10069-account-of-the-romansh-language-in:
Joseph Planta, a fellow of the Royal Society, wrote this account of the Romansh language in a letter to Sir John Pringle from the British Museum on June 30, 1775. A Bible lately given to the Royal Society by Count de Salis had been translated into Romansh, a language little attended to in Britain.

Planta seizes the chance to collect all he can of the language's history and present state, for readers who take pleasure in philological inquiries. His letter, printed in the Philosophical Transactions of 1776, is an early English study of a Swiss mountain tongue. Language lovers get a curious, learned snapshot.
10138-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly's second number, December 1857, concludes its Florentine Mosaics with the Carmine church. Only the Brancacci chapel escaped the fire of 1771. There stand frescoes by Masolino da Panicale, who died early in the fifteenth century: the Preaching of Saint Peter and the Healing of the Sick.

His scholar Masaccio, who lived from 1402 to 1443, continued the series, and the article follows the chapel's art with care. The number shows the young Atlantic's range: travel, art, and letters. Readers get Florence through American eyes, in the magazine's second month. The young magazine already showed the taste that made it famous.
10217-the-land-of-little-rain:
Mary Austin published this book of desert sketches in 1903, drawing on years spent in the dry country east of the Sierra Nevada. She writes about a land of lost borders, where water is scarce and life must bend to heat, wind, and stone. Native peoples, miners, hunters, and small towns all pass through her pages.

Short chapters follow water trails, scavengers, a pocket hunter, Shoshone land, and a town called Jimville. Austin watches plants, animals, and people with care, and finds dignity in hard, spare lives. Readers get vivid, humane nature writing that helped shape how Americans picture the desert West.
10224-kalitan-our-little-alaskan-cousin:
Mary F. Nixon-Roulet wrote this 1907 children's book as part of the Little Cousin series, which introduced young readers to children in many lands. Its hero is Kalitan, a Native Alaskan boy whose daily life becomes the book's lesson. The tone is gentle and simple, aimed at school-age readers in the early 1900s.

Through Kalitan, readers learn about homes, food, boats, hunting, and family work in Alaska. Scenes stress kindness, skill, and respect for elders, though some views now read as dated. Readers get a period children's portrait of Alaskan life, best read with care about how it frames Native people.
10610-letters-and-journals-of-james-eigh:
Theodore Walrond edited these letters and journals of James, eighth Earl of Elgin, with a preface by Dean Arthur Penrhyn Stanley of Westminster. Elgin served as governor of Jamaica, governor-general of Canada, envoy to China, and viceroy of India, a career tied to many critical points in British imperial history. His family sought a lasting memorial after his death.

Stanley notes that Elgin's foreign service left him little known at home, his place taken by others, his face forgotten, his party ties none. The letters and journals restore that record. Readers get a primary, authoritative life of a Victorian statesman, through his own words.
10867-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1858 leads with railway engineering in the United States, praising American engineers beside Britain's great names. Evans and Fulton, Whistler, Latrobe, Roebling, Haupt, Ellet, Adams, and Morris yield to none in skill, the essay argues, even without a Thames Tunnel or Menai Bridge. America can show a railroad bridge of eight hundred feet clear span, hung two hundred and fifty feet above a wild river.

The number mixes such technical pride with essays, stories, and poems, as the Boston magazine always did. Its pieces capture a nation building railroads over the Alleghanies. Modern readers get engineering history in lively period prose.
10983-the-young-captives-a-narrative-of-:
A short 1850 narrative for children tells the shipwreck of the English ship Charles Eaton in the Southern Ocean. Crew and passengers escape to a raft, reach an island, and fall asleep exhausted on shore, where islanders kill all but two little boys, John and William Doyley, sons of passengers. John was thirteen or fourteen, William barely two.

Passed from master to master, the boys at last find kindness with a man named Dupper, who teaches John to shoot with bow and arrow and to spear fish. They never stop longing for home, until an English vessel anchors offshore and John tells the captain their story. The tract teaches courage and providence through a true, harrowing tale.
11055-lord-dolphin:
Harriet A. Cheever wrote this 1903 children's fantasy in which a dolphin tells his own story. Born deep in the Mediterranean, a sea whose name means midland sea, Lord Dolphin travels by sea and by land, visiting coral groves, a mermaid's cave, gardens, and treasure grounds. Diantha W. Horne's illustrations picture great vessels straining, fishes fleeing in terror, and a first ride on land.

Lord Dolphin explains seaweeds as sea-gardens, with crimson leaves, cups, bells, and tassels like flowers ashore, and he marvels at human folk and their ways. The tone is playful and instructive, inviting children to wonder at ocean life. Cheever, author of Billy Trill and Mother Bunny, writes for young readers who enjoy talking animals and undersea marvels.
11093-trailin:
Max Brand wrote this 1919 western about Anthony Bard, a young easterner drawn west by a Wild West show at Madison Square Garden. Two men sit unmoved through the best show ever seen there, while all New York, rich and poor, cheers riders who lived under limitless western skies. Bard's quest begins there, leading to stalking, a dark town called Eldara, and a swimming of the Saverack River.

Chapters follow Nash, Sally, Joan, and a stage show, with a lamp, a candle, and a critique of pure reason among the titles. Brand writes fast, vivid action, with horses, rivers, and gunmen, and a hero learning the West by living it. Trailin remains one of Brand's popular early westerns, full of the romance and danger of the frontier.
11103-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1860 opens with a biographical essay on Thomas Hood, the English poet and humorist. Hood, meant for business, left a mercantile house at fifteen for health reasons, spent two years in Scotland, and tried engraving before turning to letters. At the London Magazine he met Charles Lamb, who liked the young sub-editor and helped his talent ripen.

Both men, the essay notes, were playful in manner but melancholy by constitution, tender in mirth and mirthful in tenderness, and born punsters. Hood worked incessantly through prose and verse, gravities and gaieties, until his early death, owing no man anything in mind, though much in money. The issue shows the Atlantic honouring English letters on the eve of the American Civil War.
11117-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for February 1861 opens with Our Artists in Italy, on the painter William Page. Page, the writer insists, is a painter in the full sense: not everyone who uses pigments can say, I also am a painter. Colour-manifestation, least simple of art-utterance, demands form, light and shade, and the mystery and power of colour together.

Later pages give an honest memorial of a woman indulgent to every sort of individuality, even epicurean tendencies remote from her own, who gave to the Sicilian cause and to American antislavery. Published on the eve of the Civil War, the issue shows the Atlantic joining art criticism with antislavery sympathy.
11159-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for December 1862 opens with The Procession of the Flowers, an essay on flowers marching across the year. In Cuba, a blossoming shrub bears crimson bells so seductive to humming-birds that petal and wing seem one, and the fallen bells are called Cupid's Tears. Frederika Bremer watched the flowers ascend her wall in a crimson line, each borne by a tiny colourless ant.

To a watcher from the sky, the march of flowers across any zone would seem as beautiful as that West Indian pageant. In the Northern United States, active plant growth is condensed into ten weeks, while in England it runs sixteen, with something always in bloom. Later pages visit an old religious house endowed by the Earl of Leicester as a home for twelve poor, war-broken soldiers. The issue blends natural history with English antiquarian lore.
11415-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1861 leads with George Sand, reviewing her Histoire de ma Vie as a royal-souled woman capitulating with the world without surrendering her secrets. The article applies Horace's lines on Cleopatra to Sand, praising her decency in withholding the passionate loving woman and whom she loved, and refusing to fill gaps from scandal chronicles. Parentage, birth, education, study, religion, marriage, maternity, authorship, friendship, travel, and litigation are all detailed.

The reviewer takes Sand as she gives herself, bringing out the significance of what she says without interpolating gossip. The piece shows the magazine's literary seriousness during wartime. For Sand readers, it offers a contemporary American judgment, respectful and not prying into scandal.
11465-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for December 1860 leads with the United States and the Barbary States, correcting patriotic delusions about the Tripoli war. Most Americans know only Preble's attack, the article argues, forgetting twenty-five years of tribute, and wrongly claim America first refused to pay Moorish pirates. The money question was amount: Washington would pay anything in reason, but Tripolitan prices were too high. Burning the Philadelphia and bombarding Tripoli supply rhetorical fireworks, but not the whole story.

The article pictures Brother Jonathan with liberty cap and bag of dollars, bowing before a whiskered Mussulman, against Fourth-of-July oratory. Its debunking tone is characteristic Atlantic. For naval historians, the number offers a contemporary corrective to popular memory.
11524-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-:
December 1861 brings a young American to Paris. He calls on Lafayette in the Rue d'Anjou. Visitors had crowded the old general since his 1824 trip to the United States. The boy, sixteen, follows their example with a cabriolet ride. A brisk French porter meets him at the door.

The masthead names literature, art, and politics as the magazine's ground. Later pages turn to other matter. One prose story deals with a factory share and a marriage bargain. Another man weighs a plain business paper. The issue mixes travel memory, talk, and fiction.
11560-the-barbarism-of-berlin:
G K Chesterton's 1914 book opens with the facts of the case. England's entry into the European war can be told plainly, he argues. It is as plain as a man falling down a coal-hole. If a man sets a house on fire, both master and mistress burn because he fired it.

Chapters follow on the war on the word and the refusal of reciprocity. The appetite of tyranny and the escape of folly come next. A later passage turns to marriage as a duel. It compares the treatment of women in America and France. The book is a short, fierce defence of the Allied cause.
11606-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for February 1859 opens with a question: ought women to learn the alphabet? It recalls Paris in 1801, when Sylvain Maréchal thrust in a plan to forbid the alphabet to women, with eighty-two clauses and one hundred and thirteen reasons.

Maréchal's satire, the essay says, still bites, and his friend Madame Gacon Dufour answered it in earnest. Later pieces in the number turn to Dante's Vita Nuova, called the first book where modern sentiment finds free expression, set against Petrarch's sonnets. The issue pairs a witty argument with literary history.
11625-the-wrong-twin:
Harry Leon Wilson's 1921 novel opens at the Foto Art Shop in Newbern Center. A window shows twin sons of Dave Cowan at four years old. One sits forward, composed, with neat curls. The other scowls, with curls mussed by a raging hand.

He fought the camera to the bitter end, the book says. The twins grow into the wrong-twin comedy of the title. A girl glowers and threatens to run away. A banker is never kept waiting by one twin. A palm reader finds cruelty in Wilbur's hand. Golf adds to the fun, with strict scorers mocked as golf lawyers.
11981-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Volume 1 of The World's Great Sermons, compiled by Grenville Kleiser, formerly of Yale Divinity School faculty and author of How to Speak in Public, runs from Basil to Calvin. Published by Funk and Wagnalls in New York and London, it opens a ten-volume anthology that would close, in volume 10, with Drummond to Jowett.

The sermons in this first volume span the early church to the Reformation, showing how preaching changed from patristic eloquence to reforming argument. Kleiser's biographical notes and full texts, with an introduction by Lewis O. Brastow in the series, make the volume a survey of Christian oratory for general readers and for students of public speaking alike.
12048-our-little-korean-cousin:
H. Lee M. Pike's Our Little Korean Cousin, illustrated by L. J. Bridgman, introduces young readers to Korea through a boy named Yung Pak. Chapters follow some queer things, Yung Pak's home, a glimpse of the king, Yung Pak at school, a lesson in history, and the monk's story.

Later chapters describe a journey, the monastery at Chang-An-Sa. Yung Pak as a full-fledged top-knot, with illustrations of a street in Seoul and boys sitting upon the floor at school. Written in the Little Cousin series' manner, the book teaches geography and custom through a child's daily life, though its outsider's view now reads as a period piece.
12066-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-:
The February 1862 Atlantic Monthly, volume 9, number 52, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, opens with Julia Ward Howe's Battle Hymn of the Republic. Its famous lines, mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord. He hath loosed the fateful lightning of his terrible swift sword, gave the Union a song in the Civil War's second year.

The number's appearance in February 1862, with the war barely a year old, shows the Atlantic speaking directly to a nation at war, through poetry, essays, and political argument. Howe's hymn, written to the tune of John Brown's Body, became the issue's enduring contribution, outliving the magazine's other contents by more than a century.
12144-the-continental-classics-volume-xv:
Issued in 1909 as volume eighteen of The Continental Classics, this anthology gathers mystery tales from Russia and Hungary in English translation. Its Russian half runs from Pushkin and Dostoevsky to Chekhov, with stories of gambling, murder, forgery, and false identity.

Pushkin opens with a card player chasing a secret winning sequence, while Dostoevsky contributes a long excerpt of crime and guilt. The Hungarian half adds tales of a living death, a cursed dinner table, and a sealed room. Read together, the stories show how European writers of the period built suspense from obsession, greed, and the slow pressure of a guilty conscience rather than from police procedure alone.
12199-the-chase-of-saint-castin-and-othe:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood published this story collection in 1894, about the French in the New World. Catherwood wrote historical fiction of the Great Lakes and Mississippi valley, drawing on French colonial records.

The title story opens in April woods around a bark-and-pole lodge, where a human dwelling stands out against the wilderness by its very humility. Other stories follow French soldiers, traders, missionaries, and settlers among Native peoples. Catherwood favors atmosphere: forests, rivers, and isolated posts, with romance held in check by history. The book preserves a romantic view of New France, written when American readers were rediscovering their French past.
12319-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-:
The February 1858 Atlantic Monthly, volume one, number four, leads with The Great Failure, on the commercial catastrophes of 1857. The essay argues that the crucial fact is not the stoppage of Smith, Jones, and Robinson, nor bank suspensions, but paralysis of the trade of the civilized globe.

The number describes a sudden overthrow of business in the United States, Britain, and Europe within one quarter. Other pieces include a Chinese scene with opium boats, leaden canisters, and a heavy gate with lanterns admitting a stranger. The issue shows the young Atlantic tackling economics with scope. It remains a vivid record of the panic of 1857 as contemporaries felt it.
1239-the-spirit-of-the-border-a-romance-:
Zane Grey sets this romance among the early settlers of the Ohio Valley, where the border hero Lewis Wetzel fights Indian wars and the pioneers defend their forts. The tale follows the Zane family and their neighbors through raids, captures, and escapes on the frontier.

Grey writes the border wars with action and sentiment, and Wetzel, the silent scout, anchors the tale. The novel, an early Grey, draws on the Zane legends of West Virginia. It suits readers who like frontier adventure in the old, hearty style. Grey's border tale suits readers who like frontier adventure in the old style.
12768-penny-plain:
O. Douglas set this warm Scottish novel in Priorsford, a small town on the River Tweed, in the years after the First World War. Its households gather for tea, church, and talk, while newcomers, old friends, and poor neighbours test the town's kindness. Peel Tower and the hills round the town give the place a quiet, lived-in feel.

Much of the charm lies in small acts: a visit paid, a slight felt keenly, a shy guest drawn into company. The book treats snubs, pride, and goodwill as matters of real weight, not mere manners. Readers who like gentle domestic fiction will find here a close, fond picture of Border town life.
12785-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-:
This February 1863 number of the Atlantic Monthly shows a leading American magazine in the middle of the Civil War. It opens with an essay on Prince Albert, praising his learning, taste, and quiet influence on British public life after his sudden death. Further pieces mix literature, art, and politics for educated readers.

Serial fiction runs beside the essays, with characters and scenes drawn in careful, novelistic detail. The mix gives a feel for how Northern readers took in the war: not only through news, but through books, ideas, and stories. As a single issue it is a useful window into American thought in 1863.
12871-the-insurrection-in-dublin:
James Stephens wrote The Insurrection in Dublin in 1916 as a day-by-day diary of Easter Week, from Monday to Sunday, with chapters on the Volunteers, leaders, labour, and the Irish question. Guns sounding across a peaceful city took Dubliners by surprise, and Stephens records streets cut off, news failing, and rumour filling the gap.

By the third day, he notes, people who expected a one-day rising began to feel gratitude that the Volunteers held out at all, even while sure of defeat. The diary captures fear, humour, and street talk with literary skill. It remains one of the most readable first-hand accounts of the Rising.
12910-early-britain-roman-britain:
Edward Conybeare's Early Britain: Roman Britain, published in 1903 with a map, surveys the Roman occupation for general readers. A bibliography notes that much valuable material lies only in journals like the Antiquary and in local archaeological reports, beyond any one book's scope. Errata correct Caesar's date to 55 B.C. and other slips.

A campaign passage shows the narrative. Forty ships are shattered in a storm, the rest saved and repaired, and a fresh fleet ordered from Gaul. Caesar returns to find a larger British army under Caswallon at Barham Down. Conybeare writes clearly and carefully. The book remains a solid introduction to Roman Britain.
13048-where-the-sabots-clatter-again:
Katherine Shortall wrote these sketches as a member of the Radcliffe Unit in France, working with the French Red Cross after the Armistice. She served as a chauffeuse in the devastated regions, and her impressions come from roads, villages, and ruined houses. The book was printed for the Radcliffe College Endowment Fund in a limited edition of 150 copies in 1921.

Shortall describes brides in broken halls, flowers blooming against mouldy walls, and an old man who lived alone in his cellar among ruins. Her title points to wooden shoes heard again on streets where war had silenced them. The sketches are short, vivid, and humane, a record of France beginning to live again after ruin.
13054-a-thane-of-wessex-being-a-story-of:
Charles W. Whistler's historical novel follows a young thane of Somerset through the Viking raids of Wessex. The hero, aged twenty-two and long motherless, takes up his father's hall at Cannington above the Parret. His quiet life ends when he stands before judges at the folk moot on Brent hill, outlawed and cast out.

Chapters run from the fight with two men to secret meetings, Viking landings, flight through Sedgemoor, and a great levy. Ships with hidden lights slip toward the haven at night, and Bridgwater burns as monks flee to the Quantock woods. Whistler builds his tale on Saxon law, war, and loyalty, and it reads as adventure grounded in the age it claims.
13066-lord-elgin:
Sir John George Bourinot's Lord Elgin, in the Makers of Canada series, Toronto 1903, tells the life of the governor who shaped responsible government in Canada. Bourinot finished and revised the book shortly before his death, and editors praise its grasp of constitutional law. Chapters cover Elgin's early career, politics in Canada, and the great reforms of his years.

One key vote, on a bill for French Canadians, passed the assembly by forty-seven to eighteen and the council by fifteen to fourteen. Elgin later wrote that the Church of England's tone drove away even those most willing to work with her. The book is a compact political life, clear on how a governor learned to let a colony rule itself.
13069-the-minister-and-the-boy-a-handboo:
Allan Hoben, a Chicago professor of practical theology, wrote this 1912 handbook for clergy who worked with boys. Hoben also served as field secretary of the Chicago Juvenile Protective Association, and he draws on that city work throughout. His chapters treat boyhood itself, village and city life, organized play, choice of work, citizenship, faith, and the church boys' club.

Hoben argues that boys need group play more than drill, and that games teach fair dealing, courage, and self-knowledge. He urges ministers to meet boys where they live, to use talks by tradesmen on real work, and to tie moral teaching to choices boys actually face. The book stands as an early, practical guide to youth work, written before clubs and camps became common.
13076-the-life-of-john-ruskin:
W. G. Collingwood's 1911 life of John Ruskin follows the critic from boy poet to art teacher and prophet of social reform. Books run from The Boy Poet, 1819 to 1842, through The Art Critic, to later years at Coniston. Collingwood, once professor of fine art at Reading, writes with close knowledge of Ruskin's circle.

Early chapters trace mountain worship, the germ of Modern Painters, a love story, and an Oxford degree. Later pages show Ruskin pressed by letters, lectures, and new work in botany and minerals, including Proserpina. The life also notes illness, prayer, and sermons that shaped his thought. It remains a solid, readable portrait of a restless Victorian mind.
13209-the-second-violin:
Grace S. Richmond's 1906 novel The Second Violin opens with a crash, as John Lansing Birch lays down his viola in despair during The March of the Pilgrims. Book one follows the second violin, book two the Churchill latch-string. Richmond, known for Red Pepper Burns, writes domestic fiction with humor and heart.

Dr. Andrew Churchill loses his first patient in private practice, a young mother, and faces a baby not yet two years old left behind. Friends argue over adopting other people's children, while Churchill, frank and genial, turns steely when challenged. A hospital visit shows convalescents, not grave cases, to a young visitor. The novel is a warm tale of music, medicine, and family duty.
13315-a-prince-of-cornwall-a-story-of-gl:
Charles W. Whistler sets this historical novel around 710, when Ina of Wessex and his kinsman Nunna defeated Gerent, king of the West Welsh. Owen, a Cornish prince, and Oswald, a young Saxon, move between Sussex, Glastonbury, the Quantocks, and the Welsh coast as Saxon power pushes westward.

Oswald's road runs through feasts, vows, sea voyages, cliff paths, hunts, ransoms, and a meeting with Nona, a Welsh princess. Whistler grounds the tale in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and in the frontier country itself, then lets loyalty, faith, and forgiveness decide who keeps land and who loses it. Adventure and old border politics carry the story throughout.
13365-the-ethics-of-drink-and-other-soci:
James Runciman's 1892 essays, subtitled Joints in Our Social Armour, start with drink and widen to time, company, and character. He warns that bare statistics leave most readers cold: millions of gallons and millions of pounds mean little beside the ailments of a pet terrier. The ethics must be felt in single lives, not counted in totals.

Runciman attacks wasted time, from the young dandy galloping across grass country to the idler lounging round stables, and shows how bad company pleases at first because idleness tempts our lower nature. Work, he insists, needs effort and habit. The book is Victorian social criticism with a preacher's eye for the small choices that shape a life.
13454-aylwin:
Theodore Watts-Dunton's novel Aylwin opens on crumbling cliffs at ebb tide, with a narrator floating toward the open sea and bidding farewell to brown cliffs, beloved sand, and a little boat. The story that follows, with a key reprinted from Notes and Queries and a note on D'arcy, turns on love, loss, and a woman glimpsed in Wales.

Winifred Wynne, seen by a man who knew her in Wales, and a picture by Wilderspin, dressed in an azure tunic bordered with stars, haunt the narrator's search. Scenes move between Welsh cottages, lakes, and London rooms where folding doors open on a longed-for face. Watts-Dunton blends romance, poetry, and gipsy lore into a tale of a love that survives separation.
13470-bertha-our-little-german-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade's Bertha, Our Little German Cousin, from the Little Cousin series, introduces American children to Germany through a girl's year. Bertha works by candlelight two nights before Christmas with her mother and older sister, then learns toy-making, hears of a wicked bishop, and joins a coffee party.

Stories of Heidelberg Castle, Frederick the Great, a brave princess, and a magic sword follow, with a stork mother who dies in a chimney fire rather than leave her babies. Hans describes a palace with hundreds of halls, painted walls, silk hangings, and shining floors. Wade teaches German life through tales, pictures, and a child's curiosity about castles, kings, and neighbours.
13575-how-to-observe-in-archaeology-sugg:
The British Museum's 1920 guide How to Observe in Archaeology gives travellers in the Near and Middle East practical rules for fieldwork. Sir F. G. Kenyon prefaces the volume, G. F. Hill writes the introduction, and Flinders Petrie sets out method, with chapters by specialists on flint implements, Greece, Asia Minor, Cyprus, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt.

Palestine advice insists that study of local pottery from actual specimens is an absolute preliminary. Any sherd with character must at once be assigned to its period, or field research has no value. Knowledge of Semitic alphabets follows. Lists of British institutions, societies, and the archaeological joint committee make the book a working handbook for amateurs who want to observe well and record truly.
13601-expositions-of-holy-scripture-roma:
Alexander Maclaren expounds Romans and Corinthians to Second Corinthians chapter five in this volume of Expositions of Holy Scripture. Sermons take up the witness of the resurrection, privilege and obligation, Paul's longing, debtors to all men, the gospel as God's power, and world-wide sin and world-wide redemption.

Maclaren promises that beholding Christ's glory changes believers into his likeness, with faces shining and lives ennobled by serene beauty. Death, in his preaching, comes as a messenger to paupers telling them of a great estate, lifting Christians from an ill-lighted workshop into the King's presence. The volume is Victorian pulpit exposition, verse by verse, for readers and preachers alike.
14173-the-romanization-of-roman-britain:
F. Haverfield's second edition of 1912, greatly enlarged, asks how far Roman ways took hold in Britain. Chapters cover the empire at large, then language, material life, art, local government, land, and chronology. A closing chapter traces the Celtic revival in the later empire, when native ways pushed back against Roman forms.

Language evidence leads the case. Agricola encouraged Latin, and Tacitus says Britons who once hated the foreign tongue grew eager to speak it well. Plutarch mentions Demetrius of Tarsus teaching in Britain around the year 80, and Juvenal notes British lawyers trained by Gaulish masters. Inscriptions, town plans, and the Gorgon head from Bath's temple of Sul Minerva add stone proof. Haverfield writes with scholarly care, and the book remains a standard guide to Roman Britain.
14239-golden-steps-to-respectability-use:
John Mather Austin lectured youth of both sexes in Golden Steps to Respectability, Usefulness, and Happiness, published at Auburn in 1851. Lectures cover good reputation, character, principles, associates, amusements, religion, and marriage. A motto urges onward, upward, eyes fixed on skies, content only when rising. Austin, author of Voice to Youth and Voice to Married, writes as a friendly lecturer, not a scold.

Temperance leads the habits. Austin calls it most important, underlying and coloring all others, since intemperance destroys property, health, and reputation, overthrows family peace, and reduces victims to want and misery. Later lectures warn against violent debate: few converts ever came by sword or wrangling, and furious bigotry, in man or woman, wanders beyond proper limits. Persuasion, earnest talk, and a consistent serious life win where argument fails. Earnest mid-century counsel for young people starting out.
14245-the-fall-of-the-grand-sarrasin:
William John Ferrar set this tale in Guernsey in 1057, in the Norman seas. Its hero is Nigel de Bessin, a knight of sixteen who leaves his island home for war. Ferrar wrote it as a string of holiday sketches, drawn from walks among cliffs, ruined castles, and old abbeys. The prose keeps an old voice, full of swordplay, greetings, and court manners. It reads like a chronicle told by the hero himself.

Nigel fights his bouts with sword and shield, and learns the heat of war on his field. He meets a vicomte and his sons, and is led in to a lady at her frame, working a tapestry of deeds of arms. The tale moves between courts, camps, and sea roads, with cousins, lords, and foes in turn. Its charm lies in the old detail: armor, oaths, and the pride of a boy proving himself a soldier.
14279-the-ancient-life-history-of-the-ea:
H. Alleyne Nicholson, professor at St. Andrews, wrote this outline of fossil life on earth. It treats palaeontology two ways: as the study of extinct forms in the rocks, and as a history told by fossils in their order of time. Shells, corals, fishes, and birds pass in review, each placed in its age. The book speaks to students who want facts, not a heap of names.

Among Silurian snails the book notes Euomphalus, with its flat coiled shell hollowed on one side. Platyceras follows, thin and barely coiled, with a wide mouth, while its kin run on through Devonian and Carboniferous rocks. Cretaceous birds of North America get a look, above all Ichthyornis, a pigeon-sized bird with teeth set in sockets in both jaws. No living bird has teeth, so the find links birds to reptiles. The book turns fossils into a story of life's long past.
14366-argentina-from-a-british-point-of-:
Campbell P. Ogilvie edited this 1910 book on Argentina, written from a British point of view. It grew from a paper he read before the Royal Society of Arts, and was printed for shareholders of the Santa Fé Land Company. Photographs and diagrams fill its pages. The book covers land, cattle, trade, and the daily life of settlers and townsfolk. Its tone is that of a man who knows the country firsthand.

One settler tells how a meat buyer took his cattle at fifteen shillings a head, though he had sold them at twenty dollars paper. The buyer soon ruled the market and charged what he liked, while the seller could not raise his price. Wet weather and thin grass made roundups hard, yet the buyer pressed for beasts twice a week. A coachman called the Jehu closes the sketches, driving four horses over trunks and tussocks with skill and pride.
14380-the-life-of-john-milton-volume-5-o:
David Masson's massive biography reaches its fifth volume with the years 1654 to 1660, when John Milton served as Latin secretary under Oliver Cromwell's Protectorate. Masson, a professor at Edinburgh, set the poet's life inside the politics of his age.

The volume follows Cromwell's parliaments, foreign policy, and fall of the republic, alongside Milton's writings, blindness, marriages, and secretarial work. Letters and state papers fill many pages. The book is dense Victorian scholarship, valuable for its detail on Milton's public years and the end of the Commonwealth. Later volumes carry the story through the Restoration and beyond.
14488-elsie-s-kith-and-kin:
Martha Finley's 1886 novel continues the Elsie Dinsmore series, reuniting a large Southern family at the homes of Ion and Viamede. Edward Travilla and his young wife Zoe open the story, parted from kin who have traveled on.

Lulu, a headstrong girl, struggles to master her temper under her family's watchful eyes, while cousins, tutors, and suitors fill the household with talk, music, and small crises. Finley writes in a warm, moralizing style, praising obedience, faith, and family affection. The book pleased the series' loyal readers with familiar characters in a gentle domestic round.
14659-muslin:
George Moore's Muslin, originally A Drama in Muslin in 1886 and reissued in 1915, follows Irish convent girls from prize day onward. The girls leave the Convent of the Holy Child for society, love, and marriage. Moore wrote as a realist of Irish life.

White dresses flutter like doves in the convent garden, while elder girls run timidly to favorite sisters. Olive Barton writes anxiously to Captain Hibbert, begging him to explain what she has heard about the Lawlers. The novel satirizes the marriage market and the Church's hold on girls. It remains a landmark of Irish naturalism.
14872-the-tale-of-squirrel-nutkin:
Beatrix Potter's 1903 tale, a story for Norah, is about a tail belonging to a little red squirrel named Nutkin. He has a brother called Twinkleberry and many cousins, and they live in a wood at the edge of a lake.

In the middle of the lake stands an island covered with trees and nut bushes, and among them a hollow oak, home of an owl called Old Brown. One autumn, when nuts are ripe and hazel leaves are golden and green, Nutkin and his kin come out to gather. Nutkin's teasing of Old Brown drives the comedy, and the tale warns, gently, that rude jokes with a powerful neighbour can cost a squirrel dear.
14891-the-rulers-of-the-lakes-a-story-of:
Joseph A. Altsheler sets this French and Indian War story just after Braddock's defeat, with Lake George and Lake Champlain as its prizes. Young Robert Lennox and his friend Tayoga, an Onondaga Indian, undertake a dangerous trek across northern wilderness to warn settlers and soldiers at Fort Refuge.

Afterwards they join the army as scouts, preceding an expedition to the lakes and meeting fierce encounters on trail and water. Heralds of peril, a kindly bridge, a flight, a forest concert and a naval combat lead to a lake battle and a sinister siege. Altsheler writes frontier war as adventure and friendship, with the lakes themselves as characters in the fight.
15034-stories-for-the-young-or-cheap-rep:
Hannah More and others wrote these moral tales for young readers, gathered here in a revised American edition of the Cheap Repository Tracts. Volume six leads with Black Giles the Poacher, a family tale in three parts, and adds stories of a waterman, a porter, and a Christmas tract. A vision of the Valley of Tears closes the set.

Each tale teaches a plain lesson: honest work beats living by wits, fortune-telling misleads, and burdens are best borne together. The style is simple and direct, meant for reading aloud in homes and schools. As a sample of early popular moral fiction, the book shows what reformers thought children should learn from stories.
15200-selections-from-the-works-of-john-:
Edited by Chauncey Tinker for Yale students, this 1908 Riverside selection gathers Ruskin's best prose with introduction and notes. Modern Painters supplies pieces on mountain glory, sunrise on the Alps, and the pathetic fallacy. Stones of Venice adds St. Mark's and Gothic character, while Seven Lamps gives memory and obedience.

Lectures on art, traffic, and life round out the set, showing Ruskin as critic, teacher, and moralist. Tinker's notes help new readers follow Ruskin's dense, brilliant style. Students of art and Victorian thought will find the selection a strong, well-chosen introduction to a great prose writer.
15222-looking-seaward-again:
Walter Runciman's 1907 sea sketches, dedicated to his wife, gather fireside tales told without literary strain. He left home early to learn the harsh discipline of sailing ships before steam took the wind from their sails, and he kept memories of voyages and shore stays. The preface explains, not apologizes, for plain telling.

Stories of ships, crews, storms, and distant ports fill the book, with a seaman's eye for detail and humor. Runciman writes as a man who lived the life, not a landsman imagining it. Sea lovers will find the sketches vivid, honest, and full of salt.
15520-with-methuen-s-column-on-an-ambula:
Ernest N. Bennett, fellow of Hertford College, Oxford, published this Boer War narrative in London in 1900, with Swan Sonnenschein. Profits went to Lady Lansdowne's fund for widows and families of officers, a cause Bennett took up at a friend's suggestion after returning from South Africa. Lady Lansdowne approved the plan, and Bennett hoped sales would justify the little volume.

The narrative opens with a first view of Capetown from the sea, at sunrise behind Table Mountain, houses still in shadow between hills and water. Bennett then follows Methuen's column on an ambulance train, tending wounded men in a hard campaign. The book is a plain, humane war memoir, less about battles than about care, endurance, and the cost borne by soldiers' families at home.
15546-the-last-of-the-peterkins-with-oth:
Lucretia P. Hale published this last Peterkin book in Boston in 1906, with Little, Brown, copyright 1886 by Roberts Brothers. It is dedicated to the lady from Philadelphia, beloved by the Peterkin family. A preface explains the sad frame: the Peterkins left their native land and never returned, and Elizabeth Eliza's commonplace book, found among family papers, appears here first.

Chapters follow Elizabeth Eliza's paper and commonplace book, the Peterkins practicing travel, an excursion for maple sugar, and Mrs. Peterkin in Egypt, fainting on the Great Pyramid. Later tales add Lucilla's diary, Jedidiah's Noah's Ark, and Carrie's three wishes. The humor lies in a well-meaning family's literal logic, applied to travel, housekeeping, and the world. Readers of the earlier Peterkins will find the same gentle absurdity, now with a melancholy close.
15819-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-:
One monthly issue of the Atlantic Monthly, dated February 1864, issued by Ticknor and Fields in Boston. The Atlantic, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, spoke for the educated North during the Civil War. Each number mixed essays, fiction, poetry, and reviews. This issue, volume thirteen, number seventy-six, shows the magazine at mid-war.

The lead essay on genius opens with Paul Morphy playing seven chess games blindfold, and young Colburn solving vast sums in his head. Such powers, the writer holds, strike us with hopeless wonder. Other pieces treat war, letters, and public life. For a modern reader, the issue gives the mind of the wartime North: grave, curious, and eager for art even in crisis.
15913-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for December 1863, volume twelve, number seventy-four, issued by Ticknor and Fields in Boston. This number carries a tale that made American history: Edward E. Hale's The Man Without a Country. It opens with a death notice in the New York Herald for Philip Nolan, late of the corvette Levant. Readers who missed that corner missed a classic.

Hale's tale follows Nolan, cursed never to hear of his country again, through years at sea. Other pieces treat literature, politics, and the Civil War. The issue shows the Atlantic at its wartime best: grave, literary, and patriotic. For modern readers it holds a first appearance worth seeking: a story that taught a nation what country means.
16028-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1863, volume twelve, number seventy-three, issued by Ticknor and Fields in Boston. In the Civil War years the Atlantic mixed history with literature for a Northern audience. This number leads with a sequel: The Spaniard and the Heretic. An August piece, The Fleur-de-Lis in Florida, told of Huguenot attempts in Florida.

Spanish jealousy of the Huguenot colony gave rise to the crusade whose history follows here. A monk opens the narrative of faith, empire, and massacre. Other pieces treat literature and the war. The issue shows the Atlantic's historical bent: old Florida bloodshed, retold while a new war raged at home.
16130-judgments-of-the-court-of-appeal-o:
Heard over six days in October 1981, these judgments come from New Zealand's Court of Appeal, sitting as Woodhouse, Cooke, Richardson, McMullin, and Somers. The case reviewed aspects of the Royal Commission report on the Mount Erebus aircraft disaster, in proceedings brought by Air New Zealand and others against Commissioner Peter Thomas Mahon and the Attorney-General. The New Zealand Airline Pilots Association also appeared.

The judgments weigh how far a court may review a commission's findings and process, a question of law rather than a retelling of the crash itself. Lawyers, students, and readers of public inquiries will find the reasoning careful and closely argued. The volume stands as a key legal record of one of New Zealand's most painful public controversies.
16196-king-olaf-s-kinsman-a-story-of-the:
Charles W. Whistler's historical novel follows the last Saxon struggle against the Danes in the days of Ironside and Cnut. Chapters trace the coming of the Vikings, Olaf the King, the breaking of London Bridge, Earl Wulfnoth of Sussex, and Redwald's fate at Penhurst. Sexberga, the thane's daughter, the fight at Leavenheath, and the treachery of Edric Streone deepen the tale.

Whistler's preface admits no English chronicler mentions King Olaf the Saint in England, yet two churches at either end of London Bridge testify to gratitude for his great deed there. Battles, flights from London, and a last great battle close the story. Readers who like Saxon England will enjoy its sturdy, old-style adventure.
1634-the-foolish-virgin:
Thomas Dixon's Foolish Virgin follows a young woman from a friendly warning through temptation, fate. Doubts and fears, to wings of steel, a vain appeal, and a wedding that promises until death. Jim's trial, Ella's secret, and the lotos-eaters close a tale of a girl's choices in a world of men and money.

Dixon, best known for The Clansman, writes here a melodrama of innocence and experience, with moral lessons worn plainly. The novel is a period piece, dated in its views. It will interest readers of early American popular fiction and of Dixon's controversial career.
16417-spadacrene-anglica-the-english-spa:
Edmund Deane, a doctor at Oxford, wrote the first book on the waters of Harrogate, and this 1922 reprint pairs his old text with a fresh introduction and life notes. In 1626 Harrogate was a small hamlet in the royal forest of Knaresborough, and Deane's praise of its spring helped start the spa town that grew there.

The reprint keeps Deane's early modern voice while the editors explain his world for new readers. Cures, wells, and the rise of a watering place form the core of the book. For local historians and spa buffs, it is both a source text and a short history of how one spring made a town.
16524-the-nursery-no-107-november-1875-v:
This November 1875 number of The Nursery, a monthly magazine for youngest readers, was published in Boston by John L. Shorey at a dollar sixty a year. Its contents mix stories, verses, and pictures: Flora's Looking-Glass, Chinese Scenes, Grandma's Garden, Great-Aunt Patience and Her Little Lion, Grandpa's Pigs, Captain Bob, and The Soldier-Dog, among others.

The pieces are short and gentle, made for reading aloud to small children. Kindness, home life, and small adventures fill the pages, with simple language a young listener can follow. As a period piece, the number shows what American nurseries read in the 1870s: wholesome, cheerful tales, simply told and brightly meant.
16602-the-major-operations-of-the-navies:
A. T. Mahan, captain in the U.S. Navy and author of The Influence of Sea Power upon History, treats naval war in the American Revolution in this 1913 volume, with portraits, maps, and battle plans. The opening argues that wars tend to spread, using Frederick the Great, the Balkans of 1912, and the Revolution itself as proof, then traces the war's naval train.

Mahan writes as a strategist, weighing fleets, coasts, and alliances. The book suits readers of naval history who want operations, not mere anecdote. It remains a classic study of sea power in the war that made America, by the thinker who defined the field.
16790-anglo-saxon-britain:
Grant Allen wrote this short book on Anglo-Saxon Britain for the Early Britain series, issued by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London. His preface says the book sketches Britain under early English conquerors from the social side, not the political side. Kings and statesmen get little space; monuments, life, and thought of the folk get the most.

Allen asks what in modern British life comes from purely English or Low Dutch roots, judging by what remains in land, speech, and custom. A map of Britain in 500 opens the book. The volume gives a clear, compact social history for general readers, and a fine sample of Victorian popular history at its most readable.
1690-marie-an-episode-in-the-life-of-the:
H. Rider Haggard returns to Allan Quatermain as a young man in this South African romance, set among Boer farms on the edge of Zulu country. Allan falls in love with Marie Marais, daughter of a French Huguenot settler. Their courtship is broken by her ruthless suitor Hernando Pereira and by the wars that close around them.

The story follows Allan from a shooting match and a farm attack to Dingaan's court, where a promise and a betrayal decide Marie's fate. It is an adventure tale, but its weight lies in the love story: a first love remembered by an old hunter, and the price of pride and revenge given room to act.
17132-the-makers-of-canada-champlain:
N. E. Dionne's life of Samuel Champlain, in the Makers of Canada set, follows the French founder from Brouage to Quebec. Chapters trace his first voyage, Acadia and Port Royal, the founding of Quebec in 1608, wars with the Iroquois, the fur trade, and the loss and return of Quebec in 1629. Jesuit and Recollet missions get full space beside trade and war.

Dionne draws on early records and keeps dates, places, and names in clear order, with a time list and index at the back. The tone is that of a national biography for general readers. For anyone new to New France, this is a solid first life of the man who mapped and held its early towns.
17239-the-destiny-of-man-viewed-in-the-l:
John Fiske's Destiny of Man, first copyrighted in 1884 and here in its twentieth edition, grew from an address at the Concord School of Philosophy on immortality. Fiske starts within known science: Copernicus, Darwin, infancy, brain growth, and the shift of natural selection toward psychical life. Later chapters treat society, morality, warfare's end, Christianity's message, and a future life.

Dedicated to his six children, the essay argues that evolution points beyond brute inheritance toward a moral destiny. Fiske writes in clear, hopeful Victorian prose. Readers of science and faith will find a classic statement of evolution with a spiritual horizon, still debated today.
1757-the-cruise-of-the-dolphin:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich lifts this episode from The Story of a Bad Boy, with Tom Bailey himself as narrator. Every Rivermouth boy, Tom says, looks on the sea as mixed up with his destiny. The cruise of the Dolphin gives Tom and his friends a taste of it: clouds scudding, breakers moaning, and rain lisping down as they dress for a day on the water.

The episode is a boy's adventure in miniature, full of boats, weather, and the pride of handling a craft. Readers who know Tom Bailey will enjoy the return to Rivermouth, and newcomers will find a short, sunny introduction to Aldrich's best-known hero and his seaside town.
17648-the-land-of-contrasts-a-briton-s-v:
James Fullarton Muirhead, author of Baedeker's handbooks to Great Britain and the United States, published this Briton's view of his American kin in Boston, New York, and London in 1898. He dedicates the book to the land that has given him what makes life most worth living. The contents open with an introductory chapter, then survey American life chapter by chapter.

Muirhead, a guidebook writer turned observer, notes contrasts between Britain and America in manners, towns, work, and public life. Readers get a friendly, well-travelled account of the United States in the 1890s, written by a Briton who knew it well. The book suits readers of travel writing and of Anglo-American relations.
17655-observations-of-an-orderly-some-gl:
Lance-Corporal Ward Muir, Royal Army Medical Corps (Territorial), wrote these observations of an orderly, glimpses of life and work in an English war hospital, published by Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company. Chapters open with a first day and life in the orderlies' huts. Washing up, a hut hospital, and wards from D block follow.

When the wounded arrive and laundry problems close the early set, readers see hospital war work from the orderly's lowly, essential place. Muir writes with humour and compassion about routine, comradeship, and suffering. The book suits readers of Great War medical memoirs from below stairs.
17782-animal-children-the-friends-of-the:
Edith Brown Kirkwood wrote Animal Children, with drawings by M. T. Ross, printed in Chicago by P. F. Volland in 1913. The book is dedicated to all children who find friends in the forest or on the plain, and most of all to Samuel and Gilbert.

Short verses give each beast a child's voice. There is a lion prince who is still a baby, a tiger smeared with stripes by bold jungle boys, and a monkey who thinks a leopard's spots are pasted on. The rhymes are light, funny, and kind. It is a sweet picture-book verse set for the very young, full of beasts at play.
17993-young-peoples-history-of-the-war-w:
Prescott Holmes wrote this young people's history of the war with Spain in 1900, printed in Philadelphia by Henry Altemus with eighty-six pictures. Holmes tells the brief 1898 war in plain words for school readers, opening with a sea battle off Manila.

He frames the war as America's stand for Cuba, against Spanish cruelty and starvation, and he notes the scandals of the war effort without dwelling on them. Chapters run from the cause of the war to the fighting at sea and on land. It is a patriotic school book of its day, best read now beside cooler, fuller histories of 1898.
18343-the-pied-piper-of-hamelin:
Robert Browning's poem The Pied Piper of Hamelin appears here illustrated by Kate Greenaway, published by Frederick Warne and Company in London and New York. Browning sets his tale in Hamelin town in Brunswick, by famous Hanover city, where the river Weser washes the wall on the southern side. Almost five hundred years ago, the townsfolk suffered from vermin, and that suffering opens the ditty.

Rats fought dogs, killed cats, bit babies in cradles, ate cheeses from vats, licked soup from ladles, split kegs of salted sprats, and made nests in Sunday hats. The piper's bargain and its breaking follow, with the children led away. Readers get Browning's best-known tale poem: a town, a piper, and a price unpaid, told in rollicking verse with Greenaway's pictures.
18349-in-the-irish-brigade-a-tale-of-war:
G. A. Henty wrote this tale of war in Flanders and Spain for young readers. Its hero comes fresh from Ireland to join the Irish Brigade, the Irish soldiers who served France after religious persecution drove them from home. Henty's preface names the evils of sectarian hatred that sent such men abroad to fight for a foreign king.

Chapters carry the hero to Versailles, Paris, Scotland, and an escape from Newgate, then to kidnapping a minister, the frontier, and the battle of Oudenarde. Missions, treachery, capture, and an old friend mark the road, with a search for a family near the end. Readers get Henty's usual fare: a brave lad, hard fighting, and history told through adventure rather than dates.
18681-across-the-fruited-plain:
Florence Crannell Means wrote this children's novel for the Friendship Press around 1940, with a companion guide for teachers of migrant children. It centers on boys and girls whose families follow seasonal farm work, the hoeing, picking, and weeding shown in its pictures.

The story opens with ten-year-old Rose-Ellen Beecham in her grandparents' house, where her mother has died and her father cannot find work. Grandma keeps house while Grandpa minds his cobbler shop, and the children watch the grown-ups worry over milk and money. The book follows such families with plain sympathy, showing how children carry hope and steady affection through hard moves and thin times. Its dedication names migrant children themselves, which sets its purpose: to help young readers see these neighbors as real children, not as strangers passing through.
18831-time-and-time-again:
H. Beam Piper first published this science fiction story in Astounding Science Fiction in April 1947. It opens on a battlefield, where a wounded soldier named Hartley lies dying after an atomic blast, blinded by the flash and dulled by a painkilling injection. Around him, medics sort the living from the dead as he slips away.

The story's premise is stated in its opening lines. Upsetting the stable stream of time would take enormous energy. A man would not expect a second chance at life, yet an atomic blast might grant both. Piper uses that idea to send his hero back through time. Readers get a compact time-travel tale built on war, chance, and the hope of doing a life over.
18832-a-cardinal-sin:
Eugène Sue's novel, translated by Alexina Loranger and published by W. B. Conkey of Chicago in 1892, opens in Paris on a bright May morning. A pale girl of about eighteen, worn by want, walks timidly through the Charnier des Innocents, a quarter crowded with public scribes.

She seeks a letter writer, pauses before several open doors, and at last enters the shop of a kindly old man with a benign face. Too shy to speak at first, she admits she cannot write and asks him to write a letter for her. The old scribe answers with care, promising that confidences from the untaught are sacred to him. Mariette's errand, begun in embarrassment, opens a tale of poverty, trust, and secrets told through another's pen.
18897-the-epic-of-gilgamish-a-fragment-o:
Stephen Langdon's edition of the Epic of Gilgamish, issued by the University of Pennsylvania Museum as volume ten, number three of its Babylonian Section, presents a fragment of the Gilgamish legend. The excerpt shows the cuneiform text in transliteration, column by column, with broken lines marked.

Gilgamish tells his dreams to his mother, who speaks in answer, and Enkidu sits before the harimtu and is led toward Uruk, the city of Anu. Later columns show Enkidu eating bread and drinking beer until he is full, clothing himself, and taking up weapons as a man among men. The fragment gives readers the ancient epic in the scholar's working form, close to the clay itself.
18937-my-first-picture-book-with-thirty-:
George Routledge and Sons published this children's picture book in London and New York, with thirty-six pages of pictures printed in color by Kronheim. It opens with an alphabet section, each letter paired with a simple word and picture, from ark and baby through zebra. No pictures were made for the letters J and X in the original.

After the alphabet come five nursery favorites. They are the little old woman who lived in a shoe, the babes in the wood, Little Bo-Peep, the five little pigs, and old Mother Goose and her son Jack. Short texts sit beside bright images made for very young readers. The book gives a clear window into Victorian picture books, where learning letters and enjoying a story went hand in hand.
18945-robin:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1922 novel Robin continues the story begun in The Head of the House of Coombe, following its heroine from Edwardian Mayfair society into the shadow of war. The book opens with a summary of the earlier novel's world, where Robert Gareth-Lawless and his ethereal young wife, known as Feather, lived in a narrow slice of a Mayfair house.

Robin herself grows up amid that glittering, fragile society, and the novel follows her into a world transformed by battlefields and loss. There she grieves for boys lying dead and seeks comfort in a cottage hearth with an older friend. Burnett contrasts the light, airy manners of pre-war London with the sobbing grief of wartime, tracing how a young woman formed by one world endures another. The novel blends society romance with a poignant account of war's domestic cost.
19057-red-robin:
Jane Abbott wrote this 1922 girls' novel about Beryl Lynch, a poor child whose mother crochets lace for a living. Beryl finds a fine doll left on a park bench and brings it home in wonder and fear, unsure whether a found treasure can be hers. Her mother questions her with loving care.

The Forsyth house, a prince, an heir, and a girl named Red-Robin weave into Beryl's story as wealth and poverty meet. Christmas scenes and home warmth soften the hard parts. Young readers get a kind tale of honesty, family love, and a child learning what is truly hers.
19120-the-saddle-boys-of-the-rockies-or-:
Captain James Carson wrote this 1913 Saddle Boys tale, Lost on Thunder Mountain. Frank and Bob, of Circle Ranch, take up a challenge about a fearful booming in the mountain that has scared superstitious cowmen for years. A rival named Peg may beat them to the secret.

Old Hank Coombs bears a message, a note warns at a spring hole, and rustlers loom as the boys ride toward the lonely peak. They plan to let Peg arrive first so none can say they stole his thunder. Young readers get a lively Rockies tale of pluck, rivalry, and a mountain mystery.
19133-practical-rules-for-the-management:
Charles Hutton Gregory, civil engineer, wrote these practical rules for managing a locomotive engine in the station, on the road, and in cases of accident, from the 1841 edition. He sent the paper to the Institution of Civil Engineers, noting that books on theory abounded but none on use. Safety and efficiency were his aims.

Gregory explains water levels over the fire box, blowing off from bottom, middle, and top cocks, steam pressure, feed pumps, and grades, where more water must be kept on a slope. Rules for appointing engine men close the work. Readers get a concise early railway manual, clear on the daily care of steam engines.
19164-lectures-on-art-delivered-before-t:
John Ruskin gave these lectures on art before the University of Oxford in Hilary term 1870. They open with an inaugural address, then link art to religion, morals, use, line, and landscape. The volume forms part of his collected works in library edition.

Ruskin argues that art made only for profit fails, since skill cannot grow under a view to gain, and that nations learn taste slowly through age and ease. New wealth brings vast patronage, often harmful in his view. Readers get a passionate Victorian theory of art as moral work, not mere trade.
19206-under-drake-s-flag-a-tale-of-the-s:
G. A. Henty wrote this boys' tale of Drake's flag on the Spanish Main. It opens with a wreck on the Devon coast, where a lad called the Otter saves a child from the sea with the help of a great mastiff dog. Friends, foes, and the Golden Hind soon follow.

Chapters carry the boys across the Spanish Main, through forests, over the Cordilleras, to the Pacific coast, the prison of the Inquisition, and a rescue. Wholesale conversions and a Portuguese settlement add colour. Young readers get a rousing historical adventure of sea dogs, courage, and Elizabethan daring.
19295-the-outdoor-girls-at-ocean-view-or:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this Outdoor Girls tale at Ocean View, about a box found buried in sand. Betty Nelson, Amy Stonington-Blackford, Grace Ford, and Mollie Billette plan a summer by the sea, after earlier books on Deepdale, Rainbow Lake, motors, and winter camp. The series sold at fifty cents a volume.

Amy's past mystery is recalled: ward of the Stoningtons, she found a long-lost brother Henry Blackford while unravelling a five-hundred-dollar bill, and kept her old name among friends. A box in the sand now promises fresh adventure. Young readers get a sunny girls' tale of seaside fun and mystery.
19351-curlie-carson-listens-in:
Roy J. Snell wrote this boys' adventure novel about radio, published in Chicago in the early nineteen twenties. Curlie Carson, a keen young wireless listener, picks up a strange message that pulls him into a much larger affair, with a mysterious map, a millionaire, and a yacht voyage to come.

Later chapters take Curlie out to sea, through a storm, and into an SOS crisis, with a girl companion who insists on sharing the risk. The book mixes the thrill of early radio with a classic treasure hunt, and it captures a moment when listening in felt like magic to its young fans.
19394-you-ll-git-dar-in-de-mornin: You will git dar in de mornin, with music by H. T. Burleigh and words by F. L. Stanton, is a short song in dialect verse. Its chorus urges keeping on looking for bright skies, hoping the sun will rise, singing when the world sighs, and staying faithful till the curtain drops. Only the song words and score notes are present here, so the piece is a brief spiritual-style song, not a book.
19423-the-story-of-porcelain:
Sara Ware Bassett wrote this story of porcelain for young readers, published in Philadelphia in the late nineteen teens with pictures by Isabel W. Caley. It belongs to her series on everyday things, from lumber and wool to glass and silk, each told through lively scenes.

One chapter visits the empress's china factory in Vienna, busy supplying Austria and Turkey. There painters decked ware with stags and hounds until Turkish buyers, barred from images of living things, refused them. The book teaches craft history through story, not lecture. In the Maine woods, Theo Swift listens while Mr Croyden begins the tale of a second great potter.
19451-double-trouble-or-every-hero-his-o:
Herbert Quick wrote this novel of a divided self, published in the early nineteen hundreds. Eugene Brassfield lives two lives at once, and a commanding hypnotist, Madame le Claire, can call forth the self he keeps hidden. Under her sway he sleeps, wakes changed, and finds strange rooms familiar.

The plot asks what a man owes to the part of himself he would rather not own, and how love and will can pull one person in two ways. Quick wraps the question in romance and stage-like scenes, making an early popular take on the double that still moves at a brisk pace.
19459-born-again:
Alfred Lawson wrote this novel of a man remade, opening on a Detroit street where a ragged beggar asks for coins for food. The narrator watches the beggar pass a saloon and hurry to a restaurant, then pause to help a poorer cripple, a small act that starts a larger change.

Later the hero clings to a beloved woman and vows they will die together rather than part, a scene of high feeling typical of Lawson's earnest style. The book mixes street realism with romance, and it shows Lawson's faith in willpower as a force for new life.
19538-the-broncho-rider-boys-with-funsto:
Frank Fowler wrote this boys' adventure of the Broncho Rider Boys with General Funston at Vera Cruz, brought out by a New York house in the mid nineteen teens. Billie, Donald, and Adrian ride, hide behind giant cactus, and dodge Mexican foot soldiers on a parade ground.

When flight seems too late, Billie spurs his horse and dashes through, holding the honor of the flag as the series promises. The book mixes real history, the American landing at Vera Cruz, with boy-hero action in Fowler's brisk style. The boys first spy a band of horsemen through a field glass above the plain of Quesco, guessing at bullion on the train.
19589-a-svmmarie-and-trve-discovrse-of-s:
This contemporary account, with maps by Baptista Boazio, tells of Sir Francis Drake's West Indian voyage, printed in London in the late fifteen hundreds. Drake's men took Santiago, Santo Domingo, Cartagena, and St. Augustine, and the narrative describes each town and each approach.

Mornings were spent firing stone houses outside the trenches, while soldiers stood guard and sailors labored till heat stopped work. Kept in old spelling, the book is a vivid primary source for England's first great sea raid on Spain's empire. One landing faces a barred haven whose shore stands well fortified, with a castle furnished with great store of artillery.
1975-the-legacy-of-cain:
Wilkie Collins's Legacy of Cain opens with a married couple of little more than two years' standing. The husband, a gentleman by birth who had offended his relations by marrying below his rank, meets his death at his wife's hand. The husband's reckless extravagance had already brought him fast toward poverty.

The novel follows the legacy that death leaves: two daughters, one good and one touched by the mother's crime, and the question of whether evil is inherited. Collins writes the sensation novel with his usual skill. The book's interest lies in its central doubt: whether a child can escape a parent's sin, or whether the legacy of Cain runs in the blood.
19995-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for February 1860 is volume 5, number 28. One essay here ponders ancient counting systems. Counting by five fingers and two hands produced the numbers, it argues. Multiplication by five and by two alternately explains the pattern. The Romans adhered to their own mode through it all. Such learned miscellany filled the young magazine's pages. The Atlantic was then barely three years old.

Boston's magazine was already America's literary flagship by 1860. Emerson, Longfellow, and Holmes stood among its founders' circle. Fiction, poetry, science, and review shared each number. February 1860 sits on the edge of a nation about to split. Its calm learning is itself poignant evidence. The issue preserves prewar American intellect at ease.
20033-quin:
Quin appeared in 1921, a novel that opens in the world of dance and wounded men. One man has lain on his back for six months. His legs are still too shaky to hold him well. A friend asks, in sharp words, why he wants to go to a dance at all.

That clash sets the tone for a story about pride, loss, and the wish to live fully again. Talk runs fierce and plain between the men. Readers meet a lead figure who refuses to accept a smaller life. The dance floor becomes a test of will.
20088-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1865 gathers essays, tales, and verse from leading writers. Volume sixteen, number ninety-seven, came just months after the Civil War ended. One piece weighs beliefs about death across many peoples and faiths. It names Charon and his boat, Dante, and the Muslim hope of paradise.

Monthly issues like this one shaped American thought in the 1860s. Readers of the day found new poems beside grave essays on faith. The issue shows a nation turning from war to deep questions again. It still serves as a window on postwar American letters and belief.
2010-the-autobiography-of-charles-darwin:
Charles Darwin wrote these recollections for his children, without thought of print, and his son Francis later edited them for this volume. The account runs from Cambridge and the voyage of the Beagle to marriage, the move to Down, and his books. Francis Darwin added notes and context, so readers can see where the recollections were written and why.

Darwin speaks plainly about his reading, his health, his doubts, and the slow growth of his ideas on species. The result is a modest self-portrait, valuable because it shows a great naturalist as a working man rather than a monument. The modesty of the account is itself revealing, since Darwin credits friends, books, and chance as much as genius.
20195-wood-block-printing-a-description-:
F. Morley Fletcher wrote Wood Block Printing, a craft guide based on Japanese practice. Fletcher laments that design was long treated as mere surface looks. Ornament was copied in a mechanical way from an artist's drawing. That artist often knew little of how the work was truly made.

Japanese woodcut craft joins design and making in one skilled hand. Fletcher teaches cutting, inking, and printing step by step for artists. His book helped revive fine woodblock work in the West. Readers get clear craft teaching rooted in respect for the maker's hand.
20203-autobiography-of-benjamin-franklin:
Benjamin Franklin wrote his Autobiography, one of the most read American life stories. This 1916 edition opens with Thomas Jefferson's tale of Franklin at court. Franklin played chess with the old Duchess of Bourbon in France. When he took her king, she said kings are not taken so.

We do in America, Franklin replied, in Jefferson's fond retelling. Inside, Franklin tells of his rise from printer's boy to famed statesman. He shares his plan for moral growth and his shrewd worldly wit. Readers get the classic American tale of self-making, told by its hero.
20232-three-score-years-and-ten-life-lon:
Three Score Years and Ten holds life-long memories of Fort Snelling and the West. One scene recalls a Hartford sitting-room when the century was nineteen. A fair young matron sat beside a cradle in that bright room. In it slept a beautiful boy of a year and a half.

From that tender start, a long life runs west to frontier posts. Fort Snelling stood where rivers meet, at the edge of settlement. Memory books like this one save daily life that histories skip. Readers get seventy years of family, army, and western change in one voice.
20430-the-after-glow-of-a-great-reign-fo:
The After-Glow of a Great Reign collects four addresses given after the death of Queen Victoria. Speakers looked back on her long reign and what it had meant to Britain. The addresses mix praise, mourning, and moral teaching in the manner of sermons.

One speaker takes up a hard question from his text and answers it first. The answer, he says, comes from one who understood human nature, who had sinned and been forgiven. Such turns show how the addresses use scripture and the late queen's example together, to steady a nation in its grief.
2053-the-american-republic-its-constitut:
Orestes A. Brownson published this 1866 study of the American republic, its constitution, and its destiny, dedicating it to the historian George Bancroft. Written as the Civil War closed, it asks what holds the Union together. Brownson, a convert to Catholicism, argued from natural law rather than from party feeling.

Brownson works through the origin of government, sovereignty, and the relation of states to the nation, defending the constitution as a living order. The book is dense but clear, and it stands as a serious Catholic voice in American political thought. His defence of the constitution as a providential order set him apart from many thinkers of his day.
20585-sartor-resartus-and-on-heroes-hero:
Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus and On Heroes appear together in this volume, his two most famous works. Sartor Resartus, or The Tailor Retailored, hides a philosophy of life inside a mad German professor's theory of clothes. On Heroes gathers Carlyle's lectures on hero worship through history.

Carlyle loves vast facts. Our theory of gravitation is as good as perfect, he writes. Lagrange has proved the planetary system will endure forever on this scheme, and Laplace guesses it could not have been made on any other. Such sweeps of science serve his real subject: the great souls who steer the world.
20643-the-character-and-influence-of-the:
The Character and Influence of the Indian Trade in Wisconsin is a scholarly study of the fur trade and its effects. It follows the trade from the French era into American hands. Trade goods, posts, and credit bound Native nations and European empires together across the Great Lakes.

The study opens with the broad forces at work. It considers what follows when a higher and a lower civilization meet in commerce, to use its period terms. The Phoenicians, it notes, built trade into a great historic agency, closely tied to piracy at first. Wisconsin's trade is then judged against that long history.
2068-keziah-coffin:
Joseph C. Lincoln sets a Cape Cod tale around Keziah Coffin, a sharp-tongued widow who takes charge of neighbours, a parson, and a sea captain's affairs. Proposals, a prowler, a guardianship, and a minister's voyage tangle her plans. Lincoln, a Cape Cod writer, set many novels in the fishing towns he knew from boyhood.

Captain Nat, Captain Eben, and a cast of coastal folk drift in and out of Keziah's house, while she fights, schemes, and softens by turns. Lincoln writes the dialect and humour of the Cape with affection, and Keziah carries the book. Keziah's plain speech and sharp management make her a favourite among Lincoln's strong Cape women.
20713-a-campfire-girl-s-first-council-fi:
Jane L. Stewart's A Camp Fire Girl's First Council Fire opens her series about the Camp Fire Girls, the girls' organization founded alongside the Boy Scouts. Its heroine, Bessie, works as a hired girl before the Camp Fire changes her life. The first scenes show her home burden plainly.

There were tears in Bessie's eyes as she went at her dishes. Mrs. Hoover glared at her for a minute, then turned and left the kitchen, muttering about ingratitude. Against that drudgery, the council fire of the title offers friendship, ceremony, and the outdoors. The series sold the new movement to girl readers.
20833-exciting-adventures-of-mister-robe:
Sticks, grass, and mud build Mister Robert Robin's nest in a big basswood fork. Ben Field, in this 1928 tale, hides it so well that none below can spot it. From that safe perch, the robin family's adventures unfold for young readers.

Field wrote nature tales that teach while they charm small children. Robin parents feed, guard, and school their young through the season. Foes, storms, and first flights supply the small thrills. The plain, warm telling suits reading aloud, and its bird lore rests on close watching of real robin life in American yards and woods.
20868-cat-and-dog-or-memoirs-of-puss-and:
Puss the cat looks back on a life of more joy than grief in Cat and Dog. Constant kindness, the cat says, made that happy sum. Memoirs of Puss and the Captain lets two pets tell their own tales.

Mary Martha Sherwood wrote improving tales that mixed fun with moral care. Here, cat and dog recount masters, homes, and scrapes in turn. Animal voices let her teach kindness to beasts by stealth, in warm early children's writing. The tale is told for young readers. Both pets tell their tales in the first person.
20873-albert-gallatin:
No European-born citizen, says this 1883 life, rose higher in American service than Albert Gallatin. His gifts in lawmaking, finance, and diplomacy won praise on both Atlantic shores. Men of science, too, held his name in high regard worldwide.

Henry Adams wrote this compact life of the great Treasury chief. Gallatin funded a young nation, haggled peace at Ghent, and studied native tongues. Adams, himself a sharp historian, keeps the tale lean and keen. The book still serves as a crisp first path into the life of a founder too often left in Jefferson's shade.
21307-fire-island-being-the-adventures-o:
The Planet rides a tremendous sea in the eastern oceans as George Manville Fenn's tale opens. Her crew cling on while Mr Lane advises a life belt. A party of naturalists has shipped aboard her, bound for the island of the title. Their science offers no protection from what waits there.

Chapter after chapter drops the little group and their sailors into fresh danger, with the reader left guessing how each problem can be solved. Fenn was at his best in this mode. Uncertain naturalists face a remote island and perils from sea, weather, beasts, and men, right up to the closing chapters.
21348-benjamin-franklin:
John T. Morse Jr. wrote this life of Benjamin Franklin for the American Statesmen series, published in Boston in 1899. Fifteen chapters run from Franklin's early years through his life as a Philadelphia citizen. They continue through his two missions to England and his years as minister to France. The Hutchinson letters affair and the Privy Council scene get a chapter of their own.

Later chapters cover his financing work and his habits of life and business. The peace talks and his last years at home follow, ending with the Constitutional Convention and his death. Illustrations include Franklin's portrait and Independence Hall. Morse aimed at a compact political life for general readers, in the standard series of its day.
21463-voyages-and-travels-of-count-funni:
Count Funnibos and Baron Stilkin set out to see the world in W. H. G. Kingston's comic tale for the young. The two elderly nobles plan a grand voyage of discovery. In fact, their travels never take them beyond Holland, the land they start from.

Mishaps pile up, the pair part, and chance brings them back together. The Baron vows never to let a problem stop him, however daft his plan.
