One boot shared between two travellers is a fair sample of the logic. Kingston, rarely comic in his sea tales, here writes pure farce, with many pictures to match.
21654-in-and-around-berlin:
Minerva Brace Norton, an American living abroad, describes Berlin in In and Around Berlin, published in 1889. The approach to the city recalls the newer parts of New York, she writes. There the likeness ends, for Berlin is the heart of a very different nation.

Chapters treat family and social life, education, churches, and museums. The Reichstag and the Prussian Parliament get a chapter, as do famed personages. Norton dedicates the book to her countrymen who have visited Berlin, hope to go, or travel by armchair. Her Berlin is the stiff, bright capital of the young German Empire.
21821-the-mark-of-cain:
A duty dinner at the Olympic Club opens Andrew Lang's novel The Mark of Cain, published in 1886. Maitland of St. Gatien's watches his twenty guests linger over wine and olives, wishing they would go. Even at his own party he feels like an outsider. A strong hand on his shoulder wakes him from his reverie among the scattered fruit.

Lang, known for fairy tales and essays, here tries the modern novel of clubs and society. The title hints at a brand of guilt or fate that a man carries through polite life. Tobacco smoke, cold streets, and close talk fill the opening world. The tale that follows works in Lang's lighter register, curiosity and irony over melodrama.
21842-the-boy-scouts-of-lenox-or-the-hik:
A new scout patrol takes shape in Lenox in this 1915 boys' novel by Frank V. Webster. Tom Chesney, George Cooper, and Carl Oskamp count noses among themselves and find nearly a full patrol. George ought to make a fair scout, his friends allow, even if he is always finding fault. Their big test is the hike over Big Bear Mountain.

The frontispiece shows a rescue, with a boy hoisted to a limb while the next is hauled up. Webster wrote dozens of brisk books for boys, from farm lads to airship pilots. This one rides the first wave of the scouting craze. Woods craft, teamwork, and cheerful grit carry the troop over the mountain and back.
21968-the-finer-grain:
Late tales by Henry James fill The Finer Grain, published in 1910, five stories of success, visits, and quiet desolation. The Velvet Glove opens the book: novelist John Berridge, drunk on his prodigious hit, is sought out in Paris by a young lord. The lord begs the celebrity's judgment on a literary case. Berridge reads the whole scene as one more quaint act on the stage of European society.

A Round of Visits, Crapy Cornelia, and The Bench of Desolation follow in the contents. One tale, Mora Montravers, is missing pages in this text and was removed, as the note explains. James's late style is dense and circling, built for readers who savor motive over event. The finer grain of his title is the grain of feeling itself.
22041-mary-rose-of-mifflin:
Frances R. Sterrett published Mary Rose of Mifflin in 1910. Mary Rose is an orphan, the only child of her aunt's dead sister. When the girl needs a home, her aunt insists on taking her in. Her husband Larry Donovan grumbles at the plan, and the small town of Mifflin watches to see how it will end.

A child who has known little kindness changes the house she enters. Sterrett builds the tale from small scenes, neighbours, and slow softening of hearts. The fight is never about money or villains, only about whether a gruff man can learn to love a child. It is a gentle domestic novel of its period.
22230-hortus-inclusus-messages-from-the-:
John Ruskin wrote Hortus Inclusus as letters to the ladies of the Thwaite at Coniston. The Latin title means "a garden enclosed," and the subtitle calls the pieces messages from the wood to the garden. Ruskin sent them in happy days and dedicated the book to his dear friends in gratitude. They are among the gentlest things the great critic ever wrote.

The letters wander from flowers and woods to womanhood and the names of living creatures. Ruskin finds a small Paradise in a Lake District garden and in the friends who kept it. Late in life his prose here turns soft and grateful. The book is a quiet corner of his vast collected works.
22304-nicanor-teller-of-tales-a-story-of:
Nicanor, Teller of Tales is a story of Roman Britain by C. Bryson Taylor. Even its back matter shows the care behind the tale. A glossary pairs Roman place names with the British places they became.

Readers can match Abus with the Humber River and Tamesis with the Thames. Corinium becomes Cirencester, and Isca Silurum becomes Caerleon. Such a list tells you the fiction rests on a real Roman map. The story brings that occupied Britain to life through its teller, Nicanor. History readers get both a tale and a small gazetteer of Roman Britain in one volume.
22337-history-of-the-moors-of-spain:
History of the Moors of Spain tells how Muslim rulers shaped the Spanish peninsula. The French original had long enjoyed a high reputation. An American lady made the translation offered here.

Her taste and learning, the preface says, well fitted her for the task. Of all Muslim peoples, the Moors of Spain stood renowned in arts and arms. Their story fills the following pages in full. Readers meet a Spain of conquest, courts, and learning. The book also recalls the revival of learning in later medieval centuries. It remains a period account of a civilization that left deep marks on Spain.
22345-memoirs-of-the-private-life-return:
Memoirs of the Private Life, Return, and Reign of Napoleon concerns the emperor in 1815. That was the year of his return from exile and final reign. The writer promises facts that merit close attention from readers.

Study shows a character full of contrasts, the memoir argues. Napoleon appears by turns mistrustful and open, ardent and reserved. He is enterprising yet irresolute, vindictive yet generous. He favors liberty and yet acts the despot. Such a portrait refuses simple praise or blame. Readers get an insider's view of the Hundred Days. It remains useful for anyone tracing how contemporaries judged Napoleon's baffling mix of gifts.
22550-old-mackinaw-or-the-fortress-of-th:
Old Mackinaw, or the Fortress of the Lakes, recounts Michigan's straits country. Mackinac stood guard where Lakes Huron and Michigan meet. Its bibliography alone shows the depth of sources behind the history.

Schoolcraft's works, in three volumes, stand among the chief sources. Shea's Catholic Missions and Discovery of the Mississippi also appear. Lanman's History of Michigan and Parkman's Siege of Pontiac are listed. Foster and Whitney's Geological Report covers the land itself in science. Ferris's Great West and Disturnell's Trip to the Lakes add travel accounts. Readers get a fortress town's story built from many witnesses. French missions, British guns, and American trade all passed that island.
22737-john-gayther-s-garden-and-the-stor:
John Gayther's Garden and the Stories Told Therein is a story collection built around an old gardener and the tales his garden draws out of him; it appeared in 1902. The catalog record names no author. The frame is simple and warm: a garden, its keeper, and the people who pass through it.

John Gayther did not own the garden; he only had charge of it. At busy seasons he had men to help him. For most of the year, though, he preferred to do everything himself. That modest opening sets the book's pace: work, weather, and talk among the beds. Stories told therein grow naturally from the place. Readers who enjoy frame tales and quiet village worlds will find a gentle specimen here.
22874-frank-merriwell-s-pursuit-or-how-t:
Burt L. Standish sends Frank Merriwell into danger in Frank Merriwell's Pursuit, published in 1904. The talk in the excerpt runs hot. Lives hang on the outcome, one man insists. He offers money for aid and asks, practically, whether the house holds any whisky. Merriwell tales rarely pause for breath.

Frank was the clean-living Yale hero of a hugely popular dime-novel series. Each adventure tested his nerve, honesty, and athletic skill against plotters who played dirty. How to Win, the subtitle, states the formula plainly. Modern readers meet here a piece of the reading that shaped American boys a century ago. The values are dated, the pace is not, and the period flavor is the real attraction.
22912-phyllis-a-twin:
Dorothy Whitehill's Phyllis, a Twin, published in 1920, opens in sunshine off Fifth Avenue. In a house a short distance from Central Park, every window stands open. Soft white curtains flutter in a crisp breeze, and cool yellow light floods the rooms. A girls' story could hardly ask for a brighter start.

Phyllis shares her life with a twin, and twinship drives the fun and the mix-ups of this series for young readers. School, friends, and small adventures fill the chapters in the manner of the period's girls' books. Whitehill keeps the tone bright and the stakes friendly. The volume preserves a whole style of wholesome series fiction, written to be passed hand to hand among sisters and friends.
2292-yet-again:
Max Beerbohm, the dandy essayist and caricaturist, collects witty pieces on books, theater, and modern life in Yet Again. The essays range from literary parody to social observation, all delivered in Beerbohm's polished, amused voice. He treats fame, fashion, and folly as equal subjects for elegant mockery.

The volume's pleasure lies in its sentences: balanced, ironic, and never hurried. Beerbohm never shouts where a raised eyebrow will do. Readers who enjoy the essay at its most civilized will find this collection a fine companion. Beerbohm's caricatures of literary London add a visual wit to match his prose.
22921-the-death-and-burial-of-cock-robin:
Who'll carry him to his grave, asks The Death and Burial of Cock Robin. The Kite volunteers to bear the body to burial, so long as daylight lasts. The Linnet offers to fetch a torch and carry the light for the procession. So the old rhyme calls its mourners one by one.

Bird after bird takes a part in the burial, the Lark serving as clerk and saying Amen. The verses have taught children rhyme and rhythm for centuries, and picture editions made the procession famous. This printing pairs the familiar questions and answers with illustrations. It is a nursery classic in its simplest form, solemn and playful at once, and built to be read aloud.
23012-elder-conklin:
A girl refuses plainly in Elder Conklin, Frank Harris's story of frontier courtship. Why, just the plainest kind of refusal, I guess, she says. She told the other man only that she felt bound to go with a stranger instead. The refusal, she insists, could not have been plainer. Afraid, she repeats, as if the word stung her. But he'll lose nothing by waiting, nothing. You hear me talk. And her eyes flashed.

The flash promises the story's real subject, a young woman managing rival claims in a raw settlement. Elder Conklin's name carries the respectability she is weighing against a stranger's pull. Harris builds the scene almost wholly from talk, and the talk crackles. His western women rarely wait quietly to be chosen, and this one states her terms herself.
23023-notes-and-queries-number-201-septe:
Notes and Queries, number 201, dated September 3, 1853, trades in literary suspicion. One note quotes a warning about Swinney, a wretched but dangerous fool. He had the impudence, the writer says, to go to Lord G. Sackville, a stranger to him, and ask outright whether he was the author of Junius, the famous anonymous letters. Take care of him, the note ends.

That appetite for attribution fills the whole weekly number. Readers sent questions on books, proverbs, families, and forgotten facts, and other readers answered them. The journal called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men and artists. Bound runs became a Victorian reference web in print. This single number preserves the correspondence mid-flow, quarrels and all.
23473-lectures-on-land-warfare-a-tactica:
A field officer, named on the spine but not on the title page, wrote this nineteen twenty two tactical manual for infantry officers, printed by William Clowes in London. It examines the principles behind the art of warfare, testing each rule against examples from military history.

Cases run from Thermopylae in four eighty before Christ to the Battle of the Sambre in November nineteen eighteen, with notes on the Boer War and other modern campaigns. The lectures suit officers studying how ground, fire, movement, and surprise combine, and how old battles still teach new wars. Readers of military history will find a clear, example rich guide, serious in tone and practical in aim.
23560-carl-and-the-cotton-gin:
Sara Ware Bassett wrote this nineteen twenty four book of the Invention Series, with pictures by William F. Stecher, about Carl and the cotton gin. Chapters open with the McGregors, Carl telling a story, a tragedy, problems, a tangle of surprises, and the web widening, before a fairy godmother arrives and the romance of cotton unfolds.

North and south, mills, and the gin's place in American life follow, as Carl learns how a simple machine changed farming, trade, and labour. Bassett writes for young readers, mixing family story with clear accounts of invention and industry. Children who like stories of how things work will enjoy Carl's path from farm boy to inventor's friend, and the cotton story that grows around him.
2366-the-beldonald-holbein:
Henry James's short tale The Beldonald Holbein turns on a portrait: a beautiful woman whose likeness, painted like a Holbein, becomes the obsession of her circle. The narrator, an artist's friend, watches as the painting's fame and the woman's aging collide, with James's usual irony about art, beauty, and social cruelty. The story is slight in plot and rich in observation.

James uses the portrait to ask what art preserves and what it falsifies. The tale's quiet ending carries a sting. Readers of James's shorter fiction will enjoy this polished gem.
23918-the-little-quaker-or-the-triumph-o:
The Little Quaker, or The Triumph of Virtue, printed in London for William Cole, is a tale for the instruction of youth. Pope's lines serve as epigraph: teach me to feel another's woe, and show the mercy I would receive. Its frontispiece shows the little Quaker remonstrating with George and William Hope for their cruelty.

George and William are the only children of a Berkshire gentleman of fortune, and their father's misfortune is two very perverse and disobedient sons. Home from school for the holidays, they roam with low company, learn profane language and cruelty to animals, and laugh at their parent's lessons. The little Quaker's example sets against their conduct the virtues of mercy, feeling, and duty.
23922-dead-man-s-land-being-the-voyage-t:
George Manville Fenn's Dead Man's Land sends two teenaged boy cousins, the father of one, and a family tutor from dear old England to Africa, on a voyage to Zimbambangwe. Adventures befall them there, some pleasurable and many not, in the manner Fenn's readers expected: tight situations that seem to have no solution.

One awkward moment comes when a boy is pounced on by a lion, and the party escapes, possibly minus one of their bullocks. The book opens just before dinner, with Doctor Robertson the tutor napping by the library fire, dreaming of climbing with an ice axe. By the end, the travelers are glad indeed to return to England and home.
24452-nights-rome-venice-in-the-aestheti:
Elizabeth Robins Pennell published this memoir in Philadelphia and London in 1916, with sixteen illustrations. It recalls evenings spent with her husband, the artist Joseph Pennell, and their circle in four cities. Rome and Venice belong to the aesthetic eighties, while London and Paris belong to the fighting nineties.

Chapters move from old and new Rome to Venetian cafes, London windows, and Paris streets. Artists, writers, and actors pass through, among them Aubrey Beardsley, William Henley, and Toulouse-Lautrec's cabaret singer Aristide Bruant. The book gives a warm, firsthand portrait of artistic life before the First World War, told by a woman who lived at its centre.
24548-shiloh-as-seen-by-a-private-soldie:
Warren Olney, late captain of the 65th U.S. Colored Infantry, read this paper before the California Commandery of the Military Order of the Loyal Legion on 31 May 1889. He argues that the time has come for the private soldier to be heard, beside the generals whose battle descriptions fill the books.

A private's field of vision is narrow, Olney admits, but it is his own. His account of Shiloh gives the battle as a common soldier saw and felt it, with personal memories of the fighting. The paper remains a valuable voice from the ranks, plain and direct, for readers who want the Civil War from ground level.
24574-loss-and-gain:
John Henry Newman wrote this novel, subtitled The Story of a Convert, published at London in 1881 in an eighth edition. It follows a young Oxford man whose doubts about the Church of England lead him, step by step, toward the Roman Catholic Church. Newman himself had made that journey, and the novel draws on his own experience.

The story mixes university life, friendship, argument, and prayer, as its hero weighs faith against family, friends, and future. Newman's prose is clear, earnest, and deeply felt. Readers interested in Victorian religion will find here a classic conversion novel, and a window onto Oxford in the age of the Tractarians.
24604-rene-e-mauperin:
Edmond and Jules de Goncourt wrote Renee Mauperin, published here in the French Classical Romances series, edited by Edmund Gosse with critical introductions by Henry James, Andrew Lang, and others. The novel follows Renee, a spirited young woman of the French bourgeoisie, through love, family, and society.

The Goncourts, masters of naturalist detail, paint Parisian life with close, vivid observation, from drawing rooms to sickrooms. Renee's story turns on youth, passion, and the costs of convention. Readers of French literature will find this novel a fine example of the Goncourts' art, and a moving portrait of a young woman ahead of her world.
24690-anting-anting-stories-and-other-st:
Sargent Kayme wrote these strange tales of the Filipinos, published at Boston in 1901. An anting-anting is a charm or amulet, believed to protect its bearer, and Kayme's stories turn on charms, spirits, and magic in the islands just after the American occupation. Contents include the anting-anting of Captain Von Tollig.

Later tales tell of a cave in Coron, a conjure man of Siargao, a nurse named Mrs. Hannah Smith, a fifteenth wife, Our Lady of Pilar, and the spirit of Mount Apo. Kayme writes with local colour and a taste for the uncanny. Readers get a vivid, if dated, collection of Filipino wonder tales.
24704-on-the-vice-of-novel-reading-being:
Young E. Allison wrote this defence of the novel, read before the Western Association of Writers at Winona Park, Indiana, on 29 June 1897, and printed at Louisville in 1897. Its subtitle calls it a brief in appeal, pointing out errors of the lower tribunal, that is, the critics who condemned novel reading as a vice.

Allison argues that the novel, since it reached its modern form, has proved the most ingenious vehicle for conveying the thought and fancy of man. He pleads for fiction as a serious art, not a waste of time. Readers who love novels will enjoy this witty, lawyer-like brief for the defence.
24718-memoirs-of-the-private-life-return:
M. Fleury de Chaboulon, ex-secretary of Napoleon and of his cabinets, wrote these memoirs of the private life, return, and reign of Napoleon in 1815. The second volume, published at London in 1820 by John Murray, carries the motto of Scipio: ungrateful country, you shall not even have my bones.

Chaboulon writes from inside the Emperor's circle, describing Napoleon's return from Elba, the Hundred Days, and his second reign. His memoirs mix court detail with political judgement. Readers of Napoleonic history will find here a firsthand account of 1815, by a man who served the Emperor to the end.
24885-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1864, volume fourteen, number eighty-five, opens with Leaves from an Officer's Journal. The writer records the first Black regiment raised in the South, the First South Carolina, and its trial as a momentous experiment. It set out to prove freed slaves apt for drill, loyal, brave under fire, and steady in success.

Officers knew the regiment was watched with microscopic scrutiny, since one mutiny or rout might end all efforts to arm Black men for a century. The journal watches Port Royal, where sons of Massachusetts faced the descendants of Puritans and Huguenots. Later pages turn to housekeeping and the wants of a home. The issue gives a firsthand record of emancipation in arms.
24930-glances-at-europe-in-a-series-of-l:
Horace Greeley's letters from Europe, written in the summer of 1851 and published in New York the same year, report from Great Britain, France, Italy, and Switzerland. The Great Exhibition in London anchors the tour, and Greeley measures the continent's industry, farming, and customs against American practice. His eye is that of a working editor, curious about wages, workshops, and the daily life of ordinary people.

Trade policy runs through the letters as a steady argument: Greeley opposes trading American specie and land for imported silks, liquors, and laces. He wants a country that makes its own goods and keeps its wealth at home. The result is both travel writing and a campaign document, vivid on the ground and firm in its convictions.
24970-the-story-of-a-robin:
Agnes S. Underwood's 1898 story, published by T. Nelson and Sons, follows a robin family through a summer of growing up. Two old robins consult one fine morning about breaking up their household. Five young birds crowd a nest now too small, quarrel over the best place, and risk tumbling the weakest over the side. The parents, worn thin by constant feeding trips to the gardener's early potato plot, decide the young must find food for themselves.

Cock Robin announces a holiday and change of air, leaving the fledglings to fend for themselves. The young hero later admires his own reflection in the water, a beautiful cock robin, and forgets Jenny Wren's impudence as he considers which Miss Robin to court. A second tale, Apple-Pie Order, completes a gentle volume for young readers.
25216-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
The October 1866 number of the Atlantic Monthly, volume 18, number 108, shows the Boston magazine a year after the Civil War. Ticknor and Fields billed it as a magazine of literature, science, art, and politics, and the issue ranges accordingly.

It opens with Childhood: A Study, a lyrical sketch of wind, willows, and river water near an old brick city. Another article surveys the priestly pomp of ancient Etruria, from gold vessels in the Vatican and Campana collections to temple treasures plundered and destroyed. The number captures the Atlantic's high, curious tone.
25522-freedom-in-service-six-essays-on-m:
F. J. C. Hearnshaw, professor of medieval history at the University of London, gathers six essays on Britain's safety and good government, published in 1916 during the First World War. He dedicates the book to the memory of Lord Roberts, a leading voice for national service.

The essays trace England's old duty to serve, from militia and medieval rules through Tudor, Stuart, and later practice, then argue about compulsory service and liberty. Hearnshaw weighs liberty as freedom from foreign control, as responsible government, and as room for service, and he defends a voluntary spirit inside a shared national duty.
25753-radio-boys-loyalty-or-bill-brown-l:
Wayne Whipple and S. F. Aaron write this 1922 Radio Boys tale, Radio Boys Loyalty, or Bill Brown Listens In, published by Donohue in Chicago and New York. Whipple and Aaron had written Radio Boys Cronies together before.

Bill Brown and Gus open the tale discussing the Tech's fine new wireless station. Bill, keen to get access to the station, has set a time when Professor Gray and Mr. Hooper can hear the boys' first broadcast. Students, fooling, hazing, and good will fill early chapters, as radio loyalty means sticking by friends and by the station.
26322-peterkin:
Mrs. Molesworth's Peterkin, issued by Macmillan in 1902 with pictures by H. R. Millar, is a children's story told from the nursery. It opens at tea, with everyone present except Peterkin, and a servant named James asking nurse, called Mrs. Brough, where the boy has gone. James reports that Peterkin's mamma herself wants to know, and his red face hints at trouble.

Chapters promise Found, an invitation, stratagems, Margaret, a great plan, a terrible idea, and a fog. A frontispiece shows mamma hugging Peterkin as if he had been lost for a year. Later pictures show a parrot, a poetry book in a brown-paper parcel, and a bath chair. The book mixes mystery, jokes, and family warmth.
26442-true-to-his-home-a-tale-of-the-boy:
Hezekiah Butterworth's tale of Franklin's boyhood follows young Ben from Boston toward Philadelphia, in the author's popular series of boyhood lives. One adventure shows Ben as a poet, and another sends him friendless and forlorn by sea, with only a few shillings in his pocket. A friend's advice points him to Philadelphia, city of Penn.

Crossing the Delaware, Ben helps row the boat and offers the boatman his fare. The boatman refuses, saying Ben earned his passage by rowing. Ben, holding one silver dollar and a copper shilling, insists the ferryman take the coin. He later reflects that a person is sometimes more generous with little money than with plenty.
26490-lord-milner-s-work-in-south-africa:
W. Basil Worsfold's 1906 history, with portraits and map, follows Lord Milner's work in South Africa from 1897 to the Peace of Vereeniging in 1902. Worsfold draws on hitherto unpublished information and opens with Lord Goschen's praise of a man whom difficulties could not conquer, disasters could not cow, and obloquy could never move. The book is frankly admiring of its subject.

Chapters move from Downing Street and the man on the spot through the creed of Afrikander nationalists, a year of observation, and playing for time. Then come the ultimatum and the fall of the republics. Rebellion in the Cape Colony, conciliation, disarmament of the Dutch population, and preparation for peace lead to the surrender at Vereeniging. The volume serves as a pro-Milner record of war and settlement.
26518-journal-of-an-american-prisoner-at:
An unnamed American kept this pocket journal after his capture in the War of 1812. Editor G. M. Fairchild prepared it for private printing at Quebec in 1909. Fairchild argues from the handwriting and the story that the writer was Surgeon's Mate James Reynolds. Reynolds had charge of the sick aboard the packet Cuyahoga when British forces seized her off Fort Malden in July 1812. A companion schooner carrying stores was seized with her.

Daily entries, often only a line or two, record prison ships, crossings of troops and Native allies, rumors, weather, and the dull wait for release. The journal ends when the writer is ordered to prepare to leave Quebec for Boston. Spelling stays rough and unpolished, which is part of its value. It gives a plain, day-to-day view of captivity from inside, rather than a polished history written long after.
26522-george-mu-ller-of-bristol-and-his-:
Arthur T. Pierson wrote this 1899 life of George Müller of Bristol, the German-born preacher famous for his orphanages and his trust in prayer. James Wright, Müller's son-in-law and successor, introduces the book and endorses it as the authorized memoir for British and American readers. Pierson draws on Müller's own Narrative of the Lord's Dealings, in four volumes, plus annual reports.

Chapters trace Müller from his birth and conversion through his pastorate to the founding of the Scriptural Knowledge Institution and its orphan work. Trials of faith, answered prayer, and the daily practice of looking to God for supplies form the heart of the story. Readers meet a man whose helpers prayed with him daily and shared the work's secrets through years of strain and triumph.
2662-under-the-greenwood-tree-or-the-mel:
Thomas Hardy sets this rural painting in Mellstock, where the village quire still sings in church and the seasons turn the story. Winter opens with Mellstock Lane, the tranter, and the assembled quire going the rounds at Christmas, dancing more wildly at the tranter's party.

Spring brings Dick's courtship of the new schoolmistress, and the quire's fate under a new organ. Hardy writes with affection for old customs and quiet humor about change. The novel charms as a portrait of Dorset village life before the modern world swept the quire away.
26797-something-else-again:
Franklin P. Adams published this book of light verse with Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City, New York and London, in 1920, dedicating it to Montague Glass. Adams had already written By and Large, In Other Words, Tobogganing on Parnassus, and Weights and Measures. His pieces parody classics, newspapers, and modern life in turn.

The book opens with the Doughboy's Horace, modernizing Horace's odes for an American soldier. Present Imperative advises Leuconoë to sweep the floor and wash the dishes rather than dream about 1928. Later pieces imagine Amy Lowell as James Whitcomb Riley, the advertising man as Gilbert, Praed, or Locker, and a vers librist addressed directly. How Do You Tackle Your Work asks whether the reader grapples each day's task with a confident, easy mind.
26991-a-short-system-of-english-grammar-:
Henry Bate's Short System of English Grammar, written for the boarding school in Worcester, argues that usage and custom, not borrowed rules, should govern a language. Its preface attacks grammarians who forced Latin rules onto English as if one language's rules could serve another.

Latin has only eight parts of speech, Bate notes, while English, with its article, has nine. English nouns, he insists, have no true cases: of a rose is not a genitive of rose, but a preposition showing relation. The book teaches grammar from English itself, plainly and briefly.
27008-notes-and-queries-number-211-novem:
November 12, 1853 brings Notes and Queries number 211, with notes on Grammont by G. Steinman Steinman and Thomas Keightley on the changing meaning of proverbial expressions. Extracts from Colchester corporation records and a note on convocation under George II follow.

Minor notes touch Pepys's grammar, Roman remains, curfew at Sandwich, and the natural history of Balmoral. Queries range from Days of my Youth and the birthplace of King Edward V to the derivation of chemistry. The chemistry query asks whether Chemi, the name of Egypt, explains the word. A query on Taylor's Holy Living and one on the return of gentry under Henry VI also appear.
27009-notes-and-queries-number-212-novem:
Number 212 of Notes and Queries, dated November 19, 1853, opens with party similes of the seventeenth century: Foxes and Firebrands and The Trojan Horse. Cuthbert Bede adds testimonials to donkeys, and William Durrant Cooper writes on longevity in Cleveland, Yorkshire.

Folk lore notes record an ancient custom in Warwickshire and customs of Nottinghamshire. Minor queries ask about currency, Donatus Redivivus, ash trees and lightning, and the drainage of the marshes near Great Yarmouth, a typical bundle of Victorian puzzles. Minor notes add a centenarian couple, autumnal tints, and straw paper, and a note on the Reverend Josiah Pullen sits among the contents.
27010-notes-and-queries-number-213-novem:
Notes and Queries number 213, for November 26, 1853, opens with William Sidney Gibson on the state prison in the Tower. Thomas Nimmo prints an inedited letter from Henry VIII of England to James V of Scotland, and Bolton Corney reviews a handbook to the library of the British Museum.

Folk lore notes cover Derbyshire, weather superstitions and rhymes, and Cambridgeshire, while D. Jardine argues that rapping is no novelty. Queries ask about grammar in relation to logic and the coronet of Llewelyn ap Griffith, Prince of Wales. Minor notes add Bond the poet, the late harvest, and Sir Joshua Reynolds's baptism, and the number opens at page 509.
2702-the-lion-s-skin:
Rafael Sabatini opens this historical romance with a fanatic, then moves to the Adam and Eve tavern, a witness, and Mr. Green. Moonshine, Hortensia's return, and a father and son at odds follow, with temptation and a champion waiting.

Spurs to the reluctant, an assault at arms, and sunshine and shadow lead to a forlorn hope, Lady Ostermore, and love and rage. Mr. Green executes his warrant among graves, where a ghost of the past walks. Sabatini writes with dash and color, and the lion's skin of the title proves a hard disguise to wear.
27548-the-art-of-promoting-the-growth-of:
Thomas Watkins, many years foreman with Mr. Grange of Hackney and then with W. Knight of Highbury Park, published this gardening manual in London in 1824. Harding of St. James's Street published it, and seedsmen and fruiterers in Covent Garden, Fleet Street, and Cornhill sold it.

Watkins gives directions for the best means of bringing cucumbers and melons to a complete state of perfection. He had meant to include an engraving of his own fine fruit, executed at considerable expense. He dropped the plate because, though accurate, it did not show the qualities that made his fruit superior. Practical growers get a foreman's own methods here.
27683-the-world-i-live-in:
Helen Keller, author of The Story of My Life, published this book with Hodder and Stoughton in London, New York, and Toronto, copyrighted in 1904 and 1908, and dedicated to Henry H. Rogers, her dear friend of many years. A portrait shows Keller in her study.

Its chapters are called The Seeing Hand, The Hands of Others, The Hand of the Race, and The Power of Touch. Keller writes of the world as it reaches her through touch, and of how hands speak for others and for the race. Press praise quoted at the front calls her autobiography a record of extraordinary victory over physical disabilities, and a human document without parallel in literature.
28021-pictures-and-stories-from-uncle-to:
Pictures and Stories from Uncle Tom's Cabin, published by John P. Jewett and Company in Boston in 1853, adapts Harriet Beecher Stowe's narrative for the youngest readers, to plant warm fellow-feeling for the wronged Negro race of America in young hearts. The editor's preface explains that verses were written by the authoress for the youngest readers in large bold type, while prose parts, in smaller type, suit reading aloud in the family circle.

The book opens with The Sale of Little Harry, whose curls and bright eyes delight the rich man's house until a wicked trader buys him one winter day. The little work shows how Stowe's novel reached children, in picture-book form, within a year of its first publication.
28093-the-confessions-of-arse-ne-lupin:
Maurice Leblanc's The Confessions of Arsene Lupin, copyrighted in 1912 and 1913, collects ten tales told by Lupin's friend and chronicler. Lupin, the gentleman thief already famous in French papers, here explains cases the public only half knew. A reward notice, a wedding ring, and a red silk scarf each open a new puzzle.

The stories move from Paris rooms to a forest and a prison that seems to have no door. Lupin steals, disguises himself, and outwits police, yet often gives money away or rights a wrong. Readers get fast, witty crime tales in which the thief, not the detective, solves the mystery.
28115-the-great-sioux-trail-a-story-of-m:
Joseph A. Altsheler's The Great Sioux Trail, published in 1918, is a boys' adventure of mountain and plain. Set during the wars on the western frontier, it follows young scouts and soldiers through Sioux country, where a warning, a narrow escape, and a long flight drive the plot. Charles L. Wrenn supplied the pictures.

The boys meet old chiefs, cross rivers, and learn woodcraft as they carry news and dodge war parties. Altsheler, author of many boys' series on the Civil War and the frontier, keeps the action brisk and the morals plain. The book suits readers who enjoy old-style western tales of courage and loyalty.
28293-the-tale-of-jolly-robin:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote The Tale of Jolly Robin in 1917 as a Tuck-Me-In Tale for bedtime. Jolly Robin, once a spotted nestling with two brothers and a sister, learns to fly, meets Jasper Jay and Mr. Crow, and blunders through snowballs, hermits, and a white giant. Harry L. Smith drew the pictures, and Grosset and Dunlap published the book.

Chapters follow Jolly from nestlings to the top of the barn, with lessons on manners, jealousy, and courage in small, funny doses. Bailey, author of Sleepy-Time Tales, writes in short, clear sentences for very young readers. The book suits parents reading aloud at night.
28380-life-of-charles-darwin:
G. T. Bettany wrote Life of Charles Darwin in 1887 for the Great Writers series, edited by Eric S. Robertson. Bettany traces Darwin from ancestry: grandfather Erasmus, physician and poet of The Botanic Garden, father Robert Waring Darwin, physician, and maternal grandfather Josiah Wedgwood, potter. Charles, born at Shrewsbury on February 12, 1809, lost his mother in 1817.

Chapters follow Darwin at Edinburgh and Cambridge, his friendship with Henslow, his Beagle voyage from December 27, 1831, and his letters home. Walter Scott published the short life in London. Bettany writes clearly for general readers, making Darwin's youth and voyage vivid.
28618-from-farm-house-to-the-white-house:
William M. Thayer's From Farm House to the White House, published by Hurst and Company of New York, tells the life of George Washington from boyhood to manhood. Its subtitle promises his public and private life and services, and the volume belongs to Thayer's Log Cabin to White House series. A preface urges every American, old or young, to know Washington's life.

Washington's own letter to his college stepson opens the moral frame, warning that habits formed young stick for life. The twig bent early shapes the tree, the letter says, and idleness approaches like a thief. Readers get an improving biography built to confirm patriotism and steady character.
29025-roman-catholicism-in-spain:
An Old Resident wrote this 1855 study, Roman Catholicism in Spain, published in Edinburgh by Johnstone and Hunter. The opening argues that Roman Catholicism shifts more with outward practice than other faiths do. Spain's excesses, it says, grow from Spanish history: Goths and Moors, conversion, and the national character shown by Isabella the Catholic, Charles V, and Philip II.

The first chapter treats the Spanish clergy: their early state, order, wealth, lands, and power, with their stance against the sciences and their backing of papal power over kings. Later matter covers barraganas, tithes, and the poverty of parish priests after Mendizabal abolished tithes. Readers get a Protestant resident's critical survey, valuable as a period view of Spanish religion and society.
29080-plain-words-for-christ-being-a-ser:
Reginald G. Dutton, curate of St. Martin's in the Fields, wrote this 1880 book, Plain Words for Christ, a series of readings for working men, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Dutton dedicates it to the working men of England, among whom he counts many firm friends. His preface says he touched only topics working men likely needed advice on, in language as simple as possible.

Following scripture's example, Dutton illustrates meaning from nature's teachings wherever he can. The contents run through life, birthdays, temptation, drink, idle words, excuses, poverty, and being out of work, to masters and men, forgiveness, courtship, marriage, and home. Readers get a kind, plain Victorian devotional book, written for men at work rather than scholars at leisure.
29150-holbein:
Beatrice Fortescue wrote this short life of Hans Holbein the Younger for Methuen's Little Books on Art series. It was first published in 1904 with forty-six illustrations. Holbein was the German painter of the northern Renaissance. He worked in Augsburg and Basel, then found fame at the court of Henry VIII in England, where his portraits fixed the faces of a whole age.

Fortescue traces Holbein's family and Augsburg home, his move to Basel, and his brother Ambrose. She covers his dealings with Erasmus, whose Praise of Folly he illustrated. She also surveys his paintings and closes with a catalogue of his principal surviving works. Readers get a compact, picture-filled introduction to an artist whose sharp-eyed portraits still shape how the Tudor world looks to us.
29197-a-short-history-of-spain:
Mary Platt Parmele wrote this short history of Spain, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1906, copyrighted in 1898. Parmele states her method in the preface: she leaves out the mass of confusing detail that makes history dreary, and keeps only the facts vital to the nation's development.

Fourteen chapters trace Spain from its early peoples through its kingdoms, its empire, and its later fortunes, with Charles V among the figures illustrated. The book aims at the general reader who wants the shape of Spanish history without a scholar's apparatus. Readers get a concise, readable survey, dated in places but clear about what Parmele thought mattered most in Spain's story.
29316-sir-henry-morgan-buccaneer-a-roman:
Cyrus Townsend Brady published this romance of the Spanish Main in New York in 1903. Its hero, Sir Henry Morgan, resolves in his old age to go a-buccaneering once more, and the book follows his cruise with the buccaneers across the seas. Later books treat the tangled love affairs of the Pearl of Caracas.

A further book tells of the taking of La Guayra by the buccaneers, with the dreadful perils of Donna Mercedes de Lara and Captain Alvarado in that city. Brady, author of For Love of Country and For the Freedom of the Sea, writes in the swashbuckling mode. Readers get a full-blooded pirate romance, with sea fights, love, and a legendary buccaneer at its center.
29382-the-ladies-work-table-book-contain:
Printed in New York in 1844 by J. Winchester, this practical manual teaches plain and fancy needlework, embroidery, knitting, netting, and crochet. Its full title promises clear directions and many engravings that show each stitch, and its chapters move from tools and materials to body linen, house linen, and finer fancy work. The book speaks to women as makers of home comfort and good taste.

Each lesson gives steps a beginner can follow, with care for neatness, thrift, and skill. The prose reflects its era's view of women's home role, stated plainly in its introduction. Modern makers, historians of craft, and readers of domestic manuals will find a useful, detailed record of stitches and standards from the 1840s.
29388-memoir-of-an-eventful-expedition-i:
This memoir, rendered from the Spanish of Pedro Velasquez of San Salvador, tells of a journey into an unexplored part of Central America. It claims the discovery of Iximaya, an idolatrous city of ruined temples. The party, described by John L. Stevens and other travellers, is said to have brought back two Aztec children, descendants of a priestly caste now nearly extinct. The tale blends travel, wonder, and the era's hunger for lost cities.

Readers should take its bold claims as claimed, not proven: a hidden city, ancient founders, and living heirs to a vanished priesthood. Its value lies in the vivid picture it gives of nineteenth-century exploration lore. Those who enjoy lost-world tales and old travel yarns will find a lively, if fanciful, account of a quest into the unknown.
29400-murder-point-a-tale-of-keewatin:
Coningsby William Dawson published this novel in 1910, with Hodder and Stoughton in London and George H. Doran in New York. Dawson, author of The House of the Weeping Woman, sets his tale of Keewatin, the northern Canadian district, at Murder Point. John Granger of Murder Point opens the book, and an unbidden guest follows.

Later chapters bring the devil in the Klondike, Spurling's tale, and cities out of sight. Dawson writes a northern adventure of remoteness, rumor, and reckoning, where the wilderness presses on every choice. Readers get an early twentieth-century Canadian north tale, atmospheric and tense, about a man at a place named for murder.
29469-a-supplementary-chapter-to-the-bib:
George Borrow wrote this short essay as a study of Richard Ford's Hand-Book for Travellers in Spain, a work Ford spent more than sixteen years compiling and first printed in 1845. Borrow had meant the piece for The Quarterly Review, and the 1913 pamphlet printing, made for private circulation, presents it as a supplementary chapter to his own Bible in Spain. Ford himself had praised that book, and the two writers admired each other's Spain.

Borrow's essay reads less as a review than as a fresh chapter of travel writing: sharp, learned, and full of Spanish color. It weighs Ford's handbook against lived knowledge of the land. Readers of Borrow, of Ford, or of old Spain will find a compact, vivid link between two great books about the same country.
29482-benjamin-franklin:
Paul Elmer More's short life of Benjamin Franklin is third in the Riverside Biographical Series from Houghton Mifflin. It follows the printer, scientist, and statesman from his early days in Boston to his work in Philadelphia and his first voyage to England. Later chapters take up his religious beliefs, the Junto club, and his rise to fame at home and abroad. Each volume in the series runs about 140 pages, made for school and home reading.

More sums Franklin up with a borrowed Napoleonic line: after meeting Goethe, Napoleon said, in effect, this is a man. The book stresses industry, wit, and public service over myth. Readers seeking a compact, classic life of Franklin, written for general readers, will find a clear and admiring portrait.
29516-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-:
Volume fourteen, number eighty-six of The Atlantic Monthly, dated December 1864 and printed by Ticknor and Fields, gathers literature, art, and politics for a nation at war. Its opening piece, The Highland Light, describes the Cape Cod light. It stands as the first great sea-coast light seen by ships entering Massachusetts Bay from Europe, some twenty rods from the edge of a wasting clay bank.

The issue's mix of essays, tales, and verse shows the magazine's Civil War-era range: close observation, moral reflection, and literary craft. Readers get a single month of a great American magazine at a turning point in its history. Historians and lovers of period writing will find a vivid slice of 1864 letters.
29571-nan-of-music-mountain:
Frank H. Spearman, author of Whispering Smith, set Nan of Music Mountain in the West, printed in 1916 by Grosset and Dunlap with pictures by N. C. Wyeth. Its chapters open on Frontier Day, follow the Thief River stage line and the Spanish Sinks, and reach first blood at Calabasas. Rounding up Sassoon, heels for it, and a gambling room follow, with a cup of coffee and a glass moon among later scenes.

Lefever, rotund and fond of sitting sidewise on a table's edge when a chair would not do, adds color to a tale of ranch, rail, and romance. Nan herself stands at its heart. Readers of western fiction will find a lively, well-illustrated novel from the classic age of the range.
29591-getting-to-know-spain:
Dee Day wrote Getting to Know Spain, printed in 1957 by Coward-McCann of New York, with pictures by Don Lambo and Sabra Holbrook as series editor. The book opens with the queen who made America possible: Isabella of Spain, whose backing sent three little ships from a Spanish village in August 1492. The Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria sailed under an Italian sailor, Christopher Columbus.

Day writes for young readers, telling Spain's story through places, people, and history, from Columbus to modern times. The book's seventh impression shows its classroom success. Young readers and families will find a bright, friendly introduction to Spain, its past, and its pride.
29664-notes-and-queries-number-218-decem:
Number 218 of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, December 31, 1853, priced at fourpence, served as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, reads: when found, make a note of. Its contents list notes on St. Stephen's Day, the Holy Trinity Church at Hull, and minor notes on Italian-English words, American names, and rulers of the world in 1853.

Queries seek the derivation of Silo, the character of the song of the nightingale, inscriptions in books, and ladies' arms borne in a lozenge. The number shows Victorian scholarship as a conversation, question answering question. Readers of antiquarian history will find a lively, crowded issue from the journal's early years.
29694-the-treasure-trail-a-romance-of-th:
Marah Ellis Ryan's 1918 romance of the land of gold and sunshine, printed by A. C. McClurg of Chicago with pictures by Robert Amick, opens with Kit and the girl of the lark call. Later chapters tell the red gold legend, a verified prophecy of Senorita Billie, and scenes in the adobe of Pedro Vijil. A dead man under the cottonwoods, the province of Altar, and the slave trail follow.

Ryan's horseman speaks forceful Mexican, a tongue supposed to be Spanish and often not, and a picture vows to hit any trail except Mexican politics. The novel mixes treasure, love, and border peril. Readers of southwestern romance will find a colorful, sunlit tale of gold and daring.
29697-the-heart-of-thunder-mountain:
Edfrid A. Bingham published this mountain novel in 1916, with a frontispiece in color by Anton Otto Fisher. It opens in a silent pasture where tall grass ripens bronze in the breeze. A girl on a cow pony watches the high land that will shape her fate. Seth Huntington, Hillyer, Smythe, and Diana move through a tale of bids, stratagems, and hearts in revolt.

Avalanche, storm, a narrow pass, and the challenge of a brute test the folk of Thunder Mountain. The chapters close with a lamp relit and a voice in the hurricane. Bingham writes the range in full color, with ranch work, hard weather, and love affairs wound tight. The book is a full-blooded western romance of the high country.
29760-the-dominant-strain:
Anna Chapin Ray sets this 1903 novel among well-to-do young people in a Boston social season. Talk at balls and horse shows masks real stakes there. Beatrix, weary and sharp-tongued, faces a choice about marriage. Her friend Sally presses her, half in jest and half in earnest, to say what she will tell a suitor. That suitor is sure to speak before Lent ends.

Sidney and Thayer move through the same set, and the plot turns on temper, pride, and the pull of old family traits. Ray lets talk do much of the work, so a light scene can carry a hard truth about what each person wants. The title points to the trait that wins out when charm, duty, and will pull in unlike ways.
29774-a-yankee-flier-over-berlin:
Al Avery published this wartime flying tale in 1944, with pictures by Paul Laune. It follows American fighter pilots of the Third Fighter group as they fly escort for heavy bombers bound for Berlin. At the edge of German defenses they must turn back and leave the bombers to press on alone. Colonel Holt and his weather men weigh cloud, fuel, and flak before each run.

The chapters move from rugged sorties and scout runs to a hidden airfield, a prisoner, an escape, a spy, and a zero hour. Stan, the young flier at the heart of it, learns the work of war in the air and on the ground. The book is a boys' war tale, brisk and plain, about nerve, teamwork, and the cost of each mission.
30133-notes-and-queries-number-217-decem:
Notes and Queries for Saturday, December 24, 1853, gives one weekly number of the journal that served literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists as a shared notebook. Notes in this issue cover folk lore from the reign of King James I, the ballad of Sir Hugh, Pennsylvanian folk lore at Christmas, county rhymes, and legends of County Clare. Short miscellanies add Yorkshire and Cornish customs, saints' day feasts, and New Year practice.

Queries and answers fill the rest, with readers asking after regicides, knights, old families, Greek epigrams, and translations from Aeschylus. The mix shows the journal at work: a small fact offered here, a correction there, and a chain of letters that slowly builds a record. For students of Victorian antiquarian life, the number is a compact sample of the whole project.
30157-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-15-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for February 1865, volume 15, number 88, gives one wartime number of the magazine of literature, art, and politics. Its lead essay treats Washington Allston, called the first great American painter, who died on July 8, 1843. It recalls his first Boston show in 1827, his long retired life after years in Europe, and the strange charm of a genius rooted in imagination rather than fashion.

Ticknor and Fields entered the issue in 1865, in the last months of the Civil War, and the number mixes art, letters, and public life in the Atlantic manner. Allston stands as the issue's anchor, praised for work that still led in imagination after twenty-one years of change. For readers of period magazines, the issue is a window on how Boston judged art while the nation fought.
30257-the-founder-of-new-france-a-chroni:
Charles W. Colby chronicles Champlain, founder of New France, in a Toronto and Glasgow volume from 1915. Early years open, followed by Champlain in Acadia, at Quebec, and in the wilderness, then his last years and his writings and character. A bibliographical note and index close the book, and a colour drawing by C. W. Jefferys fronts it, showing the Order of Good Cheer at Port Royal in 1606 and 1607.

Other pictures give a portrait of Champlain ascribed to Moncornet, a map of coasts explored from 1604 to 1607 by Bartholomew, and Champlain's own drawing of the habitation at Quebec. Henri de Bourbon, Prince de Condé, appears among the figures of the narrative. Colby writes popular history in the Brook chronicle manner, brisk and clear, for readers who want the French founder of Canada in one readable volume.
30574-shadow-mountain:
Dane Coolidge writes Shadow Mountain, copyrighted in 1919, with a frontispiece by George W. Gage showing a woman reaching out smiling wistfully to touch a man. Coolidge, author of The Desert Trail, opens with the last of ten thousand, the shotgun widow, the shadow, and the ghost man.

Later chapters add a load of buckshot, all crazy, between friends, the tip, a peace talk, and the best head in town. A touch, the expert, a sack of cats, the explosion, and the god of ten per cent follow, with a showdown with the widow and peace at a price. Coolidge mixes western humor, feud, and romance in a fast, colorful tale.
30580-the-fairy-books-of-andrew-lang-a-p:
David Widger edits The Fairy Books of Andrew Lang as an index to twelve volumes by various authors and Andrew Lang, with links to all stories in the HTML version. The Blue Fairy Book opens the set, with the Bronze Ring, Prince Hyacinth and the Dear Little Princess, East of the Sun and West of the Moon, and the Yellow Dwarf.

Later tales add Little Red Riding Hood, Sleeping Beauty in the Wood, Cinderella, Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp, Rumpelstiltzkin, Beauty and the Beast, and Puss in Boots. The White Cat, the Water-Lily, the Gold-Spinners, and the Terrible Head follow, with Pretty Goldilocks, Whittington, the Wonderful Sheep, Little Thumb, and the Forty Thieves. Widger's index guides readers through Lang's rainbow fairy canon.
30594-notes-and-queries-number-215-decem:
Notes and Queries, number two hundred fifteen, dated Saturday 10 December 1853, serves as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, genealogists, and others. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

Contents open with original royal letters to the grand masters of Malta by William Winthrop, penny sights and exhibitions in the reign of James the First by A. Grayan, and the impossibilities of our forefathers. Parallel passages by Rev. John Booker follow, with astrology to come. Priced at fourpence, the weekly gathers queries, answers, and odd knowledge.
30595-notes-and-queries-number-216-decem:
Notes and Queries, number two hundred sixteen, dated Saturday 17 December 1853, serves as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, genealogists, and others. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

Contents open with teaching a dog French by Arthur Paget, the religion of the Russians, Leicestershire epitaphs by William Kelly, and Longfellow's Reaper and the Flowers. Minor notes add receipt versus recipe, the death of Philip the Third of Spain, and churchwardens. Priced at fourpence, the weekly gathers queries, answers, and odd knowledge for Victorian scholars.
30803-books-before-typography-a-primer-o:
Frederick W. Hamilton, educational director of the United Typothetae of America, wrote this 1918 primer for apprentices in the printing trades. It covers the history of book making up to the invention of movable types, and it belongs to a technical series for learners. Hamilton starts, as he says, with the earliest dawn of civilization, not with the press itself.

Six chapters trace the origin of the alphabet, writing materials, the growth of the book, the making of manuscripts, old and medieval libraries, and the dawn of a new era. Hamilton explains why people needed marks for property, records, orders, and news, even in simple societies. It is a short, clear guide for readers who want to know how books existed long before print.
30841-the-rover-boys-in-the-land-of-luck:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, wrote this Rover Boys adventure, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Its full subtitle promises stirring adventures in the oil fields, and an early picture shows Andy yelling that oil has been struck. The Rover Boys had already been to school, to sea, and on a hunt in earlier volumes of the series.

Chapters move from a storm and a rescue through school sports, a rival school, and a trip home from France, before the boys head for Texas. There the oil country gives them work, danger, and luck in turn. It is a wholesome boys' adventure of the Stratemeyer kind: team spirit, pluck, and a new American industry as the backdrop for fun.
30995-indian-methodist-hymn-book-hymns-u:
Held here is an Indian Methodist hymn book, with hymns used on the Fraser River Indian Mission of the Methodist Church, British Columbia Conference. Hymns in Chinook, and the Lord's Prayer and Ten Commandments, are appended. The hymns were translated by the Reverends Thomas Crosby, Charles M. Tate, and William H. Barraclough, missionaries, and compiled and printed by Barraclough at Chilliwack, British Columbia, in 1898.

Its notes say the hymns are in the Chilliwack dialect of the language of the Alkomaylum nation, who live along the Fraser River from Yale to the coast. They also live on Vancouver Island at Cowichan and Nanaimo. As spoken by the Cowichans, the language is sweet and rhythmical, while the Chilliwack dialect is harsher and more guttural. The Nanaimos, Yales, Sumas, Kwantuls, and Nooksaks each speak a slightly different dialect of the same language. It is a mission hymn book in an Indigenous language.
31155-the-academy-keeper-or-variety-of-u:
Printed in London in 1770 for Thomas Peat at one shilling, The Academy Keeper is a handbook for running a boys' boarding school. Its author made his own fortune at it. Having married the mistress of a boarding school, he learned to manage boys' tempers and parents' dispositions, handed the school to a favorite usher, and set down his rules for others.

The directions cover terms, diet, lodging, recreation, discipline, and instruction, with advice on addressing parents and guardians of every rank and on choosing and treating ushers, academy-wives, and servants. Candid about money and manners alike, the little book is a rare, practical glimpse of eighteenth-century private education as a business.
31339-the-black-phalanx-african-american:
Joseph T. Wilson was a veteran of the Second Louisiana Native Guard Volunteers and the 54th Massachusetts Volunteers. He wrote The Black Phalanx, first published at Hartford in 1890, with a new foreword by Dudley Taylor Cornish in this edition. Wilson covers African American soldiers in the War of Independence, the War of 1812, and the Civil War, in a long, detailed history drawn from service records and firsthand knowledge.

Chapters move from recruiting and organizing to departments of war, the Army of the Frontier, and battles in the Gulf and the South. Wilson's aim is record as much as argument: to set down what Black soldiers did, where they served, and under what officers. The book remains a foundational source for the military history it covers and a landmark of Black historical writing.
3158-our-american-cousin:
Tom Taylor's comedy in three acts sends an American cousin among English gentlefolk. Asa Trenchard, rough, frank, and rich, collides with the manners of a family that needs his money but not his ways. Lord Dundreary, with his tangled sayings, stole the show in performance, and the transcriber's note to this 1869 printing remarks how few of his famous Dundrearyisms it keeps.

The play lives on for a somber reason: Abraham Lincoln sat watching it at Ford's Theatre on the night he was shot. That fact should not hide its comic craft. Taylor built a durable stage machine from national contrast, and audiences still enjoy the clash between American bluntness and English polish that drives every scene.
3191-goldsmith-s-friend-abroad-again:
Mark Twain presents these letters as plain fact, with a note to match. No experience in them had to be invented, he says, because fancy is not needed to vary the history of a Chinaman's sojourn in America. Plain fact proves amply sufficient. The letters run from Shanghai outward, addressed to Ching-Foo, as the writer leaves an oppressed native land for a realm he calls noble.

What follows is the immigrant's America seen from inside: work, prejudice, law, and small kindnesses, reported home in plain speech. The book's power lies in that reversal. A Chinese voice judges the land of promise by its treatment of strangers, and Twain lets the judgment stand without softening its edge.
31921-the-land-of-nome-a-narrative-sketc:
Lanier McKee's 1902 book The Land of Nome, a narrative sketch of the rush to the Bering Sea gold fields, covers the country, its mines and people. It also covers the history of a great conspiracy in 1900 and 1901. Gold at Cape Nome, Alaska, almost in the Bering Strait and some one hundred and fifty miles off Siberia, was found by a small party of prospectors in late autumn 1898.

News spread like wildfire down the Pacific coast and up to Dawson. The spring of 1900 brought an unprecedented mad rush of eighteen thousand persons, after beach gold easy to extract was found in 1899. Readers get a firsthand account of the Nome rush, its hybrid city, inland mines, and the McKenzie conspiracy that seized its courts.
31966-cathedrals-of-spain:
John Allyne Gade's Cathedrals of Spain, published in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in February 1911 and fully illustrated, travels through Spain's great churches. Its chapters cover Salamanca, Burgos, Avila, Leon, Toledo, Segovia, Seville, and Granada, with a list of books consulted and an index.

Illustrations include the new cathedral of Salamanca, photographed by J. Lacoste of Madrid, and the old and new buildings' towers at Salamanca. The new cathedral of Salamanca is the frontispiece. Readers get an architectural travel book, learned but readable, that treats each cathedral as a history in stone.
3200-the-entire-project-gutenberg-works-:
This file gathers the whole Project Gutenberg Mark Twain collection in one place. An editor's note explains the scale: over sixty files, prepared by many different volunteers over many years. Each work also exists in a much smaller separate file, for readers who want one book at a time. As new Twain works became available, the collection grew.

The omnibus runs from the early sketches to the late letters, speeches, and novels, in a single searchable text. Its size is its point and its problem: everything together, at the cost of easy navigation. For a reader who wants Twain entire, without hunting file by file, this compilation remains the simplest route through his complete Gutenberg works.
32023-the-boy-s-voice-a-book-of-practica:
J. Spencer Curwen's 1891 book The Boy's Voice, is a book of practical information on the training of boys' voices for church choirs. It was written by a fellow of the Royal Academy of Music and president of the Tonic Sol-fa College. Curwen says its value depends less on his own work than on the large number of choirmasters whose experience he gathered.

Chapters cover the healthfulness of singing, management of the breath, the art of managing choir boys, voice training, pronunciation in singing, and singing by ear and by note. Readers get a practical Victorian manual for choir trainers, full of hints from working choirmasters for producing good results from poor material.
32127-wheels-within:
Charles de Vet's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1952, opens in a neurologist's office with a question about identity. The cover line warns readers not to probe their own roots and self, since what they learn may shock them. Dr. Hall asks Bennett, a contractor, when his headaches first started, and Bennett answers about six months ago.

Bennett is happy in his work, preferring it to any other occupation he knows. When his headaches grow severe, he says, he has hallucinations. At first he felt only that he was in a place completely unlike anything he had ever known. Each time, his impressions grew sharper, until his mind returned with a fairly clear picture of a room in a tall building. Readers get a quiet, unsettling story about a man whose headaches may be memories.
32142-marley-s-chain:
Alan E. Nourse's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in September 1952, follows a poor traveller named Tam. The cover line sums up his trouble in short form: the world around him was owned by other people. Tam arrives at a spaceport in shabby clothing, carrying a small, weather-beaten bag. Staff pull him out of the passing crowd to pore over his bundle of travel papers with unusual strictness.

Ordered to wait, Tam watches helplessly for fifteen minutes as the spaceport empties. A huge liner from the outer Asteroid Rings is hauled by great cranes back to its berth for repair. Its curved, meteor-dented hull gleams dully in harsh arc lights. Hungry and cold, Tam shivers in the night air, with dread gnawing at his stomach. Readers get a story of poverty and paperwork in a future owned by others.
32237-assassin:
J. F. Bone's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in February 1958, turns a visitor tale into an assassination plot. The cover line says the visitors courted Earth with presents, love, patience, and peace, and asks who could turn them down, since nobody fires at Santa Claus. The story opens with a rifle lying comfortably in a man's hands, a gleaming instrument smelling faintly of gun oil.

It is a gunsmith's perfect work, a semi-automatic rifle with a telescopic sight, a tool that hurls death with pinpoint accuracy for half a mile. Daniel Matson eyes the weapon with gray hunter's eyes in a passionless executioner's face. His blunt hands are steady as he lifts the gun, tries a dry shot at an imaginary target, and nods: he is ready. Readers get a tense thriller, where the assassin waits.
32498-the-brain:
Alexander Blade's tale, printed in Amazing Stories in October 1948, centres on a gigantic mechanical brain filling a whole mountain, described as a weapon mightier than the atom bomb. A young flight engineer, legs stretched across gadgets in a crowded compartment, tells a tall doctor they are almost there. The doctor protests they cannot be near Washington after crossing California only half an hour earlier.

The engineer grins that they will soon see Cephalon, where one professor and fifteen tons of equipment mark their destination. Repairs, an illustration shows, must be made in great haste at night while the Brain's machines sleep. Blade builds a story of a machine that comes to life, asking what happens when a weapon built to think begins to think for itself.
32727-women-of-modern-france-illustrated:
Hugo P. Thieme of the University of Michigan traces the influence of French women in the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries. His book is volume seven of the Woman in All Ages series, published by George Barrie and Sons. He divides his subjects into three classes.

Queens, as wives, stood for virtue, education, and family life. Mistresses drove political intrigue. Authoresses and educated women patronized art and literature. Thieme sets gentle queen-consorts against regent-mothers such as Louise of Savoy and Catherine de' Medici, and against Diana of Poitiers, first in a long succession of ruling mistresses.
328-a-heap-o-livin:
Edgar A. Guest dedicates this little book of verse to Marjorie and Buddy, from their daddy. A Heap o' Livin' opens with When You Know a Fellow, a plea to judge neighbors by their burdens, not their blemishes. Guest's plain rhymes preach kindness and understanding.

Later poems celebrate home, work, friendship, and the daily heap of living. Guest, the people's poet of Detroit, wrote for newspaper readers in simple, warm lines. His verse drew both love and mockery for its sentiment. The book remains a snapshot of homely American optimism.
32809-the-west-indies-and-the-spanish-ma:
James Rodway tells the story of the West Indies and the Spanish Main, published in London by T. Fisher Unwin in 1899 in a second impression, in the Story of the Nations series. The shores of the Caribbean, he writes, stirred many nations with adventures, struggles, pain, and disaster.

Rodway names the islands from north to south: the Bahamas, the Greater Antilles, and the Caribbees, once called the Antilles from a traditional island west of the Azores. He sets Spanish explorers, lured by golden cities, pearls, and emeralds, beside Mediterranean wanderers such as Ulysses and Aeneas. Hurricanes, earthquakes, and starvation follow. Later chapters weigh Royalists against Roundheads in Barbados, and a Demerara capitulation demanded on unknown terms.
32915-sir-hilton-s-sin:
George Manville Fenn's novel opens at a breakfast table, where a fussy aunt watches her darling Sydney eat marmalade and butter while he chatters about chemistry lessons at Loamborough. Acids and alkalis, he explains, form new combinations and go off in gas, and his talk of carbon in sugar and butter sets a light, comic tone. The household world of aunts, schoolboys, and small talk is the stage on which a graver story will play.

The sin of the title belongs to Sir Hilton, and the novel follows how an old wrong reaches into the lives of the young people around him. Fenn, a prolific Victorian storyteller, mixes domestic comedy with melodrama, letting secrets, family duty, and youthful high spirits carry the plot. It is an easy, old-fashioned read, fond of its characters even when it judges them.
32940-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume nine, gathers the entries running from England to English finance. Its long opening article treats England as the southern part of Great Britain, then works through its shape, coasts, rivers, climate, and counties before turning to history, government, trade, and church life. Shorter entries sit beside it on places, people, and topics that fall in the same alphabetical span.

The value of the slice lies in its period view of a country at the height of its imperial reach. Readers get the facts, maps in words, and judgments that educated readers of the day were expected to trust, from the length of a coastline to the sources of public revenue. As a reference text it is dated, but as a record of how England saw itself, it is hard to match.
33008-landolin:
Berthold Auerbach's Landolin, translated by Annie B. Irish and published by Henry Holt in 1878, opens with spring returning to the hills and valleys of a German home. Day awakes, a strong breeze moves through the forest as if to carry away the lingering night, birds twitter, and an early lark sings. Pine trees whisper and rustle and the sun shines on dew-glittering fields. Cherry fragrance and hawthorn hedges fill the valley air.

From that spring morning Auerbach unfolds a village story of work, family, and moral choice in the Black Forest manner he made famous. Auerbach is the author of On the Heights and Villa on the Rhine. Landolin's tale is told with warmth and attention to country life, letting seasons and labor carry its meaning. It is a gentle, well-translated novel for readers who enjoy German village fiction and its quiet, steady humanism.
33009-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The December 1865 number of the Atlantic Monthly, volume sixteen, opens its fiction with Griffith Gaunt. Or, Jealousy, in which a husband and wife face each other pale and furious over a priest who shall or shall not darken their doors. Catharine Peyton, a tall, imperious beauty of ancient Cumberland family, stands at the center of a marriage already strained by pride and jealousy. The quarrel that opens the serial promises trouble to come.

The Atlantic was a magazine of literature, science, art, and politics. It surrounded its serial with essays, poems, and reviews for a serious readership in the months just after the Civil War. This number therefore doubles as a record of American letters at a turning point, when the war was over and writers were turning back to domestic and moral themes. It is a rich single issue for students of the period.
33059-the-towns-of-roman-britain:
The Rev. J. O. Bevan's Towns of Roman Britain, published in London in 1917, studies the towns founded under Rome in Britain, the coloniae and municipia that grew where Roman quarters had stood. A frontispiece map shows Roman Britain with its chief roads. The book moves town by town, using walls, roads, and remains to explain how a Roman town was laid out and lived in. Bevan, a Cambridge man and fellow of antiquarian societies, writes for readers who want history on the ground.

The volume suits walkers and students alike, matching ancient names to modern places and showing how Roman order shaped later English towns. Its maps and plans help a reader follow a road or a wall across country that still bears Roman marks. As a guide to Roman Britain, it is clear, compact, and rooted in the evidence of stones and streets.
33204-subspeciation-in-the-meadow-mouse-:
Sydney Anderson's Subspeciation in the Meadow Mouse, Microtus pennsylvanicus, in Wyoming, Colorado, and Adjacent Areas, studies geographic variation in a common mouse. It was published as volume nine, number four of the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, on May 10, 1956. To study color variation, Anderson devised a method using a single skin. The skin is KU 42407 from east of Buckhorn in Weston County, Wyoming, chosen as a representative paler mouse and arbitrarily given the number two.

The paper, running from page 85 to 104 with two figures, compares mice across Wyoming, Colorado, and neighboring areas, asking how local populations differ and where subspecies boundaries fall. Anderson writes for mammalogists, with methods, measurements, and specimens cited so others can check his work. For students of North American mammals, it remains a precise, citable study of how one widespread species varies across the high plains and mountains.
33335-worrying-won-t-win:
Montague Glass's book, copyrighted in 1918, gathers comic dialogues in which Potash and Perlmutter discuss the war and the worries of the day. Its first chapter finds the pair debating President Wilson's hand, with Abe noting that if Wilson showed it, he might as well throw the game to Germany. Glass, known for his New York business humor, writes in the lively dialect talk of his famous partners.

The volume's humor lies in turning wartime anxiety into laughter, as two shrewd traders weigh news, rumors, and politics. Its title gives its moral: worry wins nothing, while wit and work carry a man through. For readers who enjoy period comedy, Worrying Won't Win is a brisk, funny record of American talk in 1918.
33522-little-frankie-and-his-cousin:
Little Frankie and His Cousin, in Mrs. Leslie's books for little children, follows Frankie with a young kinsman. The Little Frankie series, written or edited by A. R. Baker, was sold by all booksellers, alongside question books on Christ's Sermon on the Mount and Sabbath school books. Frankie's tale with his cousin offers young readers a gentle story of family, play, and good conduct.

The book's charm lies in its simple, Sunday-school tone, where cousinly love becomes a lesson in kindness and sharing. Its short chapters suit very young readers and reading aloud. For collectors of children's books, Little Frankie and His Cousin is a sweet, old-fashioned volume from a popular series for little ones.
33601-the-master-s-violin:
Myrtle Reed writes a sentimental novel of music, friendship, and healing in this 1904 book. The story opens by a fire on an April evening, as an old lady's love of warmth keeps a blaze on the hearth while spring fragrance enters through an open window. The master plays his violin, and a Cremona instrument, a gift of peace, and a secret chamber become threads in a tale of people learning to live again.

Twenty-one chapters follow Lynn into his own, a bit of human driftwood, rosemary and mignonette, a garden, a false line, and a letter to Iris. Reed's world is one of flowers, old silver, and mahogany, where kindness and music mend what life has broken. Readers who enjoy gentle, old-fashioned domestic romance with a musical center will find the book warm and consoling.
33637-victory-out-of-ruin:
Norman Maclean reflects on Britain after the Great War in this 1922 collection, most of whose chapters first appeared in the Glasgow Herald and the Scotsman. Maclean argues that wars and strikes are only symptoms of a hidden disease, and that soothing a symptom without healing the disease is the most dangerous course. People forget peril quickly, he warns, and settle back into slumber once the immediate danger passes.

Thirteen chapters move from the only hope and the supreme need through liberty, tyranny, the peril of the crowd, and the way of peace. The book is a minister's plea for spiritual renewal as the remedy for social division, written for readers troubled by postwar unrest and searching for a moral path forward.
33721-the-barren-ground-caribou-of-keewa:
Francis Harper studies the barren-ground caribou of Keewatin in this 1955 University of Kansas Museum of Natural History publication, with twenty-eight figures and a map. The work centers on the Windy River area at the northwestern extremity of Nueltin Lake, in what is now the Kivalliq region of Nunavut.
