Chapters trace migrations: southern limits of winter range, spring movement in the Churchill and Nueltin Lake regions, a summer interlude, fall migration and retrograde autumn movement. Ecology sections cover habitats, trails, weather, food, insects, relations to people, bears, foxes, wolves, birds of prey, flies, parasites, and reindeer. Harper's study remains a classic of northern wildlife research.
33833-glories-of-spain:
Charles W. Wood wrote this travel book on Spain, published in London and New York in 1901 with eighty-five pictures. The journey starts at Calais, crosses France by way of Paris and the Garonne, and then turns to Spanish towns, cathedrals, and inns. Wood lingers over Zaragoza Cathedral, whose interior fronts the book.

Chapters mix road scenes, hotel talk, and notes on art, faith, and local custom. Wood writes as a leisurely English traveler, keen to praise beauty and to note odd characters met on the way. The book gives a rich, old-world picture of Spain before modern travel changed it.
33964-the-man-who-rose-again:
Joseph Hocking wrote this novel, printed at Cincinnati in 1907 with four color pictures. Hocking says its central idea came from a real incident told him by C. Hagberg Wright of the London Library. A cynic's challenge is accepted, a man and a woman meet, and a double personality tightens its chain through Leicester's wooing.

Later chapters follow Olive's life in Devonshire, a man with a fez, Signor Ricordo, and the coming of Winfield, toward revelations and a chapter called God and the Man. Hocking writes of fall and rising again. The novel offers a moral romance of a man remade.
34108-the-sacred-egoism-of-sinn-fe-in:
Gnathaí Gan Iarraidh wrote this Irish political tract, published in Dublin and London in 1918 by Maunsel and Company, as passed by the censor. The opening chapter, The Cult of Altruism, argues that in an age of sacred egoisms and oppressed nationalities, small nations became distressed heroines whose rescue inspired professions of altruism.

The author notes that presses of the Latin and Anglo-Saxon worlds poured out sentiment on subject races, though before August 1914 small nations were glad to escape notice. The tract defends a nation's right to its own interest. It remains a sharp document of Irish nationalist thought in wartime.
34208-the-law-of-hemlock-mountain:
Hugh Lundsford's 1920 novel The Law of Hemlock Mountain opens among army officers at cards, then moves to a mountain land where written law runs weak. Lieutenant Spurrier, the young officer at its centre, must live among folk who settle wrongs by their own code.

Spurrier shares a roof with Sam Mosebury, a man the law could not hang, and guards his conduct toward a mountain girl with no road out of her world. The tale weighs formal justice against mountain custom, and asks what law means where the court sits far away. The frontispiece shows Spurrier owning that he took pets for wild birds.
3463-the-boys-life-of-mark-twain:
Albert Bigelow Paine writes a life of Mark Twain meant for young readers, drawn from his larger biography of the author. The chapters follow Samuel Clemens from his Missouri family and his uncle's farm through school, his apprenticeship in print, and his years learning the Mississippi River as a pilot. Later chapters cover the wreck of the Pennsylvania, the end of piloting, and his turn to soldiering and the frontier.

Paine keeps the story brisk and full of incident, from Tom Sawyer's band of boys to Twain at seventy, honored by Missouri. The book gives boys and girls a true account of how a river boy became America's most famous humorist. Older readers will also enjoy it as a clear, short life of Twain.
365-the-land-of-little-rain:
Mary Austin sketches the dry country of eastern California in this set of linked essays. She names the land by its scant rain, then walks its water trails, mesas, and small towns. The Ceriso desert, Shoshone land, Jimville, and the grape-vine town all take their turn in her pages.

Austin watches pocket hunters, basket makers, scavengers, and neighbors with a poet's eye and a neighbor's ear. She gives places Indian names where they fit better than map names. The book endures as a loving, close portrait of desert life, where water rules all and small things matter most.
3744-the-trial-or-more-links-of-the-dais:
Charlotte Yonge continues her Daisy Chain family chronicle in this long sequel, subtitled The Trial. The May family gathers at Cocksmoor and at home, where Richard, the young incumbent, tends a parish shadowed by scarlatina and bad drains. Letters from Edinburgh, family jokes about an infants' honeymoon, and the knell for a dead child mix the comic and the sorrowful in Yonge's usual way.

Later chapters follow orphaned girls Minna and Ella as a year of growth parts them, one learning to comfort and the other still fleeing pain. Yonge writes for readers who know the Mays already, though newcomers can still follow the parish round. The book rewards patience, with church life, family duty, and quiet heroism taking the place of grand adventure.
4014-arse-ne-lupin:
Edgar Jepson and Maurice Leblanc team up for a tale of Arsene Lupin, the gentleman thief, now cast as a duke's rival in love and crime. A letter from Lupin sets the game in motion, while the duke smokes on a terrace and studies the morocco case that holds a pendant.

Sonia, the duke, and Lupin move through drawing rooms and country houses, trading charm, theft, and pursuit. The novel mixes romance with detection, as Lupin steals hearts and jewels with equal ease. Readers who enjoy suave, fast-moving adventure will find a polished entry in the Lupin series.
4017-the-hollow-needle-further-adventure:
Maurice Leblanc's mystery follows the schoolboy detective Isidore Beautrelet as he tracks Arsene Lupin, the gentleman thief, through a puzzle of carts, inns, and a river crossing. No motor car crossed on Thursday the twenty-third of April, and a waiter who came back from training saw a cart that did not cross.

Beautrelet pieces small clues into a bold theory about a secret hiding place, the Hollow Needle, said to hold the treasure of French kings. Lupin stays one step ahead, witty and cool, while the boy reasons his way after him. Readers who like clever, fast-moving detective tales will enjoy this duel of brains.
4203-wake-robin:
John Burroughs's Wake Robin, his first book of nature essays, takes its name from the spring flower and the birds that return with it. A scarlet bird in holiday suit, black wings and tail set against deep red, turns dull yellow-green in fall, like the female all season.

The purple finch, or linnet, sings apart on a dead hemlock, one of the finest songsters in the choir of the old barkpeeling. Burroughs writes of walks, songs, and seasons with a naturalist's ear. Readers who love birds and spring will find a gentle classic of American nature writing.
4213-the-founder-of-new-france-a-chronic:
Charles W. Colby's chronicle of Champlain follows the founder of New France to Port Royal. Lawsuits had kept one party from returning to Acadia, so the roadstead stood empty when De Monts, Champlain, and Pontgrave brought the people of St. Croix thither in August 1605.

Not only the people went: even the framework of houses was shipped across the bay and set up in a haven of better hope, on the bay's north side. Colby tells the founding in the clear style of the Chronicles of Canada. Readers who like exploration history will enjoy a brisk life of Champlain.
4336-an-inquiry-into-the-nature-and-prog:
The Reverend T. R. Malthus, professor of history and political economy at the East India College, published this inquiry on rent in London in 1815. It grew from notes he had collected for his teaching, and the pressure of current debate hastened its appearance. Rent, he argues, follows principles that can be stated and tested.

Malthus examines how rent arises from differences in soil and situation, and how it moves with prices and cultivation. The tract is short and technical, aimed at fellow economists rather than general readers. It stands beside his corn law pamphlet as a key text of classical political economy.
4346-the-effects-of-cross-self-fertilisa:
Charles Darwin wrote this large experimental work on the effects of cross-fertilization and self-fertilization in plants. His first chapter sets out the means that favor crossing, the benefits it brings, and the history of the subject. He then explains his experiments, carried on over successive generations under uniform conditions.

Darwin measured crossed and self-fertilized plants with care, weighing sources of error and the amount of pollen used. The work supports his broader argument that crossing generally strengthens offspring, while close self-fertilization weakens them. It is a patient record of experiment, and a key text for the history of plant breeding.
4369-the-verse-of-alfred-lichtenstein:
Alfred Lichtenstein wrote this self-critique of his own verse, because he believed many readers misunderstood it. He divides his work plainly: his first eighty pieces are love lyrics of the usual kind, much like garden verse. Their content is the distress of love, death, and universal longing.

Lichtenstein adds that the impulse to write in a cynical vein, like cabaret songs, may have come from a wish to seem above it all. Most of the eighty poems, he says, are insignificant and were not shown to the public. The text gives a rare thing: a poet judging his early work aloud, with one quoted poem on burying himself in the night.
4386-life-of-chopin:
Franz Liszt wrote this life of Frederic Chopin, translated from the French by Martha Walker Cook. The present text follows the fourth revised edition of 1880, reproducing the 1863 original essentially unabridged, with original spellings kept and italics shown as capitals. Liszt knew Chopin well, and he writes as a fellow artist.

The eight chapters trace Chopin's youth in Poland, his Paris years, his music, and his early death. Liszt treats the piano works as the key to the man, with passages on national feeling and on the poetry of the nocturnes and mazurkas. The book is both biography and criticism, by one great pianist about another.
4907-moths-of-the-limberlost-a-book-abou:
Gene Stratton-Porter's book about the Limberlost Cabin follows moths through their whole lives in a northeastern Indiana swamp. Chapters take up eggs, caterpillars, and winter quarters, then turn to individual kinds: the Robin Moth, the Yellow Emperor, the Lady Bird, moths of the moon, and the King of the Poets.

Stratton-Porter writes as a naturalist who lived beside her subject, and the Limberlost itself becomes a character in the account. Readers learn how to find, raise, and watch moths, and why a swamp's night life rewards patience. The book remains a warm introduction to field study for anyone curious about insects.
5087-the-treasure-train:
Arthur B. Reeve's collection presents twelve cases for Professor Craig Kennedy, the scientific detective, and his friend Walter Jameson. Each story turns on a new device or trick of its day: a truth detector, a love meter, a submarine mine, a sunken treasure, and a phantom destroyer, among others.

Kennedy solves crimes with laboratory method rather than simple deduction, testing poisons, codes, and machines to catch the guilty. The stories are brisk pulp mysteries from the early twentieth century, and they show how popular fiction of the period mixed detective work with faith in science and invention.
5092-the-coming-of-cuculain:
Standish O'Grady retells the youth of Ireland's great hero, known in childhood as Setanta, from the Ulster cycle of Gaelic legend. The book follows the boy among the Red Branch knights, through his running away. His feats among the boys of Ulster, his knighting, and his first wars follow, until Setanta becomes Cuculain.

O'Grady drew on old Irish tales and shaped them into a connected narrative for modern readers, keeping their heroic scale and strange magic. The result serves as a clear doorway into Irish myth, introducing the champions, kings. Sacred horses of Ulster join them, in the order a young hero meets them.
5304-my-robin:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's My Robin answers a question from a young reader of The Secret Garden: did the author own the original of the robin, or was he mere fantasy? Burnett, thrilled to find a reader intimate with English robins, writes of the real robin who visited her garden and of the letters that followed.

The short book, illustrated by Alfred Brennan, tells how a wild robin became a companion. It also tells how a children's author learned from a bird. Readers who loved the robin of The Secret Garden will find here the true story behind him, told with warmth and delight.
5621-baron-d-holbach-a-study-of-eighteen:
Max Pearson Cushing wrote Baron d'Holbach as a study of eighteenth-century radicalism in France, submitted for a doctorate in political science at Columbia University in 1914. The book examines Holbach the man through early letters to John Wilkes and his family. It also traces his relations with Diderot, Rousseau, Hume, Garrick, and other leading figures, closing with an estimate of his character and personality.

Later chapters treat Holbach's works, his translations of German scientific books, and the philosophy of his Systeme de la Nature, with bibliographies of editions. Readers get a scholarly life of a radical atheist philosopher, set among the French Enlightenment's salons and debates.
565-the-zincali-an-account-of-the-gypsie:
George Borrow studies the gypsies of Spain, the Zincali, in this work written over five years on the road. Borrow, distributing scriptures in ventas and posadas, gathered lore on gypsy names, language, law, clans, and fortune-telling. Chapters treat colonies, forges, counts, and the Gitana of Seville.

Borrow writes with vivid, partisan energy, mixing travel, philology, and anecdote. An introduction surveys gypsies from Russia to England. The book endures as a pioneering, if prejudiced, portrait of a people Borrow knew by campfire talk and long road days, not by library alone.
5663-the-prose-of-alfred-lichtenstein:
Alfred Lichtenstein's short prose gathers sharp, unsettling pieces from a German writer of the early twentieth century, including a fragment from an unfinished novel. The opening piece, called The Winner, follows Max Mechenmal. He runs a newspaper kiosk, eats and drinks well, and keeps careful control of his many affairs. Quietly, he also takes money from Ilka Leipke. His comfort rests on calculation, not on luck.

The prose is blunt about greed, fear, and the wish to look grand without being caught. Lichtenstein watches people who dream of fine clothes and fine company yet shrink from the risk their schemes would need. Readers looking for polished heroes will not find them here. Instead they meet vivid, flawed figures drawn in a few hard strokes. Their city world pulls desire one way and caution the other.
6136-bars-and-shadows-the-prison-poems-o:
Ralph Chaplin's Bars and Shadows gathers prison poems with an introduction by Scott Nearing. Chaplin was serving a twenty-year sentence in the Federal Penitentiary, not for violence against person or property, but solely for expressing opinions, accused with fellow prisoners of conspiracy to obstruct the war.

The introduction notes the government produced no single witness to show the war had been obstructed in the relevant way. Poems titled Mourn Not the Dead, Taps, Night in the Cell House, Prison Shadows, and Song of Separation follow. Chaplin writes from a cell about freedom, comrades, and the cost of dissent.
644-the-haunted-man-and-the-ghost-s-barg:
Charles Dickens writes a Christmas ghost tale in this novella, where a learned chemistry teacher is haunted by more than a ghost. The haunted man, hollow-cheeked and grizzled, lives in a chamber part library and part laboratory, where students hang on his lips. A spirit offers him a bargain: to forget his sorrows and lose the power to recall pain.

Dickens writes with rich, somber prose, full of fog, bells, and inner echoes. The gift proves a curse, as a man without memory loses pity too. The tale endures as a lesser-known Christmas book, where Dickens warns that sorrow, rightly borne, keeps the heart human.
6446-greifenstein:
F. Marion Crawford opens Greifenstein with Frau von Sigmundskron, called the old baroness though not really much past middle age. Her hair is very white, she is thin and pale, and her bold, almost emaciated features show the framework of departed beauty. She carries her head erect and walks with firm, elastic step, though her looks promise little strength, and she has never been ill in her life.

Her leanness has the most natural of causes, the narrator hints, but she herself would be last to mention it. A mid passage turns to Rex, an enlightened man, learned and cultivated, scorner of old prejudices and cheap theories. He yet trusts astrology enough to risk serious personal interest on what he pretends to foretell. Crawford writes a German castle novel of pride, family, and a rational man caught by an irrational faith.
6475-facts-and-arguments-for-darwin:
Fritz Muller, translated from German by W. S. Dallas in 1869, offers Facts and Arguments for Darwin after reading On the Origin of Species. One mode of testing Darwin seemed most certain. Apply his views as specially as possible to some particular group of animals, building a genealogical tree for families, genera, or species. Pictures of common ancestors should be as complete as possible. If Darwin were false, detailed application should breed irreconcilable contradictions.

Muller tests, chapter by chapter, whether the tree holds or breaks. A mid passage treats a worm of the Amphinomidae family, guest in the floating Lepas. Its place is intelligible at once from the Darwinian standpoint, while its relation to free living sea worms stays unintelligible otherwise. Muller writes natural history as evidence, where small sea creatures argue a great theory.
6873-mark-twain:
Archibald Henderson writes Mark Twain with photographs by Alvin Langdon Coburn. He opens with Bliss Carman's verse on Twain jesting in Avalon, isle of dreams. Chaucer, Shakespeare, Molière, and Cervantes listen and smile there. Henderson's preface speaks of a debt of personal gratitude owed by men, women, and children worldwide for Twain's humor and charm.

From childhood, Henderson says, his feeling for Twain was warm and personal, drawn first from the books alone, from Tom, Huck, Jim, and Brer Rabbit. The biography that follows traces that beloved life. Mark Twain is a fond, early life of America's great humorist, full of affection and anecdote.
698-memoir-of-fleeming-jenkin:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this memoir of Fleeming Jenkin, the Scottish engineer and teacher who was his friend. Jenkin worked on telegraph cables, taught at Edinburgh, and wrote on many topics, from drama to trade. Stevenson draws him as a man of restless mind, warm talk, and strong views, liked by students and peers alike.

The memoir first served as an introduction to a set of Jenkin's papers, and it stands alone here. Stevenson blends fact with fond recall, showing Jenkin's work, his home life, and his talk. It gives a vivid portrait of a Victorian man of science who was also a man of letters, seen through the eyes of a novelist who knew him well.
7046-annals-and-reminiscences-of-jamaica:
Harriet Manning Whitcomb prepared her annals and reminiscences of Jamaica Plain at request, to be read before the Jamaica Plain Ladies Tuesday Club. A wish to preserve the paper led her to print it for sale at a fair for the Jamaica Plain Indian Association, though she felt reluctant to appear in public print. She drew on the Memorial History of Boston, Drake's Town of Roxbury, Doctor Thomas Gray's Half Century Sermon, and the memory of older residents.

If any date or incident proves wrong, she begs readers charity and courtesy for indulgent criticism. The sketch that follows collects and reviews the circumstances and events of a Boston neighborhood, from early days to the author's own time. It is a local history written by a neighbor for neighbors, plain, fond, and careful.
708-the-princess-and-the-goblin:
George MacDonald wrote this fairy tale about Princess Irene, a small girl who lives in a mountain house watched over by her nurse. Below the mountain live goblins, who plot to steal her and marry her to their prince. Curdie, a miner's boy, hears their plans in the mines and warns the household.

Irene finds help from a mysterious great-grandmother, who gives her a thread to follow through dark halls. Courage, trust, and kind deeds guide the children past traps and tunnels. The tale blends wonder with moral weight, and it has long been a favourite first fantasy for young readers.
7112-erema-or-my-father-s-sin:
R D Blackmore's Erema, or My Father's Sin, opens with a biblical curse that has followed the heroine always. It speaks of the sins of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation. If she had not known her father, loved him, and closed his eyes in desert silence deeper than the grave, her path might have differed. The common business of the world might have led her down the general track that leads to nothing.

Until her father fell and died, she never dreamed he could die, so resolute was he in seeing her safe in a new home before starting again for remoter solitudes. His mind once made up, no one had ever known him fail of it, and he showed that resolve in the last and fatal act of his fatal life. The novel that follows is a daughter's reckoning with a father's sin.
7298-william-tell-told-again:
William Tell Told Again joins two children's books in one volume, as its transcriber's note explains. One is a picture book of sixteen full-colour illustrations by Philip Dadd, described in verse by John W. Houghton, while the other is a humorous novel by P. G. Wodehouse based on that picture book, with a lengthier story, a more intricate plot, and fuller characterisation.

The bound volume mingled picture book and novel, with illustrations and poems at regular intervals, though most pictures stood distant from the novel page they reflected. This text version keeps placeholders for the plates, so the two Tell tales can still be read together. Young readers get legend twice over, in verse pictures and in Wodehouse comedy.
7318-the-bravest-of-the-brave-or-with-pe:
G. A. Henty's Bravest of the Brave, or With Peterborough in Spain, rescues the Earl of Peterborough from oblivion in his preface to his dear lads. Peterborough's career as a general lasted little more than a year, Henty writes. Yet in that time he showed a genius for warfare never surpassed, with feats of daring worthy of chivalry's leaders.

History slighted him, Henty argues, because Marlborough's glory overshadowed his campaigns, and because his cause could scarcely be called England's. The novel follows a young hero through those Spanish campaigns, mixing battle craft with boyish pluck. Henty writes history as adventure, brisk and loyal to his general.
7361-a-brief-history-of-panics-and-their:
Clement Juglar's Brief History of Panics and Their Periodical Occurrence in the United States, third edition, translated and edited by DeCourcy W. Thom, brings the account down from 1889 to date. Thom, a former member of the Baltimore and New York exchanges, dedicates the edition at Blakeford. He recalls golden days at Wakefield Manor in Virginia in 1891 and at his old Maryland home in 1915, where the book proved a pleasant companion of two visitations.

Juglar, member of the Institute and vice-president of the Societe d'Economie Politique, traces American panics as recurring events with a pattern, not as mere accidents. His history joins finance to a theory of cycles, studied through crashes and recoveries. The book remains a classic early study of boom and bust.
7556-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
Mark Twain's humor, anger, and wisdom fill this collection of short passages, chosen among an editor's favorites and paired with pictures. The passages range across his books and speeches, from jokes to bitter judgments. Each one can be traced to its full context. That link matters, since Twain's punch often lands in the setup around it.

Read together, the passages sketch a writer who distrusted cant in law, politics, and polite talk. Human folly, good intentions gone wrong, and the gap between ideals and conduct recur across them. The tone shifts fast: funny one moment, bleak the next. It is Twain in flashes, a good way to hear his voice before settling into a full book.
8410-jack-of-the-pony-express-or-the-you:
Frank V. Webster wrote this boys' adventure about Jack, a young rider of the mountain trails, carrying mail for the pony express. Contents promise narrow escapes, important letters, a secret mine, strangers, night attacks, bonds, queer discoveries, dummy letters, and a ride for life, with Jennie, the postmistress, among the friends who help him.

The book belongs to the Stratemeyer-style adventure series, written for boys who loved horses, danger, and pluck. Jack's rides through mountain country, pursued and aided in turn, deliver excitement without gore. Readers of classic boys' fiction will find a brisk, old-fashioned tale of a young rider doing a man's job well.
8498-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-0:
The first number of The Atlantic Monthly, November 1857, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, announced a new American voice. Contents list the Abbé de l'Epée, Agassiz's Natural History, Akin by Marriage, and American Antiquity. My Aquarium, Domestic Architecture, Art, and the Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table follow, alongside the Battle of Lepanto, Beecher, Beethoven, Béranger, and Birds and their Ways.

The Atlantic, founded by Boston's literary circle, became America's leading magazine, and this first issue shows its ambitions: science, art, politics, and literature together. Readers get the magazine at its birth, with Holmes's Autocrat already a feature. It is a landmark for American periodical history, and a rich miscellany in its own right.
877-little-britain:
Washington Irving sketched this small London neighbourhood, Little Britain, a cluster of streets in the heart of the great city. He quotes Nashe on the grave ancients within hearing of Bow bell, and he paints a world of old shops, narrow lanes, and neighbours who keep old customs amid new London.

Irving writes with affection for a place that time seems to have passed by, where shopkeepers, clerks, and idlers live by old rules. His sketch is gentle and nostalgic, a piece of local colour from the age of the Sketch Book. It charms readers who love old London, in miniature, before the modern city swept it away.
8776-the-impostures-of-scapin:
Moliere's farce Les Fourberies de Scapin, acted May 24, 1671, at the Palais Royal with Moliere himself as Scapin, appears in Charles Heron Wall's prose translation with introductions and notes. Wall notes its great success, while calling it nothing but a farce, taken partly from classical, partly from Italian or French sources. The cast sets two fathers, Argante and Geronte, against their sons Octave and Leandre and the young women they love, Hyacintha and Zerbinetta, the latter believed a gypsy girl.

Scapin, servant to Leandre, with Silvestre beside him, runs the plots, tricks, and beatings that untangle the lovers' troubles. His famous bag scene and his extortions from the fathers are the farce's highlights. The play moves fast, laughs loudly, and asks nothing deep of its audience. Readers and student actors will find Wall's version a practical, funny introduction to Moliere at his most knockabout.
89-north-american-free-trade-agreement-1:
Trade deals turn on annexes, and this file holds part of one. The North American Free Trade Agreement annex dated October 7, 1992 sets out reservations on investment and services. Each party lists measures that depart from national treatment, most-favored-nation treatment, or local presence rules.

Entries name a sector, sub-sector, industry class, and the obligation concerned. Performance requirements and senior management nationality rules appear alongside. The dry legal form matters: reservations define what the deal does not open. Lawyers and scholars use the annex to read the treaty's true reach.
8924-home-again:
George MacDonald writes Home Again as a duplex edition, opening in the dusk of an old-fashioned farmhouse best room. Two elderly persons sit in the faint glow of a buried July sun through sods of his grave. Roses unseen send their odour through twilight and open window, but one sitter scarcely notices, believing mainly in mahogany, linen. Hams, while the other finds the scent too sad, issuing like sunlight from the grave of vanished youth. He is not sad by nature, only one who found the past more delightful than the present and never left his first loves.

From that elegiac parlour, the novel follows a man coming home to reckon with old affections, family duty, and faith. MacDonald's late fiction is reflective and domestic, less adventurous than his earlier work, but rich in character.
8941-lord-kilgobbin:
Charles Lever wrote this Irish novel late in life, in breaking health, and it ran in Cornhill Magazine from 1870 to 1872 before book form. Set in Ireland in Lever's own time, it follows Lord Kilgobbin's family, their estate, and the young people caught between old landlords, new politics, and Fenian plots.

Lever dedicates the book to a lost companion whose death left him helpless, and sorrow shades its humor. The tale mixes romance, political intrigue, and Irish country life. It stands as Lever's farewell novel, a fond yet uneasy look at an Ireland changing fast under his eyes.
9069-saint-augustin:
Louis Bertrand wrote this life of Saint Augustin, translated into English by Vincent O'Sullivan. Augustin, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, wrote the Confessions, one of the great books of the Christian West. Bertrand draws on those Confessions, with quotes taken from Canon Bigg's version in English.

The life follows Augustin from sin and restless youth to conversion and his work as bishop and thinker. O'Sullivan notes where Bertrand's reading of the Latin differs from Bigg's. Readers get a vivid, French-flavored portrait of a saint whose inner life still moves modern minds.
9150-dick-sands-the-boy-captain:
Jules Verne wrote this sea tale in French in 1878 as Un capitaine de quinze ans, translated by Ellen Frewer. Dick Sands, a boy of fifteen, must captain a ship when disaster strikes its crew. Day after day at sea, he faces storms, navigation, and the tricks of a villain aboard. The French edition held ninety-four illustrations.

Verne keeps the trials coming with almost mechanical regularity, yet the boy's courage holds the reader. The tale was reprinted often, in the Parke edition and beyond. It remains a rousing boys' adventure of duty and pluck on the open sea.
9391-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-2:
November 1859 brought the twenty-fifth issue of the Atlantic Monthly, a magazine of writing, art, and public affairs. Its lead piece tells of Eleuterio Felice Foresti, an Italian exile who reached New York in 1836 after years held by Austrian rule. The number also prints a long serial tale, short poems, and a piece called Lion Llewellyn. Reviews of new books end the issue.

Foresti's story moves from prison and watchful spies to the relief of a free land, where free speech and self-rule greet him. The serial chapters and poems around it give the issue its mix of high feeling and plain tale telling. A reader today gains a window on how Americans in 1859 read exile, freedom, and the fate of nations abroad.
9467-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-2:
The December 1859 issue of the Atlantic Monthly gathers essays, verse, and fiction from a range of hands. It opens with a first-person tale, The Experience of Samuel Absalom, Filibuster, about a failed California gold seeker. Later pages carry poems, a piece on boots and shoes, and a story of Elkanah Brewster's temptation. Book reviews close the number.

Samuel Absalom, broke and ragged in Oroville, sets off to join General Walker in Nicaragua, chasing a fresh start by force of arms. The other pieces shift tone fast, from homely craft to moral trial to verse. Taken as a whole, the issue shows a young American magazine testing many kinds of writing at once, for readers keen on news, wit, and argument.
9607-from-boyhood-to-manhood-life-of-ben:
William M. Thayer wrote From Boyhood to Manhood, a life of Benjamin Franklin for young readers, printed in 1889. Thayer, famed for White House lives, traces Franklin from old England to New England, where persecution drove his kin across the sea. Chapters follow Josiah Franklin's trade, the family Bible, and Boston in early days. The fifteenth child, born on a Sunday, gets his own chapter.

Later chapters follow printer-boy days, table-talk learning, a new newspaper, and brighter days, toward philosopher and statesman. Thayer writes with moral warmth for boys. A reader gets a lively, old-style Franklin life, full of industry, wit, and the making of a founder.
9657-the-mutineers-a-tale-of-old-days-at:
Charles Boardman Hawes wrote The Mutineers, a tale of old days at sea and Far East adventure, as set down by Benjamin Lathrop. The book opens with a sail for Canton, China, aboard the ship Hunter, whose voyage forms the tale's backbone. Hawes thanks Captain David Woodard, wrecked on Celebes over a century before, and other skippers for journals and tales. The story blends true sea lore with fiction.

Later parts meet an Arab ship, a council in the cabin, and a crisis at sea, as mutiny brews and fortunes turn. Hawes writes with salt, pace, and care for old ships. A reader gets a stirring boys' sea tale, rich in Canton trade, island wreck, and the code of blue-water men.
a-brief-history-of-panics-and-their-peri:
Clément Juglar, a French economist of the Institute, wrote A Brief History of Panics to show that American financial crises return in a pattern, not by chance. The hosted copy is the third edition, translated and edited by DeCourcy W. Thom, who brought the story down from 1889 toward his own day and dated his dedication in October 1915.

Juglar traces crisis after crisis in the United States, comparing prices, credit, speculation, and liquidation as each boom breaks. Thom's additions carry the sequence into the twentieth century, arguing that panic grows from real business conditions, not mere fear. Bankers and students of cycles valued the book because it treated panics as a recurring disease with observable symptoms.
a-cardinal-sin: Eugene Sue opens this novel on a bright May morning in the Charnier des Innocents quarter of Paris. A young girl of about eighteen, worn by poverty, makes her timid way among the public scribes of the district. Gold soon enters the story, and covetous delight at shining pieces hints at the sin of the title. Sue builds a melodrama of want, temptation, and fate in old Paris.
a-heap-o-livin:
Edgar A. Guest collected these homey verses in a little book dedicated to his children, Marjorie and Buddy, as their Daddy. The opening poem, When You Know a Fellow, sets the program: most faults shrink once you know the burdens a man carries. Poem after poem works the same ground in plain rhyme — fathers and children, work and neighbors, grief taken patiently.

Titles such as The Rough Little Rascal show the domestic focus: a small boy with a smudged nose becomes an emblem of what a parent waits all day to meet. Guest wrote for newspaper readers across America, and his verse aims at comfort rather than surprise. The collection preserves the voice of the people's poet at his most characteristic: simple, warm, and certain that home is the center of life.
a-prince-of-cornwall-a-story-of-glastonb: Charles Watts Whistler sets this story around Glastonbury and the western country during the reign of Ina of Wessex, following Owen of Cornwall and the young Oswald. The chapter titles trace wanderings to Sussex, a thane keeping faith, a king's feast marred, a perilous landing, crossings of the Dyfed cliffs, and a fall from Cheddar cliffs. Through messages, hunts, and moonlit warnings, the tale builds a Saxon world of loyalty, exile, and return.
a-svmmarie-and-trve-discovrse-of-sir-fra: Walter Bigges gives a summary and true discourse of Sir Francis Drake's West Indian voyage, printed at London in 1589. The expedition took the towns of Saint Iago, Sancto Domingo, Cartagena, and Saint Augustine, each exactly described with geographical maps by Baptista Boazio showing situations and the armies' approaches. Dedicated to the Earl of Essex, the tract keeps its original inconsistent spelling, corrected only where the endnotes say so.
a-thane-of-wessex-being-a-story-of-the-g: Charles Watts Whistler tells a thane of Wessex in this story of the great Viking raids into Somerset, opening with the narrator outlawed before the folk moot on Brent hill. Raised in his father's hall at Cannington above the Parret, he succeeded as thane at two-and-twenty, motherless. He governed three years before bold feast talk criticizing the king undid him. Fights, secret meetings, Viking arrivals, the fires of Stert, and flight through Sedgemoor follow.
account-of-the-romansh-language-in-a-let: Joseph Planta gives an account of the Romansh language in this letter to Sir John Pringle, printed in the Philosophical Transactions in 1776. A Romansh Bible, presented to the Royal Society by the Count de Salis, prompts the inquiry into a language little attended to. Romansh is spoken in the mountain parts of the Grisons, by the headwaters of the Rhine and the Inn. Its two main dialects differ so widely that they are almost two languages, though books printed in both are understood in their districts.
across-the-fruited-plain: Florence Crannell Means writes Across the Fruited Plain, published by the Friendship Press with illustrations by Janet Smalley. A teacher's guide on the migrants for young people accompanies it. Dedicated to a troop of children across the fruited plain, Tomoko, Willie May, Fei-Kin, Nawamana, Candelaria, Isabell, and Mary Margaret, the book opens with Seth Thomas striking twelve. The house of Beecham, Rose-Ellen's library book, and grandma's kitchen follow a journey of picking and weeding.
agobard-de-grandine-et-tonitruis-latin:
Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, wrote his book on hail and thunder around 815, in the age of Charlemagne's heirs. The Latin treatise attacks a belief common among his flock. Farmers held that weather magicians, called tempestarii, raised storms and sold the stolen crops to sky sailors.

Agobard calls the belief folly and proves it from Scripture and reason. He tells of a crowd ready to stone supposed sky travelers, whom he talked down himself. His work is the earliest systematic church attack on folk magic. Theologians quoted him for a thousand years. The Latin text preserves a bishop thinking clearly against the panic of his own parish.
agrippa-de-occulta-philosophia-1533-lati:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in Latin at Cologne in 1533, the first full edition. The work is the foundational synthesis of Renaissance magic. Astrology, Kabbalah, number lore, and natural magic all find their ordered place in Agrippa's vast system.

Book by book, he rises from the elemental world through the celestial to the divine. Every later magus drank from this spring, and most admitted the debt. The Latin text of 1533 is the form in which Europe first read him. Agrippa aimed to restore magic as a learned, pious discipline. His bible of Renaissance magic still anchors any serious study of the occult tradition.
agrippa-de-vanitate-1564-latin:
Agrippa published On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences in 1530, and this Latin edition of 1564 kept his great skeptical performance in print. The book demolishes the arts and sciences one by one. Grammar, medicine, law, theology, and magic itself all stand accused of vanity and error.

The joke cuts deep, since Agrippa's own Occult Philosophy had taught several of these arts. Readers have debated for centuries how much of the attack he meant. As rhetoric, the De vanitate is a masterpiece of learned doubt. As a companion to the Occult Philosophy, it is unmatched: learn magic first, Agrippa seems to say, then learn to doubt everything, including the lesson.
albumasar-introductorium-1489-latin:
Abu Ma'shar of Baghdad, called Albumasar in Latin, wrote the Great Introduction to astrology in the ninth century. It became the book that taught the Latin West the Arabic system of the art. Hermann of Dalmatia turned it into Latin, and the version here was printed in 1489. No English version in the public domain exists.

Albumasar grounds the power of the stars in physics, sorting signs, planets, houses, and aspects into one great scheme. Kings and scholars across Europe used his book to read the heavens for three centuries. The printed Latin of 1489 shows the work at the height of its fame. It stands as the record of how Arabic astrology remade a science in the West.
alcabitius-isagoge-1521-latin:
Al-Qabisi, a scholar of Aleppo in the tenth century, wrote the Isagoge as a short first book for students of astrology. For the rest of the Middle Ages it served as the standard beginner's text in the Latin West. The edition here is the Latin printing from Venice in 1521, with the commentary of John of Saxony.

Five chapters lay out the signs, the planets, the houses, and the terms a judge of the stars must know. John of Saxony, a Paris master of the 1300s, explains each point for the classroom. No English version in the public domain exists. The little book shows how a whole science was taught, one clear rule at a time.
allan-quatermain:
H. Rider Haggard sent his hunter hero Allan Quatermain on his last trek in this book of 1887. It is the mate to King Solomon's Mines, the hit of two years past. Haggard wrote it while the fame of the first book was still fresh and high.

Quatermain, now old, joins a last hunt for a lost white race in the heart of Africa. Strange priests, a vast cave world, and a doom that hangs on the band fill the tale. The book turns the brisk hunter of the first tale into a figure of myth.
an-inquiry-into-the-nature-and-progress-:
Thomas Robert Malthus published his Inquiry into the Nature and Progress of Rent in London in 1815. Malthus, a clergyman and professor at the East India College, drew the tract from his lecture notes. Its subject is rent, the share of farm produce that stays with the landowner. The argument speaks directly to the corn law debates of that year.

Malthus defines rent by what remains after the costs of cultivation and ordinary farm profits are paid. He asks why raw produce sells at a high price and disputes the answers of Adam Smith and the French Economists. Rent, he argues, is no mere monopoly gain but grows from fertile soil and rising demand. The pamphlet helped shape classical economics and the case over grain imports.
anglo-saxon-britain: Grant Allen writes Anglo-Saxon Britain in the Early Britain series, appointed by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London. The book traces the Saxon settlement of Britain, its kingdoms, laws, and conversion. Allen's compact history served schools and general readers as a clear guide to early England. Short chapters keep the early story clear.
animal-children-the-friends-of-the-fores: Edith Brown Kirkwood writes of animal children, the friends of the forest and the plain, in a book lovingly dedicated and indexed for young readers. The stories follow young beasts and birds through their first lessons in wild life. Kirkwood's gentle tales teach natural history through affection and adventure. Each tale ends with a kind, plain moral.
annals-and-reminiscences-of-jamaica-plai:
Harriet Manning Whitcomb explains the making of her sketch. She prepared it to be read before the Jamaica Plain Ladies' Tuesday Club. She then printed it at her friends' wish. She sold it at a fair for the Jamaica Plain Indian Association. She drew on the Memorial History of Boston, Drake's Town of Roxbury, and the memory of older residents, and she begs indulgent criticism for any errors. The imprint is Cambridge, 1897.

Her annals follow Jamaica Plain, once part of Roxbury and now a Boston neighborhood, through its farms, ponds, great houses, churches, and the families who held them. Reminiscence mixes with record: who lived where, what stood before the streetcars came. Local history of this kind preserves what no larger history bothers to keep.
argentina-from-a-british-point-of-view-a: Campbell Patrick Ogilvie presents a paper first read before the Royal Society of Arts in 1910, with notes from staff of the Santa Fe Land Company. He surveys Argentine land, trade, and daily life from a British business view, and he draws on men who lived and worked there. Facts and figures anchor the account, though the author admits its limits. The book serves as a period guide to investment hopes and settler experience.
arse-ne-lupin:
Arsène Lupin, the English novel credited on its title page to Edgar Jepson and Maurice Leblanc, brings France's gentleman thief to the château of the Dukes of Charmerace. A millionaire's daughter writes among her family's treasures as the story opens. The Duke of Charmerace arrives, motor-cars vanish, and a letter from Lupin announces more thefts to come. Detective Guerchard opens the inquiry, with secretary Sonia caught between suspicion and loyalty.

Inside, pendant, cars, and telephone wires disappear or fail in a duel of wits across twenty-three chapters. Lupin moves through the house in plain sight, since disguise is his native country. Guerchard picks up the true scent only to find his quarry bargaining from strength. Readers get the Lupin formula in early, polished form: crime as sport, the police a move behind, and a thief whose charm is meant to make honesty look slow.
augustine-de-divinatione-daemonum-latin:
Augustine of Hippo wrote De divinatione daemonum, on the divination of demons, around 413. The short Latin treatise asks a sharp question. If demons foretell the future truly, as pagans claimed, why must Christians refuse their oracles?

Augustine answers that demons guess shrewdly rather than know. Keen senses, long memory, and swift travel let them predict much, he argues. Their hits prove no divine gift, and their aim is to trap human souls. The treatise became foundational for all medieval demonology. Later writers on witchcraft built on Augustine's frame. Here it stands in its original Latin, brief and decisive.
aylwin:
Theodore Watts-Dunton wrote this romance, issued here with two appendices: a note on the character of D'Arcy and a key to the story reprinted from Notes and Queries. The dedication recalls sunny days and starlit nights rambling with C. J. R. on crumbling cliffs now at the bottom of the sea. An opening sonnet, Caught in the Ebbing Tide, farewells those Raxtox cliffs.

Love, art, and gypsy life on the Suffolk coast drive the plot, around a hero pressed hard on his unbelief. One scene turns on a cross: asked what he will do with it, he answers he will lock it up safely, and hears himself named a rationalist. His disbelief in a supernatural world is itself the story's battleground. Watts-Dunton, friend of Swinburne and Rossetti, loads the tale with poetry, folklore, and argument.
bacon-epistola-secretis-1618-latin:
Roger Bacon, the thirteenth-century Franciscan, addressed his Letter on the Secret Works of Art and Nature to a learned reader of his day. John Dee edited this Latin printing of 1618, a fitting match of editor and author. The epistle ranges over marvels, magic, and natural philosophy in Bacon's bold voice.

Bacon describes wonders that art and nature can work without demons. Flying machines, great ships, and burning mirrors pass in review as things knowledge might achieve. He writes like a prophet of experimental science. Dee, who owned more Bacon manuscripts than anyone, gave the letter to the press. Readers meet the medieval friar whom later ages turned into a magician, arguing here for nature's hidden powers.
baron-d-holbach-a-study-of-eighteenth-ce: Max Pearson Cushing's 1914 Columbia study examines Baron d'Holbach, the radical philosopher of eighteenth-century France. It traces his life, his friendships with Diderot, Rousseau and Hume, and his works, from translations of German science to the atheist Système de la Nature. Cushing weighs Holbach's character and influence, printing five unpublished letters to John Wilkes in an appendix.
bars-and-shadows-the-prison-poems-of-ral: Ralph Chaplin's 1922 prison poems were written during a twenty-year federal sentence imposed, as Scott Nearing's introduction stresses, for opinions and organising rather than violence. Night in the cell house, prison shadows, taps and a prison nocturne sit beside songs for the I. W. W., Wesley Everest and the girls who sang for prisoners. Freedom, distance and retrospect run through verse made behind bars.
bertha-our-little-german-cousin:
Mary Hazelton Wade wrote this volume of the Little Cousin series at Boston in 1904, with pictures by L. J. Bridgman. Bertha is a German girl whose family Christmas opens the book: two nights before the feast the children sit back to back by candlelight, each busy on a secret gift. Toy-making, a coffee-party, and the wicked bishop of the Rats' Tower carry the German year.

Sightseeing teaches the history. At Heidelberg Castle, father explains that the fortress-palace was not built all at once: parts rose over four hundred years, and enemies stormed, burned, and plundered it in turn. Frederick the Great has his chapter, and a brave princess hers. Wade wrote the series to give American children foreign playmates; Bertha's Germany is all castles, Christmas trees, and kindly lessons.
born-again:
Alfred William Lawson wrote Born Again, a utopian novel he dedicated to a Detroit beggar who gave his last dime to a worse-off man. Lawson, later known for straight-line economics and aircraft, here tells a life across lives. His hero learns from wise Sagemen how souls return in new bodies.

Death frees a soul to begin again in a fresh form, the Sagemen teach, perhaps in want made by a selfish system. Lawson uses that frame to attack strong men who squeeze light and hope from the weak. The hero vows to better earthly states for souls yet to come, among them Arletta's. Talk outweighs plot, as in most message novels. Readers meet an early, earnest draft of Lawson's later creed.
brentano-das-marchen-von-dem-myrtenfraul:
Clemens Brentano wove Italian folk material into his fairy tale of the myrtle maiden, Das Maerchen von dem Myrtenfraeulein, given here in German. A plant, a maiden, and a secret life hidden inside green leaves carry the story. Brentano was the most musical of the German Romantics, and his tales sing on the page.

Love and transformation govern the plot, as folk wonders receive a poet's lush retelling. The marvelous feels natural in Brentano's hands, which is the fairy tale's oldest trick done perfectly. Readers of German will hear his verbal music at full strength. The tale shows why his name anchors the Romantic fairy tale. Small in size, the piece holds a whole enchanted garden inside it.
britannica-1911-abauzit-firmin:
Firmin Abauzit receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abauzit, born of Protestant parents at Uzès in 1679, fled France as a boy when the edict of Nantes fell. Two years as a fugitive in the Cevennes ended at Geneva, where his mother joined him.

Languages, physics, and theology filled his youth in Holland and England. Newton counted him an early defender and fixed a Principia error at his word. William the Third failed to keep him in England, and Geneva gained a librarian and New Testament hand instead. Rousseau praised him in print, and Voltaire pointed strangers his way. Heirs burned most of his papers for their faith's sake, the entry laments.
britannica-1911-abbey-edwin-austin:
Edwin Austin Abbey receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbey, an American painter born at Philadelphia in 1852, left art school at nineteen for Harper and Brothers in New York. Pen work beside Howard Pyle and Joseph Pennell made his name as an illustrator.

Harpers sent him to England in 1878 for Herrick's poems, and Goldsmith and Shakespeare sets followed. Water-colours and pastels matched the pen work's success, and oil painting came in 1890 with A May Day Morn. London made him a full Royal Academician in 1898. His Quest of the Holy Grail frescoes fill Boston Public Library walls. Edward the Seventh gave him the coronation picture to paint in 1901, portraits and all.
britannica-1911-abdera-spain: Abdera in Spain is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names an old seaport on Spain's south coast, between Malaca and New Carthage, among the Bastuli. Carthaginians founded it as a trading station. After decline it rose under Rome as a leading town of Hispania Baetica, set on a hill above modern Adra. Old coins bear the Phoenician word abdrt with Heracles' head and a tunny-fish. Coins of Tiberius show the town temple flanked by two tunny-fish standing as columns.
britannica-1911-about-edmond-francois-va:
Edmond François Valentin About receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed by Frank Thomas Marzials and read here inside a shared chunk of text. About, a French novelist and journalist born at Dieuze in 1828, took second place at the École Normale behind Taine. Athens school service ended in a frank turn to letters in 1853.

La Grèce contemporaine hit at once, and Tolla drew charges of borrowing that fed years of feud. Farcical novels hold his best work, the entry judges: Le roi des montagnes, Le nez d'un notaire, and L'homme à l'oreille cassée. His paper the XIXe Siècle powered republican fights in the 1870s. A schoolmaster's verdict stands as prophecy: never more than a little Voltaire. The Academy elected him in 1884, weeks before his death.
britannica-1911-achin:
Achin, in Dutch spelling Atjeh, was a Dutch government forming the northern end of Sumatra, an area of more than twenty thousand square miles. Mountain ranges run along the island's spine and reach about twelve thousand feet, while the coasts are low and the rivers small. Its seat, Kotaraja, sits inland among kampongs, villages of timber and thatch buried in fruit trees, linked by rail to its port Olehleh. Pepper heads exports worth far less than imports.

History and resistance fill the entry. English envoys carried letters from Queen Elizabeth and James I to Achin's kings, and traders of many nations crowded its anchorage, yet factories never lasted. Dutch expeditions in the early nineteen hundreds met heavy fighting, and revolt still smouldered when the entry closed.
britannica-1911-agriculture-the-trade-in:
Irish stock crossed to Britain under a rule that spared them a harsh fate: forced slaughter at the port where they landed, the lot of foreign beasts. That break meant a great deal to Irish breeders, whose best buyers sat just across St George's Channel. A part of the Agriculture article on the Irish live stock trade sets out the scale of that traffic.

Table XXV counts the cattle, sheep, and pigs shipped year by year from 1891 to 1905, with the horses shipped shown as well. Store beasts, sent over for fattening or breeding, made up a bit more than half the cattle on most counts. Fattening those Irish stores filled yards across Norfolk and other English counties in bulk. Calves came to about one in twelve of all the cattle. Year in, year out, the flow stayed heavy, feeding British farms from Irish herds.
britannica-1911-aidin:
Aidin names both a province and a town of Asiatic Turkey, covered together in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The vilayet, or province, lay in the southwest of Asia Minor and took in ancient Lydia, Ionia, Caria, and western Lycia. The entry calls it the richest, most productive province of Asiatic Turkey. Its government sat at Smyrna, and it took its name from a Seljuk emir.

The town of Aidin, also called Guzel Hissar for its beautiful site, stands in the valley of the Menderes, the ancient Maeander. Seljuks took it late in the 1200s, and by about 1390 it acknowledged Ottoman rule. On the Smyrna to Dineir railway, it ran large tanneries and sweetmeat works and exported figs, cotton, and raisins. An earthquake badly damaged it in 1899, and the ruins of ancient Tralles crown a nearby height.
britannica-1911-aimoin:
Aimoin (about 960 to about 1010), a French chronicler, spent most of his life inside one set of walls. Born at Villefranche de Longchapt, he joined the abbey of Fleury young, took the monk's habit there, and stayed. From that quiet base came the histories that spread his name through the middle ages.

His chief work, the Historia Francorum, runs the tale of the Franks from the first times down to 653. Later hands carried it on into the twelfth century. Medieval readers drew on it much, though men now rate its worth as slight. Aimoin also wrote a life of Abbo, abbot of Fleury, the one life of that house's abbots still left. Books two and three of the Miracula sancti Benedicti, the wonders of St Benedict, came from his pen as well.
britannica-1911-ain:
A river splits the French department of Ain into two unlike halves. The Ain runs south through the middle of the eastern border department, which was put together in 1790 out of old Burgundy districts: Bresse, Bugey, Dombes, Valromey, and the Pays de Gex. In 1906 its 345,856 people lived across 2,248 square miles.

East of the river stand the southern Jura hills, ridge behind ridge, each line lower as they step west. The tallest ground, with the Cret de la Neige at 6,653 feet, lies in the Pays de Gex. Westward spread plains famed for Bresse pigs and fowls and for Dombes geese and turkeys, all shipped far and wide. Vineyards in Bugey and Revermont make good wines. Asphalt from Seyssel heads the list of minerals, and silk making, milling, and wood work give many their jobs.
britannica-1911-alboin:
Alboin, who died in 572 or 573, led the Lombards out of their Danube lands and made himself master of much of Italy. He took the throne after his father Audoin near 565, when his folk dwelt in Noricum and Pannonia, west of the river. Joined with the Avars, he crushed the Gepidae, slew their king Cunimund, and had the dead man's skull made into a cup for drinking.

He seized Cunimund's daughter Rosamund as well and wed her, a match that stored up grief. In 568 he swept into Italy, overran Venetia, and took the wide tract now called Lombardy. Pavia shut its gates to him for three years and fell in 572. By then Lombardy, Piedmont, and Tuscany were most likely his, with Spoleto and Benevento past them. Inside a year his chamberlain Peredeo had slain him, and the conquest passed to lesser hands.
britannica-1911-albumin:
Albumin, or albumen, an organic substance central to living bodies, is treated in a long scientific article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. From the Latin albus, white, the name covers a whole group of bodies of very complicated chemical composition. They are called proteids, or histogenetic bodies, because they are essential to building up the animal organism.

Plants are the original source of albuminous substances, which gather most richly in seeds, and they occur throughout the fluids of living bodies. Their chemistry is among the hardest in organic science and has drawn a huge literature. Workers such as Kossel and Emil Fischer studied how albumin molecules break down, since knowing the breakdown products is the road to building an albumin up again. Classes follow, from casein in milk curd to vitelline in egg yolk and the basic histones.
britannica-1911-alcuin:
Alcuin, a celebrated churchman and scholar of the eighth century, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at York in 735, he liked the Latin name Albinus and took the surname Flaccus at Charlemagne's palace academy. He was educated at York's cathedral school under the master Aelbert, travelling with him to Rome in search of manuscripts. When Aelbert became archbishop in 766, Alcuin succeeded him as head of the school.

Returning from Rome in 780, Alcuin met Charlemagne at Parma, and the king persuaded him to court. The royal dream was to teach the Franks correct Latin, create schools, and revive learning, and Alcuin became his chief helper in that work from 781. Great abbeys rewarded him. His letters, the entry adds, are filled with pious meditation yet form a mine of information on his age. They are the most reliable authority for humanism in the Carolingian age. He died in May 804.
britannica-1911-algonquin:
Algonquin, or Algonkin, a collective name for North American Indian peoples, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word was once taken for a French form meaning those on the other side of the St Lawrence river. It is now believed to come from a Micmac word meaning at the place of spearing fish. The Algonquins proper dwelt in the Ottawa river valley and around the St Lawrence's northern tributaries.

The Algonquins allied with the French against the Iroquois, and many were driven west to become known as Ottawa. French missionaries found their language to be the key to many related dialects, now grouped as the Algonquian stock. Chief tribes of that stock are listed, from Cree and Ojibway to Delaware, Cheyenne, and Shawnee. Peoples of Algonquian stock numbered between 80,000 and 90,000, split between the United States and Canada. Of the Algonquins proper, about 1,500 remained in Quebec and Ontario.
britannica-1911-alizarin:
Alizarin is a vegetable dyestuff once obtained from madder root, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry treats it as a chemical substance with a known formula and structure. The root holds a glucoside, a sugar-linked compound, called ruberythric acid. Acids or ferments split that glucoside into glucose and alizarin itself.

Until 1868 the dye came entirely from madder, a source known since ancient times. The entry then traces the synthetic route found by Graebe and Liebermann, who linked alizarin to anthracene and anthraquinone, and the cheaper sulphonation method found at the same time by Perkin. Industrial steps follow, from purifying crude anthracene to oxidation and fusion with caustic soda. Related coloured compounds, including quinalizarin and other oxyanthraquinones, close the account.
britannica-1911-alloxantin:
Alloxantin is a chemical compound formed by combining alloxan with dialuric acid. The entry gives its formula, notes that it carries three molecules of water, and suggests one of those may be part of its constitution rather than simple water of crystallisation. It can also be made by acting on alloxan with sulphuretted hydrogen, a gas now called hydrogen sulphide.

The substance forms small hard prisms. Exposed to air containing ammonia, the prisms turn red because murexide, or ammonium purpurate, forms on them. That colour change has a practical use: evaporating uric acid with dilute nitric acid yields alloxantin, and adding ammonia brings out the purple-red colour, giving chemists a test for uric acid. A tetramethyl derivative, amalic acid, is described as well.
britannica-1911-angel-coin:
Angel was a gold coin first used in France in 1340. Edward IV introduced it into England in 1465 as a new issue of the noble. At first it was called the angel-noble. Its value varied over its life. It ranged from six shillings and eightpence up to ten shillings. It was last coined in the time of Charles I. The name came from the design it bore. That design showed St Michael and the dragon.

The angel also served a ceremonial purpose. It was the coin given to sufferers who came to be touched by the sovereign. The touching was a ritual cure for the disease known as king's evil. After the coin ceased to be minted, medals replaced it. These medals were called touch-pieces. They carried the same device of the archangel and the dragon. They were given to those who came for the touching instead.
britannica-1911-bailly-jean-sylvain:
Bailly, Jean Sylvain (1736-1793), was a French astronomer and speaker born in Paris, drawn from painting and tragedy to science by Lacaille's influence. He worked out an orbit for Halley's comet of 1759, cut down Lacaille's star observations, and entered the Academy of Sciences in 1763.

His essays on Jupiter's satellites showed real original power, and praise pieces on great men won him seats in all three French academies, a triple honour unseen since Fontenelle. Histories of ancient and modern astronomy followed, learned but marred, the entry says, by wild speculation. Revolution swept him into politics: president of the Third Estate, leader at the Tennis Court, then mayor of Paris. The Champ de Mars shooting of 1791, done by guards under his orders, destroyed his standing with the crowd.
britannica-1911-baker-sir-benjamin:
Baker, Sir Benjamin (1840-1907), was an English engineer. He was born near Bath in 1840. A South Wales ironworks trained him early. London work followed with Sir John Fowler. He helped build the Metropolitan railway there. He designed the vessel that carried Cleopatra's Needle in 1877.

That ship brought the obelisk from Egypt to England. Baker was already a bridge authority then. The Forth Bridge made his public reputation. He designed and erected that great work. Its completion came in 1890. A knighthood and Royal Society fellowship followed. He advised on the Assuan dam in Egypt. Its opening in 1902 brought another knighthood. Baker also spread London's deep tube railway system. Those lines use cast iron tunnel segments. His practice ranged over nearly all civil engineering. He died at Pangbourne in 1907.
britannica-1911-balmain:
Balmain was a town in Cumberland county, New South Wales, Australia, on the western shore of Darling Harbour at Port Jackson. It lay two miles by water from Sydney and counted as a suburb of it. Its population in 1901 was 30,881.

Great numbers of Sydney's working people lived there, and some of the city's largest factories and most important docks stood on its shore. The 1911 Britannica entry lists saw-mills, iron foundries, chemical, glass, and soap works, and shipbuilding yards. One soap-linked works made coconut oil, tied to Port Sunlight in England. Balmain became a municipality in 1860.
britannica-1911-banjermasin:
Banjermasin is the chief town in the Dutch portion of Borneo, in the East Indies, on the river Martapura near its meeting with the Barito. It lies 24 miles from the Barito's mouth, on the south coast. The Dutch resident of South and East Borneo has his seat there.

Many of its nearly 50,000 people live in houses floating on the river or built on piles in it. Large vessels can sail up to the town, making it a trade centre for benzoin, rattans, wax, gold, diamonds, iron, and weapons from the river districts. The 1911 Britannica entry recalls an East India Company factory of 1700, abandoned after attack, and a British seizure in 1811 undone by restoration in 1817.
britannica-1911-barentin:
Barentin is a town of northern France, in the department of Seine-Inférieure, eleven miles north-west of Rouen by rail. Its population in 1906 was 5,245. The town sits in the valley of the Austreberthe, a small stream flowing to the Seine.

One structure dominates the entry: a fine railway viaduct, 540 yards long, crossing the valley at a height of 100 feet. Cotton cloth making is the town's principal industry. The 1911 Britannica entry is very short, and it keeps to place, size, the viaduct, and the cotton trade, offering readers a compact gazetteer notice rather than any history of the place.
britannica-1911-bartenstein:
Bartenstein, a town in the kingdom of Prussia in Germany, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as standing on the Alle, thirty-four miles south of Königsberg by rail. Its population in 1900 was 6805. The town carried on a considerable trade in corn and livestock, the farm produce of the country around it. Its people also worked in small industries serving that agricultural district.

Those industries are listed plainly: founding, carriage-building, tanneries, breweries, and potteries. History, though, is what made the town's name known beyond its region. Bartenstein is celebrated, the entry says, for the treaty concluded there on 26 April 1807 between Prussia and Russia. That agreement, made during the Napoleonic wars, is the single event the entry picks out from the town's past, and it closes the short account of the place.
britannica-1911-basin:
Basin, once also spelled bason, is a word whose technical uses are set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At root it names a round vessel for holding liquids, from a late Latin word probably tied to bacca, a bowl. From that sense the term spread widely. It can mean a dock with flood-gates on a tidal river, or a canal widening where barges unload. In geography it means a river's whole drainage area.

Geology gives the word its strictest use. There a basin is a broad, shallow syncline, a downward fold of the rock beds. It must not be confused with a river's drainage basin, even when the two partly coincide. The London and Hampshire basins and the Paris basin serve as large examples, and coal basins such as South Wales as smaller ones. Rock-basins scooped by glaciers, and lake basins, are also distinguished.
britannica-1911-bassein:
Bassein was a district and town in the Irrawaddy division of Lower Burma, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The district, in the Irrawaddy delta, had shrunk to 4127 square miles after giving up a large tract to the new Myaungmya district in 1896. A coastal range runs through it, and the great river reaches the sea at its eastern edge through a delta cut by salt-water creeks. Farmed delta land formed a vast sheet of rice.

Town and trade complete the picture. Bassein town, the capital, stands on the Bassein river and held 31,864 people in 1901. It was an important seat of the rice trade, with several steam rice mills. It also commanded the great outlet of the Irrawaddy, giving it military as well as trading value. The British took it in May 1852 during the second Burmese war. Flotilla steamers linked it with Rangoon, and a railway opened in 1903.
britannica-1911-battakhin:
Battakhin is the name of an African Arab people of Semitic stock, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They hold the banks of the Blue Nile near Khartum, in the Sudan. The entry ties their name to a famed siege. General Gordon fought most of his battles near that town against the Battakhin in 1884, holding Khartum against the rising in the Sudan.

One fight sealed the town's fate. Their sheikh, El Obeid, routed Gordon's troops on 4 September 1884. That defeat led to the close investment of Khartum, the ring of foes that cut the town off and starved it toward its fall. An older voice ends the entry. In the 1700s the traveller James Bruce described the Battakhin in blunt words as “a thieving, pilfering lot.”
britannica-1911-benjamin:
Benjamin is the tribe of Israel named for Jacob’s youngest son by Rachel. Alone among the brothers he was born in Palestine itself, between Bethel and Ephrath. His dying mother called him Ben-oni, “Son of my sorrow,” and his father changed it to Benjamin, likely “Son of the right hand.”

Jacob’s blessing calls Benjamin a tearing wolf, and the tribe’s fighters kept that fierce name: Ehud, Saul and Jonathan came from it. Its slingers were famed as left-handed, some even skilled with both hands. In the days of the judges the tribe was nearly wiped out, six hundred men escaping, then rebuilt. Bethel and Jerusalem both lay in its story, giving the least of the tribes an odd weight in Israel’s religion.
britannica-1911-bennett-charles-edwin:
Charles Edwin Bennett (born 1858) was an American classical scholar born at Providence, Rhode Island. Brown University graduated him in 1878, and he studied further at Harvard and in Germany. After school teaching in Florida, New York and Nebraska, he held Latin chairs at Wisconsin, Brown and, from 1892, Cornell.

Bennett’s studies of Latin syntax, above all his papers on the subjunctive, rest on counting through texts, a fresh method with new names for its findings. He led the “New American School” of syntax scholars, who demand a fresh look at all the evidence first. His Latin Grammar of 1895 recast the short scholarly school grammar for America, and he edited school texts of Tacitus and Cicero.
britannica-1911-benzoin-resin:
Benzoin, also called gum Benjamin, is a balsamic resin drawn from Styrax benzoin, a fair-sized tree of Sumatra and Java, and from other Styrax kinds. The name may come from an Arabic word for frankincense, its first syllable lost in European mouths. The resin is not secreted freely: it forms as the tree’s answer to cuts in its bark.

Siam benzoin is the finest sort, small “tears” of resin with a sweet smell owing partly to vanillin, rich in benzoic acid. Sumatra benzoin comes in dull red masses holding white tears and carries cinnamic acid too. Palembang benzoin ranks lowest of the three. Much benzoin is burned as incense, and its medical uses rest on the benzoic acid inside it.
britannica-1911-berlin:
Berlin, capital of Prussia and of the German Empire, receives one of the longest city articles in the 1911 Britannica. It lies on both banks of the Spree. The ground is flat and sandy, 110 feet above sea level. The city is the seat of the emperor, the Reichstag, and the imperial offices. It also hubs a great railway network and busy waterways.

The article covers the site, quarters, public buildings, industry, trade, and growth of the city. Its history runs from medieval trade through occupation in the Seven Years' War. It also covers the French occupation of 1806 to 1808. The hosted text adds a companion account of the Congress and Treaty of Berlin of 1878. That treaty redrew the Balkan settlement after war.
britannica-1911-bertin:
Bertin is a family name of weight in French journalism. Its head was Louis François Bertin (1766–1841), called Bertin aîné and born in Paris. He wrote for papers during the Revolution. After the 18th Brumaire he founded the Journal des Débats. The consulate suspected his royalist views and exiled him in 1801. He returned in 1804 to run the paper under censorship.

Napoleon renamed the paper Journal de l'Empire in those years. In 1811 the government took its conduct and profits over entirely. Bertin regained it in 1814 and restored the old title. He is often called the father of modern French journalism. His brother and his two sons carried the paper on after him.
britannica-1911-bilin:
Bilin, in Czech Bilina, is a town of Bohemia in Austria, 90 miles north of Prague by rail. Its 1900 population was 7,871, chiefly German. The town is very old and stands on the river Biela. A castle of the 17th century, held by Prince Lobkowitz, stands in it. Large lignite mines work in the ground nearby. Basalt rocks ring the town on every side.

Bilin is famous above all for its mineral springs, the Biliner Sauerbrunnen. Their water holds a large share of bicarbonate of soda, at a temperature of 45.6 degrees Fahrenheit. About four million bottles of the water are exported every year. Salt recovered by evaporation is a second export of the town. The 1911 Britannica entry also praises the Biliner Stein, a phonolite crag south of town. Rare plants grow on it, and the view is fine.
britannica-1911-bin:
Bin is a word for a receptacle of various kinds, first made of wicker or basket-work. The word appears in most European languages, the 1911 Britannica entry says. The Italian benna and the German Benne match it closely. Etymologists trace the family to a root meaning to plait. That root fits the woven basket the first bins plainly were.

The entry lists the forms the word keeps in daily speech. A dust-bin holds refuse, and a wine-bin holds bottles in a cellar. Hop-bin, coal-bin, and corn-bin name store boxes for farm and fuel use. Each keeps the old sense of a fixed container for loose goods. The entry is a short glossary note of a few lines.
britannica-1911-bisharin:
Bisharin are a nomad tribe of African Arabs, of Hamitic origin, in the eastern Nubian desert. The ancients knew them as the Ichthyophagi, the fish-eaters. In the middle ages they were known as the Beja. The 1911 Britannica entry calls them the most characteristic of the Nubian Arabs. With the Ababda and Hadendoa they stand for the Blemmyes of classical writers. In language and geography they link the Hamitic peoples with the Egyptians.

Nominally the Bisharin are Muslims, the entry says. Yet they keep some non-Islamic practices alive beside that faith. Traces of animal worship show in one firm rule: they never kill the serpent or the partridge, holding both sacred. The entry is a short ethnographic note of a few lines. It gives the tribe's desert home, its old names, and that striking custom. No numbers or chiefs are named.
britannica-1911-bissell-george-edwin:
George Edwin Bissell (1839– ) was an American sculptor, born at New Preston, Connecticut, on 16 February 1839. His father was a quarryman and marble-cutter. During the Civil War Bissell served as a private in the 23rd Connecticut volunteers. That service ran in the Department of the Gulf in 1862 and 1863. On mustering out he became an acting assistant paymaster in the South Atlantic squadron. After the war he joined his father's business at home.

He studied sculpture abroad in 1875 and 1876. He lived much in Paris from 1883 to 1896, with visits home between. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his chief works across two countries. They include the Waterbury soldiers' and sailors' monument, a Lincoln statue at Edinburgh, and Burns and Highland Mary at Ayr. A statue of President Arthur stands in Madison Square, New York. Chancellor Kent's statue went to the Congressional library in Washington.
britannica-1911-black-mountain:
Black Mountain is a range and border district on the Hazara side of the North-West Frontier Province of India. The range runs 25 to 50 miles and averages about 8000 feet high. It rises from the Indus basin. Yusafzai Pathan groups lived on its western face. Among them were the Hassanzais, the Akazais, and the Chagarzais.

Most of the entry lists four British expeditions into the district. Forces went in during 1852–53, after two customs officers were murdered. They went again in 1868, after a police post at Oghi was attacked. The Hazara expeditions of 1888 and 1891 followed years of raids. Each time, large forces crossed the tribal country. The tribes then submitted and agreed to keep the peace.
britannica-1911-bonnat-leon-joseph-flore:
Léon Joseph Florentin Bonnat (born 1833) was a French painter famed for strong, lifelike portraits. Born at Bayonne, he was schooled in Spain under Madrazo at Madrid. His long line of portraits shows the mark of Velasquez and the Spanish realists, the entry says.

At Paris he won the medal of honour in 1869 and became one of the leading artists of his day. In 1888 he took the painting chair at the École des Beaux Arts. In May 1905 he followed Paul Dubois as its director. Portrait painting in a vivid manner is called his most characteristic work. His subject pictures also won fame, among them the Martyrdom of St Denis in the Panthéon.
britannica-1911-boos-martin:
