Martin Boos (1762–1825) was a German Catholic priest whose warm, inward piety won him followers and enemies in turn. Born at Huttenried in Bavaria on Christmas Day 1762, orphaned at four, he was raised by an uncle at Augsburg and sent to the university of Dillingen. There he formed the modest piety that marked his whole life.

After serving in Bavarian towns he moved in 1799 to Linz in Austria, welcomed by Bishop Gall, and in 1806 became pastor at Gallneukirchen. His movement spread among Catholic laypeople and drew some fifty or sixty priests. When Gall and other protectors died, persecution began about 1812, with endless charges in the church courts. Prussia sheltered him at last, with a Düsseldorf professorship in 1817 and the pastorate of Sayn in 1819.
britannica-1911-brierley-benjamin:
Benjamin Brierley (1825–1896) was an English weaver who became a popular writer in Lancashire dialect. Born near Manchester to humble parents, he started work in a textile mill and taught himself in his spare time. At about thirty he began placing pieces in local papers, and sketches gathered as A Summer Day in Daisy Nook in 1859 won him notice.

In 1863 he turned fully to writing and journalism, bringing out Chronicles of Waverlow that year and the long tale The Layrock of Langley Side in 1864, later put on stage. He ran Ben Brierley's Journal, a weekly, from 1869 to 1891, and gave public readings of his work, touring America in 1880 and 1884. His Ab-o'-th'-Yate sketches and scenes of Lancashire common life sold widely. A building society failure cost him his savings in 1884, a fund was raised for him, and a statue rose in Queen's Park, Manchester, two years after his death.
britannica-1911-bruce-alexander-balmain:
Alexander Balmain Bruce (1831–1899) was a Scottish divine born at Aberargie near Perth on 31 January 1831. His father suffered for holding to the Free Church at the Disruption of 1843 and moved to Edinburgh, where the son was educated and showed exceptional ability from the first. Early religious doubts, stirred above all by Strauss's Life of Jesus, made him lifelong sympathetic to others under the same stress.

After serving as assistant at Ancrum and Lochwinnoch he was called to Cardross in 1859 and to Broughty Ferry in 1868. He published his first considerable exegetical work, The Training of the Twelve. His Cunningham Lectures of 1874 became The Humiliation of Christ. In 1875 he took the chair of Apologetics and New Testament exegesis at the Free Church College, Glasgow, holding it twenty-four years.
britannica-1911-bucer-martin:
Martin Bucer (1491–1551) was a German Protestant reformer. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his career. He was born at Schlettstadt in Alsace. In 1506 he entered the Dominican order. He studied at Heidelberg and read Erasmus and Luther. In 1521 he left the order by papal dispensation. He married a nun and preached the new doctrine. After his excommunication in 1523 he settled at Strassburg.

Bucer worked hard for Protestant unity. His views on the Lord's Supper leaned toward Zwingli. Still, he sought a formula to unite Lutherans and Swiss. That effort brought him charges of ambiguity. In 1548 he refused the Interim agreement at Augsburg. Cranmer then invited him to England. In 1549 he became regius professor of divinity at Cambridge. He advised on the revision of the prayer book. He died on 27 February 1551. Mary later had his body dug up and burnt. Elizabeth had his tomb rebuilt. The entry credits him with ninety-six treatises.
britannica-1911-buchez-philippe-joseph-b:
Philippe Joseph Benjamin Buchez (1796–1865) was a French author and politician. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his ideas and career. He was born on 31 March 1796 at Matagne-la-Petite. He finished his schooling in Paris. He then studied natural science and medicine. In 1821 he helped found a secret society. It copied the Italian Carbonari. Its aim was an armed rising against the government.

Buchez took his medical degree in 1825. He joined the Saint-Simonian society for a time. He left it over its strange religious turn. He then built his own Christian socialism. His journal L'Européen spread those views. His Introduction to the science of history appeared in 1833. It divided the past into four great epochs. Each epoch rested on a universal revelation. Later works include a Traité de politique, published in 1866. He died on 12 August 1865.
britannica-1911-buckstone-john-baldwin:
John Baldwin Buckstone (1802–1879) was an English actor and playwright. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his stage career. He was born at Hoxton on 14 September 1802. He was articled to a solicitor at first. He soon left the law for the stage. After years in the provinces he reached London in 1823. He played Ramsay at the Surrey theatre. In 1827 the Adelphi took him on as leading low comedian.

Buckstone later joined the Haymarket theatre. He was its lessee from 1853 to 1878. There he acted in his own plays and farces. Luke the Labourer was one popular piece. As manager he built a strong company. It included Sothern and the Kendals. He staged plays by Gilbert, Planché and Robertson. He wrote 150 plays in all. Some of them stayed popular for years. He died on 31 October 1879.
britannica-1911-captain:
Captain is a rank and title in the army and navy. The word comes from the Latin caput, meaning head. It passed through the late Latin capitanus. This 1911 Britannica article explains its many uses. At sea, anyone who commands a ship is called captain. That holds even without the substantive rank. A lieutenant in command is addressed as captain.

The master of a merchant ship is her captain too. On a warship, petty officers also carry the title. There are captains of a top, of the forecastle and of a gun. A post captain in the British navy is a full captain. The name comes from being posted on the captains' list. Admirals are chosen from that same list. The captain of the fleet serves as an admiral's chief of staff. The article then turns to the army rank. It gives the French, German and cavalry forms of the title.
britannica-1911-carpenter-william-benjam:
William Benjamin Carpenter (1813–1885) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English physiologist and naturalist born at Exeter, the eldest son of Dr Lant Carpenter. He studied medicine at University College, London, and took his M.D. at Edinburgh in 1839. His thesis dealt with the nervous system of invertebrate animals, a line of work that grew into his Principles of General and Comparative Physiology.

The Royal Society elected him in 1844 and gave him a Royal medal in 1861, and he became Fullerian professor of physiology at the Royal Institution in 1845. The entry stresses his gift as a lecturer when popular science was young. His deepest research lay in marine zoology, above all the Foraminifera and Crinoids. That work helped spur deep-sea exploration, leading to the Lightning expedition of 1868 and later the famous Challenger voyage.
britannica-1911-cartagena-spain:
Cartagena is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a fortified seaport of south-eastern Spain, in the province of Murcia, on the Mediterranean. Its population in 1900 was 99,871. The city holds an arsenal and naval dockyards, and an admiral with the title of captain-general governs it, as at Ferrol and San Fernando. It is also an episcopal see and the end of a branch railway from Murcia.

The city stands on a hill above its harbour, with a fertile valley to the north and east and high mountains closing the south and west. Its grey houses look neglected, being built of a friable, crumbling stone. The harbour, the largest in Spain after Vigo and the finest on the east coast, is a deep bay guarded by four hills and a narrow entrance with forts on either hand. Tramways run through modern suburbs to the mining district about two leagues inland.
britannica-1911-cautin:
Cautin is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a province of southern Chile. Arauco, Malleco, and Bio Bio bound it in the north. Argentina lies to the east. Valdivia lies to the south. The Pacific washes its west. Its area is officially put at 5832 square miles. The province sits in the temperate farming and forest belt. It produces wheat, cattle, lumber, tan bark, and fruit.

The state railway from Santiago to Puerto Montt crosses Cautin north to south. Two rivers cross it east to west. Both give good transport. The province once formed part of Araucanian land. Its political existence dates only from 1887. Its people in 1905 numbered 96,139. Many of them were European settlers, chiefly Germans. The capital is Temuco, on the Rio Cautin. Lautaro and Nueva Imperial are the other chief towns. Both were Spanish outposts in the long Araucanian struggle.
britannica-1911-chatelain:
Châtelain is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French feudal title, from the medieval Latin castellanus, the commander of a castle. In England the word stayed at that plain sense. In France it gained a special weight. It came to imply the jurisdiction of which the castle was the centre. The châtelain began, in Carolingian times, as an official of the count.

With the growth of feudalism the office became a fief and then hereditary. In rank the châtelain usually matched the simple sire, between the baron and the chevalier. In the Low Countries some were great nobles with wide jurisdiction. In the towns their power turned on their struggle with superiors and, from the twelfth century, with the rising communes. The châtellenie, the district under their justice, survived the office itself and lasted until the Revolution.
britannica-1911-cochin-denys-marie-augus:
Denys Marie Pierre Augustin Cochin (born 1851) was a French politician born at Paris. He studied law and entered the chamber of deputies in 1893. Over time he rose to lead the Conservative party in debate. The entry marks him as one of that party's main speakers.

His public stands give the shape of his career. He fought the income tax plan in 1894 and the reopening of the Dreyfus case in 1899. He also fought the split of church and state in 1905. The entry lists his books as well. They run from L'Évolution de la vie in 1895 to Ententes et ruptures in 1905.
britannica-1911-coffin:
A coffin is the box or case in which a corpse is confined. The word comes from a Latin term for a basket or chest. That older word never held the present sense. Greeks and Romans both buried and burned their dead. Greek coffins took the shape of an urn, a plain box or a triangle. The body in the last kind sat upright.

Burnt clay was the common Greek stuff, at times moulded round the body and then baked. Rome burned its dead until the Christian era brought stone coffins. Stone finds in London and other English towns fill much of the entry. In early England only the rich used stone. The poor were wrapped in cloth or laid under hay and flowers. By the late 1600s coffins served all ranks. Notes on American Indian practice close the account.
britannica-1911-coin:
Coin names, at root, the wedge-shaped die used to stamp money. The word comes through French from the Latin cuneus, a wedge. In time the name passed from the die to the money it stamped. A coin is thus a piece of money. Older English forms of the word are coyne, quoin and coign.

Those old forms live on in split uses. Quoin names the outer angle of a building. Coign also names a jutting angle. Shakespeare's phrase, a coign of vantage, keeps that sense alive. The entry is short and word-based. It gives no account of how coins are made or used. A reader gains the root, the shift in sense and the two building terms. That is the whole scope of the piece.
britannica-1911-cousin:
Cousin is a term of kinship that comes through French and Italian from a Latin root. Children of brothers and sisters are first cousins to each other, or cousins-german. Children of first cousins are second cousins to each other. The count runs on in that same step pattern. A child of a first cousin stands as first cousin once removed to that cousin's kin.

A second use of the word sits far from the family tree. Since the 1500s sovereigns have used cousin as a style of honour in speech. It fits persons of high rank who are not equal sovereigns. Brother is kept for one sovereign to a second. In Britain the sovereign calls dukes, marquesses and earls cousin in royal writs. In France the style went to princes of the blood, cardinals and marshals. In Spain it forms a set right of the grandees.
britannica-1911-craufurd-quintin:
Quintin Craufurd (1743–1819) was a British author born at Kilwinnock on 22 September 1743. In early life he went to India and entered the service of the East India Company. He came back to Europe before he was forty with a handsome fortune in hand. Paris became his home from that point. There he gave himself to letters and art.

He built a good library and a rich collection in that city. Paintings, coins and other objects of old interest filled his rooms. He stood on close terms with the French court, most of all with Marie Antoinette. He was one of the men who arranged the flight to Varennes. He fled to Brussels when that flight failed in its aim. In 1792 he came back to Paris in hope of saving the royal prisoners. Through Talleyrand's sway he kept his Paris home when war broke out anew. He died there on 23 November 1819.
britannica-1911-dammartin:
Dammartin is a small town of France in the department of Seine et Marne, 22 miles north-east of Paris. It stands well on a hill of the Goële plateau. Its weight in the entry is historical, not modern. Dammartin was the seat of a countship whose holders played a large part in French history. A certain Hugh first made himself master of the town in the 900s.

Reynald I, count of Dammartin, fell with the coalition crushed by Philip Augustus at Bouvines in 1214. His two heiresses carried the countship into other houses by marriage. Through Fayel and Nanteuil it reached Antoine de Chabannes, a favourite of Charles VII. He founded the town's collegiate church in 1480, and his tomb stands in its chancel. Sold to the Montmorency dukes in 1554, the countship was seized by Louis XIII in 1632 and given to the princes of Condé.
britannica-1911-demmin:
Demmin is a town of Prussia on the navigable river Peene, where the Trebel and Tollense join it, 72 miles west-north-west of Stettin on the Berlin-Stralsund railway. Its people numbered 12,541 in 1905. Textiles, breweries, distilleries and tanneries employ the town, and an active trade in corn and timber passes through it.

The town is Slavonian in origin and of great age, already a place of weight in Charlemagne's time. A German army besieged it in 1148 and Henry the Lion took it in 1164. The Thirty Years' War brought repeated fights over it, and Swedes and the electoral prince took and retook it after the peace. It passed to Prussia in 1720, and its walls were dismantled in 1759.
britannica-1911-estebanez-calderon-seraf:
Estébanez Calderón, Serafín (1799–1867), was a Spanish author best known by his pen name “El Solitario.” He was born at Málaga on 27 December 1799. His first literary effort was El Listón verde, a poem signed “Safinio” and written to mark the revolution of 1820. He was called to the bar and settled for a time at Madrid.

At Madrid Estébanez published a volume of verses in 1831 under the name “El Solitario.” He died at Madrid on 5 February 1867. His most interesting work is Escenas andaluzas of 1847. It is written in a curiously affected style, its word-hoard part archaic and part provincial. Yet, for all its odd mannerisms, the entry calls it a vivid record of picturesque scenes and local customs. He also left an unfinished history of the conquest and loss of Portugal, printed in 1883 under his nephew's editing.
britannica-1911-ettingshausen-constantin:
Constantin, Baron von Ettingshausen (1826–1897), was an Austrian geologist and botanist born in Vienna on 16 June 1826. He took a medical degree there. In 1854 he became professor of botany and natural history at Vienna's medical and surgical military academy. In 1871 he moved to the botany chair at Graz. He held that post until his death at Graz on 1 February 1897.

His name rests on work with fossil plants. He studied the Tertiary floras of many parts of Europe. He also worked on the fossil floras of Australia and New Zealand. His books include a study of living ferns as a key to fossil kinds, issued in 1865. His Physiographie der Medicinal-Pflanzen appeared in 1862. With J. Starkie Gardner he produced a monograph of the British Eocene flora, whose fern volume came out in 1879–1882.
britannica-1911-feval-paul-henri-corenti:
Paul Henri Corentin Feval (1817-1887), French novelist and dramatist, was born at Rennes in Brittany on 27 September 1817, and much of his best work draws on his native province. Trained for the bar, he left law after his first brief and gained a footing in Paris with the Club des phoques in 1841. His Mysteres de Londres of 1844, where an Irishman plots England's ruin to avenge his countrymen, appeared under the pen name Sir Francis Trolopp.

The entry lists a long shelf of novels: Le Fils du diable, Les Compagnons du silence, Le Bossu, Les Habits noirs and others. Some were staged, Le Bossu with Sardou as collaborator most successfully. His crime chronicles, the entry says, did harm that he himself later saw. In old age he turned ardent Catholic, revising his early books and writing religious pamphlets. Overwork broke his health, and he died in Paris on 8 March 1887.
britannica-1911-flavin: Flavin, from Latin flavus, yellow, is the commercial name for an extract or preparation of quercitron bark, from the tree Quercus tinctoria. It serves as a yellow dye. Growers and dyers use it in place of the ground and powdered bark itself, which the entry points to under the head Quercitron. The hosted text is a genuine short article of a few lines. It gives the name, its Latin root, the bark it comes from, and the dyeing use that made it an article of trade.
britannica-1911-fluorescein:
Fluorescein, or resorcin-phthalein, C20H12O5, is a chemical compound discovered in 1876 by A. von Baeyer. He made it by joining phthalic anhydride with resorcin at about 195 to 200 degrees. The entry describes the making in detail. The two substances are heated, the melt is boiled out and washed, then dissolved in sodium hydrate. Acid throws the product down again. Repeated two or three times, the process yields fluorescein pure.

The pure compound is a yellow powder that will not dissolve in water but dissolves in alcohol, crystallizing in small dark red nodules. In caustic alkali it gives a dark red solution. Diluted, that solution shows a brilliant green fluorescence, the trait that gave the substance its name. Brominating it yields eosin, a dye that colours silk, wool and cotton a fine pink.
britannica-1911-folkes-martin:
Martin Folkes (1690-1754), English antiquary, was born in London on 29 October 1690. He was educated at Saumur and at Clare College, Cambridge. There he so excelled in mathematics that at only twenty-three he was chosen a fellow of the Royal Society. He joined its council in 1716, and in 1723 Newton, the society's president, made him a vice-president. On Newton's death Folkes stood for the presidency but lost to Sir Hans Sloane, whom he succeeded in 1741.

In 1733 Folkes toured Italy and composed his Dissertations on the Weights and Values of Ancient Coins. He was president of the Society of Antiquaries from 1749 to 1754. Before it he read papers on the Trajan and Antonine pillars at Rome, among other studies of coins, weights and antiquities. The French Academy made him a member in 1742, and Oxford and Cambridge gave him honorary degrees in 1746. The entry traces a life at the centre of learned London.
britannica-1911-fountain:
Fountain, from late Latin fontana, from fons, a spring, names outlets of water that bear the work of human art where the water emerges. An early example is the carved Babylonian basin of about 3000 B.C. found at Tello. Layard also found an Assyrian fountain in a gorge of the river Gomel. It was a series of basins cut in the rock, stepping down to the stream, the lowest carved with two rampant lions.

The word covers simple gear that lets water gush into an ornamental basin, and grand gear that forces it into high jets. A fountain may be the basin or the jet itself. The long article follows fountains through history, from market-place columns with masks at their spouts to ornate Gothic structures with figures of virgins, saints and warriors. The hosted file opens with the end of the Foundling Hospitals article before reaching this survey.
britannica-1911-fouquier-tinville-antoin:
Antoine Quentin Fouquier-Tinville (1746-1795), French revolutionist, was born at Herouel, a village in the department of the Aisne. He was first a procureur attached to the Chatelet at Paris. He sold that office in 1783 and became a clerk under the lieutenant-general of police. He seems to have taken up revolutionary ideas early, though little is known of his part at the Revolution's outbreak. His name was made by the tribunal that judged the Terror's victims.

When the Revolutionary Tribunal of Paris was set up on 10 March 1793, Fouquier-Tinville was made its public prosecutor. He held the post until 28 July 1794. His work was less to convict the guilty than to carry out, in due form, the proscriptions ordered by whatever faction held power. That work earned him a name as one of the most sinister figures of the Revolution. The entry follows him to his own trial and execution.
britannica-1911-frahn-christian-martin:
Christian Martin Frahn (1782-1851), German numismatist and historian, was born at Rostock. He began oriental studies under Tychsen at the university of Rostock and continued them at Gottingen and Tubingen. In 1804 he became a Latin master in Pestalozzi's famous institute. He went home in 1806, and the next year he was chosen for the chair of oriental languages in the Russian university of Kazan. A German coin scholar was thus planted deep inside the Russian empire, among Tatar and Mongol money.

In 1815 Frahn was invited to succeed Tychsen at Rostock, but he chose St Petersburg instead. There he became director of the Asiatic museum and a councillor of state, and there he died. He wrote over 150 works. The entry names his studies of oriental coin cabinets and of Bulgar coins. It also names his work on the Mohammedan coins of the St Petersburg Academy.
britannica-1911-franklin: Franklin is a short word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Late Latin francus, meaning free, and at first meant simply a freeman. In England it later named a landholder who was free born but not noble. Some older writers also used it for a free or liberal host. The Latin form given is franchilanus. The entry runs to a few lines only and gives no more than these senses and the word origin.
britannica-1911-frobisher-sir-martin:
Sir Martin Frobisher (about 1535-1594), English navigator, was born at Altofts in Yorkshire and went to sea young, sailing to Guinea in 1544. By 1560 or 1561 he had fixed on the great aim of his life: a North-West Passage to Cathay and India. For fifteen years he sought backing in vain.

In 1576, helped by the earl of Warwick, he sailed with two tiny barks and a pinnace and 35 men. The pinnace was lost and one bark deserted. Alone, he reached Labrador and entered Frobisher Bay, losing five men to capture there. A lump of black earth brought home was rumoured to be gold ore. In 1577 a far larger expedition sailed with a royal ship and a Company of Cathay. Later he served as Drake vice-admiral in the West Indies and won his knighthood against the Armada. He died at Plymouth in November 1594 of a wound taken at Fort Crozon.
britannica-1911-galicia-spain:
Galicia is a region in the north-west of Spain, bounded by the Bay of Biscay, Leon and Asturias, Portugal and the Atlantic. It held 1,980,515 people in 1900 over 11,254 square miles, divided since 1833 into Corunna, Lugo, Orense and Pontevedra. Mountains cross it, reaching 6593 feet in the Peña Trevinca, and the Miño runs 170 miles to the Atlantic. The coast, 240 miles, is bold and cut, with Ferrol among Europe's best harbours and the port of Corunna.

The coast climate is mild, the interior colder and rainy. The soil is fertile, with grain crops in the lowlands and cattle herds on the pastures. The Galicians resemble the Portuguese in speech and habits, and Gallego has become in Madrid almost a synonym for a labourer. Corunna is the largest town; Santiago de Compostela is the capital. The Suevian kingdom fell to the Visigoths in 585, and after 1072 Galicia remained part of Castile or Leon.
britannica-1911-gastein:
Gastein is a side valley of the Pongau in Salzburg, Austria, famed for its mineral springs. The 1911 Britannica entry describes a valley some 25 miles long, set between 3,000 and 3,500 feet, with the Tauern peaks behind it. The river Ache runs through it, forming great waterfalls near Wildbad-Gastein. The Tauern railway reached the valley in 1905, through a tunnel over five miles long.

Two watering places share the waters. Hof-Gastein, the valley capital, receives thermal water by a five-mile conduit built in 1828, and was once rich from gold and silver mines worked since Roman times. Wildbad-Gastein, or Bad Gastein, draws over 8,500 guests a year to springs of 77 to 120 degrees. The entry also records the Gastein Convention of 1865 and Bismarck's 1879 talks there, which led toward the Triple Alliance.
britannica-1911-gawain:
Gawain, in the 1911 Britannica, is the most famous hero of Arthurian romance. The entry opens with his many name forms, from the Welsh Gwalchmei to the Latin Walganus. He is made son of King Loth of Orkney and nephew to Arthur through his mother.

The article traces his figure through the early records. William of Malmesbury tells of his tomb found in the Welsh province of Ros, and calls him a king over Galloway. In Geoffrey of Monmouth and in Wace he acts as Arthur's envoy to the Roman emperor and dies fighting Mordred's landing. English poems make him the model of chivalrous courtesy, 'the fine father of nurture.' The entry notes that before Malory, Gawain, not Arthur, was the typical English hero, and contrasts his smaller place in Chretien de Troyes.
britannica-1911-gedymin:
Gedymin (died 1342) was grand-duke of Lithuania. The 1911 Britannica entry questions the old chroniclers who made him a servant of Prince Witen, and makes him more probably Witen's younger brother. He inherited a vast domain: Lithuania proper, Samogitia, Red Russia, Polotsk and Minsk.

Around him stood greedy foes, above all the Teutonic Knights, whose raids under colour of conversion had united the Lithuanian tribes. Gedymin aimed higher, at a dynasty that would make Lithuania mighty, not merely safe. In 1322 he wrote to Pope John XXII seeking protection, and in 1325 he invited settlers of every rank from the Hanse towns, with free choice of settlement and their own laws. The entry then follows his gains in the Russian principalities, Kiev among them, his marriage alliances, and his even-handed rule over Catholic and Orthodox clergy.
britannica-1911-gitschin:
Gitschin, in Czech Jicin, is a town of Bohemia, Austria, 65 miles north-east of Prague by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 9,790 people in 1900, mostly Czech. Its parish church was begun by Wallenstein on the model of Santiago de Compostela, and its castle, finished in 1630, stands beside the church.

Wallenstein made the town capital of his duchy of Friedland, and in 1813 the emperor Francis I signed there the treaty joining the Allies against Napoleon. The entry recalls his murder and the town's fall in the Thirty Years' War, and its later passage to the Trauttmannsdorf family. On 29 June 1866 the Prussians won a great victory there over the Austrians. That win let two Prussian armies join, leading on to the Austrian defeat at Koniggratz.
britannica-1911-griffin:
The Griffin, Griffon or Gryphon, from the Greek gryps, was in the natural history of the ancients an imaginary creature of the eagle kind. The 1911 Britannica entry describes it with four legs, wings and a beak: eagle in front, lion behind, and in some writers a serpent's tail. It watched over gold mines and hidden treasure.

Consecrated to the Sun, whose chariot the ancient painters showed drawn by griffins, it was said to inhabit Asiatic Scythia. There gold and precious stones abounded, and the griffins tore apart strangers who came to gather them, chastising human greed. The one-eyed Arimaspi warred with them constantly, Herodotus is cited as saying. Mandeville made the griffin eight times a lion's size. The entry then follows the beast into heraldry and architecture, from Persepolis capitals to the table supports of Pompeii.
britannica-1911-groin:
Groin carries several distinct meanings. One old sense comes from the Latin grunnire. It meant the grunting of swine, and hence a pig's snout. That sense probably gave rise to groyne. A groyne is a small coastal breakwater of timber or masonry. It checks the drift of sand and shingle. A second sense names part of the body. It is the fold between the lower abdomen and the thighs.

Architecture takes its meaning from that fold. A groin is the angle where two vaults cross. Equal vaults meet in a vertical plane. Unequal vaults produce winding curves. Those curves were hard to centre without ribs. The entry also explains the Welsh groin. There the main vault stands higher than the cross vaults. It explains groin centering too. That is the timber support used while vaulting is built.
britannica-1911-grossenhain:
Grossenhain is a town in the kingdom of Saxony, 20 miles north of Dresden on the main railway line to Berlin, with 12,015 people in 1905. It has an Evangelical church, modern and commercial schools, a library and an extensive public park. Its industries are important, covering woollen and cotton cloth, buckskin, leather, glass and machinery.

The town began as a Sorb settlement, was held and strongly fortified by the Bohemians, and then passed to the margraves of Meissen, from whom Brandenburg took it in 1312. It suffered in all the great German wars and was nearly destroyed by fire in 1744. On 16 May 1813 French and Russian forces fought a battle there during the Napoleonic wars.
britannica-1911-guest-edwin:
Edwin Guest (1800–1880) was an English antiquary. He was educated at King Edward's school, Birmingham. At Caius College, Cambridge, he graduated as eleventh wrangler. He became a fellow of his college. He was called to the bar in 1828. After some years of legal practice he turned to research. Antiquarian and literary studies filled the rest of his life.

In 1838 he published his History of English Rhythms. That exhaustive work made his name. He also wrote many papers on Roman-British history. Dr Stubbs edited them after Guest's death as Origines Celticae (1883). Fresh material for a history of early Britain joined them. Guest became master of Caius College in 1852. He served as vice-chancellor in 1854–1855. He died on 23 November 1880.
britannica-1911-hohenstein:
Hohenstein, or Hohenstein-Ernstthal, is a town of Germany, in the kingdom of Saxony, on the slopes of the Erzgebirge, 12 m. N.E. of Zwickau. Its population was 13,903 in 1905. It has two fine Evangelical churches, a town hall restored in 1876, and monuments to famous men. Cotton spinning and weaving lead its industries, with machines, stockings, gloves, woollen and silk fabrics, printing and dyeing.

Many townsfolk also work in the copper and arsenic mines nearby, and a mineral spring with baths lies close. Hohenstein is the birthplace of the physicist G. H. von Schubert and of C. G. Schröter, an inventor of the pianoforte. The town joins two older towns, Hohenstein and Ernstthal, united in 1898. A second Hohenstein, in East Prussia, founded by the Teutonic Order in 1359, is noted at the end.
britannica-1911-holguin:
Holguín is a town of the high plateau country in the interior of Oriente province, Cuba, about 65 m. N.W. of Santiago de Cuba. Its population was 7,592 in 1907. It stands near the Marañon and Jigüé rivers, on a plain ringed by hills except to the east, where it lies open to the plateau winds. For long it was the chief station where Spanish troops were acclimatized.

The town's oldest public buildings are two churches, built in 1800 and 1809. Its trade is in cabinet woods, tobacco, Indian corn and cattle products, exported through Gibara, its port some 25 m. N.N.E., linked by railway. Holguín was settled about 1720 and became a city in 1751. In the Ten Years' War of 1868–1878 and the revolution of 1895–1898 it was an insurgent centre.
britannica-1911-john-margrave-of-branden:
John, or Hans (1513–1571), margrave of Brandenburg-Cüstrin, was the younger son of Joachim I, elector of Brandenburg, born at Tangermünde on the 3rd of August 1513. Despite a family law that barred division of the electorate, he inherited the new mark of Brandenburg on his father's death in July 1535.

Raised a strict Catholic, he moved by 1538 to the side of the Reformers and joined the league of Schmalkalden. Imperial promises then drew him back to Charles V. He opposed the Augsburg Interim of 1548 and led the princes who formed a league in February 1550 to defend Lutheran teaching. After fresh quarrels he returned to the emperor's side. His last years went to ruling the new mark with care and thrift. He bought Beeskow and Storkow and fortified Cüstrin and Peitz. He died at Cüstrin on the 13th of January 1571, leaving no sons.
britannica-1911-kain:
Kain is the name of a sub province and of a town in Khorasan, Persia. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kailas entry. The sub province runs about 300 miles north to south, from Khāf to Seīstān, and about 150 miles west to east, from the hills of Tūn to the Afghan frontier. It is very hilly, with wide plains and rich villages at a mean height of 4000 feet.

About 150,000 people lived there. The land rears great numbers of camels and yields much grain, saffron, wool, silk, and opium. Its felts and woollen goods are famed, above all its carpets, the best made at Darakhsh. The town of Kain was the capital until 1740, when Birjend took its place. It stands 65 miles north of Birjend, walled in mud, with barely 5000 people, and a ruined castle on a hill above the plain.
britannica-1911-kammin:
Kammin, or Cammin, is a town in the Prussian province of Pomerania. It stands 21 miles and a half from the Baltic, on the Kamminsche Bodden, a lake joined to the sea by the Dievenow. Its population in 1905 was 5923. Among its four Protestant churches, the cathedral and the church of St Mary stand out. Iron founding and brewing are carried on, with some fishing and shipping, and steamers run to Stettin, about 40 miles south southwest.

Kammin is of Wendish origin and gained town rights in 1274. From about 1200 until 1628 it was the seat of a bishopric. The see then became a secular principality, and in 1648 the town was folded into Brandenburg. The entry is a compact gazetteer note: place, waters, churches, trades, and four centuries of church rule summed in a few lines.
britannica-1911-kaolin:
Kaolin is a pure white clay, known also as china clay, since it is a chief material in the making of china, or porcelain. The word is said to be a corruption of the Chinese Kau ling, High Ridge, the name of a hill east of King te chen. From that hill came the first samples sent to Europe, by the Jesuit Père d'Entrecolles, early in the 18th century.

His samples, tested in Paris by Réaumur, showed that true porcelain held two chief materials. They came to be known as kaolin and petuntse, our china clay and china stone. Kaolin gives the paste its shaping power in the kiln. Petuntse gives the glassy quality of porcelain. Early finds were made at Aue in Saxony and St Yrieix near Limoges. In England it was found in Cornwall about 1750 by William Cookworthy.
britannica-1911-kazvin:
Kazvin is a province and town of Persia, northwest of Teheran and south of Gilan, with Khamseh on its west. The province pays a yearly revenue of about £22,000. It holds many rich villages that yield much grain and fruit, great amounts of the fruit being dried and sent abroad.

Kazvin, the capital, stands at 4165 feet, 92 miles by road from Teheran. The city is said to have been founded in the 4th century by the Sassanian king Shapur II. Earthquakes have damaged it again and again. Many streets and most of the grand buildings seen by Chardin in 1674 now lie in ruins. The chief remains are the palace of the Safawid shahs and the mosque with its large blue dome. In the 16th century Shah Tahmasp I made Kazvin his capital, and it stayed so until Shah Abbas I moved the seat of rule to Isfahan.
britannica-1911-keewatin:
Keewatin is a district of Canada. Hudson and James bays bound it on the east, and the Albany and English rivers, Manitoba, and Lake Winnipeg on the south. The 100th meridian bounds it on the west and Arctic straits on the north. It takes in 445,000 square miles.

Its surface is in general barren and rocky, studded with countless lakes, with forest below 60 degrees north and bare moss and lichen ground beyond, the so called barren lands. Save for a strip of younger rocks and a few patches of older ones, the district is built of Laurentian rock. Its chief river is the Nelson, which with its great feeder the Saskatchewan runs 1450 miles. The Hayes and the Severn also drain it. The survey treats a vast, thinly known north in the gazetteer's order of bounds, rock, river, and climate.
britannica-1911-kennicott-benjamin:
Benjamin Kennicott (1718–1783) was an English divine and Hebrew scholar, born at Totnes in Devonshire on the 4th of April 1718. He followed his father as master of a charity school. By the kindness of friends he was able to go to Wadham College, Oxford, in 1744, where he stood out in Hebrew and divinity.

While still an undergraduate he published two studies, on the Tree of Life in Paradise and on the offerings of Cain and Abel. They won him his bachelor's degree before the set time. In 1747 he was elected fellow of Exeter College, and in 1750 he took his master's degree. In 1764 he joined the Royal Society, and in 1767 he became keeper of the Radcliffe Library. The entry goes on to the great task of his life, the gathering and comparison of Hebrew manuscripts of the Old Testament.
britannica-1911-kreutzer-konradin:
Konradin Kreutzer (1780–1849) was a German composer, born on the 22nd of November 1780 at Messkirch in Baden. He died on the 14th of December 1849 at Riga. His fame rests almost wholly on one opera, Das Nachtlager von Granada (1834). Written in the manner of Weber, it held the stage for half a century, through all the changes of musical taste, thanks to its flow of true melody and depth of feeling.

The same gifts mark Kreutzer's part-songs for men's voices, once very popular in Germany. Among them "Der Tag des Herrn" ("The Lord's Day") is named as the finest. Kreutzer wrote many operas for the Vienna stage, but they have vanished and are not likely to return. He was Kapellmeister to the king of Württemberg from 1812 to 1816, and in 1840 he became conductor of the opera at Cologne. His daughter Cecilia was a singer of some note.
britannica-1911-krotoschin:
Krotoschin, in Polish Krotoszyn, is a town of Germany in the Prussian province of Posen, 32 miles S.E. of Posen. In 1900 it held 12,373 people. It has three churches and a synagogue, steam saw-mills and a steam brewery, and trades in grain and seeds.

Its castle is the chief place of a mediatized principality. That small state was formed in 1819 out of lands of the Prussian crown. It was granted to the prince of Thurn and Taxis, to make up for his giving up the monopoly of the Prussian postal system, which his family had held before.
britannica-1911-la-voisin:
Catherine Monvoisin, known as "La Voisin" (d. 1680), French sorceress, was a chief figure in the affaire des poisons of the reign of Louis XIV. Her husband was a failed jeweller, and she built their fortunes back up by palmistry and face-reading, then by witchcraft. With the renegade priest Étienne Guibourg, who celebrated a "black mass," she practised medicine and midwifery, procured abortions, and sold love powders and poisons. Her own article sits inside a chunk file that also carries neighbouring articles.

The great ladies of Paris flocked to her, among them the comtesse de Soissons and Mme de Montespan. After the Brinvilliers executions of 1676 a royal commission opened in April 1679. When Montespan's plan to poison the king came out, Louis closed the court, and La Voisin was executed on the 20th of February 1680. Thirty-five others were executed, five sent to the galleys and twenty-three banished.
britannica-1911-labe-louise-charlin-perr:
Louise Labé (c. 1525–1566), French poet called La Belle Cordière, was born at Lyons about 1525, the daughter of a rich ropemaker. At the siege of Perpignan she is said to have fought on horseback in the dauphin's ranks. Before 1551 she married Ennemond Perrin, also a ropemaker. She built up a library and gathered round her the learned ladies of Lyons — Pernette du Guillet, the Scève sisters, Clémence de Bourges. Poets such as Maurice Scève and Pontus de Tyard came too, with Marot and probably Rabelais among the visitors.

About 1550 the poet Olivier de Magny passed through Lyons and she fell in love with him. Her passion for Magny fired her verse: the elegies voice her grief at his absence, and her Sonnets, printed in 1555, quickly won great popularity. Magny's jealous ode to her husband, the "Sire Aymon," ruined her reputation.
britannica-1911-lanolin:
Lanolin is the trade name for a skin mix. Wool-fat and water form the mix. The British list of drugs sets the mix at seven ounces of wool-fat. Three fluid ounces of water go with it. The fat comes from raw sheep's wool. Workers wash out a brown grease before spinning. Cleaning makes that grease fit for use.

Clean wool-fat is clear and soft. It takes up large amounts of water. Such mixes split apart only slowly. The fat sinks into skin with ease. Plain wool-fat and lanolin thus form the base of many ointments. Blends with vaseline or fatty oils are common. Two traits help its use. It acts mildly against germs. It does not turn rancid.
britannica-1911-lantara-simon-mathurin:
Simon Mathurin Lantara (1729-1778) was a French painter of landscape scenes, born at Oncy on 24 March 1729. A weaver's son who began as a herd boy, he caught the eye of his master's son and was placed with a painter at Versailles. Quick skill won him early notice.

Steady life chafed him. While money from a sale lasted he lived free of care among plain workmen, and rich patrons who took him in found that ease and fine living stopped his hand. He died in Paris on 22 December 1778. His works are few and now prized; the Louvre holds one signed landscape, Morning, dated 1761. Other painters, Vernet among them, are said to have added figures to his scenes.
britannica-1911-linares-spain:
Linares is a town of southern Spain in Jaen. It sits among the south foothills of the Sierra Morena. Height above the sea is 1,375 feet. The Guadalimar runs three miles south-east. The count of 1900 gave 38,245 people. Four branch rail lines tie it to rich lead mines north-west.

Town growth came late and fast. Town hall, bull-ring, and theatre rose in the late 1800s. A fine fountain of Roman birth is the chief old thing. Lead rules work life here. Powder, dynamite, blasting fuse, and rope serve the pits. Plant comes from abroad, chiefly England. British firms smelt the ore and roll its sheets and pipes. Linares lead holds top rank for grade, though yield tends to fall. Grain, wine, and oil feed a brisk home trade. Old Castulo's scraps lie two miles south.
britannica-1911-loisy-alfred-firmin:
Alfred Firmin Loisy (born 1857) was a French Catholic scholar of the Bible. Ambrières in Lorraine was his birthplace. Peasant kin had tilled that soil for ages. A frail boy, he went to church school at St Dizier. No priestly path was planned. He chose it all the same and entered the seminary in 1874.

Orders came in 1879 and two village cures followed. Paris study at the Institut Catholique began in 1881. Abbé Martin taught him Bible tongues and text craft. Abbé Duchesne gave him a sharp eye for hard Bible facts. His degree came in March 1890. A first book, on the canon of the Old Testament, came that year. Chair work at the Institut followed. Books on the New Testament canon, on Bible text and versions, and on the first three Gospels poured out by 1894. His own journal carried much of it.
bruno-de-magia-latin:
Giordano Bruno wrote De Magia, on magic, in Latin near the end of his wandering life, around 1590. Bruno treats magic as the art of bonds. All things, he argues, are linked by attractions and sympathies, and the magus works by knowing and pulling those links.

 His system sorts magic into kinds and traces how images, words, and desires bind souls. The treatise is the philosophical peak of Renaissance magic theory. Bruno the thinker of infinite worlds stands behind every page. Burned at Rome in 1600, he left this calm, daring account of his art. Readers meet the mind for which the cosmos itself was the great web of bonds.
c-f-meyer-die-richterin:
A woman holds the power of justice in Charlemagne's age and must judge her own family's crimes. C. F. Meyer's Die Richterin, given here in German, builds its tragedy around Stemma, the judge of its title. Few heroines in German fiction carry her sternness and sorrow in equal measure.

Guilt and atonement govern the plot, as hidden sins surface under her own tribunal. Meyer writes the early medieval world with his usual lapidary force, every scene cut clean. Stemma's strength is real, and so is the price it exacts from her heart. Critics call the novella the master's late masterpiece. Magnificently written, it closes his career on a note of stern, tragic grandeur.
canon-episcopi-latin:
The Canon Episcopi is a church law text from around 900, passed down through Regino of Prüm's collection. It treats the belief that certain women ride at night with Diana or Herodias. The canon declares the night flight an illusion worked by demons, not a bodily fact.

That ruling mattered for centuries. Canon lawyers quoted the text for six hundred years, and it long held back full-blown witch persecution. Later demonologists had to argue around its plain denial. The canon shows the early medieval church as the skeptic in the room. Its Latin lines are brief, but few texts on witchcraft have been cited more often or fought over harder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-lehn: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Lehnin describes a Cistercian abbey founded in 1180 by Otto the Second, Margrave of Brandenburg. It stood about eight miles south-east of Brandenburg, and its church showed fine Romanesque building. Lehnin matters chiefly for the famous Vaticinium Lehninense, a prophecy supposedly penned by a monk called Hermann in the 1200s or 1300s. First printed in 1722, it laments the Ascanian line's end in 1319, portrays later margraves, and ends the Hohenzollern house with Frederick William the Third.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abthain:
Abthain, or abthane, is the English or Lowland Scotch shape of middle-Latin abthania, from Gaelic abdhaine, meaning abbacy. The word's exact sense was lost, so people took it to denote some ancient dignity, whose holder went by abthanus or abthane. Dr. Skene holds that the correct meaning is abbey or monastery, not abbot or over-thane.

The word refers chiefly to territories of churches and monasteries founded by old Celtic or Columban monks, chiefly from the Mounth range to the Firth of Forth. Many of these abthains passed into lay hands, descending from father to son. They paid certain church tributes and matched the early Irish church's termon lands closely. Skene recommends the forms abthany or abthanry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adele-amalie-:
Adele Amalie Gallitzin, or Golyzin, was a princess born at Berlin on 28 August 1748. She died at Angelmodde near Munster on 17 April 1806. Daughter of Prussia's General Count von Schmettau, she was educated Catholic but soon grew estranged from religion. In 1768 she married Russia's Prince Dimitry Gallitzin, ambassador under Catherine II at Paris, Turin, and The Hague.

There her beauty and qualities of mind and heart won her a brilliant role. At twenty-four she suddenly left society and devoted herself to her children's education. She studied mathematics, classical philology, and philosophy under Franz Hemsterhuis, who kindled her Socratic-Platonic enthusiasm. Drawn to Munster by Furstenberg's educational reform, she became centre of an intellectual circle including Overberg, Droste-Vischering, Stolberg, and Hamann. She later returned to the church, and her gentle charity blessed many.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-akhmin:
Akhmin is a city of Upper Egypt on the Nile's banks. Of late years it has gained great importance from discoveries in its cemeteries. Akhmin's hill, some two miles long, is filled with remains piled in pits of eight or ten small chambers, a dozen coffins in each.

Heathens and Christians lie heaped together, so often one cannot say whether a body's little articles belonged to a heathen, a Christian, or a sect member. Eutychianism had become almost the whole Coptic nation's religion from the fifth century onward. Papyri and tapestries chiefly famed the city. Among the papyri, the Gospel of Peter, Apocalypse of Peter, and Book of Henoch fragments hold first place. The tapestries have supplied first-rank material for ancient textile handicrafts' history, in excellent preservation and great variety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-jean-b:
Albert Jean Belin was a French prelate, a senior churchman, and writer. He was born at Besançon early in the seventeenth century and died in April 1677. He entered the Benedictine monastery of Faverney in 1629 and later served as prior and abbot at houses including Charité-sur-Loire, Nevers, and Paris. He was consecrated Bishop of Belley in February 1666.

Belin wrote in French, and his books ranged from works on the philosopher's stone and talismans to proofs of Christian truth and eucharistic emblems, many dated 1653. The entry notes he is probably the same man as Alphonsus Belin, prior of Charité-sur-Loire, author of a 1683 defence of Catholic teaching against the Reformed faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albrecht-von-:
Albrecht von Wallenstein, also called Waldstein, was an imperial general, born in Bohemia in September 1583 and dead at Eger in February 1634. He came from a Czech noble family of the Bohemian Brethren and studied at the Lutheran university of Altdorf. He travelled in France and Italy and turned Catholic, apparently at the Jesuit college of Olmütz. An elderly widow's fortune, inherited in 1614, launched his rise.

Wallenstein first commanded independently in 1621 against Bethlen Gabor in Moravia. After lending Ferdinand large sums, he gained confiscated Bohemian estates that became the principality of Friedland in 1624. In April 1625 Ferdinand made him captain over all imperial forces, and he raised an army of 20,000 men. Later campaigns drove Mansfeld from Silesia and carried him to Jutland and Mecklenburg. The entry judges his standing as a general disputed and his later life a tangle of intrigue ending in treason.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alcuin:
Alcuin, also called Alhwin or Flaccus, was an eminent teacher, scholar, and theologian, born about 735 of noble Northumbrian parentage and dead on 19 May 804. His birthplace is disputed, though it was probably in or near York. As a child he entered the cathedral school founded there by Archbishop Egbert. When his master Aelbert became archbishop in 767, the direction of the school fell to Alcuin.

Alcuin had the largest share in the revival of learning of his age, the entry says. He worked as a teacher and gatherer of knowledge rather than an originator. His work reached beyond York to the Palace School, part of Charlemagne's broad plans for spreading learning. As a theologian he wrote on Scripture, morals, and doctrine, standing as the Church's foremost champion against the Adoptionist heresy. As a liturgist he was the chief agent of the reform of worship carried out under Charlemagne's authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-curtain:
Altar curtains once hung between the columns of the ciborium, the cupola over the high altar in most basilicas, cathedrals, and large churches. Metal rods held rings fastening curtains, called tetravela altaris, of linen, silk, gold cloth, and other precious stuffs, drawn around the altar at set parts of Mass. Roman pontiffs such as Gregory IV, Leo IV, and Nicholas I gave such curtains to Rome's churches.

When ciboria fell out of use, a dossel or dorsal hung at the altar's back, with two more at its sides, on wall rods, reredos rods, or four pillars. Angels holding candelabra crowned the pillars, candles burning there on solemn occasions. Today's sanctuary candelabra probably descend from these pillar lights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andre-garin:
Andre Garin, an Oblate missionary priest, was born in 1822 at Cote-Saint-Andre, Isere, and died at Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1895. He studied at his native town's lesser seminary and entered the Oblates of Mary Immaculate on 1 November 1842. Too young for the priesthood, he went to Canada and was ordained in 1845 by Bishop Bourget of Montreal.

For twelve years he served eastern Canada's Indian missions, then served as superior at Plattsburg and Buffalo. His mastery of Montagnais and English aided his early work. When Lowell needed an able man to organize its French Canadians, Garin was ordered there. His good sense, courteous manner, and kindly temper soon won him wonderful influence over his people. During some twenty-five years as pastor he built costly churches and commodious schools and founded several religious confraternities. Two years after his death his parishioners raised a statue to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-therese-:
Anne-Thérèse Guérin, Mother Theodore in religion, born at Etables in 1798, died in 1856. She entered the Sisters of Providence in 1823, professed vows in 1824, and became Rennes superior the same day. Transferred to Soulaines in 1833, she founded St. Mary-of-the-Woods, Indiana, in 1840, and became superior general in America.

The Life and Life-Work of 1904 calls her a woman of uncommon valour. Father Charles Coppens adds that she was superior in gifts and virtues, living in union with God, practising heroic faith, hope, and charity. A model of virtue for the faithful, especially religious men and women. Her mind was superior: the French Academy gave her medallions, she was skilled in medicine and theology, and her institution's expansion evidences her energetic spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-artvin:
Artvin, a Russian city in the Transcaucasian province of Kutais, stands beside Turkish Armenia on the left bank of Tehoruk, which flows to the Black Sea. By 1894 it held 5,900 people, mostly Armenian and Turkish. In Artvin and its vicinity stood nine Armenian-Catholic churches, four boys' schools and three for girls, while Gregorian Armenians held five churches and two schoolhouses.

The Armenian-Catholic diocese of Artvin was set up in 1850 by Pius IX for United Armenians in southern Russia. It was first suffragan to Constantinople's metropolitan, then answerable to the Armenian-Catholic Cilician patriarch, whose see is Constantinople. Its first bishop, Timotheus Astorgi, served from 1850 to 1858, followed by Antonius Halagi in 1859 and Joannes Baptista Zaccharian in 1878. That year Russia annexed the whole diocese and joined it to Tiraspol, blocking later bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascelin:
Ascelin, ambassador of Innocent IV, pope from 1243 to 1254, to the Tartars, entered the Dominican order, likely at Paris, in 1221 or 1222. Distinguished for learning and great zeal for spreading Christian faith, he was chosen in 1245 with three fellow Dominicans by Humbert de Romanis, provincial of France. The pope had ordered Humbert to pick fit men for an embassy to convert Sultan Melik Saleh, then camped in Persia.

On Vincent of Beauvais's authority, drawn from embassy member Simon of St. Quentin, they met the sultan's first great army on 24 May 1247. Their mission failed, since they brought no presents to win mercenary courtiers, and Ascelin refused to kneel three times in honour of the khan's dignity. Condemned to death, the friars faced the khan's threat to flay their leader Ascelin, and the entry follows a mission undone by protocol and pride.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-august-allers:
August Allerstein, also called Hallerstein, was a Jesuit missionary in China who died there probably about 1777, after the suppression of his order. His skill in mathematics and astronomy won him favor at the imperial court in Peking. Emperor Kiang-long raised him to mandarin rank and put him in charge of the Department of Mathematics, where he stayed for many years. The court post gave him access to figures few Europeans could obtain.

His lasting gift to Europe was a census of China for the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth years of Kiang-long's reign, reaching the West in 1779. The work mattered because the Tatar rulers disliked census-taking, fearing the Chinese might grasp their own strength and grow restless. It also confirmed the reckonings of his predecessor Father Amiot. It showed a rising population, with 196,837,977 souls counted in the first year and 198,214,624 in the next.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustus-welb:
Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin was an English architect and archaeologist born in London in 1812, who died at Ramsgate in 1852. He was the only child of Augustus Charles Pugin, a French Protestant draughtsman who had fled France for London. The boy learned drawing from his father, inheriting his delicacy and dexterity, and force of character and piety from his mother. At fourteen he prepared drawings of Rochester Castle. The next year he sketched in Notre Dame in Paris while suffering from overwork.

In youth he designed furniture for Windsor Castle, built a model stage at home, made scenery for Kenilworth, and rearranged Drury Lane's stage machinery. A passion for the sea gave him his own smack, a small sailing boat. His creed was the Gothic embodiment of art as the only true Christian architecture. His merit, it says, was restoring architecture in England and reviving medieval forms across the land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldwin:
Baldwin was Archbishop of Trier and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, born in 1285, who died in 1354. He belonged to Luxemburg's noble counts and was brother to Emperor Henry VII. His father died in battle when Baldwin was three, so his mother Beatrix and his brother schooled him. At thirteen he went to Paris University under two private tutors and gained a thorough education.

In 1305 Henry sought Mainz for his nineteen-year-old brother, but Clement V refused so great a see to a youth. When Aichspalter cured the pope's severe sickness, he won Mainz himself, with Baldwin to follow Diether at Trier. Diether died in 1307, and Baldwin, consecrated at Poitiers in March 1308, took Trier that June. Aged only twenty-two, he filled the triple office of bishop, prince, and elector, paying old debts without new taxes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bassein:
Bassein is a town twenty-nine miles north of Bombay, a historic old Portuguese settlement in India. St Gonsalo Garcia, the only Indian saint, was born here, later crucified with Japan's first martyrs at Nagasaki in 1597. Founded in 1536 by Nunho de Cunha, who took the island from Bahadur Shali of Gujerat, it became Portugal's chief northern Indian settlement.

Rich timber, fertility, and a healthy climate made it a commercial center and home to many Portuguese noblemen. Franciscan Antonio do Porto, the Apostle of Bassein, is credited with converting 10,156 pagans. Mahrattas took it in 1739 and the English in 1802, leaving a ruined town whose fort ranks among India's finest Portuguese ruins. It remains a Christian oasis with nine churches, twelve priests, and 16,119 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benin:
Benin, the Vicariate Apostolic of the Coast of Benin, is a mission entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It covers a wide stretch of Upper Guinea on the Gulf of Guinea, once part of a great West African kingdom. A mission founded in Dahomey in 1860 took the Benin name because local people disliked the Dahomey title.

Splits soon shrank the vicariate, with Dahomey cut off in 1882 and the Niger mission in 1894. What remained lay between Dahomey, the Niger country, and the sea. The entry lists stations, clergy, schools, and converts, giving a working report on a young African mission at the century's turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benjamin:
Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob, receives a scriptural entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. His Hebrew name means son of the right hand, though his dying mother Rachel first called him Ben-oni, son of my sorrow, and Jacob changed it. After Joseph's loss, Jacob lavished affection on Benjamin, his last link to Rachel.

Reluctance marks the story: Jacob only let Benjamin travel to Egypt for corn under pressure, and Joseph showed him marked favour there. The entry then follows the tribe of Benjamin, its land, its warriors, and its later place in Israel's history. It joins a family tale to a tribal history in one compact piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berlin:
Berlin, capital of the German Empire and of Prussia, receives a substantial entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The city, on the Spree in Brandenburg, held just over two million people in 1905, of whom about 224,000 were Catholics. It grew from two Wendish settlements, Kölln on a Spree island and Berlin across the water.

History dominates the piece, from medieval revolts against Hohenzollern electors to the castle that became the royal residence. Later sections cover Catholic parishes, schools, hospitals, and orders in a largely Protestant capital. The entry joins civic history to a census of Catholic life in imperial Berlin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-dorni:
Bernard Dornin, the first American publisher of books distinctly Catholic in character, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Ireland in 1761, he died in Ohio in 1836 after political trouble drove him from home in 1803. Arriving in New York, he opened a book-selling and publishing business.

A New Testament printed in Brooklyn in 1805 and Pastorini's History of the Church in 1807 began his list. Moves to Baltimore in 1809 and Philadelphia in 1817 kept him at the head of American Catholic publishing for years. Archbishop Carroll and other bishops prized him as a vigorous writer and a trusted friend of the hierarchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-frowin:
Blessed Frowin, Benedictine abbot of Engelberg, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Nothing is known of his early life, save that historians of both Einsiedeln and St. Blasius claim him as their monk. His first sure fact is election as abbot of Engelberg in 1142, succeeding St. Adelhelm in the newly founded Swiss house.

As abbot he stood out for holiness, learning, and able rule, greatly enlarging the abbey's lands and privileges, civil and church alike. Its fame for study grew under him. He died in 1178, leaving Engelberg a strong and honoured monastery. The entry presents an abbot known mainly by his works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-ralph-sher:
Blessed Ralph Sherwin, an English martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1550 at Rodesley near Longford in Derbyshire, he died at Tyburn in 1581. Nominated by Sir William Petre to a fellowship at Exeter College, Oxford, he took his M.A. in 1574, famed as an acute philosopher and a fine Greek and Hebrew scholar.

Fleeing abroad in 1575, he was ordained at Douai in 1577 and returned to England's mission. Arrested and racked in the Tower, he was tried for treason as a priest and executed with Edmund Campion's companions. The entry presents a scholar-priest among the first Douai martyrs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cain:
Cain, the first-born of Adam and Eve, took his name from the Hebrew root kanah, to possess, recalling his mother's words at his birth. Genesis casts him as a tiller of the soil while his brother Abel kept flocks, and both offered sacrifice to God. Cain gave fruits of the earth, Abel the firstlings of his flock, and God accepted Abel's offering while rejecting Cain's, for reasons the text leaves unstated.

Commentators long debated the cause. One view, from the Septuagint, holds that Cain offered well but divided badly, keeping the better share for himself. Saint Augustine held that Cain gave God goods but not his heart. Angered by the rejection, Cain killed Abel, and Saint John ascribes the murder to Cain's evil works set against his brother's just ones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cartagena-spa:
Cartagena in Spain is a diocese suffragan to Granada since the concordat of 1851, and before that to Toledo. It covers Murcia and Albacete with towns in Alicante and Almeria, and its bishop lives at Murcia, a city of 111,539 people. Vandals nearly destroyed Cartagena in 425, and some writers infer it then lost metropolitan rank, though a Bishop Hector signed the decrees of Tarragona in 516.

Byzantines rebuilt the city. Bishop Licinianus wrote theological epistles late in the sixth century. After the Byzantine expulsion in 674 the see lapsed, with a Bishop John recorded under Moorish rule in 998. The city returned to Christian hands in 1247, and the see was restored under the Franciscan Pedro Gallego, confessor of Alfonso X. Nicholas IV moved the bishop's residence to Murcia in 1291 to escape pirate raids. Later bishops include Siliceo, tutor of Philip II, and Cardinal Belluga.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chaplain:
Chaplain comes from Latin capellanus, from capella, chapel. The favored derivation, drawn by Du Cange from earlier writers, traces capella to St. Martin of Tours' capa or capella, a short cloak the kings of France kept as a relic. Carried into war and enshrined under a tent on the field, the relic gave the tent the name capella, and its custodians became the capellani.

Others hold that capella simply means a covering. They say the name came from the tent-like structure French kings raised over the altar for soldiers in the field, with no link to St. Martin's relic. If the St. Martin derivation is right, court chaplains began as the clerics guarding sacred relics in royal palaces. In time they gained leave to say Mass in the oratories under their care, with spiritual jurisdiction over palace residents. They became confessors and teachers of all frequenting the court chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dumou:
Charles Dumoulin was a French jurist born at Paris in 1500 and dead there in 1566. He came of a noble family related to Anne Boleyn, mother of Elizabeth of England. After his doctorate in law he lectured at Orléans in 1521 and became an advocate of the Parlement of Paris. He soon left that post to study law alone, winning a great reputation for jurisprudence.

In 1542 he embraced Calvinism, then soon passed to Lutheranism, and violent attacks on the papacy forced him to seek refuge in Germany. He lectured on law at Tübingen in 1553 and afterwards at Strasburg, Dôle, and Besançon. Back in Paris in 1557, he was soon forced out again to Orléans and Lyons, returning to Paris in 1564. On his deathbed he renounced his errors and made peace with the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles-Francois Toustain was a French Benedictine of the Congregation of St-Maur, born at Repas in 1700 and dead at St-Denis in 1754. He came of a family of note and made his vows at Jumièges in 1718. After philosophy and theology at Fécamp, he went to Bonne-Nouvelle at Rouen to learn Hebrew and Greek. Ordained priest only in 1729, he approached Mass nervously and only after long preparation.

In 1730 he entered St-Ouen, later moving to St-Germain-des-Près and Blancs-Manteaux, and died while taking a milk cure at St-Denis. Fasts and ascetic practices had worn out his body. For twenty years he worked with his fellow monk Tassin on an edition of St. Theodore of Studium that never found a publisher. Their joint Nouveau traité de diplomatique, in six volumes from 1750 to 1765, treated its subject more fully and thoroughly than before.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-josep:
A biographical entry on Charles Joseph de Harlez, a Belgian priest and scholar of the ancient East who taught at Louvain. Born at Liège in 1832 to an old noble family, he first studied law with distinction, then abandoned a promising legal career for theology and ordination in 1858. After teaching posts at Huy and Louvain, he took up the chair of Oriental studies in 1871.

De Harlez poured his energy into the Zend-Avesta, the sacred writings of Zoroastrianism, a religion founded by the prophet Zoroaster. His French translation of 1875 to 1877, revised in 1881, advanced study of the text and of Old Persian language. He also argued that the Avesta and the Rig-Veda, the early hymns of India, differ more deeply than they seem to agree, a view his critics came to accept.

A short life of Charles Joseph Tricassin, a seventeenth-century Capuchin theologian from Troyes who died in 1681. Little is known of his personal history. The entry presents him as a deep student of Augustine, the early Church father whose teaching on grace shaped Catholic debate for centuries. Tricassin defended Augustine's doctrine against the Jansenists, a movement that stressed human helplessness without grace.

His books take up predestination, the belief that God destines some people for glory, the freedom of the fallen will, and grace sufficient for every person. They include Latin treatises printed at Paris between 1669 and 1679, a commentary on Augustine, and a French version of Augustine on grace and free will. His opponents, unable to answer him, reportedly bought up his books and burned them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-louis:
An entry on Charles de la Vallée Poussin, the Belgian geologist who created the teaching of geology and mineralogy at Louvain. Born at Namur in 1827, he studied humanities there and mathematics in Paris, spending ten years on literature and philosophy before turning to science. Appointed professor in 1863 on Omalius d'Halloy's recommendation, he built the university's courses in geology, the study of the earth, and mineralogy, the study of minerals, from scratch.

His papers, scattered through journals from 1876 to 1903, put him among the foremost Belgian geologists and crystallographers, students of crystal structure. Memoirs with A. F. Renard on the microscopic study of crystalline rocks won a Royal Academy prize and became a classic. He also fixed the true layering of Belgian coal-bearing limestone, studied how the Meuse valley formed, and helped prepare the official geological map of Belgium before his death at Brussels in 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-rolli:
A life of Charles Rollin, the French educator and historian who wrote his famous books only in retirement. Born in Paris in 1661, the son of a cutler, he won a college scholarship through his piety, studied theology, and taught rhetoric at the Collège de Plessis. At thirty-three he became rector of the university, and in 1696 principal of the Collège de Beauvais, dismissed in 1722 for opposing the papal bull Unigenitus.

Rollin began his Traité des Études, a guide to teaching literature, near the age of sixty. It urged studying national history and schoolbooks in the everyday language. His Ancient History ran to twelve volumes, and his Roman History, left unfinished at his death in 1741, shows warmth and ease but little critical bite. The entry also notes his share in the Jansenist St. Médard cemetery scenes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christophe-pl:
An entry on Christophe Plantin, bookbinder and publisher of Antwerp, born near Tours in 1514. The son of a servant, he learned binding and printing at Caen from 1535 to 1540, knew Latin early, and loved scientific books. After a short stay in Paris he reached Antwerp in 1548 and opened a bindery famed for inlaid bindings. In 1555 he founded a publishing house that within five years ranked first among typographers of his time.

Charged in 1562 with dealing with two religious reformers, Plantin fled Antwerp, then cleared himself. Only after two centuries did his Familist links and his printing of heretical works come to light. His great feat was the Biblia Regia, the eight-volume royal polyglot Bible finished in 1573 with Philip the Second's backing. The king then made him Royal Architypographer for breviaries, missals, and psalters, a privilege his successors held for two hundred years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-latin:
An entry on church Latin, the Latin of the Church's official books, the Bible and the liturgy, and of Western Christian writers expounding or defending the faith. It differs from classical Latin chiefly by new idioms and new words, while in syntax and literary method Christian writers match their contemporaries. Those differences come from the origin and purpose of church Latin itself.

Early Rome spoke prisca latinitas, the old tongue of Latium, until Ennius and others, trained by Greeks, enriched it for cultured circles. That polished idiom became classical Latin, preserved purest in Caesar and Cicero, while the populace kept the old speech, the sermo vulgaris. Daily contact forced cultured writers to borrow vulgar words, producing a mixed everyday idiom, the sermo cotidianus. From that living speech, shaped by Scripture and worship, church Latin grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-de-lor:
Claude de Lorrain, a French painter and etcher, was born in 1600 at Chamagne on the Moselle and died at Rome in November 1681 or 1682. He grew up poor in a large family and was orphaned by twelve. He lived with a wood-carver elder brother at Freiburg, learning to draw ornaments and arabesques. Sandrart says he was apprenticed to a pastry-cook, though pistori may misprint pictori, painter. About 1613 a relative took him to Rome and abandoned him.

He sought Gottfried Wals at Naples, who taught him perspective and landscape. Back in Rome in 1615, he joined Agostino Tassi's household as half servant, half assistant. After Venice in 1625, a Loreto pilgrimage, and wanderings through Tyrol, Bavaria, the Black Forest, and Nancy, he settled in Rome in 1627 for life. Popes, Emperor Leopold the First, and Philip the Fourth of Spain commissioned him, and in 1644 alone he finished seventeen important canvases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cochin:
Cochin, on India's Malabar coast, became suffragan to Goa by Paul the Fourth's bull of 4 February 1558. Leo the Thirteenth reorganised it under the Concordat of 23 June 1886 and the constitution Humanae Salutis Auctor of 1 September 1886, leaving it suffragan to Goa. The diocese forms two coastal strips, the first about fifty miles long and eight at its broadest, the second thirty miles long. Its higher institutions stand at Cochin and Alleppi.

When the Portuguese arrived, Malabar professed Hinduism, the Christianity of Saint Thomas, Islam, and Judaism, the last in a large colony. The Catholic community drew mostly from Nestorians and Hindus, with a fair share from Islam and rare converts among Jews. Portugal began Catholic mission work in India, and Cochin claims honour as its cradle. Eight Franciscan friars sailed from Lisbon with Cabral in 1500. Three were slain at Calicut on 16 November 1500, and the survivors reached Cochin about 26 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-la-r:
Pierre Marique's entry follows the Comte de La Rochejacquelein, French politician born at Citran on 28 September 1805, dead on 7 January 1867. His old family name runs back to Saint Louis's Crusade of 1248. His father Louis and uncle Henri won fame as royalist generals in the Vendée wars. His mother left much-edited memoirs. At sixteen he entered Saint-Cyr, won a cavalry commission in 1823, and fought in Spain and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828.

Made a peer in 1825, he resigned after the Revolution of 1830 brought younger Bourbons to the throne. Morbihan sent him to the legislature in 1842, where he sat with the Legitimist Right, sometimes backing liberal measures. In 1848 the Gazette de France backed his presidential candidacy, with few votes. Napoleon III made him senator in 1852, to Legitimist surprise. In the senate he defended Catholicism, though Marique faults his imperial foreign policy backing. He published works on taxes, pensions, and France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-convent-schoo:
George Cyprian Alston's entry treats convent education in Great Britain. Educating the young ranks nearly as old as religious life for women. From earliest times English children learned in convents. Eighth-century Wimborne nuns, helping Saint Boniface evangelize Saxony, founded convent schools wherever they went, reaching high scholarship. Medieval writers show English convent schools comparing favourably with boys' schools. All this ended at the Reformation in England.

Numerous convents opening in later nineteenth-century England produced numerous convent schools. Secondary schools stand almost all under Government inspection, with wide studies and fully qualified teachers. Over two hundred Catholic secondary schools in England serve under about sixty orders. Only Catholic students had been admitted hitherto, but September 1908 Board regulations changed admission. Higher education for women through convents barely leaves experiment. Ireland's and Scotland's convent schools compare favourably with England's. Superiors of England's principal teaching orders supplied most information.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-leo-thu:
A biographical entry traces Count Leo Thun-Hohenstein, an Austrian statesman born in Bohemia in 1811 and dead in Vienna in 1888, whose career linked prison reform, Czech culture, and imperial politics. Educated at Prague in law and philosophy, he studied England's political system and, in Paris, its prisons and charities for working people.

His first publication urged moral reform of prisons, and a later treatise defended Czech language and literature. During the 1848 revolution he became the effective ruler of Bohemia, was captured by insurgents at Prague, and later served as minister of education and religion. In later life he led Bohemia's Federalist party, defending full autonomy for the kingdom, and founded its newspaper, the Vaterland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demetrius-aug:
A biographical entry follows Demetrius Augustine Gallitzin, born at The Hague in 1770 and dead at Loretto, Pennsylvania, in 1840, who lived as prince, priest, and missionary. He came of one of Russia's oldest and richest families. His father had served fourteen years as ambassador to France, moving among Diderot, Voltaire, and d'Alembert. He professed godless philosophy despite nominal Orthodoxy.

His mother Amalie, baptized Catholic but religiously neglected, became fervent in 1786, and young Demetrius, baptized Orthodox and strictly disciplined, became a sincere Catholic near seventeen.
