Ordained for America, he reached Pennsylvania in 1792 and laboured forty years in the Alleghenies. At Loretto he built church and community, wrote books in defence of the Faith, and became known as the Apostle of the Alleghenies, dying amid the flock he had served. He gave his life to a rough frontier flock, riding long miles to sick beds and far farms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-lambin:
A life of Denis Lambin, a French scholar of Greek and Latin born about 1520 at Montreuil-sur-mer, who died at Paris in 1572. Service with Cardinal de Tournon took him twice to Italy, where he met leading Italian scholars and began translating Aristotle. Shock at the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew is said to have hastened his death.

At the Collège de France he held the Latin chair, then moved to Greek, while his editions of Horace, Lucretius, Cicero, and Nepos opened a new era in their texts. His translations also covered Aristotle's Ethics and Politics plus speeches by Aeschines and Demosthenes. Wide commentary marks the Horace and Lucretius editions, though he names his manuscripts less exactly than later scholars wish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dolphin:
The dolphin served early Christians as a symbol tied to the wider use of the fish. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that its swiftness pictures the eagerness with which Christians, sharers in Christ the true Fish, should seek knowledge of him. Pairs of dolphins are thus shown turning toward the sacred monogram or another emblem of Christ. In other cases the idea is love and tenderness.

Aringhi prints a dolphin with a heart, and other stones bear the motto thou hast a pledge of love. On tombs the dolphin can mark simple married love, while with an anchor it pictures the Christian clinging to Christ crucified. The entry thus reads a small sea creature as a sign of the single believer rather than of Christ himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-san-a:
Domingo Chimalpain was a Mexican Indian scholar of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. He was schooled in the colleges for Indians at Mexico City under clerical direction. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his family, having gained some wealth, backed his study of the antiquities of his own people. He wrote several works in Spanish and Nahuatl on the Mexican past.

Bustamante printed one of his works as Gomara's chronicle, though it seems a copy or paraphrase of it. He is credited with an ancient Mexican history, a chronicle from 1068 to 1597, notes on events from 1064 to 1521, and relations of the kingdoms of Aculhuacan and Mexico. The entry cautions that the attribution of some works is not yet certain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominique-par:
Dominique Parrenin was a Jesuit missionary born at Russey near Besancon on 1 September 1665. He joined the order in 1685 and was sent to China in 1697, reaching Peking the next year. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his wide knowledge and easy use of Chinese and Tatar-Manchu won the favor of the emperor Kangxi. Parrenin used that favor for religion and for science alike.

While feeding the emperor's curiosity about physics, medicine, and European history, he showed how Western science owed its rise to Christianity. Traveling with the court, he visited native Christians and won great persons to look kindly on the spread of the faith. He died at Peking in 1741, a courtier-priest of two worlds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dublin:
Dublin is an archdiocese covering about sixty miles of Ireland's middle eastern coast and reaching some forty-six miles inland. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives its bounds as County Dublin whole, Wicklow nearly whole, and parts of Kildare and Wexford. Its suffragans are Kildare and Leighlin, Ferns, and Ossory. The whole spans nearly seven hundred thousand statute acres.

Ptolemy in the second century marked Eblana on his map at Dublin's latitude. The annals first name Duibhlinn, black pool, under the year 291, for a river where the king of Ireland fought the Leinstermen. The entry follows the see from those early notices through centuries of Irish church history, citing Shearman, Halliday, and the public records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dunedin:
Dunedin is a diocese covering the Otago provincial district of New Zealand, with Southland, Stewart Island, and nearby isles. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry praises its lake and fiord scenery, the most picturesque in the country. Its area runs to about twenty-four thousand square miles, with four thousand of goldfields and more than two thousand of forest. Captain Cook may have visited this coast in 1770.

Beyond a few traders, no white settlers came until 1840, when families settled at Waikouaiti. In 1848 the Otago Association colonized the district on a large scale under the Free Church of Scotland, hoping to keep it a Free Kirk reserve. Catholic newcomers at first faced a cool welcome, and the entry traces how the diocese grew despite it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durand-ursin:
Durand Ursin was a Benedictine of the Maurist congregation, born at Tours on 20 May 1682. He took vows at Marmoutier at nineteen and gave himself to diplomatics, the study of old charters. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how in April 1709 he joined his brother Edmond Martene on a literary tour of France, gathering matter for a new Gallia Christiana. Having searched over eight hundred abbeys and a hundred cathedrals, they came back in 1713 to Saint-Germain-des-Pres.

Their haul filled the Gallia Christiana in part, while the rest appeared as the New Treasury of Anecdotes in five folio volumes from 1717. In 1718 the two set out anew, and the entry follows Durand to his later years. Branded a Jansenist appellant, he was sent to Noyon, then allowed to retire to Paris, where he spent his last years in letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durandus-of-s:
Durandus of Saint-Pourcain was a philosopher and theologian born at Saint-Pourcain in Auvergne. He died at Meaux on 13 September 1332. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he joined the Dominicans at Clermont and took his doctorate at Paris in 1313. Summoned to Avignon by John the Twenty-Second, he became Master of the Sacred Palace, explaining Scripture there. In 1318 he became bishop of Le Puy, moving to Meaux in 1326.

He earned the name Most Resolute Doctor for his vigorous defense of views new to the schoolmen. His works include commentaries on the Sentences and treatises on jurisdiction and on souls after death. His nominalism ran so far against the realism of his day that scholars date the third age of scholasticism from him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-cosin:
Edmund Cosin, also spelled Cosyn, was a Cambridge scholar whose birth and death dates are not known. Born in Bedfordshire, he entered King's Hall as a Bible clerk and took degrees in 1535, 1541, and 1547, holding fellowships at King's Hall, Saint Catharine's, and Trinity. Under Queen Mary he became Master of Saint Catharine's and chaplain to Bishop Bonner.

In 1558 he was chosen Vice-Chancellor of Cambridge, but as a Catholic he would not accept the Elizabethan church settlement. He gave up all his posts in 1560, lived in retirement at Caius College, and in 1568 chose exile over a forced oath. He was still living abroad in 1576, and the record then goes silent. The entry is a short, honest sketch of a career cut off by conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-coffin:
Edward Coffin, also known as Hatton, was an English Jesuit missionary born at Exeter in 1570 and dead at Saint-Omer in 1626. After study at Reims and Ingolstadt he was ordained at the English College in Rome and sent to England. He entered the Society in 1598, but on his way to the novitiate in Flanders the Dutch seized him near Antwerp and took him to England.

There he spent five years in prison before banishment in 1603. For twenty years he served as confessor at the English College in Rome, and he died on the road while volunteering for England once more. His writings include a preface to Father Persons, a reply to Dean Hall, and an Art of Dying Well drawn from Bellarmine, plus a short life of Bellarmine in his last illness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-sorin:
Edward Sorin founded the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, living from 1814 to 1893. Born at Ahuille near Laval in France, he was taught at first by his mother and then in the diocesan seminary, where he stood out for ability and good life. Drawn at first to China, he instead joined the Congregation of the Holy Cross, newly founded at Le Mans by Abbe Moreau.

Chosen to plant the congregation in America, he landed at New York in the autumn of 1841 with six brothers and pushed on to Indiana. In a harsh winter, in poverty, he began the work that became Notre Dame. Its schools spread to a dozen states, its sisters nursed nearly eighty soldiers in the Civil War, and Sorin founded the Ave Maria in 1865. He led his order as superior-general from 1868 until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elisha-john-d:
Elisha John Durbin was the patriarch-priest of Kentucky, born in Madison County in 1800 and dead at Shelbyville in 1887. Sent in 1816 to the preparatory seminary of Saint Thomas in Nelson County, he spent four years in work and study under missionaries such as David, Flaget, and Rosati. At Bardstown's Saint Joseph Seminary he learned under Francis Patrick Kenrick, and Bishop David ordained him in 1822.

Early in 1824 Bishop Flaget gave him the west and south-west of Kentucky, some thirty counties and more than eleven thousand square miles. From Union County he rode on horseback for over sixty years, building churches, planting stations, and visiting lone families, with yearly trips to Indiana and Nashville. Enfeebled in 1884, he took the small Princeton mission, then a Shelbyville academy chaplaincy, where he died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth-gal:
Elizabeth Galitzin was a Russian princess who became a Religious of the Sacred Heart, born at Saint Petersburg in 1797 and dead in Louisiana in 1843. Her father was Prince Alexis Andrevitch, and her mother was a friend of Madame Swetchine. When her mother left Orthodoxy for the Catholic faith, at risk of exile or death under Russian law, Elizabeth swore never to change her own religion.

Four years later, moved by her mother's steady life and by other family conversions, she examined the question and submitted. Father Rozaven found her an austere teaching order, the Society of the Sacred Heart. She took the habit at Metz in 1826, made vows at Rome in 1828, and professed at Paris in 1832. As secretary-general to foundress Madeleine Sophie Barat from 1834, and assistant-general and visitor to America from 1839, she served with ardour, though her strict rule made mistakes the foundress excused.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elphin:
Elphin is a diocese in Ireland, suffragan of Tuam, founded by Saint Patrick. This entry tells its first days from early Irish sources. On his tour through Connaught in 434 or 435, Patrick crossed the Shannon near Battlebridge. He came to Corcoghlan. There the chief, a noble Druid named Ono, gave him land and then his castle to found a church and monastery. The place, once Emlagh-Ono, took the name Elphin, rock of the clear spring.

That name came from a great stone Patrick raised from a well he opened. It also came from the crystal stream that still runs through Elphin's street. Patrick built Tempull Phadruig, Patrick's church, set up the see, and placed Saint Assicus over it as bishop, with Bite and Cipia beside him. Assicus, Patrick's goldsmith, made chalices, patens, and metal book covers for new churches. His successors kept a school of Celtic art in the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enrico-martin:
Enrico Martin was a hydraulic engineer in Mexico whose birthplace and birth date are unknown, dead there in 1632. Some call him Spanish, Humboldt thought him German or Dutch, others say a Mexican schooled in Spain. Most likely he was a Frenchman, Henri Martin, his name turned Spanish. He served as king's cosmographer, interpreter for the Inquisition, and publisher.

In 1607 Viceroy Luis de Velasco gave him the task of draining the valley around Mexico City. The valley was a closed basin, and in heavy rains the lakes of Zumpango and San Cristobal rose above Texcoco and flooded the city. Martin's plan was a canal outlet for Lake Zumpango, begun in November 1607 and finished in May 1609. Water and corrosion caved in the tunnel and blocked it. Later officials reported the work wanting, with sums spent and over a million workmen engaged. Martin wrote to the king to dispute their account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etschmiadzin:
Etschmiadzin is an Armenian monastery, since 1441 the ecclesiastical capital of the schismatic Armenians and seat of their catholicos. It stands in Russian territory, in the extreme south of the Caucasus, on the River Aras near Erivan. As early as the fifth or sixth century a monastery existed there attached to the royal residence of Valarshapat, the national centre of Armenia.

According to national tradition, the primatial see of Armenia was founded here by Saint Gregory Illuminator, Apostle of Armenia, early in the fourth century. On the site of his vision of the descent of the only Begotten One, Etschmiadzin, still kept as a national feast, he built a chapel. In time a church and monastery arose, centre of Armenia's national and religious life until the mid-fifth century. Then invasions of Caucasian hordes and Persian persecution began long wanderings, recalling the monks of Durham with Saint Cuthbert's body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-fromen:
Eugene Fromentin was a French writer and artist, born at La Rochelle on 24 October 1820 and dead at Saint-Maurice, near La Rochelle, on 26 August 1876. His father, a distinguished physician and art connoisseur, intended him for the bar. After brilliant studies, he came to Paris in November 1839 to study law. In 1843 he joined Maître Dénormandie, an attorney. But his literary and artistic inclinations made his profession insupportable.

Seeing Marilhat's 1844 exhibition settled him on painting as his calling. He became a pupil of Cabat, one of the restorers of modern landscape painting, with Flers, Huet, Corot, and Rousseau. A brief 1846 trip to Algeria clarified the path his work would take. In 1848 and 1852 he again visited Algeria for material. He exhibited at the Salon in 1847. In 1850 he sent eleven paintings and won a second-class medal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Expectation of the Blessed Virgin falls on 18 December in Spain. It began when Spain moved the Annunciation feast into Advent. The Tenth Council of Toledo fixed it to 18 December in 656. People call it Nuestra Senora de la O, for the long O sung after Vespers.

Gregory XIII approved the feast for Toledo in 1573 as a double major. It later spread to Venice, Tuscany, and the Papal States in turn. The Mozarabic Office gives special antiphons for each day of the octave. At Milan the Annunciation is still kept on the last Sunday before Christmas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-hemmerl:
Felix Hemmerlin was a Swiss provost and a fierce writer for church reform. Born at Zurich in 1388, he studied canon law at Bologna for four years. He became provost of St Ursus's collegiate church at Solothurn in 1421. There he reformed clergy, worship, and choir life with vigour and stubborn energy.

Hemmerlin wrote over thirty polemical treatises against ecclesiastical abuses of many kinds. He attacked friars, Beguines, cardinals, Curia, and pope alike. His enemies seized him in 1456 and had him condemned to lifelong confinement. He spent his last years writing in mild confinement at Lucerne until about 1460.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-joseph-:
Felix Barbelin was a Jesuit known far and wide as the apostle of Philadelphia. Born in Alsace in 1808, he entered the Jesuits in 1831. After years at Georgetown College, he moved to Philadelphia in 1838. There he pastored Old St Joseph's for over twenty-five years.

Barbelin founded St Joseph's Hospital and sodalities for men, women, and the young. He became first president of St Joseph's College in 1852. His charity and love of children won the veneration of Protestants as well as Catholics. He died in Philadelphia in 1869, still held in benediction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-martin:
Felix Martin was a French Jesuit antiquary, architect, and founder in Canada. Born in Brittany in 1804, he joined the Jesuits in 1823. Sent to Canada in 1842, he helped restore the Society there after long extinction. He became superior of the whole mission in Lower Canada in 1844.

Martin founded St Mary's College in Montreal, opening in a temporary building in 1848. Fire, plague, and typhus delayed the permanent college building for years. He designed St Patrick's Church in pure thirteenth-century Gothic style. He also gathered the archives of New France's colonial and missionary past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-baldw:
Francis Baldwin, also called Baudoin, born at Arras on 1 January 1520 and dead at Paris on 24 October 1573, was a celebrated jurist of the Reformation age. Sent young to Louvain, he studied law with great success and came to the court of Emperor Charles V at Brussels. He taught in turn at Bourges, Strasburg, Heidelberg, Douai, Paris, and Angers, travelling widely between Catholic and Protestant lands.

A story that he changed religion seven times cannot be proved. Early in life he showed a friendliness to Calvinism that sat uneasily with Catholic conviction, and princes used him to settle religious questions between the confessions. From 1560 his attachment to the faith grew stronger, and he defended Catholicism against Calvin in serious study. He died as a devout Catholic attended by the Jesuit Maldonatus, leaving prolific writings on law and church questions, including a work on Constantine the Great.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frankfort-on-:
Frankfort-on-the-Main, once the scene of the choosing and crowning of German emperors, lies on both sides of the Main in Hesse-Nassau, twenty-four miles above its meeting with the Rhine at Mainz. On 1 December 1905 it counted 334,978 people, of whom 105,814 were Catholics and 23,476 Jews.

Of twenty-five Catholic churches and chapels the most important is St. Bartholomew's Cathedral, where emperors were elected and crowned. It stands where Louis the German built the Saviour's church between 850 and 875, rebuilt in Gothic style in 1239 and renamed for St. Bartholomew, its choir remodelled from 1315 to 1338, transept added in 1346, and famous tower built between 1415 and 1512. After the fire of 1867 Denzinger, architect of Ratisbon Cathedral, restored the whole church and completed the tower by 1880.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederic-loui:
Frédéric-Louis Colin, a French Sulpician who moved to Canada in 1862, led his order there from 1881 until his death in 1902. Born at Bourges in 1835 and ordained at Paris in 1859, he taught theology and ran the higher seminary at Montreal before becoming superior. The entry presents him as both a noted preacher and a practical builder of schools.

Colin founded the Canadian College at Rome in 1885 so young Canadian priests could study at Roman universities, and opened a Montreal seminary of philosophy in 1892. For lay students he pushed Laval University forward, paid for a French literature chair himself, and brought lecturers from France and Belgium. He also began the custom of inviting a preacher from abroad for the Lenten sermons at Notre-Dame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-w-v:
Frederick von Egloffstein, a Bavarian who emigrated to America, earned the title Father of Half-tone Engraving in America. Born near Nuremberg in 1824, he served in the Prussian army before crossing the Atlantic. His method joined ruled glass screens with photography to print pictures in tone. The entry traces an inventor whose art met war and business in turn.

In 1861 he had glass plates ruled with wavy lines for his process, then left the work to fight for the Union. Wounded in North Carolina in April 1862, he retired as a brevet brigadier general. Backed by Archbishop McCloskey, he formed a company to engrave bank notes against counterfeiting, but the government refused his method. He later served on submarine works at Rock Island and Hell Gate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-bucel:
Gabriel Bucelin, a Benedictine historian born in Thurgau in 1599, wrote some fifty-three works on Germany's church and nobility. He entered Weingarten at thirteen, was ordained in 1624, and restored fervor and study at Saint Trudpert in the Black Forest. Driven by Swedish troops, he fled to Admont, then served as prior of Saint John's at Feldkirch from 1651 until near his death in 1681.

Bucelin ranks among the first writers of German church history. His Germania Sacra of 1655 lists the great churchmen and monasteries of Germany, while his topo-chrono-stemmatographia traces clergy and noble lines across the centuries. He also wrote on Constance, on Rhaetia, and on his own Benedictine order, leaving many works still in manuscript at Stuttgart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffroi-de-v:
Geoffroi de Villehardouin, marshal of Champagne and first historian in the French tongue, wrote the Fourth Crusade from inside its councils. Born about 1150 and marshal by 1191, he took the cross at Ecry in 1199 and joined the embassy to Venice. He helped elect Boniface of Montferrat leader in 1201 and labored to hold the host together at Zara and Constantinople.

After the Latin Empire rose in 1204, Villehardouin became marshal of Romania, settled Baldwin's quarrel with Boniface, and after Adrianople's disaster in 1205 rallied the army's retreat. Under Henry he fought at sea and won the fief of Messinople. His Conquest of Constantinople, dictated after 1207, stands among the oldest French prose, sober, exact, and vivid on Byzantine splendor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georges-chast:
Georges Chastellain, a Burgundian chronicler born in Flanders in 1403, recorded his age for the dukes he served. Schooled at Louvain, he soldiered briefly, traveled England and France, and entered Philip the Good's service. When Charles the Bold held a Golden Fleece chapter at Valenciennes in 1473, he knighted Chastellain with the title Indiciarius of the order. Chastellain died at Valenciennes in 1475.

His Chronicle of the Things of My Time, covering 1417 to 1474, survives only in fragments. His disciple Jean Molinet continued it after his death, and Buchon edited it in 1827, Kervyn de Lettenhove in eight volumes. His Recollections of Wonders and his delightful life of Jean de Lalaing complete the prose. Despite open partiality to Burgundy, his history holds accurate information, and as a poet he mastered the artificial grands rhétoriqueurs school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerald-griffi:
Gerald Griffin, an Irish novelist, dramatist, and lyricist born at Limerick in 1803, won fame with The Collegians and died a Christian Brother. Youngest of nine boys, he grew up at Fairy Lawn by the Shannon, schooled chiefly by his gifted, devout mother, roaming ruin-rich country and gathering folk tales. In 1820 his parents emigrated to Pennsylvania, leaving Gerald with a physician brother at Adare.

At nineteen Griffin carried tragedies to London, calling it a laughable delusion, and starved through two years of refused dramas and cheating magazines before steady work as a publishing reader. Tales of the Munster Festivals followed, and The Collegians, published when he was twenty-five, assured fame and fortune. He then burned nearly all his unpublished manuscripts and entered the Christian Brothers, who teach poor children. He died at Cork in 1840.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-chois:
Gilbert Choiseul du Plessis-Praslin was a French bishop born in 1613, who died at Paris in 1689. A Sorbonne doctor of 1640, he became Bishop of Comminges in 1644, visiting his diocese, restoring clerical discipline, and founding schools and colleges. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a pastor famed for charity into the stormier waters of French church politics.

In famine he pawned his own property for the poor, and in plague he nursed the sick until the disease struck him. Transferred to Tournai in 1671, he showed the same zeal. Yet he leaned toward the Jansenists, asking Rome in 1651 to issue no decision on their propositions, and he championed the Gallican Liberties. In the Assembly of 1682 his draft propositions gave way to Bossuet's four articles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-goscelin:
Goscelin, also spelled Gotselin, was a Benedictine biographical writer who died about 1099. Born in northern France, he became a monk of Saint Bertin's at Omer, and Bishop Hermann of Salisbury brought him to England, probably in 1053. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a tireless collector of materials for lives of English saints.

He visited many monasteries and cathedrals, gathering material wherever he went, and William of Malmesbury praised his industry in the highest terms. At Ely about 1082 he wrote a life of Saint Etheldreda. At Ramsey between 1087 and 1092 he wrote a life of Saint Ivo, and at Canterbury in 1098 his account of the translation of Saint Augustine's relics. His chief work was a two-part life of Saint Augustine of Canterbury, based on older records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-green-bay-wis:
Green Bay, Wisconsin, is a diocese established on 3 March 1868 from Milwaukee, covering sixteen Wisconsin counties over 15,387 square miles. At its founding it held thirty-one churches and forty-two stations, thirty-one priests, and about fifty thousand Catholics, Irish-American, German, Belgian, and Dutch. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows its first three bishops.

Joseph Melcher, born at Vienna in 1806 and ordained at Modena in 1830, was consecrated first bishop at Saint Louis in July 1868. He died at Green Bay in 1873. Francis Xavier Krautbauer, born in Bavaria in 1824, followed in 1875 and died suddenly in 1885. Frederic Xavier Katzer, born in Upper Austria in 1844, volunteered for the American mission in 1864, taught at the Milwaukee seminary, and became vicar-general before his own episcopate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregor-zallwe:
Gregor Zallwein was a canonist born at Oberviechtach on 20 October 1712, who died at Salzburg on 6 or 9 August 1766. After studying at Ratisbon and Freising he took vows at the Benedictine Abbey of Wessobrunn in 1733, studied canon law at Salzburg, and became master of novices and prior. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a lecturer valued across borders.

Sent to the new seminary at Strassburg in Carinthia at the Prince-bishop of Gurk's request, he became professor of canon law at the Benedictine University of Salzburg in 1749. He held the post until his death, with the rector's office from 1759. Unlike most German canonists of his time, he stressed sources and historical development, and foreign students attended his lectures. His chief work is Principia juris ecclesiastici, four volumes, Augsburg 1763.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-marti:
Gregory Martin was translator of the Douai Version of the Bible from the Latin Vulgate, born at Maxfield near Winchelsea in Sussex, who died at Reims on 28 October 1582. During thirteen years at Oxford he bore a reputation as a brilliant scholar and linguist, equalled only by his industry. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the man who bore the brunt of the translation.

He entered St. John's College as an original scholar in 1557 and befriended Edmund Campion. After conforming outwardly to the Established Church, he left Oxford to tutor in the Duke of Norfolk's family. Presenting himself at Allen's College at Douai in 1570 as a candidate for the priesthood, he made the whole translation in the first instance. Other great scholars at the English College assisted him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grosswardein:
Hungary's Latin diocese of Grosswardein, suffragan of Kalocsa-Bács, covered Bihar and Szilágy counties with parts of Békés and Szatmár and the city of Debrecen. Its foundation is dated to 1083 and credited to King St. Ladislaus, its patron, though the seat first stood at Bihar before Ladislaus moved it to Grosswardein.

Tartars wrecked bishopric and city in 1241, yet the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries brought growth, a Gothic cathedral rebuild, and Bishop Johann Vitéz, a promoter of humanism. After Mohács in 1526 the diocese sank fast: the last Catholic priest left the city in 1606, and Turks ruled from 1660 to 1692. Only then did reorganization begin, with a new cathedral stone laid in 1752.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guerin:
Eugénie de Guérin, born at the château of La Cayla in Languedoc in 1805, spent her life in that lonely house. Her mother's death left her, at thirteen, helping raise her siblings. Her devotion fixed on her brother Maurice, for whom she kept a journal from 1834 and wrote long letters, urging his soul even through the years when he gave up his faith.

Maurice, born in 1810, studied at Toulouse and Paris and spent a year at Lamennais's school at La Chênaie. He lost his faith in Paris, and came home to die devoutly in 1839, months after marrying. Fame reached him only after death, when George Sand praised his poem Le Centaure in 1840. His journal, letters, and poems appeared in print two decades later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-leonhard:
Nuremberg wood engraver Hans Leonhard Schaufelin, a pupil of Dürer born in 1490, made his name chiefly as an engraver. His paintings at Nuremberg, Munich, Cassel, and Ulm show Dürer's influence and a fine sense of beauty, above all in drapery. His prints carry a curious rebus on his name, his initials joined to a shovel.

He drew the illustrations for Emperor Maximilian's Theuerdank and two important engravings for Ulrich Pinder's Mirror of the Passion, and a series of his Munich paintings follows Christ and his Mother. His only known fresco stands at Nördlingen, where he became a magistrate in 1515 and rose to prominence before his death in 1540.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-raymond:
French Canadian author Henri-Raymond Casgrain, born at Rivière-Ouelle in 1831, wrote some of the best works in his country's literature despite near blindness. A seigneur's son educated at Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatière, he studied medicine, became a priest in 1856, and retired from Beauport and Quebec parishes when eye disease struck, freeing him for letters.

Tales of early colonists in the Soirées canadiennes led to histories of Marie de l'Incarnation, the Hôtel-Dieu of Quebec, Montcalm and Lévis, and a second Acadia. Biographies of de Gaspé, Garneau, Crémazie, and Chauveau followed. Research in French archives fed Quebec's Documents de Lévis. He edited Crémazie's works in 1882, taught history at Laval, and presided over the Royal Society of Canada in 1889 and 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-lang:
Henry of Langenstein, also called Henry of Hesse the Elder, was a theologian and mathematician born about 1325 near Langenstein in Hesse who studied and taught philosophy and theology at Paris. In 1368, when a comet appeared, he refuted the astrologers' claim that it foretold future events, and at the university's instance wrote three further treatises on the subject. When the Western Schism began in 1378 he sided with Urban VI. He argued for ending it by general council or compromise in his Epistola Pacis of 1379 and Epistola Concilii Pacis of 1381.

Forced from Paris in 1382, Henry spent time at Eberbach monastery. He then accepted Duke Albert III's invitation to Vienna in 1384, helping found its theological faculty and teaching there until his death in 1397. His printed works include defences of the Immaculate Conception, the ascetical Speculum Animae, and a treatise on contracts of buying and selling valued for its political economy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hildebert-of-:
Hildebert of Lavardin was bishop of Le Mans, archbishop of Tours, and a celebrated medieval poet, born about 1056 near Montoir on the Loire and dead in 1133 or 1134. Nothing is known of him before 1085, when the bishop of Le Mans made him head of the cathedral school. He became archdeacon in 1091 and bishop five years later, despite enemies who tried to blacken his name.

His stormy career crossed kings and dukes: William II of England summoned him in 1099 suspecting disloyalty, and he was taken prisoner in the Anglo-French wars of 1111. He rebuilt Le Mans cathedral, consecrated in 1120, attended the Synod of Reims and the First Lateran Council, and became archbishop of Tours in 1125. His poems and letters kept his fame alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hilduin:
Hilduin was a ninth-century Frankish abbot and archchaplain who died on 22 November 840. A scion of a prominent Frankish family, he was schooled under Alcuin, gained wide learning, and corresponded with Rabanus Maurus. Hincmar of Reims, his pupil, praised him warmly. The abbey of St-Denis near Paris came to him in 815, later adding St-Ouen, St-Germain-des-Prés, and St-Médard at Soissons.

Then Emperor Louis the Pious made him archchaplain, and Hilduin joined Prince Lothair's expedition to Rome in 824, bringing back relics of St. Sebastian. When he backed Louis's sons against their father in 830, he lost his abbeys and was banished to Paderborn and Corvey. Restored by 831, he reformed St-Denis and later wrote, at Louis's commission, a biography of St. Dionysius of Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-intendencia-o:
A mission district in Colombia's province of Saint Martin, ringed by the Cordilleras and watered by six rivers, is described in this short geography entry. It was created as a vicariate apostolic on 24 March 1908 and entrusted to the Society of Mary. It replaced two earlier prefectures set up in 1903 and 1904. Those prefectures followed talks between the Holy See and the Colombian government dating from 1902.

Batatas, Garagoa, Guavio, Humades, Meta, and Orinoco rivers cross a vast land. That land was still largely peopled by native inhabitants, put at about 50,000. Scarcely 10,000 of them had been baptized. The entry thus records a young mission frontier: its legal shape, its rivers and mountains, and the scale of evangelizing work still ahead of its missioners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ivan-sergejew:
Prince Ivan Gagarin came from a Russian princely house traced to Starodub's old rulers. He was born at Moscow on 1 August 1814. He died at Paris on 19 July 1882. His father was Prince Sergius Gagarin, a state councillor. His mother was Barbara Pushkin.

Gagarin entered state service young. He served first as attaché to his uncle at Munich. He later worked at Vienna and at the Paris embassy. In Paris he met Madame Sophie Swetchine and the preacher Ravignan. Their influence likely aided his conversion to Catholicism in 1842. On 19 April that year he made his profession of faith. The entry follows a diplomat turned Catholic convert.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-j-m-vincent-a:
Jean Marie Vincent Audin was born at Lyons in 1793. He died at Paris on 21 February 1851. He first studied theology at Argentière seminary. He then studied law and passed his exams. He never practiced law. He chose a literary career instead.

His early books included La lanterne magique in 1811. He wrote Blanc, bleu et rouge in 1814. He also wrote a history of events after Bonaparte's return. He contributed to the Journal de Lyon. He later settled in Paris and opened a bookshop. He wrote political articles and historical tales. Then he turned to full historical writing. The entry follows a bookseller who became a historian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-denis:
Paris preacher and philanthropist Jacques-Denis Cochin, born in Paris on 1 January 1726 and dead there on 3 June 1783, was the son of Claude-Denis Cochin, a famous botanist. Theology at the Sorbonne earned him a doctorate. Ordination as priest followed in 1755. The next year he took charge of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas parish, where he spent his life improving his people's material and spiritual lot.

Preaching of great unction and strength won him wide fame. His published works include four books of Sunday sermons, issued from 1786 to 1808. They also include Exhortations on feasts, fasts, and ceremonies and Retreat Exercises, both from 1778. Spiritual Writings appeared posthumously in 1784 through his brother. His parish's needs also inspired him to found a hospital, a parish priest whose charity outlived his sermons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-fremin:
James Fremin, a Jesuit missionary, was born at Reims on 12 March 1628 and died at Quebec on 2 July 1691. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1646. In 1655 he sailed for Canada's Onondaga mission, and the rest of his life went to evangelizing Native peoples. Invited by a Cayuga chieftain, he left in 1666 for Lake Tiohero near present Cayuga, though his stay was short.

The next year he was sent to revive Father Jogues' mission among the Mohawk, founding on the way the first Catholic settlement in Vermont, on Isle La Motte. Reaching Tinnontoguen, the Mohawk capital, he quickly learned the language and, by courage and kindness, won respect from his charges, though the Mohawk answered his preaching slowly. His chief care became Huron captives already Christianized, and in October 1668 he moved onward in his mission work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-bodin:
Jean Bodin, a French thinker born at Angers in 1520 and dead at Laon in 1596, founded the philosophy of history and shaped early political science. He learned law at Toulouse and later taught it there, speaking in 1559 on training youth for public life, then moved to Paris at forty, still little known.

His Method of 1566 set out how climate shapes society and government and sketched a theory of progress. His six-book Republic of 1577 expanded into a defence of authority and a portrait of the ideal state. Drawing on modern Germany, England, Spain, and Italy rather than antiquity alone, Bodin foreshadowed Montesquieu and gave politics a new, fact-based method.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-claude-m:
Jean-Claude-Marie Colin, a French priest born in 1790 and dead in 1875, founded the Marists, the Society of Mary. He studied at Saint-Jodard, then Alix and Verrières, before entering the Lyons seminary and was ordained in 1816, joining seminarians who dreamed of a society under Mary's patronage.

Though the shyest of the group, Colin became its true founder. As assistant at Cerdon he drafted provisional rules, won backing from bishops and ministers, and in 1836 gained Gregory XVI's approval for the society as an order with simple vows. As superior-general until 1854 he built houses and colleges in France and sent Marists to the missions of Oceania.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-cousin:
Jean Cousin, a French painter, sculptor, engraver, and geometer born at Soucy near Sens in 1500 and dead at Sens about 1590, began with glass painting and maths. Trained under Hympe and Grassot, he also wrote a successful book on mathematics while still young.

In 1530 Cousin finished windows for Sens cathedral on Saint Eutropius and painted glass for nearby châteaux, then moved to Paris and worked as a goldsmith. His Sainte-Chapelle windows at Vincennes count as the finest glass painting in France. Said to be the first Frenchman to paint in oils, he was hailed as founder of the French school, though his oils owe more to Italian models.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-dieu-:
Jean de Dieu-Raymond de Cucé de Boisgelin, a French cardinal born at Rennes in 1732 and dead in 1804, gave up his birthright as family head to serve the Church. Vicar-general of Pontoise, he became bishop of Lavaur in 1765 and archbishop of Aix in 1770, winning fame as a skilled ruler and generous benefactor.

Provence owed him a canal bearing his name, a bridge at Lavaur, and schools for poor children. When revolution brought famine threats to Aix, Boisgelin rallied magistrates and merchants, gave a hundred thousand livres toward grain, and urged clergy to press the people to return looted stores. Where law had failed, his sway restored order and bread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-desmaret:
Jean Desmarets de Saint-Sorlin, a French playwright and novelist born at Paris in 1595 and dead there in 1676. He held court posts, joined the Rambouillet salon, and became the French Academy's first chancellor. Richelieu, his protector, steered him to the stage.

His tragedy Aspasie triumphed in 1636 largely through the cardinal, and plays like Les Visionnaires, Scipion, and L'Europe followed, the last picturing Richelieu's view of Europe. Turning devout in 1645, Desmarets wrote verse versions of the Virgin's Office and the Imitation of Christ, and his twenty-six canto epic Clovis traces France's monarchy to God. It remains his greatest, if flawed, work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-edme-aug:
Jean-Edme-Auguste Gosselin, a French church writer born at Rouen in 1787 and dead in Paris in 1858, studied at Saint-Sulpice and taught dogma there even before ordination in 1812. He joined the Sulpicians on their return in 1814, led the Issy seminary as vice-president, then as superior from 1831 to 1844.

Poor health from 1844 left Gosselin to serve mainly by pen and example, and Renan praised him as the most polished and amiable man he knew. His lasting works are a twenty-two volume edition of Fénelon with eleven volumes of letters, plus a revised life of the archbishop. Those labours still anchor Fénelon study today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-hardouin:
Jean Hardouin, a French Jesuit historian born at Quimper in 1646 and dead in Paris in 1729, was a bookseller's son who joined the Society in 1660. He taught letters, rhetoric, and positive theology for fifteen years, then became librarian at Louis-le-Grand, succeeding Père Garnier, whose life he wrote.

Hardouin's works on coins, Themistius, and Pliny won him learned rank, though many books are uneven and error-prone. His Old Testament Chronology of 1697 startled readers by doubting nearly all classical authors, sparing only Cicero, Pliny, Virgil's Georgics, Horace, and parts of Homer, Herodotus, and Plautus. Paris parliament banned the sale, and debate followed him for life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-hippolyt:
Jean-Hippolyte Flandrin, a French painter born at Lyons in 1809 and dead at Rome in 1864, came from poor artisans and studied under Legendre and Révoil. Two forces shaped him: Lyons itself, religious and democratic, steeped in Roman culture, and Ingres, whose pupil he became in Paris in 1829.

Flandrin knew bitter want in Paris, at times without fire or bread, yet held by quiet faith. He won the Grand Prix de Rome in 1832 with Theseus recognised by his father. At Rome, where Ingres directed the French Academy after 1834, his gifts flowered amid classical and Christian art. His Dante and Virgil and later church murals made him the classic religious painter of his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-joseph-s:
Jean-Joseph Surin, a French Jesuit born in 1600 and dead at Bordeaux in 1665, won fame for holiness, suffering, and skill as a spiritual guide. Bossuet called him consumed with spirituality, and his order inscribed his name in its French menology.

Sent to Loudun to exorcise Ursulines, Surin was so horrified by sacrileges against three hosts that he offered his own spirit to demons in atonement. For over twenty years he felt possessed, at times unable to use hands, feet, eyes, or tongue, and plunged in despair over damnation. Yet in the pulpit, after the sign of the cross, his mind cleared and his voice carried with power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-morin:
Jean Morin, a French Oratorian priest born at Blois in 1591 and dead in Paris in 1659. He was judged by Dupin, with posterity agreeing, the most learned Catholic author of his century. Born Calvinist, he was converted by Cardinal Du Perron and joined the Oratory in 1618.

Morin led Oratory houses at Orléans and Angers, attended Queen Henrietta in England in 1625. He spent months at Rome in 1640 at Urban VIII's call to work for Greek-Latin union. Recalled by Richelieu, he published learned works in Paris while converting heretics and Jews. French clergy assemblies often sought his erudition, and he debated leading scholars of his day, including Buxtorf.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jocelin:
Jocelin, a Cistercian monk and bishop of Glasgow, died at Melrose Abbey in 1199. Prior of Melrose, he was chosen abbot in April 1170 on William's resignation. In May 1174 Perth chose him as Glasgow's bishop, succeeding Ingelram, consecrated at Clairvaux in June 1175.

Jocelin opposed York's claims over the Scottish Church at Northampton council, visited Rome in 1182 to win absolution for William the Lion and bring back the Golden Rose. He negotiated long over Saint Andrews's succession. He rebuilt and enlarged Glasgow cathedral, building its fine crypt and dedicating it in July 1197, enlarged its canons and prebends, and gave richly to Paisley, Kelso, and other houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-baptis:
Johann Baptist Franzelin, a cardinal and theologian born in Tyrol in 1816 and dead at Rome in 1886, was sent young by poor parents to the Franciscan college at Bolzano. He joined the Jesuits at Graz in 1834, studied theology at the Roman College, and was ordained in France in 1849 after revolution drove him from Rome.

Returning in 1850, Franzelin taught dogma at the Roman College for nineteen years from 1857, lecturing also on Arabic, Syriac, and Chaldean. He won foremost rank among theologians of his day. Consultor to Roman congregations and papal theologian at the Vatican Council, he was made cardinal in 1876 despite protests, keeping his bare rooms, poor dress, and four o'clock rising.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-heynli:
Johann Heynlin of Stein, a German theologian born about 1425 and dead at Basel in 1496. He was likely Swabian, schooled at Leipzig and Freiburg, then at Paris in philosophy and theology. There realist masters, seeing his promise, moulded him into a fierce foe of nominalism, and succeeded.

In 1464 Heynlin sought Basle's arts faculty, where nominalism ruled, and won admission only after vigorous opposition for peace's sake. As dean in 1465 he revised university statutes and fixed a firm curriculum, purging nominalist leanings as he had hoped. Returning to Paris in 1466, he took a theology doctorate, became university rector in 1469, and with Fichet set up Paris's first press in 1470.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-ment:
Johannes Mentelin was the first printer and bookseller of Strasburg and one of the most skillful early typographers. Born about 1410, he worked as an illuminator, or painter of manuscript decoration, at Strasburg, joined the painters' and goldsmiths' guild, and learned printing at Mainz. His Strasburg press began work before 1460, and his shop soon turned out large folio volumes in a masterly finish.

Mentelin rarely signed his books, so his printed catalogues, used to sell his stock, have proved vital for identifying his output. His type, a simplified Gothic hand, cannot match Gutenberg's or Schoffer's in design, but shows original touches in its capitals. About thirty of his works survive, including Latin Bibles of 1460 and 1463, a German Bible of about 1466, and first editions of Augustine, Chrysostom, Jerome, Aristotle, and Avicenna's Canon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-reuc:
Johannes Reuchlin, called Capnion in Greek form, was the German humanist who brought the study of Hebrew into Germany. Born at Pforzheim in 1455, he studied at Freiburg, Paris, and Basle. He took law degrees at Orleans and Poitiers. During trips to Italy he met the Platonic Academy at Florence and the leading Italian scholars. He served Count Eberhard of Wurttemberg, fled to Heidelberg, and became imperial judge, teacher of Greek and Hebrew at Ingolstadt, then professor at Tubingen.

His Rudiments of Hebrew of 1506, joining lexicon and grammar, was epoch-making, and his edition of the Penitential Psalms, with a word-for-word Latin translation served beginners. His cabala writings wandered into abstruse problems of mysterious names. Through the Reformation he stayed faithful to the Church. He tried to draw his grandnephew Melanchthon away from Luther. His quarrel with Pfefferkorn over Jewish books made him a symbol of humane learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-austin:
John Austin was an English lawyer and Catholic writer who pleaded for toleration during the Commonwealth. Born at Walpole in Norfolk in 1613, he studied at St. John's College, Cambridge, and Lincoln's Inn, and embraced the Catholic faith about 1640. Esteemed in his profession and admired as a master of English style, he gave his time wholly to books and literary pursuits.

Writing as William Birchley, he argued in The Christian Moderator of 1652 that persecution for religion stood condemned by nature, God's law, and principle. He added that Catholics did not hold the odious doctrines vulgarly charged against them. His Catholique's Plea of 1659 explained Catholic belief and listed the penal statutes against recusants. His devotions, adapted later for Anglican use, were often reprinted, and he died in London in 1669.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-calvin:
John Calvin was the French theologian whose Institutes became the standard of orthodox Protestant belief in the Reformed churches. Born at Noyon in Picardy in 1509 and dying at Geneva in 1564, he never met Luther, a generation his senior, and differed from him sharply in birth, training, and temper. Calvin, a middle-class lawyer's son trained in law and the humanities, never took Catholic orders or monastic vows.

Where Luther's eloquence struck with force, humor, and rudeness, Calvin reasoned by system, spoke to the learned even before multitudes, and persuaded by a teacher's authority and a deadly logic. He wrote French as well as Luther wrote German, and both men pioneered their native tongues. If Luther was a mystic, the entry sums up Calvin as a scholastic, giving articulate form to principles Luther had thrown out in vehement pamphlets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mary-odi:
John Mary Odin was a French Lazarist who became the first Bishop of Galveston and second Archbishop of New Orleans. Born at Hauteville in France in 1801, seventh of ten children, he worked on his father's farm and studied Latin under an uncle. He answered Bishop Dubourg's appeal for the Louisiana mission and reached New Orleans in 1822 and joining the Lazarists at the Barrens seminary near Saint Louis.

Ordained in 1824, he taught and preached to Indians on the Arkansas in vacations. He gave missions to non-Catholics and natives until failing health sent him abroad to gather recruits and funds. Sent to Texas in 1840 as vice-prefect, he labored among lapsed Catholics, non-Catholics, and Comanche Indians with gentleness and self-sacrifice. He declined Detroit's coadjutorship and was consecrated Vicar Apostolic of Texas in 1842, building the Church in the new republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mcloughl:
John McLoughlin was the physician and fur trader known as the great hero of Oregon's pioneer period. Born in Canada in 1784 to an Irish father and a mother descended from a Scottish Highlander of Wolfe's army, he was schooled in Canada and Scotland. He took up medicine while young and joined the North-West Company, taking charge of Fort William on Lake Superior.

Sent to Fort George at the Columbia's mouth in 1824, he moved company headquarters to Fort Vancouver. He ruled the Oregon Country for twenty-two years as an absolute but kindly autocrat, keeping peace without an army so that travelers went unescorted among formerly hostile Indians. He aided Methodist, Presbyterian, and Catholic missionaries while still an Anglican and joined the Catholic Church in 1842. He fed, clothed, and supplied the American immigrants of 1843 to 1845, a generosity that cost him his Hudson's Bay Company post in 1846.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-stephen-:
John Stephen Bazin was the third Bishop of Vincennes, whose promising episcopate lasted only months. Born at Duerne near Lyons in 1796, he was educated in France and ordained at Lyons Cathedral in 1822. Coming to America in 1830, he labored seventeen years among the Catholics of Mobile, Alabama, teaching the young, organizing Sunday schools, and founding the Catholic Orphan Asylum Society, while serving as vicar-general.

In 1846, at Bishop Portier's request, he went to France and secured Jesuits for Spring Hill College and Christian Brothers for the boys' orphan asylum, succeeding in both efforts. When Bishop de la Hailandiere resigned Vincennes in 1847, Bazin was consecrated his successor that October. His career of great usefulness was cut short by his untimely death at Vincennes in April 1848, only six months after his consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-strain:
John Strain was the first Archbishop of St. Andrews and Edinburgh after Scotland's hierarchy was restored. Born at Edinburgh in 1810, he was educated at the High School, Aquhorties Seminary, and the Scots College in Rome, and ordained in 1833. He labored at Edinburgh, Dumfries, and Dalbeattie for twenty-three years before becoming president of Blairs College in 1858.

On Bishop Gillis's death in 1864 he was named vicar apostolic of the eastern district and Pius IX consecrated him at the Vatican that September. He spent nineteen years multiplying clergy, missions, and schools and introducing religious communities of men and women. He labored long for the restoration of Scotland's regular hierarchy, achieved under Leo XIII in 1878 largely through his efforts. He became its first archbishop, holding his first diocesan synod in 1881 before his death in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-vertin:
John Vertin was the third Bishop of Marquette in Michigan's Upper Peninsula. Born at Doblice in Carniola, Austria, in 1844, he was educated at Rudolfswert and came to America at nineteen. His devout parents presented him to Bishop Baraga, who adopted him into the diocese and sent him to St. Francis, Wisconsin, to complete his theological training.

Ordained priest on 31 August 1866, he labored zealously for twelve years, showing great administrative ability. On Bishop Mrak's resignation, Leo XIII raised him to the episcopate, and his consecration took place at Negaunee, Michigan, on 14 September 1879. The greatness of his mind and heart showed in his management of the diocese and in untold charities, and he served Marquette until his death there in February 1899.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-cretin:
Joseph Crétin was the first Bishop of St. Paul, Minnesota, in the United States. Born at Montluel in France in 1799, he was ordained in 1823 and served at Ferney, once Voltaire's home. There he built a church, founded a boys' college, and revived faith among lukewarm parishioners. Longing for a wider field, he sailed with Bishop Loras in 1838.

After eleven years of frontier ministry at Dubuque, Prairie du Chien, and among the Winnebago, he was named bishop of the new St. Paul diocese in 1850. Consecrated at Belley in 1851, he reached St. Paul that July, blessed his flock in a log chapel, and within months raised a brick building serving as school, residence, and cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-kehrei:
Joseph Kehrein was a German educator and literary historian. Born at Heidesheim near Mainz in 1808, he studied philology at Giessen from 1831 to 1834 and taught at Darmstadt and Mainz. He became pro-rector and professor at Hadamar, then directed the Catholic teachers' seminary at Montabaur from 1855 until his death in 1876.

Kehrein wrote widely on the German language, its literature, and teaching method. His best-known books cover German drama, the grammar of modern German, Catholic pulpit oratory, and a biographical lexicon of Catholic German poets. He also edited old Catholic hymns and medieval Latin sequences, and his handbook of education ran to twelve editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-eusebio-:
Juan Eusebio Nieremberg y Otin was a Spanish Jesuit theologian and one of his age's most prolific writers. Born at Madrid in 1595 to German parents, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1614 against his father's wishes, studied Greek and Hebrew, and was ordained in 1623. At Madrid's Imperial College he taught humanities, natural history, and Scripture.

Seventy-three printed works and eleven manuscripts are ascribed to him, twenty-four in Latin. His best known are On the Value of Divine Grace of 1638 and On the Difference between the Temporal and the Eternal of 1640. The latter ran to fifty-four Spanish editions and many translations. The Spanish Academy lists him among its authorities. He died at Madrid in 1658.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jules-mazarin:
Jules Mazarin was the Italian-born cardinal who ruled France after Richelieu. Born in 1602, perhaps at Rome or Piscina, he served as a papal captain and diplomat in the Valtelline and Mantuan wars. His 1630 truce won Richelieu's esteem, and after posts as vice-legate at Avignon and nuncio in France, he entered French service and was naturalized in 1639.

Made cardinal in 1641, Mazarin took power on Richelieu's deathbed recommendation and Louis XIII's death in 1643. Under Anne of Austria and then Louis XIV, he held France through the Fronde, humbly mannered and gentle, until his death at Vincennes in 1661. His rule shaped the monarchy Louis XIV inherited.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kildare-and-l:
Kildare and Leighlin is a united Irish diocese, one of four suffragans under Dublin, covering 1,029,829 acres across Kildare, Carlow, and parts of neighbouring counties. This entry explains how Leighlin joined Kildare in commendam in 1678, when each see's income ran to only about fifteen pounds a year.

Kildare takes in northern Kildare, eastern King's County as far as Tullamore, and two baronies of Queen's County. Leighlin runs north to south over half of Queen's County, all of Carlow, and parts of Kilkenny, Wexford, and Wicklow. Its history opens with St. Patrick's travels in Leinster around 448. At Naas he baptized local kings and set bishops at Kilashee and Old Kilcullen. The 1901 census put the diocese's Catholics at 130,377 out of 149,168 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-martin:
Konrad Martin (1812-1879) was Bishop of Paderborn, a scholar-priest shaped by Munich, Halle, and Wurzburg. Barred by Prussia from South German degrees, he took his doctorate at Munster in 1835 and was ordained at Cologne in 1836.

He taught religion at Cologne's Marzellengymnasium after a sharp Latin pamphlet against Hermesianism made his name, and his two-volume school textbook of 1843 ran to fifteen editions before the Kulturkampf suppressed it. As professor of dogmatic theology at Paderborn and then bishop, he stood firm against Prussian church policy, and the article follows his writings, trials, and exile to Mont St. Guibert, where he died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-krain:
Krain, or Carniola, is a duchy and crownland of the Austrian Empire, 3,857 square miles with 510,000 people, ringed by Carinthia, Styria, Croatia, Trieste, Gorizia, and Istria. The Julian and Karavanken Alps cross it, rising to Triglav at 9,300 feet.

Its rivers include the Save and the Ljubljanica, and its lakes range from high mountain tarns to Cerknisko, which swells and shrinks each year and which Dante names in the Inferno. Over 95 per cent of the people are Slovenes, kin to the Croats, with German settlers at Gotschee keeping a Tyrolean dialect. More than 99 per cent are Catholics. Farming, wine from Vipava valley, lumber, cattle, and honey drive its trade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lambert-of-st:
Lambert of St-Bertin (about 1060-1125) was a Benedictine chronicler and abbot, born to a distinguished family and schooled at St-Bertin in grammar, theology, and music, then at famous schools across France. Prior for a time, he was chosen abbot in 1095 by both his monks and the canons of St. Omer.

Closer ties to Cluny brought Cluniac monks and reforms to his run-down house, against stiff opposition, until his energy won acceptance and repaired its finances. He befriended St. Anselm and swapped verses with Reginald of Canterbury. A contemporary tract praised his learning and lists lost writings on free will, divine foreknowledge, original sin, and the soul's origin. He is probably the St. Omer canon behind the Liber floridus, a vast encyclopedia begun in 1090 and finished in 1120.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leandro-ferna:
Leandro Fernandez de Moratin (1760-1828), the younger Moratin, was a Spanish poet and playwright of Madrid. His father Nicolas was a lawyer, poetry professor, and playwright who fought to reform Spanish drama on French classical lines. Fearing literature's precarious living, the elder Moratin apprenticed his son to a jeweller.

While apprenticed, Leandro won Academy prizes in 1779 for an epic ballad on Granada's capture. In 1782 he won a second prize for a satire on popular poets. Both caught statesman Jovellanos's eye. As secretary to Count Cabarrus's French mission in 1787, he spent a year in Paris studying French drama and meeting men of letters. Back in Spain in 1789, he took up his father's reform. He staged El Viejo y la Nina in 1790 under minister Godoy's patronage, then La Comedia nueva in 1792. Travel through France, England, and Italy completed his education.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-ellies-:
Louis Ellies Dupin was a French theologian and pioneer historian of the Fathers, born in Normandy in 1657 and dead in 1719. Kin to Racine's family, he studied at the Sorbonne, took his doctorate in 1684, and gathered notes on early Christian writers from the start.

His Nouvelle bibliotheque des auteurs ecclesiastiques, begun in 1686, treated biography, literary criticism, and dogma together, in a modern tongue, ahead of all rivals. Speed brought errors, and Benedictine Petit-Didier attacked him in three volumes, while Bossuet proved a sterner foe. The entry follows Dupin's bold method, his quarrels, and his lasting place as a founder of patristic study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-eugene-:
Louis Eugene Marie Bautain was a French philosopher and theologian, born at Paris in 1796 and dead there in 1867. After the Ecole Normale under Cousin, he taught philosophy at Strasburg in 1819, studied medicine, then theology, and was ordained in 1828.

As Strasburg seminary director he shone in apologetics against atheism and materialism, yet his fideism, the view that revelation alone gives sure knowledge, drew Rome's censure. He signed sets of propositions on faith and reason in 1835 and 1840, and in 1844 promised not to teach that God's existence and the soul's immortality lie beyond unaided reason. He later served as vicar-general of Paris and taught at the Sorbonne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-hennepi:
Louis Hennepin was a Recollect Franciscan explorer of North America, born at Ath in Belgium about 1640 and dead, likely at Rome, soon after 1701. Drawn both to austere religious life and to travel, he joined the Recollects, learned Dutch at Ghent, and toured Italian and German convents after ordination.

Sent to Canada, he joined La Salle's ventures, explored the Illinois country, and was captured by the Sioux, who carried him up the Mississippi. His published travels, vivid and much disputed, spread Europe's image of the interior, from Niagara to the upper river. Later editions and quarrels over his claims fill the entry, which weighs his fame against his faults.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-jouin:
Louis Jouin was a Jesuit linguist and philosopher, born at Berlin in 1818 and dead at New York in 1899. From a Huguenot family driven to Prussia, he entered the Catholic Church in Poland, quit Prussian military service, and joined the Jesuits at Rome in 1841.

Revolution drove him from Italy in 1848 to America, where he taught at Fordham across decades, with spells in Canada, England, and Montreal. He held chairs in science, mathematics, and theology, yet philosophy was his life's work: fifty-eight years of clear, compact teaching to young students, guarding them against the errors of the age. His treatises, mostly in manuscript, served his classes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-nicolas:
Louis Nicolas Vauquelin was a French chemist, born in Normandy in 1763 and dead in 1829. Apprenticed to a Rouen apothecary, he caught a love of chemistry, moved to Paris, and worked under Fourcroy, soon outdoing his master in analysis.

All his 378 papers were analytical, describing operations and results across plant, mineral, and bodily chemistry, and they advanced knowledge of what substances are made of. He found beryllium oxide in beryl in 1798, freed chromium from lead ores, fixed the makeup of carbon disulphide with Berzelius, and found quinic acid, asparagine, and camphoric acid. He also pioneered hands-on laboratory teaching for students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-thomass:
Louis Thomassin was a French Oratorian theologian, born at Aix in 1619 and dead at Paris in 1695. He joined the Oratory at thirteen, taught literature in its colleges, taught theology at Saumur, and settled at Saint Magloire seminary in Paris until his death.

His chief work, Old and New Discipline of the Church on benefices, ran to many volumes and editions, and his Dogmatic Theology, with its masterly treatise on the Incarnation, was reprinted often. He also wrote historical and dogmatic tracts on fasts, feasts, the Divine Office, church unity, truth, alms, and usury, plus a Hebrew glossary. Hurter called him a man of staggering learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lublin:
Lublin is a diocese and city in Russian Poland, on the Bistrzyca, a Vistula tributary, with 50,152 people in 1897, of whom 30,914 were Catholics. Eleven Catholic churches grace the town, chief among them the cathedral, built 1582 to 1600 and Jesuit-held until 1722.

Founded in the eleventh century, Lublin rose through Polish-Lithuanian affairs, hosting diets whose union of 1569 bound the two kingdoms against Moscow's rising power. King Sigismund pressed for full incorporation, since loose alliance had failed against the Teutonic Order and now faced Ivan III's centralizing state. Churches of St. Stanislaus, the Assumption, and St. Paul mark the city's long Catholic story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mardin:
Mardin was a town holding an Armenian archbishopric, a Chaldean bishopric, and a Syrian bishopric, plus the Capuchin mission headquarters for Mardin and Amida. Its old Syriac name, Marda, meant fortress. It appears by Constantius's reign and again in 506. It turned Christian under Tiridates II of Armenia late in the third century.

It loomed large in Catholic and Monophysite disputes, hosting a chief Monophysite monastery, and a Jacobite bishop by 684. After 1166 the Jacobite patriarch moved there from Diarbekir. Its strong hill site saved it from Hulagu and Tamerlane, and from 1574 it belonged to the Ottoman Empire. Perched 3,600 feet up above the grassy Sea of Mardin, it counted 25,000 people, 15,500 Muslim and about 3,000 Catholics of various rites. Armenian, Syrian, and Chaldean dioceses, plus Capuchin houses, schools, orphanages, and a Protestant mission, fill out its crowded church map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-eiseng:
Martin Eisengrein was a Catholic scholar and controversial writer, son of Protestant parents in Stuttgart, born in 1535 and dead at Ingolstadt in 1578. He studied humanities at Stuttgart, arts and philosophy at Tubingen, and law at Ingolstadt from 1553 to please his burgomaster father. Within a year he moved to Vienna, taking a Master of Arts in 1554.

Jesuit company in Vienna helped draw him to Catholicism, and he later taught at Ingolstadt, where lay professors and Jesuits clashed over chairs held since 1556. With Peter Canisius he settled faction differences in 1568, and by tact he reconciled non-Jesuit professors when Duke Albert gave Jesuits the paedagogium and philosophy course in 1571. His greatest Ingolstadt service was organising its library, adding private collections of Bishop John Egolph, Chancellor Thaddeus Eck, and Professor Rudolph Clenek. His controversial sermons, some oratorical masterpieces, helped suppress Lutheranism in Bavaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-ignati:
Martin Ignatius Joseph Griffin was a journalist and historian, born at Philadelphia in 1842 and dead there in 1911. In early manhood he wrote and edited for various Catholic publications. Named secretary of the Irish Catholic Benevolent Union in 1872, he founded and edited its organ from 1873 to 1894, first as the I.C.B.U. Journal, then as Griffin's Journal.

His local Catholic history articles in that journal led to the American Catholic Historical Society of Philadelphia, founded 22 July 1884, where he served as librarian till death. In January 1887 he launched American Catholic Historical Researches, editing it till he died. A tireless delver in byways of the past, he gathered much original data for United States church history. His chief books were History of Commodore John Barry of 1903 and Catholics and the American Revolution, three volumes of 1907 to 1911. He also pushed total abstinence and building and loan associations in his native city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-von-du:
Martin von Dunin was Archbishop of Gnesen and Posen, born near Rawa, Poland, in 1774 and dead at Posen in 1842. He studied theology at Rome's Collegium Germanicum from 1793 to 1797 and was ordained in September 1797. 

On Archbishop Wolicki's death in 1829 he administered the archdiocese, was named archbishop in 1831, and was consecrated that July. He set out to reorganise his vast diocese at once. Prussian mixed-marriage law stood hostile to Catholic interests. It fined priests who refused to bless unions without promises on the Catholic party's worship and children's Catholic upbringing. Pius VIII's 1830 brief barred blessing without a children's-education promise, and Dunin enforced it. Unable to win leave to return from Berlin, he slipped secretly to Posen in October. He was seized on the night of 5 to 6 October, and held at Colberg fortress until Frederick William III died in June 1840. Freed that August, he returned to Posen amid rejoicing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-medellin:
Medellin, an archdiocese in Colombia, stands as metropolitan of Antioquia and Manizales across the departments of Medellin, Antioquia, and Manizales. Before the civil redrawing of 1908, its bounds matched the old Department of Antioquia, a name from native words meaning hill or mountain of gold. That land, over 22,000 square miles in the Magdalena, Cauca, and Atrato basins, was split into ten civil provinces, from Aures to Uraba.

The diocese lies in the Andes, where rough mountains make travel poor, though a railway is being built from Puerto Berrio to Medellin. Catholicism is professed by all, while other cults not against Christian morals are allowed. Spanish is the tongue, and the people descend from Spanish conquerors, mestizos, and negroes, living without race strife, chiefly through the Church's teaching. The Cauca valley Indians were once cannibals. Schooling is free and, as far as possible, compulsory, with 400 primary schools and more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-josep:
Michael Joseph Quin, who started the Dublin Review, was born at Thurles, County Tipperary, Ireland, in 1796 and died at Boulogne-sur-Mer on 19 February 1843. After moving to London he qualified as a lawyer at Lincoln's Inn. While waiting for briefs he turned to journalism. For the Morning Herald he wrote up his time in Spain from late 1822 through the first four months of 1823. The piece came out in book form as A Visit to Spain in 1823.

The next year brought two renderings from his pen: the Memoirs of Ferdinand VII and a Statement covering the chief events in the public life of Don Agustin de Iturbide. Later trips through Hungary, Wallachia, Servia, and Turkey supplied A Steam Voyage down the Danube in 1835, which came out in French and German as well. His most lasting work was the Dublin Review, still the leading Catholic periodical in the British Isles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michel-baudou:
Michel Baudouin, an Italian missionary born in Quebec, Canada, on 8 March 1692, entered the Society of Jesus in France at twenty-one. He reached Louisiana on his return to America in 1728, and died at New Orleans in or after 1768. Soon after landing in Louisiana he was sent to the Choctaw mission, where he laboured eighteen years.

When fruit seemed near, his superior recalled him to New Orleans, owing to English-stirred unrest among the Indians and the dangers he faced. He served as Superior-General of the Louisiana mission from 1749 until the Jesuits' expulsion from the colony in 1763. When that blow fell, Baudouin was not banished like his fellow Jesuits. With a pension of three or four hundred francs he was allowed to stay, a planter having offered the aged priest a home on his estate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-milo-crispin:
Milo Crispin was a monk and cantor of the Benedictine Abbey of Bec. He wrote the lives of five of its abbots: Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, Gulielmus de Bellomonte, Boso, Theobaldus, and Letardus. His life of Lanfranc appears in the Bollandists' Acta Sanctorum for 28 May, while the other four, those of Theobaldus and Letardus being mere summaries, are printed in Patrologia Latina, volume 150.

Milo must have been an old man when he wrote, for in the last chapter of his Lanfranc life he records something he himself heard St. Anselm say. Since Anselm died in 1109 and Letardus lived until 1149, Milo's own lifetime evidently stretched well into the twelfth century, spanning the abbey's golden age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mortmain:
Mortmain, from Old French for dead hand, means land held in such a way that it cannot be alienated. More precisely it means land held by a corporation, a body of many persons joined under one name with perpetual succession. Alienation to such a body was once expressed by the now obsolete words amortization and amortisement. The giver was said to amortize.

The entry traces how church and other corporations amassed estates that never returned to circulation. They escaped feudal dues and death duties. England answered with statutes from Magna Carta onward, culminating in the Mortmain Acts. Those acts restricted gifts of land to corporations and required licences for them. The entry follows the law's development, its evasions through uses and trusts, and its later reform and repeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-causs:
Jesuit preacher Nicolas Caussin, confessor to Louis XIII of France, paid for honest counsel with exile. Born at Troyes in 1583, he joined the Jesuits in 1609 and won fame as an orator, which brought Cardinal Richelieu to summon him to court to guide the young king's conscience.

Caussin urged the king to recall his mother and exiled kin, advice Richelieu hated. Accused of disloyal dealings, Caussin was banished to Brittany until Richelieu died in 1643. Back in Paris, he prepared his works for print before his death in 1651. His father, a physician of wide practice, helped fund the young man’s early training.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-pouss:
French painter Nicolas Poussin, born near Rouen in 1594, left a poor youth in Paris to become the classic master of French art in Rome. A wandering painter brought him to the capital in 1612, where he starved, painted in the provinces, and studied under masters who shaped him little.

Engravings after Raphael and Giulio Romano opened his eyes to antique beauty, and after three tries he settled in Rome. There he painted grave, ordered scenes from antiquity and Scripture, prizing design and story above show, until his death in 1666. Three attempts to reach Rome failed before he settled there for good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occasions-of-:
Occasions of sin are outward circumstances, things or persons, that lure a person toward sin through their nature or human frailty. The entry insists on a sharp line: the cause of sin lies in the perverse will within, while an occasion stays outside and cannot, strictly, cause the act.

Yet whoever must shun sin must also shun its occasions, since the end binds one to the means. Theologians split proximate occasions, where most people of like temper fall, from remote ones lacking that danger, and agree that proximate occasions must be fled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-original-sin:
Original sin, in Catholic teaching, means chiefly the hereditary stain borne from Adam, not only Adam's own first sin. Augustine's formula puts it plainly: the deliberate sin of the first man causes original sin in his descendants, a wound carried by birth through descent from Adam.

The entry sets the doctrine against Theodorus of Mopsuestia, who denied Adam's sin brought death, and against Pelagius's friend Celestius, who held Adam's sin hurt himself alone. Scripture, tradition, reason's objections, and the stain's nature and transmission fill the remaining sections. Theodorus of Mopsuestia opened the controversy by denying Adam’s sin brought death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulin-martin:
Paulin Martin was a French Bible scholar born at Lacam in Lot on 20 July 1840 and dead at Amelie-les-Bains on 14 January 1890. He studied at Montfaucon's little seminary and theology at Saint-Sulpice, under Le Hir's influence. Too young for ordination at theology's end, he went to Rome's French Seminary, attended Gregorian lectures, and was ordained in 1863.

Staying at Rome till 1868, he took a sacred theology doctorate and canon law licentiate and began lifelong Semitic study, chiefly Hebrew, Syriac, Aramaic, and Arabic. As a Syriac scholar he first drew notice. After ten years as Paris curate, he held the Institut Catholique's chair of Scripture and Oriental languages from 1878 to 1890. His best work, lithographed lectures of 1882 to 1886 on New Testament textual criticism, with a technical survey of Paris Greek manuscripts, crowns those twelve years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-ii-kin:
Philip II was king of Spain from 1556 to 1598, only son of Emperor Charles V and Isabella of Portugal. Born at Valladolid in 1527, he learned French and Latin yet spoke only Castilian, and loved architecture and music. He married Maria of Portugal in 1543, then Mary Tudor of England in 1554, and at Brussels in 1555 his father ceded him the Low Countries, Castile, Aragon, Sicily, and Burgundy.

Two keys unlock his reign, the entry argues: defence of Catholicism and opposition to heresy, pursued through absolutism. Wars in Italy and the Low Countries, trouble with Antonio Pérez, and the revolt of the Netherlands filled his years. The Armada of 1588, led by an incompetent commander and wrecked by storms, proved an irreparable disaster that opened Spain's decline. He died at the Escorial in 1598.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-charle:
Charles Dupin, known as Baron Charles Dupin, was a French mathematician and economist, born at Varzy in 1784. He entered the École Polytechnique at twenty-three, studied three years under Monge, and became a naval engineer, later inspector-general of the navy. His 1813 pamphlet on geometry offered new theories on the indicatrix of curved surfaces and orthogonal surfaces, and he joined the Academy of Sciences in 1818.

A professorship at the Conservatoire des arts et métiers followed in 1819, with pamphlets on geometry, the navy, industry, and shipping.
