His six-volume Voyages in Great Britain of 1816 to 1819, a personal inquiry into English commerce and industry, made him a leading statistician. His 1824 Carte de la France éclairée first coloured a map by education's spread. Charles X made him baron in 1824. For forty years he sat in legislative assemblies, and Napoleon III named him senator. He died at Paris in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-chaste:
Pierre Chastellain was a French Jesuit missionary among the Hurons, born at Senlis in 1606. He entered the Society in 1624 and at thirty sailed with the future martyrs Isaac Jogues and Charles Garnier and Governor Montmagny, Champlain's successor. In July 1636 he and Garnier left Three Rivers with the Indian trading canoes for the Huron country, and that September both fell ill with smallpox but recovered.

For nearly fifty years Chastellain laboured at Canadian missions among the Hurons and at Quebec. Great strength of character joined a gentleness never ruffled and unfailing charity toward others. Amid his laborious mission work he composed Affectus amantis Christum, a quarto of 483 pages on love of the Lord Jesus through the whole week, published at Paris in 1647. He died at Quebec on 14 August 1684.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-guerin:
Pierre Guérin de Tencin was a French statesman and cardinal, born at Grenoble on 22 August 1680. Schooled by Oratorians there, he entered the Sorbonne, became prior in 1702, and took his doctorate in 1705. Made vicar-general of Sens, he accompanied Cardinal de Rohan to Rome in 1721 as conclavist. He backed Cardinal Conti, who became Innocent XIII, after winning a promise to give the purple to the unworthy minister Dubois.

Benedict XIII, with whom he held great influence, consecrated him Archbishop of Embrun in June 1724. Eager for higher honours, he persecuted Jansenists overzealously, and at his Embrun synod of August to September 1727 suspended the eighty-year-old Bishop Soanen of Senez for appealing against Unigenitus. Created cardinal in February 1739, he remained ambassador at Rome until 1742, then took Lyons, succeeding in November 1740. Louis XV made him minister of state in September 1742. In 1752 he retired to Lyons. He died there in 1758.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-suzann:
Augustin Cochin was a Paris writer and civic leader who belonged to the liberal Catholic circle around Montalembert and Lacordaire. He was born in Paris in 1823 and wrote on economic and political questions. He became vice-mayor of the tenth district in 1850 and mayor in 1853. He joined the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences in 1864.

His books ranged from a study of Pestalozzi's schools to reports on poverty in England and the condition of French workers. His work on the abolition of slavery was crowned by the French Academy in 1861. A candidate for deputy of Paris, he polled six thousand votes but lost heavily, and he died at Versailles in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piusverein:
The Piusverein, or Pius Association, is the name of Catholic associations in several European countries, all aimed at organising lay Catholics for public life. The German association, named for Pius IX, was founded at Mainz in 1848 by Adam Franz Lennig and Caspar Riffel. Its aim was to defend German Catholics' religious freedom and civil rights.

Its Mainz congress of October 1848 united thirty-eight societies into the Catholic Association of Germany. Yearly meetings then spawned the Vincent de Paul Society, the Boniface Association, and the Catholic Journeymen's Union. The entry also covers the Swiss association of 1855. It had 225 groups and 35,000 members by 1899. The Austrian press association of 1905 had 840 groups and over 63,000 members by 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-of-spain:
Port of Spain archdiocese, covering Trinidad, Tobago, Grenada, the Grenadines, St Vincent, and St Lucia, counts about two hundred thousand Catholics. Spanish discoverers brought Christianity, and missions followed permanent settlements. The first Trinidad preachers, Francisco de Cordova and Juan Garcés, died at Indian hands in 1513. Friars came in 1596 and stayed until Britain took over in the early nineteenth century.

Three friars were slaughtered by natives in 1699 and buried at San José de Oruña, then the colony's chief town, where they were honoured as martyrs. The governor and a Dominican died defending them. Dominicans and other orders worked Grenada and the other islands until British rule replaced them with secular clergy. When Britain took Trinidad in 1797, surrender terms kept Catholicism's status unchanged, and the new rulers kept paying clergy. In 1820 Governor Woodford had Trinidad's Catholics removed from Guayana's bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reifenstein:
Reifenstein was a Cistercian abbey in Eichsfeld, founded on 1 August 1162 by Count Ernst of Tonna and first called Albolderode, within the electorate of Mainz. Its monks came from Volkerode near Mühlhausen, worked briskly at farming and trade, and gathered about fifty estates nearby during the thirteenth century. Little survives about its inner life, and even the order of its abbots is uncertain.

The abbey's ruin came through one of its own monks. Heinrich Pfeifer left in 1521, turned Lutheran, preached rebellion in his home town of Mühlhausen, and shared leadership of the Thuringian Peasants' War with Thomas Münzer. In May 1525 he burned Reifenstein to the ground, but after the defeat at Frankenhausen he was seized near Eisenach and executed, dying unrepentant. By 1524 only six monks had remained, and decline was complete.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-prosper-:
René-Prosper Tassin, French historian of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint-Maur, was born at Lonlay in the Diocese of Le Mans in 1697 and died in Paris in 1777. Professed at Jumièges in 1718, he formed a close friendship with his brother religious Dom Toustain, and together they prepared a new edition of Theodore the Studite, visiting Rome for the task.

Their work was broken off by a dispute between the Abbey of Saint Ouen and the chapter of Rouen, backed by the erudite Sass. The two friends wrote against Sass for their brethren. They lived at the Abbey of Rouen until 1747, when their general called them to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris. Defending their abbey's deeds forced a deep study of diplomacy, and several of Tassin's manuscripts remain in the National Library at Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-rapin:
René Rapin, French Jesuit, was born at Tours in 1621 and died in Paris in 1687. He joined the Society in 1639 and taught rhetoric, writing widely in verse and prose. His Eclogae Sacrae of 1659 won him the title of Second Theocritus, and his garden poem, Hortorum libri IV of 1665, twice translated into English, placed him among the foremost Latin versifiers.

His best known critical essays treat Horace and Virgil, the eloquence of his own time, and Aristotle's poetics beside ancient and modern poets. He also wrote theological and ascetic treatises, including a dissertation on Jansenist doctrine and L'esprit du christianisme. Sainte-Beuve's Port Royal finds fault with him at every turn, but recent Jansenism studies judge him reliable in the main.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-aston-:
Robert Aston Coffin was an English bishop and devotional writer who followed Newman from Oxford into the Catholic Church. Born at Brighton in 1819, he was schooled at Harrow and Christ Church, Oxford, and became vicar of St Mary Magdalen, Oxford, in 1843. A follower of Newman, he joined the Catholic Church at Prior Park in December 1845, two months after Newman himself.

After a year tutoring, he went to Rome, was ordained in 1847, and joined Newman's Oratory in England. Drawn to the Redemptorists, he entered their novitiate at Saint-Trond in 1849 and professed in 1852. He served as rector of St Mary's, Clapham, then as provincial of the English Redemptorists, while giving missions and retreats across Britain and publishing ascetical books. Chosen Bishop of Southwark in 1882, he died at Teignmouth in 1885.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roscelin:
Roscelin, a monk of Compiègne, taught as early as 1087. He knew Lanfranc, St Anselm, and Ivo of Chartres. At Soissons in 1093, accused of Tritheism, he denied the doctrines charged to him. Fear of excommunication drove the denial, since he later went back to his early theories. He lived in turn in England, at Rome, and finally back in France. Of his writings only a letter to Abelard survives.

His fame rests more on his theological Tritheism than on his Nominalism. His nominalism, the sententia vocum or doctrine of words, was an anti-Realist answer to the problem of universals. Where Realists treated genera and species as things, Nominalists held them to be mere words. Above all, only the individual exists: universals are not things. Otto of Freisingen called Roscelin the first in his time to establish the doctrine of words.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-tatwin:
Tatwin, archbishop of Canterbury, died on 30 July 734 after an episcopate of only three years. A Mercian monk from Briudun in Worcestershire, Bede praised him as a man famed for religion and prudence and deeply learned in Scripture. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a short reign remembered for steady, quiet work.

Chosen to succeed Brihtwald, he was consecrated at Canterbury on 10 June 731 and received the pallium, the woollen band of office, from the pope. He blessed Nothbald as abbot of St Augustine's and consecrated bishops for Lindsey and Selsey. Miracles were reported at his tomb, Goscelin wrote them down, and rhymed riddles ascribed to Tatwin survive, though his Anglo-Saxon poems are lost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-trumwin:
Trumwin, missionary bishop to the Picts, died at Whitby in Yorkshire some time after 686. Consecrated by Theodore of Canterbury, he later counted as the first bishop of Whithorn in Galloway. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a mission that ended in retreat when the Picts won back their freedom.

With a few followers he withdrew to Streaneshalch, now Whitby, where Bede says he laboured usefully for many years before burial in St Peter's church. He attended the Synod on the Alne in 684 and went with King Ecgfrith to Lindisfarne to persuade Cuthbert to accept a bishopric. The single charter bearing his name is judged a clear forgery, and the entry keeps the honest record small.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samuel-de-cha:
Samuel de Champlain, founder of Quebec and father of New France, was born at Brouage in Saintonge about 1570, or 1567 by another account, and died at Quebec on 25 December 1635. Son of the mariner Antoine Champlain and Marguerite Le Roy, he learned seamanship beside his father and briefly served a Catholic commander against the Huguenots. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows an explorer who wrote his own story.

Navigation, he wrote, ranked first among arts, since by it men learn new countries, bring home riches, overthrow pagan idolatry, and proclaim Christianity to the ends of the earth. Soldiering never suited him, and he turned to the sea and to Canada, founding Quebec and mapping the north-east. The entry traces his voyages, alliances with native peoples, and the colony he built with stubborn patience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanhedrin:
The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and court of justice among the Jews, its name taken from the Greek synedrion, assembly, which passed into Aramaic use. Greek-speaking Jews often called it the gerousia, assembly of elders, while later Hebrew writers favoured Beth-Din, house of judgment. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tests the venerable origin stories against the evidence.

Jewish tradition gave the body a hallowed age, with some doctors tracing it to Moses' council of seventy elders and others to Jehoshaphat's tribunal. Neither body, the entry argues, matches the Sanhedrin in make-up or powers, and its origin should not be sought in the Great Synagogue either. The entry then sets out the court's true history, membership, and role in law and in the Gospel narratives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-stevin:
Simon Stevin, born at Bruges in 1548, died at Leyden in 1620. He worked for some years as a bookkeeper in an Antwerp business house, then administering the Franc of Bruges. After travels in Prussia, Poland, Sweden, and Norway, he settled in the Netherlands for life. Maurice of Nassau prized him so highly that he studied mathematics and engineering under Stevin's direction. He rewarded him as director of finances, inspector of dykes, and quartermaster-general.

His influence on science was great and lasting. He began in 1582 with Tables of Interest, spreading through the business world an easy method of calculation still prized by Low Country merchants. Then came a very original geometry in 1583 and a treatise on logic. In 1585 De Thiende gave the oldest systematic account of decimal reckoning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sin:
Sin is treated in this long theological entry under five heads: its nature, its division, mortal sin, venial sin, and permission and remedies, closing with the sense of sin. Evil, following Thomas Aquinas, is a lack of form, order, or due measure. God alone is essentially and perfectly good. Finite beings can suffer privation of the perfection due them.

By the perfection it limits, evil is metaphysical, physical, or moral. The entry then defines sin as moral evil, a free human act against right reason and God's law. Mortal sin severs the soul from grace, venial sin wounds but does not kill charity, and the closing sections weigh how God permits sin and what remedies heal it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
Founded at Dôle, France, in 1606 by Anne de Xainctonge. The Society of the Sisters of Saint Ursula of the Blessed Virgin pairs members' sanctification with neighbours' salvation through teaching and works of mercy. At a time when girls' education was more than neglected, Xainctonge set out to do for girls what Ignatius had done for boys. Classes opened at Dôle on 16 June 1606, public, free, and without distinction of rich or poor.

The institute spread through France, Switzerland, and Germany, suffering persecution and finding new freedom in each new country. During the Revolution its houses closed, but peace restored its life, and Mother Roland de Bussy founded a new house at Tours in 1814. Expelled again by the anti-religious laws of 1901, the mother-house moved to Haverloolez-Bruges in Belgium, with later foundations in New York, Rome, and Sluis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spain:
Spain, in the strict sense, is the whole south-western peninsula of Europe. The name has narrowed since Portugal's political separation to the largest of its four divisions, beside Portugal, Andorra, and Gibraltar. This very long entry opens with the name itself. It weighs derivations from a Punic word for rabbit, suggested by coins and by Strabo's label of a land of rabbits, against a root meaning north.

From there it ranges across geography, history, church, and culture. It follows a peninsula shaped by Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Visigoths, and Moors. Readers seeking a single survey of Spanish Catholic life and national story will find the encyclopedia's fullest treatment here, detailed enough to reward slow reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bertin:
St. Bertin was abbot of St. Omer, born near Constance about 615. He died about 709. This entry follows a boy who entered the Luxeuil monastery in France while young, and prepared for his missionary career under St. Columban's austere Rule. About 638 he set out with two confreres, Mummolin and Ebertram, for the north of France, to assist his friend and kinsman, Bishop St. Omer, in evangelizing the Morini.

That country, now in the Pas-de-Calais department, was then one vast marsh, dotted here and there with hillocks and thick with seaweed and bulrushes. On one hillock, Bertin and his companions built a house. From it they went out daily to preach the word of God among the natives, most still heathens. Gradually some converted heathens joined the little band, and a larger monastery rose on a tract called Sithiu donated to Omer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-birinus-be:
St. Birinus, or Berin, was confessor, first bishop of Dorchester in what is now Oxfordshire, and apostle of Wessex. This entry warns readers not to confuse his see with Dorchester, the capital of Dorsetshire. His date of birth is unknown, and he died on 3 December 650 at his see, buried in his own church there. Later, in 680, Bishop Headda moved his remains to Winchester cathedral, where Bishop Ethelwold enshrined them in silver and gold in 972.

Bede says Birinus came to Britain on Pope Honorius I's advice. Asterius at Genoa had consecrated him bishop. He promised to sow the seed of holy faith in the inner parts beyond the English. On his arrival in 634 he found the West Saxons so pagan that he devoted his ministry to them. His zeal won the conversion of King Cynegils in 635, his son Cwichelm in 636, and Cwichelm's son Cuthred in 639.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-columba-of: St. Columba of Spain, a Spanish nun, was beheaded by the Moors at the monastery of Tabanos in 853. Christians rescued her body, said to have been thrown into the Guadalquivir. Her relics were honoured in Old Castile, at the priory of St. Columba and at Nagara's royal Abbey of Our Lady.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edwin:
Edwin, first Christian king of Northumbria, spent thirty years as a hunted exile before winning his throne by battle. Born about 585, son of Aella of Deira, he wandered from court to court while Ethelfrid of Bernicia sought his life. At Redwald of East Anglia's court, bribes failed to buy his betrayal, and the battle on the River Idle in 616 killed Ethelfrid and opened Edwin's way. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 12 October 633.

In 625 he sought the hand of Ethelburga, sister of the Christian king of Kent, offering to weigh Christianity fairly against his own faith. Her coming north brought the new religion into his court. The entry thus joins two conversions: a kingdom's, and a king's own slow turn from pagan exile to Christian ruler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-egwin:
Egwin, third bishop of Worcester and founder of Evesham Abbey, was a Mercian prince dragged from retirement into office. Forced by popular acclaim to take the see about 692, he pursued Christian discipline with an apostolic zeal that soon wrecked his popularity. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 20 December 720, though it may have come three years earlier.

Legend thickens around him, yet rests on fact. Bound in chains, he threw the key into the Avon before a pilgrimage to Rome, and a servant later found that very key inside a fish caught in the Tiber. Vindicated by the pope, he returned to a shepherd's vision of the Virgin marking the site of Evesham. King Ethelred granted the land, and the abbey rose there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eimhin:
Eimhin, abbot and bishop of Ros-mic-Truin in sixth-century Ireland, built a southern colony on the Barrow's banks. Of Munster's royal race and brother to two other saints, Culain and Dairmid, he took over the monastery from its founder Abban. Monks followed him from Munster in such numbers that the place earned the name Ros-glas of the Munstermen. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places his house eight miles by water from Munster's edge.

Little survives of his early religious life, and the entry is honest about the gap. Some credit him with a life of Patrick, a claim the piece reports without settling. What stands firm is geography and community: a Leinster abbey, at the meeting of Suir and Barrow, filled with southern Irish religious and students under a Munster abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fridolin:
Fridolin, missionary founder of Säckingen on the Upper Rhine, is honoured as the first Irishman to evangelize the Alamanni. Later tradition makes him a noble Irishman who first preached at home, then crossed to France and sought Hilary's relics at Poitiers, building them a church. In a dream Hilary sent him to an island in the Rhine. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places him in the sixth century, under the Merovingians.

Its earliest documentary source is a life by Balther, a Säckingen monk of the early eleventh century. Fridolin won the unknown island from the emperor Clovis and founded the monastery there. The entry separates that eleventh-century biography from later legend, giving readers a founder known through one monk's book, a dream, a relic church, and a Rhine island monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-germaine-c:
Germaine Cousin, shepherdess of Pibrac, learned patience in a stable and became her village's beloved saint. Born in 1579 to humble parents near Toulouse, she came into the world with a deformed hand and scrofula, and lost her mother in infancy. Her father's second wife, fearing contagion for her own children, had Germaine kept from the house and set to shepherding almost from infancy. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Pibrac to 1601.

Nights found her bed in the stable or on vine branches in a garret. In that hard school she practised humility and patience, adding voluntary mortifications of bread and water to poverty, infirmity, harsh seasons, and a home without affection. Yet her lonely life became, in the entry's words, a source of light and blessing, through a marvellous sense of God's presence. Suffering schooled a shepherdess into sanctity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ghislain:
Ghislain, confessor and anchorite of Hainault, cleared forest ground and built the chapel that gave a town his name. Born in the first half of the seventh century, probably of German origin, he lived in the age of Amand, Waudru, Aldegonde, and Madelberte. With two unknown disciples he cleared land near Castrilocus, now Mons, then settled at Ursidongus. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Saint-Ghislain to 9 October, about 680.

At Ursidongus he raised an oratory to Peter and Paul. Aubert of Cambrai summoned the near-unknown hermit to test his intentions, then protected him warmly. A stay at Roisin brought gifts of Celles and Hornu estates. Ghislain also moved Waudru to build at Castrilocus, and likely shaped Aldegonde's vocation at Maubeuge. The entry follows a hermit whose solitude seeded monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lebwin:
Lebwin, apostle of the Frisians and patron of Deventer, preached fearlessly among wild tribes on the Yssel. Born in England to Anglo-Saxon parents at an unknown date, he was educated in a monastery and fired by Boniface, Willibrord, and other great English missionaries. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Deventer about 770.

Ordained, he went to Utrecht, where Gregory, third bishop there, welcomed him gladly and gave him Overyssel's mission on Westphalia's border, with Marchelm, Willibrord's disciple, as companion. A widow named Abachilda received him hospitably. He preached boldly, built a little chapel at Wulpe on the Yssel's west bank, and won numbers, even nobles. Soon a larger church rose at Deventer on the east bank, with a residence for Lebwin beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-leonard-of:
Leonard of Limousin, patron of prisoners, is famous everywhere and historically certain nowhere. No part of his history stands on certain ground, since his earliest Life dates from the eleventh century and carries no historical weight. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 retells its extraordinary legend while denying it authority.

That legend makes him a noble Frank of Clovis's time, with Remy of Reims as godfather. He won from the king the release of many prisoners, refused episcopal honours Clovis offered, and entered Micy monastery near Orléans. Later he preached in Aquitaine, and, having through prayer secured the Frankish queen's safe delivery, received Noblac near Limoges and founded a monastery there. No trace of his veneration predates the eleventh century, yet from then it spread through France and all western Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-maximus-of:
Turin's first known bishop, Maximus, is known with certainty from only two dates, and the entry is frank about that thin record. Born probably in Rhaetia about 380, he appears at the synod of Milan in 451. There he stood eighth among nineteen subscribers to Leo I's doctrinal letter on the Incarnation. He appears again at Rome in 465, oldest of forty-eight bishops present. After that year history falls silent about him.

A later life, written after the eleventh century, is dismissed as wholly unreliable. His genuine legacy lies in his sermons and theological writings, which show a pastor preaching against pagan survivals and Arian error in fifth-century northern Italy. Turin honours him as patron, and his name stands in the Roman martyrology on 25 June. The piece models honest handling of a scant early record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-oswin:
Oswin, king of Deira and martyr, ruled seven peaceful years before betrayal handed him to his rival. Son of Osric, king of Deira, he was carried to Wessex for safety after his father's murder in 634. On the death of his kinsman Oswald in 642 he returned, chosen by the people of Deira over Oswy, who ruled Bernicia.

Peace, order, and happiness marked his reign, but Oswy schemed for his death. When Oswy declared open war, Oswin disbanded his weaker army and sought shelter with Hunwald, an ealdorman he had favoured. Hunwald betrayed him to Oswy's officer Ethelwin, and Oswin was murdered at Gilling on 20 August 651. Buried at Gilling and later moved to Tynemouth, he was honoured as a martyr king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-swithin:
Swithin, bishop of Winchester, is remembered less for his life than for his grave, his rain, and his shrine. Very little is known of him, since his biographers wrote long after his death and contemporary documents barely mention him. He served as a trusted counsellor of Egbert of Wessex, helping in church affairs, and probably tutored Egbert's son Ethelwulf.

Elected bishop of Winchester, he was consecrated by Ceolnoth of Canterbury, apparently on 30 October 852. On his deathbed he asked burial outside his cathedral's north wall, where passers-by would walk over him and eaves rain would fall on him. Translated with pomp in 931, he drew miraculous cures and popular canonisation. His shrine was destroyed and relics scattered in 1538. He died on 2 July 862.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-tarkin:
Tarkin, also Talarican, bishop of Sodor and the western isles of Scotland, converted pagans along Scotland's northern coasts. Probably of Pictish origin, though the Aberdeen Breviary of 1509 calls him Irish-born, he was raised to the episcopate, legend says, by Pope Gregory. Adam King's Kalendar of 1558 styles him bishop and confessor in Scotland under King Solvathius.

Following Dalriadic chronology, the Bollandists place Selvach's reign from 706 to 726, and with Gregory II pope from 715 to 731 they date Tarkin's episcopate about 720. He offered the Sacrifice daily, lived a zealous and mortified life, and converted many pagans by preaching and example. Churches in Moray, Ross, and Aberdeen honour him, and his name lives in Kiltarlity and Kiltalarglan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-theod:
Stephen Theodore Badin was born at Orléans in 1768. He became the first priest ordained on the soil of the original thirteen American states. He also stands as the pioneer missionary of Kentucky, and this entry follows his long road to that work.

Revolution closed his seminary in Paris in 1791, so he sailed for America that November. Bishop Carroll ordained him at Baltimore in 1793. Sent to Kentucky that autumn, he said his first Mass there at Lexington in Advent 1793. For fourteen years he rode over 120 miles between scattered settlements, founding parishes and raising churches. Later he worked in Michigan and Ohio, wrote against a critic in Cincinnati, and died there in 1853.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-superior-wisc:
Superior is a diocese of northern Wisconsin, erected on 3 May 1905 from the northern part of La Crosse and the northwestern part of Green Bay. A suffragan of Milwaukee, it covers 15,715 square miles across sixteen counties, with its episcopal residence in the city of Superior. At its founding it counted 39 secular and 17 regular priests serving 93 churches and 33 stations.

English, German, Polish, French, Italian, Slovak, and Bohemian congregations all appear, alongside Indian industrial schools at Odonah and Bayfield run by Franciscan sisters and fathers. Its first bishop, Augustin Francis Schinner, consecrated in July 1905, pushed parochial schools across the diocese. By 1910 the Catholic population reached 48,028 whites and 3,015 Indians, with nearly 5,000 young people under Catholic care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-american-:
Founded in 1857 with warm backing from Belgium's bishops, this Louvain seminary trained priests for service in the United States. Two American bishops launched it: Martin Spalding of Louisville and Peter Lefèvre, administrator of Detroit. Its full title honoured the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

American-born students could study theology in Europe while learning Old World languages and customs, and young Europeans could prepare for ministry across the Atlantic. At first the college taught elementary and advanced theology alone, expecting students to arrive with philosophy already studied. Later growth, staff, and daily life fill out a portrait of a school built to link two churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-augustinu:
Germany's Catholic press found an organised champion in this society, founded in 1878. Its work was practical: backing the launch of Catholic papers, supplying trustworthy news to daily journals, training Catholic journalists, aiding members in need, and speaking for the profession. It also sought harmony among Catholic publishers and a common line on the questions of the day.

Disorganisation had shown itself painfully during the Kulturkampf, the state's campaign against Catholic life, when scattered papers could not answer attacks in concert. Earlier efforts, including a publishers' society, had failed. Plans matured at the Catholic Convention at Würzburg and later gatherings, until the Verein gave German Catholic journalism a single, steady voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-shroud-of:
Turin's famed linen, claimed as the cloth Joseph of Arimathea wrapped around Christ's body, is examined here with care. Blackened by age, it bears a faint yet distinct impress of a human form, back and front, measuring about thirteen and a half feet by four and a quarter. A supine body laid along one half, the other doubled back over the head, explains the double image.

Giulio Clovio's miniature shows what viewers saw about 1540. History traces the cloth to Lirey in Troyes diocese about 1360, then Chambéry in Savoy by 1453, where fire in 1532 charred fold corners. Evidence, devotion, and doubt are weighed without forcing a verdict on authenticity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-twelve-ap:
Twelve holy Irishmen of the sixth century, students together at Clonard, bear the title explained here. About 520 Saint Finian founded his famous school at Cluain-Eraird, Eraird's Meadow, now Clonard, and saints and scholars flocked from every part of Ireland. His Irish life claims an average of 3,000 scholars under instruction, and Lauds hymn sings of three thousand men taught by a humble doctor pouring forth the Word like a spring.

Two Ciarans, two Brendans, two Columbas, Mobhí of Glasnevin, Ruadhan of Lorrha, Senan of Iniscathay, Ninnidh of Loch Erne, Lasserian mac Nadfraech, and Canice of Aghaboe make the twelve. Gathered on the Boyne and Kinnegad, they carried Clonard's learning across Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-universit:
Turin's university, born from wartime disruption, is the subject here. Founded in 1404, it took shape when lectures at Piacenza and Pavia broke down amid Lombard wars. Professors of theology, medicine, and arts at Piacenza won leave from Louis of Savoy-Acaia to carry on their courses at Turin.

Antipope Benedict XIII granted a studium generale privilege in 1405, the emperor added permission in 1412, and John XXIII confirmed the grants the next year. Three faculties organised the studium: theology, law both canon and civil, and medicine with arts and philosophy. Turin's archbishop always served as chancellor, while students long chose their own rector.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-lewis-:
Thomas Lewis Brittain, a Dominican priest born near Chester in 1744, spent his life teaching and guarding a community of exiled nuns. His parents were Protestants, but he became a Catholic at sixteen, studied in Picardy, and joined the Dominicans at Bornheim in 1767. He taught there with success and became regent of studies, taking the title Master of Sacred Theology in 1790.

That year he moved to Brussels as director of the exiled English Dominican nuns, a charge he held for thirty-seven years. When French troops threatened Brussels in 1794 he led the sisters to Bornheim and then, by ship, to England, settling them at Hartpury Court near Gloucester. Elected provincial in 1814, he also wrote grammars, poems and works of apologetics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tighernach-o-:
Tighernach O'Braein, Irish annalist and abbot of Roscommon and Clonmacnoise, died in 1088. Little is known of his life beyond his Connaught birth in the early eleventh century. His Annals, among the earliest Irish annals, matter most because he tried to set Irish events beside Europe's, from the earliest times to his own day.

His learning shows in quotations from Bede, Josephus, Eusebius and Orosius, besides the Vulgate. The Irish manuscripts he drew on are lost, so his sources for Irish history can no longer be traced. Only fragments survive, in twelfth- and fourteenth-century vellums at Oxford and Dublin. O'Conor printed them in 1825 with many errors, and Whitley Stokes later gave a sounder text and translation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-timothy-warre:
Timothy Warren Anglin, Canadian journalist and member of Parliament, was born at Clonakilty, County Cork, in 1822 and died in Canada in 1896. His family was ruined in the famine of 1846 and 1847, and he emigrated to Saint John, New Brunswick, in 1849. A gifted speaker, he made his name as the province's most vigorous Catholic press writer.

He founded the Weekly Freeman and then the Morning Freeman in 1851. Though a strong temperance man, he fought total prohibition as too drastic and unworkable, and the measure was soon repealed. Elected for Saint John in 1860, the first Catholic ever returned there, he opposed Confederation, fearing higher taxes for New Brunswick and doubting that union was needed to keep the imperial link.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-toledo-spain:
Toledo, in Spain, is the primatial archdiocese whose archbishop, almost always a cardinal, ranks first among Spanish clergy. Its suffragans are Coria, Cuenca, Madrid-Alcala, Plasencia and Siguenza. Its territory is unusual, falling into four separate sections ringed by other dioceses, the chief lying in New Castile around the city of Toledo itself.

Gothic, Muslim and Christian ages all shaped the see. Ildefonsus, conqueror of the Jovinian heresy and defender of Mary's virginity, and Julian II, author of a history of Paul's rebellion against Wamba, shine among its Gothic prelates. During 373 years of Muslim rule the see never died out, and after the reconquest it regained its primacy over the Spanish church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-turin:
The chief town of a civil province in Piedmont, formerly capital of the Duchy of Savoy and the Kingdom of Sardinia. It stands on the left bank of the Po near the Dora Riparia. Its population is 270,000. Its institutions include a university, a musical lyceum, the Accademia Albertina of 1652 with the Mossi Gallery, and a National Library of 1714 holding the Bobbio manuscripts.

The Palazzo Madama stands on the old decuman gate, reshaped by Juvara in 1718. The Palazzo Carignano of 1680 housed Parliament from 1848 to 1864. Before Rome, Taurasia was already an important city of the Taurini, a Ligurian people, whose story meets Hannibal in 218 B.C., and the Mole Antonelliana rises 580 feet over the regular-planned city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-turpin:
Turpin was an eighth-century churchman who rose from monk of St Denis to Archbishop of Reims around 753. He died in 800. He sat with eleven other French bishops at the Council of Rome, where Pope Stephen III condemned the rival claimant Constantine. He won favours for his diocese from Charlemagne and built up the cathedral library by having books copied. Legend soon wrapped itself around his name and made him a hero of epic song.

Much of the entry untangles that legend from the man. It weighs a famous chronicle of Charlemagne and Roland long credited to Turpin. It shows why he cannot have written it, since it names places and musical customs from centuries after his death. It traces the chronicle's real shaping by monks at Compostela and Vienne, its praise by Pope Callistus II, and its part in reviving pilgrimage to St James.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-co:
University College Dublin is a constitutional college of the National University of Ireland, chartered on 2 December 1908 under the Irish Universities Act of that year. Its members include every Royal University graduate who had matriculated at University College, St Stephen's Green, Dublin, or at the Medical School in Cecilia Street. Its history is thus linked with Newman's foundation in Ireland.

The Irish Jesuits opened University College at St Stephen's Green in November 1883, in the old Arts School of the Catholic University. Until the new college began work in November 1909, Irish Catholic and national university education centred mainly there. The entry sets out the college's two purposes, its faculties and staff, and its place in the settlement that at last gave Ireland a national university system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Louvain's splendour as capital of Brabant moved John IV of Burgundy to seek a studium generale from the papacy. The bull of Martin V, dated 9 December 1425, founded the university and required the prince to grant it advantages and privileges. At first it was incomplete: only in 1431 did Eugene IV create the faculty of theology. As a studium generale it could receive students from all lands, and its doctorate gave the right to teach anywhere.

Popes and princes vied in granting privileges and endowments, and the entry follows the university's colleges, its theologians, and its part in the religious wars of the Low Countries. It covers the suppression under French rule, the refounding, and the modern Catholic university, with its faculties and its fame in theology and philosophy. A long history, told with unusual fullness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Keewatin is a Canadian vicariate taking in the northern half of Saskatchewan, bounded by the Arctic regions, St Boniface, Temiskaming, St Albert, and Athabasca. The country is described as generally barren, though possessing timber and minerals, and thinly peopled by Indians, mixed-race families, and a few whites.

Pioneer missionaries came in the 1840s, when Bishop Provencher of St Boniface sent Abbé Thibault to Ile-à-la-Crosse, Abbé Laflèche to explore Cumberland, and Father Taché, later archbishop, to join them. Oblates of the Manitoba and Alberta-Saskatchewan provinces then served the missions, above all Ovide Charleboix. His sixteen years at Fort Cumberland led to his appointment in 1910 as titular Bishop of Berenice and vicar apostolic, resident at Le Pas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-volksverein:
The Volksverein, People's Union for Catholic Germany, was a large organization of German Catholics formed to oppose heresies and revolutionary tendencies in social life and defend Christian order in society. It was the last association founded by Ludwig Windthorst, leader of German Catholics, after the Kulturkampf, the state's struggle against the Church, when new social problems confronted Catholics.

Germany's political union and protective commercial policy from 1879 greatly strengthened economic life, manufacturing boomed, country towns became factory centres. Crowds gathered in industrial districts, making social needs ever more pressing. Catholics felt the need for protection against revolutionary Social Democracy, rooted in undisguised materialism, which was already organizing throughout Germany, even among Catholics, in anticipation of the anti-Socialist laws' fall. Windthorst saw that the Centre Party alone, championing pro-worker legislation, was not enough; the public itself must be won to supporting Christian social order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wisconsin:
Wisconsin, the Badger State, entered the Union on 29 May 1848 as the seventeenth state after the original thirteen. It lies between Lake Michigan and Lake Superior to the east and north, Minnesota and the Saint Croix to the west, and Illinois to the south. It stretches about 300 miles north to south and 250 east to west across 56,066 square miles, including the Apostle Islands and Washington Island. Its rolling plateau, from 600 to nearly 2000 feet, splits into two drainage basins.

The state's people grew from 1,686,880 in 1890 to 2,333,860 in 1910, or 42.2 per square mile. Farming leads its wealth: hay, grain, oats, corn, barley, potatoes, sugar beets, cranberries, apples, and a mighty dairy trade in milk, cheese, and butter. In 1910 it held over two and a half million cattle, a million sheep, and a million and a half swine. Mills turned out lumber, paper, pulp, leather, beer, and flour, and mines yielded iron, zinc, and lead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zamora-spain:
Zamora (Spain) is the Valladolid suffragan diocese covering most of Zamora province. The town belonged to the Vaccaei, most likely ancient Occloduri, Eye of the Duero, at the crossing of three roads. Rock-hewn tombs with head cavities lie a quarter-mile from old walls, a ruined Roman bridge survives, and a Mercury inscription in the city hall marks the crossroads.

Medieval geographers mixed Zamora with Numantia, so documents sometimes call the diocese Numantina. Jews settled there during the dispersion, and Christians lived there by Diocletian's persecution. No Gothic record survives, but the early Saracen name Medina Zamorati shows Arabic roots. From the eighth to eleventh centuries Moors and Christians traded it. Alfonso I or Fruela first retook it, Abderraman retook it in 813, and Alfonso III restored it in 893. Muslims attacked in vain in 901, and Alfonso III set up the see in 905 under Saint Atilanus.
curlie-carson-listens-in:
A radio adventure for boys by Roy J. Snell fills this tale, printed by the Reilly and Lee Company of Chicago under copyright of 1922. Curlie Carson sits in a high room full of strange instruments, behind locked doors, and picks up a message no one can explain.

Twenty-five chapters follow the trail of that message. A map, a millionaire, and a trip out to sea in a cockleshell raise the stakes. An S.O.S., the wreck of the Kittlewake, and the secret of the map crowd the close. Snell wrote for the first age of wireless. The book mixes new radio craft with plain sea peril, in brisk chapters for young readers.
dee-monas-hieroglyphica-latin:
John Dee, adviser and astrologer to Queen Elizabeth I, published his Monas Hieroglyphica at Antwerp in 1564. The Latin text here follows the Frankfurt edition of 1591. Dee built the whole book around one symbol, his Hieroglyphic Monad, a glyph he designed himself.

In 24 short theorems, Dee unpacks the glyph line by line. He reads into it math, astronomy, alchemy, and Kabbalah, claiming one sign holds the keys to nature. Scholars of magic and early science still mine the book, though much of its meaning stays locked in Dee's private code. Few Renaissance books are stranger or more studied.
dee-propaedeumata-1558-latin:
John Dee published his first book, the Propaedeumata Aphoristica, in Latin in 1558. The title promises introductory aphorisms, and the form is a chain of short numbered statements. In them the young Dee sets out the physical basis of astrology, how rays and influences from the heavens act on the world below.

The aphorisms lay the ground for Dee's natural magic. Optics, magnetism, and celestial virtue all belong to one system in his account. Latin carried the little book to scholars across Europe. It made Dee's name as a mathematical philosopher before his angelic years. Readers meet the magus of Mortlake at the start: bold, learned, and certain that nature hides an order worth mastering.
delrio-disquisitiones-magicae-latin:
Martín Antonio Del Rio was a Flemish Jesuit scholar whose Disquisitiones Magicae first came out at Leuven in 1599 and 1600. The six Latin books form a vast storehouse of demon lore. Later writers on witchcraft leaned on it so hard that some call it a new Catholic Malleus.

Del Rio works through sabbaths, pacts, fortune-telling, astrology, raising the dead, and natural magic. He sorts true wonders from fraud and from the devil's tricks, citing hundreds of older writers. The set became the learned reference on magic and witch trials for more than a century.
dick-sands-the-boy-captain:
Verne's boy captain sails again in this English rendering by Ellen E. Frewer. A note at the front says Sampson and Low published it in England in 1878, and Scribners in New York in 1879. It later stood in volume eight of the Parke edition of Verne's works, in 1911. Ninety-four pictures filled the French edition.

The Pilgrim, the apprentice Dick, a rescue, and the survivors of the Waldeck open part one. Dingo, a sagacious dog, has his own chapter head. Dick's promotion follows a catastrophe at sea. Part two needs the reader to grasp the slave trade's man-hunts, which the text says waste a continent with blood and fire. Frewer's version is stately in tone and full in detail.
doe-osti-17013571-pyarc-status-report-fy:
Status report ANL/NSE-26/57 from Argonne National Laboratory covers fiscal year 2026 work on PyARC, a Python based tool set for fast reactor analysis. Kalin Kiesling, Scott Richards, Kyle Ramey, and colleagues in the Nuclear Science and Engineering Division wrote it. PyARC links older Argonne reactor codes through a shared input system and a graphical workbench.

Upgrades include a new GAMSRC path for gamma source work, a workflow that figures core bowing effects on reactivity, and updated links to the ORIGEN code in newer SCALE versions. Input checks, workflow handling, and quality assurance tests are also covered. The report serves users who need to know what changed in the current release.
doe-osti-17121564-metal-nucleation-and-d:
Nora Shaheen, Timothy Kim, Denis Johnson, and Argonne colleagues study the spiky metal growths that plague pyroprocessing of used nuclear fuel, in report ANL/CFCT-26/26. During electrorefining, uranium and transuranic metals plate onto a cathode, but they often grow as dendrites, branching needles instead of smooth layers. Dendrites trap molten salt in their pores, carry impurities downstream, and break off without warning.

Past fixes each carry costs: scraping pauses the run, liquid cadmium pools raise handling concerns, and pulse plating needs more work. The study pairs modeling of how metal nuclei form and dendrites grow with experiments. Understanding the growth rules points toward process settings that keep deposits compact and clean, raising throughput for fuel recycling.
doe-osti-17151980-prime-prize-promoting-:
Rules for the PRIME Prize, issued by the Energy Department in September 2026 with a first modification, aim to get more solar gear certified under an ecolabel. PRIME stands for Promoting Registration of Inverters and Modules with Ecolabel. The label in question is EPEAT, which rates products on sustainability criteria across their life cycle, with silver and gold tiers.

Solar modules and inverters can register under a leadership standard plus an ultra low carbon solar rule for modules. Independent assurance bodies verify that products meet the criteria, under audit by the Global Electronics Council. The prize document sets out prize amounts, key dates, and who may compete, then walks phase by phase through the entry steps. An amended section removed one program policy factor to align with departmental priorities.
doe-osti-17197383-detecting-refined-adve:
Emma Reid, Haley Duba-Sullivan, and Tony Allen of Oak Ridge study attacks on image super resolution models, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4976 dated September 2026. Super resolution models sharpen low quality images, and small crafted input tweaks can steer their output, a risk where the images feed other systems. The team works on a refined attack method called AdvSR and on spotting its use.

Refinements include a revised loss function, gradient surgery for multi objective training, varied patch sizes during training, a clean model starting point, and a schedule for the adversarial loss. Experiments compare the old and revised pipelines, remove parts one at a time to test their worth, and check transfer across image classes and model designs. Detection methods are then judged against the stronger attack.
doe-osti-17197391-low-cost-customizable-:
Jihoon Chung, Jamie Lian, Sen Huang, and colleagues design a low cost heating and cooling control system. Their report, ORNL/TM-2026/4854 from Oak Ridge, is dated September 2026. The target users are small and mid sized medical office buildings. Clinics need steady comfort and air quality. Many run on simple controls, with no budget for high end building automation. The project aimed at a kit such buildings can afford and adapt.

Early chapters set out the building context: schedules, zones, and gear found in medical offices. The design is then validated in the laboratory. Control strategies ran against test setups before any field use. Results chapters report how the system held setpoints and where tuning was needed.
doe-osti-2575624-focal-fisheries-require:
Report NREL/TP-5000-92666, issued July 2025 for the National Offshore Wind Research and Development Consortium, asks fishermen what floating wind farms must respect. Everett J. Rzeszowski and Damian C. Brady of the University of Maine, Mike Pol of the Responsible Offshore Science Alliance, and three NREL authors ran the study. Two regions were covered: the Gulf of Maine and the Mid-Atlantic Bight.

The method was semi-structured interviews with working fishing crews. In the Gulf of Maine, fixed gear dominates, traps and pots that sit on the bottom. In the Mid-Atlantic, mobile gear, trawls and dredges, sweeps the ground. Chapters record each fleet's spatial requirements, how much room gear needs to work, and comfort-level ratings for sharing space with floating turbines and their moorings. Extra concerns, from transit lanes to cable routes, are logged as design requirements for co-designing wind areas with the fisheries in mind.
doe-osti-2583566-understanding-multifami:
June 2025 stock study by Janet Reyna, Florian Antretter, Lauren Adams, and colleagues profiles multifamily housing energy use across the greater Little Rock area. Apartment buildings are retrofit planning's blind spot: ownership is split, incomes vary, and the stock ranges from garden low-rises to towers. The report segments that stock by income, owner status, and vintage, then measures energy use and emissions end use by end use.

Heating and cooling, water heating, appliances, lighting, and miscellaneous loads each get a chapter, so a planner can see which loads dominate which segment. The three priority segments for the region are named: buildings suited to in-unit heat pumps, low-rise stock with non-ducted heating, and low-rise stock with central heating. Retrofit solutions are matched to each, with resources for next steps. The document is built for city and county staff deciding where limited retrofit money does the most work.
doe-osti-2583588-understanding-multifami:
June 2025 stock study by Janet Reyna, Florian Antretter, Lauren Adams, and colleagues turns the same lens on multifamily housing in the Boise and Twin Falls region of Idaho. The report asks which buildings use energy how, so retrofit programs can aim instead of scatter. Large multifamily stock is characterized by income, owner status, and building vintage, with geographic clusters defining the region's planning areas.

Energy and emissions are broken down by end use: heating and cooling, water heating, appliances, lighting, and miscellaneous loads. For this region the top three segments are low-rise buildings with central heating, low-rise buildings with non-ducted heating, and tall buildings with in-unit heating. Each gets matched retrofit solutions and expected savings logic, plus resources for actionable next steps. The framing is deliberately practical, telling a local official what the report can and cannot answer before the numbers begin.
doe-osti-2583616-understanding-multifami:
June 2025 stock study by Janet Reyna, Florian Antretter, Lauren Adams, and colleagues maps multifamily energy use across a four-city region: Indianapolis, St. Louis, Springfield, and Peoria. The cluster crosses state lines, so the report builds its own geographic clusters for planning. Large multifamily buildings are sorted by income, owner status, and vintage, and their energy use and emissions are tallied by end use.

Heating and cooling lead the breakdown, followed by water heating, appliances, lighting, and miscellaneous loads. The region's top three segments are low-rise buildings with central heating, low-rise buildings with non-ducted heating, and tall buildings with in-unit heating. Each segment gets matched retrofit measures, and a closing section points readers to resources for acting on them. Like its sibling volumes, the report opens by stating plainly which local questions it can answer and which it cannot.
doe-osti-2584245-membrane-electrode-asse:
HyET squeezes hydrogen with electricity instead of pistons, and its machines need membrane assemblies made like clockwork. NREL automated their production under CRADA CRD-18-00744, closed out in report NREL/TP-5900-95403 dated November 5, 2024. Scott Mauger was the contact. HyET's units deliver tens of kilograms a day at up to 700 bar. They scale from home to plant size, but high pressure demands a special assembly design, unlike fuel cell practice.

NREL built a self-running catalyst coating process fitted to these assemblies. It also added inline quality checks to catch flaws before stack assembly. Together the partners designed a fully automated production line. They then approached U.S. suppliers of the needed gear, so the line could be built at home. The work treats making as the technology: a fine design that cannot be built cheaply and evenly stays a prototype.
doe-osti-2585512-characterizing-falling-:
Matthew Sandlin of Sandia National Laboratories filed this research performance progress report, SAND2025-08595R, for Department of Energy award 51908. The project studies falling particle curtain receivers, a design for concentrating solar power plants where hot particles fall through sunlight in a thin curtain. Sandlin is the principal investigator, and the report covers January through June 2025.

Past Sandia receivers ran at pilot scale, near 1 megawatt thermal with curtains one to two meters wide. Commercial plants need 25 megawatts thermal and up, so this project built a cold flow test platform at larger scale. The platform is installed, and its pneumatic lift has carried particles to the top of the tower, though the flow rate is not yet known. Sandlin also reports budget strain: fabrication cost more than expected, nearly spending the award, and more funding is under negotiation.
doe-osti-2586396-tcf-18-15677-final-repo:
Lorelle Mansfield of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this final report, NREL/TP-5K00-95929, in August 2025 for Technology Commercialization Fund project TCF-18-15677. The project paired NREL with Ascent Solar Technologies to commercialize tandem solar cells. In a tandem, a wide-bandgap perovskite top cell sits on a CIGS bottom cell, catching more of the spectrum than either could alone.

NREL transferred its perovskite know-how to the company and co-developed a durable transparent interconnect joining the two cells in one monolithic device. The metrics table shows an inverted perovskite device reaching 18.2 percent efficiency on glass, past the 10 percent target. In the tandem, the perovskite open-circuit voltage of 0.99 volts and the CIGS value of 0.41 volts combined to a tandem voltage of 1.22 volts. Ascent Solar makes light, flexible CIGS modules aimed at portable power and aerospace uses.
doe-osti-2586986-in-situ-data-analysis-t:
Daniel Dunlavy, Eric Phipps, Hemanth Kolla, John Shadid, and Edward Phillips wrote this final report, SAND2025-10560R, printed in September 2025. The five Sandia National Laboratories researchers close out a Laboratory Directed Research and Development project. Their subject is in situ data analysis: shrinking huge simulation output while the simulation still runs, so scientists can study results they could never store in full.

The team built a low-dimensional model of simulation data based on low-rank tensor decompositions. Unlike standard versions, their goal-oriented model also matches chosen quantities of interest and conservation invariants of the data, not just the raw fields. Tests on combustion and plasma physics data used both canonical polyadic and Tucker decompositions. The goal-oriented versions modeled density and kinetic quantities of interest far more accurately, at minimal extra cost in relative error. That means analysis can stay faithful to the physics even after heavy compression.
doe-osti-2586987-roxana-paramo-ramirez-m: A single internship poster by Roxana Paramo Ramirez of Sandia National Laboratories, SAND2025-10573R, presents her MSIIP 2025-2026 project on hardware electronics validation. She wrote a C++ program that reads Gerber files, the standard design files for printed circuit boards, and converts them into an image stack. Each image shows one layer of the board, so users can inspect inner components without cutting a board apart. She reports fewer visual artifacts than commercial Gerber viewing software gives. The poster also reflects on the internship, including stronger C++ and new C skills.
doe-osti-2587139-foam-and-unreacted-mate:
Harold Baggett leads a six-author Savannah River National Laboratory team in this August 2025 report, SRNL-STI-2025-00214. Katherine Broadwater, Hoang-Kim Pham, B Swanson, C Morgan, and W Jolin complete the team. The subject is a magnesium oxysulfate grout meant to solidify liquid effluent from the Savannah River Plutonium Processing Facility's aqueous recovery system.

The grout mixed well and set within facility limits, and its leachate pH of about 9.4 sits in the range expected for Waste Isolation Pilot Plant brine. The problem was foam: at both one-gallon and 55-gallon scale, a thick foam layer threatened a nonuniform waste form with uneven shielding. Foam reduction tests settled on a final mix of 28 weight percent light-burnt magnesium oxide, 10 percent magnesium sulfate, and 62 percent dead-burnt magnesium oxide. That mix cleared the foam in under two hours, and full-scale tests confirmed no unreacted liquid remained.
doe-osti-2587565-technical-report-on-sub:
Eric Matzel, Christina Morency, and Arthur Rodgers wrote this technical report, LLNL-TR-2010654, in August 2025. All three work at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Colleagues from Mondaic, Michael Afanasiev, Christian Boehm, and Lion Krischer, share the work. The subject is monitoring the underground reservoir of the Brady Hot Springs geothermal field in Nevada. The tool is full waveform inversion, a seismic imaging method that uses the whole recorded wave, not just arrival times.

The team worked from a dense seismic dataset gathered in 2016, spanning four stages of power plant operation with different injection and production rates. A baseline model was built from the first stage. Waveform differences from the later stages were then run backward through the model to highlight exactly where the reservoir changed. For geothermal operators, such time-lapse images show how fluids move through fracture networks and how production reshapes the reservoir.
doe-osti-2587566-rheo-electric-foundatio:
Steven Hawks wrote this full technical report in August 2025 on carbon slurry flow electrodes, closing Laboratory Directed Research and Development project 22-DR-011 at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Flow electrodes are pumpable slurries of carbon particles. If their flow behavior and electrical connectivity are tuned together, they promise continuous, scalable electrochemical desalination and energy storage.

Six research threads make up the report. One built a fast centrifuge-compatible method to measure the electronic conductivity of packed slurry. Another showed that peristaltic pumping slowly damages the particles, so the team built a miniature jet pump that preserves them, with entrainment ratios of two to four. A surfactant study mapped how Tween 20 collapses the carbon gel network. Imaging work showed settling and flow-driven mixing fighting over charge transport, with dynamic bed layers concentrating carbon up to about 30-fold at the current collectors.
doe-osti-2588546-comstock-measure-docume:
Marlena Praprost of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote this measure documentation, NREL/TP-5500-95014, dated September 2025. It specifies a ComStock scenario in which commercial buildings swap their existing boilers for condensing gas boilers. Condensing models reclaim heat from exhaust vapor that standard boilers throw away, which is where the savings come from.

ComStock models the United States commercial building stock as of 2018, building by building, and a measure is a controlled what-if against that baseline. The output is an end-use savings shape: a time-series difference in energy use, split by end use and fuel, plus annual totals. This swap is deliberately narrow. Only the boiler is replaced. Coils, piping, and pumps keep their original sizes, and nothing is re-autosized to the new unit. The documentation sets applicability by heating type across the stock, then publishes the dataset openly for analysts.
doe-osti-2588816-energy-loss-of-a-short-:
Sergey Kurennoy of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this technical note, LA-UR-25-29275, dated August 19, 2025, in the Accelerator Operation and Technology division. It calculates what a short electron bunch loses as it passes through a hollow-core silica fiber channel, a structure proposed for advanced accelerator concepts.

Wake potentials and impedances were computed with the CST wakefield solver. A first run used a Gaussian bunch with root-mean-square length 225 micrometers. Its spectrum cut off below an expected resonance in the fiber channel, hiding the feature that matters most for energy loss. A shorter bunch, 100 micrometers, resolved the resonance. The note reports the resulting impedance curves, real and imaginary parts, so accelerator designers can price the energy a bunch pays to its own wake in such a channel.
doe-osti-2997460-adaptive-control-for-hy:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory final report ORNL/TM-2025/4243, by Jaydeep Karandikar, Akash Prasad, Leah Jacobs, and co-authors with CARON Engineering, covers adaptive control for hybrid manufacturing machines. The partner's TMAC system watches cutting power and adjusts feed in real time. It was installed on two machines at the Manufacturing Demonstration Facility: a Makino a51nx mill and a DMG ultrasonic machine.

A converter tool was built to turn the system's stored data files into spreadsheet form for analysis in Python. Sensitivity tests showed the power sensor catching cuts above 0.015 kilowatts, about 0.2 horsepower. Cutting power rose measurably as tools wore in titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V test paths. In worn-tool trials, the controller held cutting power near the value a validated model predicted. Shops gain evidence that power-based control can stretch tool life without a operator watching every pass.
doe-osti-2998080-vibrational-signatures-:
Micah Prange computes the vibration fingerprints of defects in a one-atom-thick semiconductor, in a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated September 2025. The material is monolayer tungsten disulfide, a sheet semiconductor studied for electronics and light sensors. Missing sulfur atoms are its most common flaw, and each flaw should shift how the sheet vibrates.

Models were built by slicing one layer from the relaxed bulk crystal, with a 13.5 angstrom vacuum gap above the sheet. A defect cell repeated three by three held a single removed sulfur atom. Calculations used the PBE density functional with an energy cutoff of 323.4 electronvolts. Comparing the pristine sheet's spectrum against the defective one names the modes a microscope should hunt. Experimentalists can then count defects by listening, in effect, to the sheet's tone.
doe-osti-2998538-pre-feed-report-on-the-:
A September 2025 pre-FEED engineering report, prepared for the National Energy Technology Laboratory under award DE-FE0032464, scopes a carbon capture hub at Port Tampa Bay in Florida. T-RICH, the Tampa Regional Intermodal Carbon Hub, would gather carbon dioxide from area industry and ship or pipe it to storage. Pre-FEED work settles siting and outline design before detailed engineering money is spent.

Partners include Aptamus Carbon Solutions and ENTR, part of Aker Solutions, alongside the port. Chapters run a facility siting study and a geology review for Florida and the proposed site, plus a weather assessment. Long specification lists govern even the chemicals allowed on site, favoring nonflammable, environmentally friendly agents for everything from fire foams to transformer oils. The public version gives stakeholders the hub's footprint logic without the protected design detail.
doe-osti-3001273-the-forward-master-equa:
Jack Agnell, Patrick O'Rourke, Scott Ramsey and Brian Temple of Los Alamos derive stochastic neutronics mathematics in LA-UR-25-31028, issued 6 November 2025. When neutrons multiply in a fission chain, the population is random. Any moment holds some probability of finding exactly n neutrons. Photons born in the same fissions deserve tracking too. So the authors ask for the joint probability of n neutrons and m photons together, and build the forward master equation that evolves it.

The starting point is a binary fission model. Each induced fission event instantly releases two neutrons and two photons. Neutrons travel at speed v, photons at light speed. Neutron capture is ignored while photon capture is kept, and a steady source emits one neutron per event. Probability balance arguments assemble the master equation term by term. The report is pure derivation, groundwork for noise analysis and fluctuation predictions in multiplying systems.
doe-osti-3001742-designing-fair-workflow:
Sean Wilkinson, Patrick Widener, Sarp Oral and Rafael Ferreira da Silva of Oak Ridge argue about workflow plumbing in ORNL/TM-2025/4241. Their subject is making supercomputing science FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable. At the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, workflows chain codes, data movers and analysis steps into pipelines rebuilt for each new machine. Flagship systems live about five years, so workflow preservation fights a losing battle against hardware turnover.

The authors propose FAIR all the way down, but aimed at components: share, discover and reuse the pieces, not just finished pipelines. Design patterns surveyed include the European EOSC-Life collaboratory, built for life scientists who keep infrastructure alive long. It contrasts with HPC churn. Sections develop an ecosystem design for reusable workflow building blocks at the facility. The paper is architecture and argument, a blueprint for how the centre's software could outlive its machines.
doe-osti-3002046-adaptive-control-for-hy: Hybrid manufacturing got adaptive control, and this DOE text covers the method. The pages detail the findings. The manufacturing folks get their tool. The control was adaptive. The manufacturing was hybrid. The folks were manufacturing. The tool was manufacturing. The method was detailed.
doe-osti-3002128-high-burnup-bwr-loca-bu:
Ian Greenquist, Aaron Wysocki, Nathan Capps, and six co-authors at Oak Ridge model a reactor accident in ORNL/SPR-2025/4182, dated September 2025. The accident is a loss-of-coolant event in a boiling water reactor running high-burnup fuel. High burnup means the fuel has produced far more energy, which changes how its cladding behaves. The question is when fuel rods would burst as coolant drains and temperatures climb.

Three linked codes do the work. VERA simulates the full core over several fuel cycles, rod by rod. Its output feeds fuel performance calculations in BISON. Together they give a detailed picture of local heating and rod stress. The study supports safety cases for running today's reactors on longer fuel cycles.
doe-osti-3002136-additively-manufactured:
Frederick A. List III, Richard H. Howard, Keith Carver, and colleagues describe new test hardware in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4179, dated September 2025. The hardware is an irradiation capsule for the High Flux Isotope Reactor, the lab's intense neutron source. The capsule carries a pressure limit, set by a rupture disc that vents before pressure can climb too far. It was built by additive manufacturing, layer-by-layer metal printing.

Printing the capsule lets complex shapes form in one piece instead of many welded parts. The report covers the design, the pressure calculations under boiler and pressure vessel code rules, and the safety basis for running the experiment. An appendix holds the formal authorization document. Reactor staff use such capsules to expose samples to neutrons safely.
doe-osti-3006107-non-destructive-three-d:
Shiva Abbaszadeh's project built the first imaging platform that watches carbon move through the rhizosphere, the soil zone around living roots, in three dimensions over time. Soil structure steers carbon, nutrient, and water cycling, yet models cannot use rhizosphere processes well because no one could measure them inside intact soil. The platform pairs Rhizo-PET, a positron emission tomography scanner tuned for carbon-11 dioxide tracing in roots, with an amorphous selenium micro-CT scanner that images soil structure at micron scale.

Together the two give 4D, non-destructive readings of carbon allocation and structural change in living plants. Three findings stand out. Root exudate spread stays highly localized. Microbial activity zones track soil structure. Soil texture changes the paths by which carbon is stabilized. The report closes with parameters Earth system models can take up, including carbon residence times, exudate diffusion rates, and microbial uptake efficiencies.
doe-osti-3006791-2024-international-conf:
Final technical report for award DE-SC0025397, from Ireneusz Janik at the University of Notre Dame, covers DOE support tied to the 2024 International Conference on Ionizing Processes. The meeting ran August 11 to 15, 2024 on the Notre Dame campus, and the Basic Energy Sciences award paid targeted support so early-career investigators could attend and present. In total 23 young investigators received help: 19 got registration discounts, 8 of those also got travel-offset awards, and 4 more received travel awards alone.

Awardees came from U.S. universities and national laboratories, with five each from Brookhaven and Idaho National Laboratory among those listed. The conclusion states the program raised early-career representation and engagement at the conference, strengthened that research community, and spread work aligned with BES missions in radiation chemistry and fundamental chemical sciences. All objectives were met and the award is closed out.
doe-osti-3008470-passive-acoustic-monito:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Emma Cotter, Joseph Haxel, and James McVey, dated December 2025, listens to a river turbine with fixed underwater microphones. Passive acoustic monitoring offers a way to watch a hydrokinetic turbine's sound footprint without divers or moving gear.

Three hydrophones recorded the site, and stretches containing distinct events such as turbine startup or passing vessels aligned the unsynchronized clocks by cross-correlation. Manual screening isolated 1,180 seconds of high-quality data from May 27 and 494 seconds from May 28, when ambient noise ran higher. Analysis of the two quieter hydrophones rests on the first day's clean samples.
doe-osti-3009129-smartflower-renewable-e:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0010801, from the Girl Scouts of Colonial Coast under Sally Swanson, covers the SmartFlower Renewable Energy Program. A SmartFlower is a solar array shaped like a flower, its petal panels tracking the sun on a rotating stem.

The team wrote two free curricula around the device, one for kindergarten through fifth grade and one for sixth through twelfth, each built on hands-on activities about the sun and sustainability. The whole project cost 16,672 dollars, and running it afterward costs little or nothing. A no-cost extension, approved June 30, 2025, carried the work to September 30 after early delays and funding uncertainty.
doe-osti-3009426-exploring-large-languag:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4288, by Brett Billingsley, Jayden Fassett, Aaron Werth, and Mathew Singleton, dated December 2025, reviews large language model agents in cybersecurity and adds the authors' own experiments. The question is how far an AI agent can go in offensive and defensive security work.

Systems surveyed include PentestGPT, which works as an interactive assistant: it reasons, summarizes, and recommends commands while a human executes them, keeping a task tree for context. The review notes PentestGPT is now largely deprecated in favour of a successor framework, Cybersecurity AI. Readers get a map of a fast-moving tool landscape with honest limits attached.
doe-osti-3010903-reducing-methane-emissi:
A plasma based fuel reformer for large bore natural gas engines is evaluated in a final report by Nicholaus Mangum of Southwest Research Institute. The report covers award DE-FE0032301 from September 2023 to August 2025. The reformer targets methane slip, the unburned fuel lost in the exhaust of lean burn engines. Testing measured slip reductions from 1 to 27 percent. The figure varied with engine and test configuration.

Plasma power stayed below one percent of engine output across the tests. Engines evaluated included the AJAX 2802 ULE and the Cummins X15N. High flow validation ran at the SwRI Metering Research Facility. Operation near 100 kHz favoured the first of two reaction routes, while 10 kHz favoured the second. Carbon buildup proved removable, though gas phase condensation was also observed.
doe-osti-3012338-tough-errors-are-no-mat:
Quantum compiling that tolerates noise advances in the final report for the TEAM project, award DE-SC0020377, by Adam Bouland of Stanford University. The performance period ran from September 2019 to September 2025 under the quantum programming and compilation thrust. A new compiling algorithm removes the need for a quantum device to exactly invert its operations.

That result answers an open problem in compiling theory dating to the 1990s and generalises the Solovay Kitaev theorem. Related work implemented zero noise extrapolation error mitigation with the Unitary Fund. The team also built algorithms for entanglement detection and constructed pseudo entangled states that look highly entangled to every efficient algorithm.
doe-osti-3012478-lighting-a-star-on-eart:
Fusion ignition results from the National Ignition Facility are summarised in a Lawrence Livermore release by Dave Schlossberg, LLNL-TR-2012943, packaged with the laboratory's abstracts for the November 2025 APS plasma physics meeting. The release is written for public communication rather than as a technical report. Experiments build on a run of successful ignition shots.

NIF plasmas are now dominated by self heating, with target gain above two. Capsule doping is the stability theme: a ramped dopant profile at 2.05 megajoules steadied the implosion and raised yield. Higher energy shots are planned to extend the confinement and performance limits.
doe-osti-3013222-energy-star-portfolio-m:
Michael Henderson's January 2025 slide deck, produced through NREL, trains nonprofit building staff to use Energy Star Portfolio Manager. The training serves NORTHH, a program retrofitting nonprofit buildings that provide health and housing services in Alaska. Portfolio Manager is the federal tool for benchmarking a building's energy, water, and waste performance against national standards.

The slides walk through account creation, adding a property, entering utility data, and reading the metrics that result, such as energy use intensity and the 1-to-100 Energy Star score. NORTHH uses the tool to track buildings before and after retrofits and to share data with auditors. Participants' building profiles were created during the proposal phase, and the deck explains how to gain access and pull reports.
doe-osti-3013866-opensg-a-multiscale-con:
Sandia report SAND2025-15297, by Akshat Bagla, Ernesto Camarena, and Wenbin Yu, printed December 2025, presents OpenSG, an open-source code for multiscale modeling of thin-walled composite structures. Thin-walled parts such as wind turbine blades are built from layered composites whose behavior depends on both the layer stack and the whole shape. Full three-dimensional simulation of every layer is too slow for design work.

OpenSG builds constitutive models, the stress-strain laws, for continua, plates, and beams from the mechanics of structure genome, a theory Yu developed. New capabilities include shell cross-section modeling, tapered beam modeling, and panel buckling analysis, a common design driver. Accuracy and speed were checked against the established VABS and SwiftComp codes and direct simulations, using a realistic wind turbine blade as the main test case.
doe-osti-3014275-oak-ridge-national-labo:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4392, by Jakob Bludau and Damien Lebrun-Grandie, dated December 2025, tackles a build system problem in Kokkos. Kokkos is the performance portability library that lets one code base run on many computer architectures. Its build instructions had grown so complex that users struggled to compile it correctly inside larger projects.

The report lists the technical requirements. They include template instantiation control and library and runtime linking. They also include in-tree versus installed builds, and use from several CMake languages. Three approaches are evaluated. One is a launcher script. One makes Kokkos its own CMake language. The third defers traversal of the target tree. The evaluation weighs automation against user burden. Large projects cannot hand-specify language and architecture for every file. The goal is a build that encapsulates the complexity once, inside Kokkos itself.
doe-osti-3014946-knowledge-based-hazardo:
