NLR/TP-6A20-96847, dated January 2026, asks whether a used solar module is hazardous waste, and whether that call needs lab testing. Curtis, Smith, and Townsend wrote it at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Federal law under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act requires a hazardous waste determination before a photovoltaic module is recycled or landfilled. An exclusion can remove that duty.

The study examines generator knowledge. It is an existing legal pathway, long used by other industries but little known in solar. A generator may rely on documented knowledge of materials and processes instead of fresh testing. Tests of substantially similar modules can count. Regulators, though, require proof that design and composition truly match. Interviews with state regulators surface a shared concern. Similarity claims fail when material makeup differs enough to change the answer.
doe-osti-3015613-enhancing-cmc-temperatu:
A Pennsylvania State University final report under award DE-FE0032226, filed January 31, 2026, develops ceramic matrix composites that survive hydrogen-rich turbine exhaust. Hotter turbines burn cleaner and stronger. But combustion water vapor attacks the barrier coatings that protect silicon carbide composites. Stephen Lynch was principal investigator.

The team made baseline composite and coating samples with field assisted sintering. Both faces were coated symmetrically. Exposed and shielded sides could then be compared after combustion runs. New recipes moved toward rare earth silicate coatings. They were chosen for stronger water vapor resistance. Defect nucleation and crack growth were tracked to explain how damage starts. Milestone, success criteria, and deliverable tables close the report. It ran from January 2023 to October 2025 on a no-cost extension.
doe-osti-3016247-collaborative-r-amp-d-w:
Bill Nemeth, Craig Perkins, Darius Kuciauskas, and five more National Laboratory of the Rockies staff served as technical contacts for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5700-98622. The partner was REEL Solar Inc. Together they worked to understand, and then overcome, the limits on performance in REEL's cadmium telluride solar cells.

The lab applied its advanced measurement tools to REEL's process. Tools included time-resolved photoluminescence, capacitance-voltage tests, electron microscopy, and mass spectrometry methods. Samples varied the buffer, absorber, and contact layers to find which choices held efficiency back. Accelerated stability testing and induced degradation checks rounded out the program. The point was practical: give REEL a clear map of which process changes should raise cell efficiency and stability.
doe-osti-3016250-unifi-specifications-fo:
The UNIFI Consortium issued this Version 3 specification for grid-forming inverter-based resources on January 30, 2026, as document UNIFI-2026-2-1. Ben Kroposki of the National Laboratory of the Rockies is among the many contributors named in its pages. The consortium is co-led by that laboratory, the University of Texas at Austin, and the Electric Power Research Institute.

Grid-forming inverters are the electronics that let solar, wind, and battery plants set grid voltage and frequency themselves, instead of just following them. The document sets shared expectations for how such equipment should behave. It also gives test procedures to confirm performance on real hardware. Model validation steps point readers to a related IEEE draft standard. A common spec matters because grids with many inverter plants need each device to respond the same predictable way during faults and swings.
doe-osti-3016951-stockpile-stewardship-a:
George H Miller of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this technical assessment, LLNL-TR-2013409, in November 2025. Its question is a hard one: can the United States keep confidence in its nuclear weapon stockpile without resuming tests that produce nuclear yield? No such test has been held since 1992. Instead, a stockpile stewardship program has carried the load.

The assessment reviews what stewardship has built on the approach validated during fifty years of testing. Cited gains include detailed knowledge of high explosive chemistry, advanced manufacturing and new materials, and high-resolution simulation codes. One highlighted success solved a long-standing mystery that had confounded weapons scientists. Miller weighs this record as new information arrives and the test moratorium continues. The report gives policymakers a technical basis for the testing debate, in plain terms.
doe-osti-3017150-hands-on-pv-experience-:
Silvana Ovaitt, Ann L Greenaway, and Rachael L Arnold of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this February 2026 final report, NLR/TP-5K00-92625, on the Hands-On PV Experience workshop. HOPE is a one-week summer school held at the laboratory for graduate students who research photovoltaics. Students and their faculty advisors come from universities across the United States.

The week mixes lectures on solar cell fundamentals with hands-on lab work in cell fabrication and testing. Specific cell technologies and measurement methods get their own sessions, led by laboratory staff. The report covers the fiscal 2022 to 2024 editions and the survey results behind them. Satisfaction ran consistently high in those surveys. For the solar field, the value is a shared training ground where future researchers learn the same measurement craft.
doe-osti-3018138-novel-non-atomizing-pro:
Amit Shyam, Jovid Rakhmonov, and Alex Plotkowski of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, with Ryan Dehoff, wrote this November 2025 CRADA final report, ORNL/TM-2025/4342. The partner was Metal Powder Works, a small business with a proprietary process called DirectPowder. Metal printing usually needs powder made by atomization, blasting molten metal into droplets with gas. This project tested making powder without atomizing.

The feedstock was DuAlumin-3D, a high-temperature aluminum alloy the laboratory developed for additive manufacturing. The phase 1 collaboration ran from July 2022 to July 2024. Extruded alloy was converted to powder by the partner's process. Mid-course, the team added an extrusion step between casting and powder making, betting that refining intermetallic particles would add strain hardening and make the process succeed. The promised gains are lower cost, lower energy use, no atomization emissions, and higher quality powder. The report is the feasibility record for that bet.
doe-osti-3018200-interpretable-deep-lear:
Fanglin Che of the University of Massachusetts Lowell wrote this final report for Early Career award DE-SC0024553. The project used interpretable deep learning to advance catalysis. Local electric fields at a catalyst can steer reactions, but they are hard to measure and harder to design. Che's approach was an interpretable deep active learning system: a model that shows its reasoning while it searches.

Three hypotheses structured the work. Fields should strengthen more than ten-fold at surface points with low coordination. Dipole moments should track partial charges and coverages in a linear way. And field-dipole interactions should change mechanisms enough to speed reactions. The test chemistry was ammonia cracking and synthesis, making and using clean hydrogen, over common metal catalysts. Aims covered probing fields under working conditions, predicting adsorption energies, and actively searching for the best field effects. The output list includes two papers in preparation.
doe-osti-3019822-high-throughput-screeni:
Jeffrey McCutcheon of the University of Connecticut led this Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office project, award DE-EE0009099, from October 2020 to March 2024. Raytheon Technologies Research Corporation partnered. The target is cooling without compressors. Electrocaloric materials change temperature when an electric field is applied or removed. Ultra-thin films maximize the effect, but testing many candidate films was slow. The project used additive manufacturing to screen them at high throughput. Heating and cooling loads justify the hunt: HVAC can reach half a building's energy use.

Measurements on terpolymer thin films used infrared imaging at 22 degrees Celsius. Applied fields exceeded 80 megavolts per meter in the reported estimates. A digital image and paired infrared frames show the temperature change across the measured area. For materials researchers, the screening platform is the deliverable: many films, one fast method. The final report records milestones, lessons learned, and the benefits case for field-driven cooling.
doe-osti-3020422-potential-solutions-to-:
A slide-based technical report by Ellie Estreich, Brittany Speetles, and Elaine Hale of the National Laboratory of the Rockies supports the Virginia Department of Energy. The pressing question: how to meet fast-rising electricity demand. Data centers already account for about 26 percent of Virginia's electricity use, and their share is expected to grow by 2030. The work was delivered through DOE's State Energy Office Direct Technical Assistance Program.

One part reviews the literature on load growth and virtual power plants, which coordinate many small devices into one flexible resource. The other part estimates how much demand Virginia could shift or trim across homes, businesses, and vehicles. Managed electric vehicle charging, for example, can move load off the top winter peak hours. The authors find the flexibility potential substantial, while noting that economic and achievable potential need further study.
doe-osti-3023001-understanding-nbi-heati:
Leonid E Zakharov of LiWFusion in Princeton, New Jersey, closes out award DE-SC0023274 with this final report, dated February 23, 2026. The reporting period ran from July 2023 through June 2025. His subject is neutral beam injection, the standard way tokamaks such as LTX-β are heated and fueled, and why much of the injected fuel never reaches the plasma core.

Zakharov works through collision cross-sections, charge exchange losses, and the secondary atoms that escape, using his GSV code to compute rate coefficients and mean free paths for a 20 keV beam. He then assesses lithium doping, which he argues could change beam fueling sharply. Later chapters turn sharply critical of the wider magnetic fusion program.
doe-osti-3023851-neutronic-effects-of-mi:
Jeff Cardoni of Sandia National Laboratories models what happens to neutron behavior when elements are missing from the Annular Core Research Reactor, in report SAND2026-18480, printed March 2026. The ACRR is a Sandia research reactor used for irradiation testing. A core loaded differently than planned, with one or more elements absent, would not behave quite like the reference core, and operators need the size of that difference.

The report lays out a modeling approach and its assumptions, names the codes and tools used, and then works the cases. Long tables and core maps give position-by-position values, with relative figures running roughly from 0.58 to 1.46 across the mapped positions in one listing. Readers get a quantitative basis for judging which missing-element loadings matter and which barely move reactor behavior.
doe-osti-3024074-co-firing-switchgrass-a:
Ajay Shah of the Ohio State University led project SWITCH under award DE-FE0032204, running October 2022 through September 2025, with this final report submitted December 22, 2025. SWITCH asks whether an Ohio River Valley power plant could co-fire switchgrass with waste coal. The report judges the idea two ways: techno-economic analysis, and life cycle evaluation of costs, energy, and emissions across the whole chain.

The work reaches down to feedstock logistics. One study inside the report compares drone photogrammetry surfaces against LiDAR for measuring stockpile volumes. Kriging-interpolated terrain models smooth out small undulations, voids, and misclassified ground points. Those flaws inflate percentage errors in the raw photogrammetry surfaces, especially around stockpile edges. That measurement care feeds the cost figures the plant decision rests on.
doe-osti-3024093-optical-trapping-and-ma:
Chuji Wang of Mississippi State University reports grant DE-SC0021030, running September 2020 through December 2023 with a no-cost extension, submitted March 23, 2026. The project developed optical trapping for magnetized dusty plasma research at Auburn University's MDPX facility. Holding and measuring one dust particle at a time, without touching it, gives cleaner plasma data than probes that disturb the system.

The main advance replaced microscope-objective traps with a scalable lens-based configuration, which fits the big MDPX chamber where microscope geometry would not reach. The team designed, built, and validated the framework for large-scale plasma systems. The report frames the result as a diagnostic upgrade: precise, non-invasive control and measurement of single particles inside plasma environments that older techniques could not manage.
doe-osti-3028574-fy-2026-midyear-report-:
David Guenaga, Monica Maceira, Omar Marcillo, and James Garner of Oak Ridge National Laboratory report a half year of seismic monitoring work in ORNL/SPR-2026/4531, dated March 2026. The project listens for underground vibration sources two ways at once: distributed acoustic sensing, which turns a fiber optic cable into a line of vibration sensors, and ordinary seismometers. Midyear reports exist to show the deployment is real and the detection works.

Fiber installation was deliberately varied, with sections coupled by sandbags or rocks and sections laid directly on the ground, to mirror real underground deployments. Datasets and ground-truth catalogs follow a 2025 Cunningham description. For event detection, the team used continuous vertical recordings from 44 geophone stations and showed a network method that spots elastic disturbances by watching the background signal's power spectrum change.
doe-osti-3029206-understanding-giant-pla: Shengtai Li of Los Alamos National Laboratory presented this slide set on April 9, 2026, on how giant planets grow in protoplanetary disks. The deck is thin, captioned figures only. Its core images show a circumplanetary disk: gas streamlines, then dust density for grain sizes, two-centimeter and 0.2-millimeter grains. Later slides ask whether dust traps leak, comparing the DustPy code against hydrodynamics with coagulation. They show coagulation modeling for the disk HD163296, with and without grain bouncing, and describe coupling hydrodynamics to the AstroChem code, with ices as layers on dust.
doe-osti-3218397-synthetic-digital-envir:
Naveen Kumar Muthumanickam of the National Laboratory of the Rockies and Frankie Zhu of Colorado School of Mines present this research poster on training robots inside fake worlds. Luke Boyd and Antar Mazumdar share the team credit. Building real test sites is slow and costly, whether the job is a solar farm on Earth or a base on the Moon or Mars. The poster offers high-fidelity digital twins instead: software copies detailed enough to teach robots hard outdoor tasks.

One twin copies a solar plant build, with pile driving, mounts, torque tubes, and panels, built in Rhino, Grasshopper, and NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The other copies the Mines lunar surface simulator, scoring a similarity index above 0.92 against the real pit. Rover and arm trials there test soil interaction before any hardware ships.
doe-osti-3233210-fast-ion-confinement-in:
William Heidbrink reports final results under award DE-SC0022131, covering June 2021 to December 2025, on fast-ion confinement in two stellarators. The project was the doctoral thesis work of Wataru Hayashi, who finished in December 2025. Fast ions carry the heat that fusion reactions make, so a stellarator must hold them well. Sites were the Large Helical Device in Japan and the W7-X device in Germany, read with fast-ion D-alpha light diagnostics.

New sightlines, proposed by the team and installed by the LHD crew, proved more sensitive to the highest-energy ions, as hoped. Hayashi two main papers treat confinement in quiet plasmas and the push that Alfven waves give fast ions. University of California, Irvine scientists led many LHD runs remotely during the pandemic, and the grant also backed stellarator modeling with the GTC code.
doe-osti-3363079-examining-respiration-a:
Allison M. Veach of the University of Texas at San Antonio, with co-investigator Brian Laub, closes out DOE award SC0023086 in this final report on streams that stop flowing. The team compared perennial and intermittent reaches of an urban river in San Antonio, Texas, using respiration chambers designed by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory scientists. Intermittent streams and ephemeral streams make up as much as 60 percent of global river length, yet their microbial activity after flooding is poorly measured.

Dry intermittent sediments showed lower microbial activity and lower bacterial and archaeal diversity than flowing reaches, likely because easily degraded carbon was scarce. Perennial sites respired faster than intermittent ones in the wet season. The report concludes that drought driven flow loss weakens nutrient breakdown and other ecosystem services.
doe-osti-3364217-reliability-of-digital-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory prepared this May 2026 study for the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Authors Johnathan Cree, Jarrett Zeliff, and Elena Peterson evaluate how to judge the reliability of digital communication systems inside nuclear facilities. Plants increasingly swap analog wiring for networked digital links, and regulators need defensible ways to assess whether those links will work when called on.

The study weighs failure sources that generic reliability methods miss. Wireless signals reflect off plant materials and can pile up into interference at some spots. Radiation can flip bits in processors and memory through single-event upsets. Aging bites too: fiber cables deform, rodents damage runs, and copper contacts corrode. The report assembles these hazards into guidance for reviewers judging communication reliability in licensing and safety cases.
doe-osti-3364551-free-piston-expander-fo:
GTI Energy's final report for DOE project DE-EE0008431, led by principal investigator Devin Halliday, covers October 2018 through March 2024. The project built a free-piston expander that recovers cooling when high-pressure hydrogen drops to dispenser pressure at fueling stations. Partners were the University of Texas at Austin, Argonne National Laboratory, and Quantum Fuel Solutions. Wasted pressure energy normally becomes a refrigeration bill; the expander turns it into cold.

Calculations cover expansion from 950 bar cascade storage down to 50 bar compressor suction, with outlet temperatures and hydrogen mass flows worked out at several efficiency levels. Cold hydrogen can chill a thermal mass heat exchanger during idle periods, storing cooling for the next vehicle. The design aims to cut the energy cost of fast hydrogen fueling.
doe-osti-3364909-hot-water-recirculation:
A February 2025 training slide deck by Meredith Cummings, Conor Dennehy, Alex Boetzel, Dana Strongin, and Deanna Cook teaches designers how to make hot water recirculation systems succeed. Recirculation keeps hot water moving through a loop so taps deliver it within seconds instead of wasting a cold slug down the drain. The training was produced for the Department of Energy's Building Technologies Office.

Sessions cover system components, piping and pump sizing, and control choices: timer, temperature, learning, and on-demand controls each trade comfort against energy use. Occupants judge 105 degrees Fahrenheit as hot and expect it within 10 seconds. Installation best practices, code compliance under Washington and California rules, heat pump and tankless combinations, and troubleshooting fill the back half. Poorly designed systems can sharply raise energy use, the deck warns.
doe-osti-3365084-project-molecular-coars: A Los Alamos National Laboratory slide, LA-UR-26-24047, by Patrick Sahrmann and issued May 18, 2026, outlines a project on coarse-grained modeling of block copolymer mixtures. Coarse-grained models lump atoms into beads to make polymer simulations fast, but a model tuned at one temperature usually fails at others. The slide shows a fix: expand the free energy around a reference temperature and learn both energy and entropy terms with machine learning score matching. A figure shows the corrected model holding accuracy across temperatures. The hosted text is one slide.
doe-osti-3365552-mitigation-for-the-demo:
Desert Research Institute cultural resources report LR120424-2-MIT, by Cheryl Collins, documents preservation mitigation for demolishing Building 25-3124, the Equipment Testing Laboratory, in Area 25 of the Nevada National Security Site. Like its companion reports in the same project series, it follows the site's agreement for historic districts: record the building thoroughly before it comes down.

The mitigation package pairs an updated resource assessment form, with photographs and drawings of current conditions, with a letter report on the building's history. Area 25 hosted the nuclear rocket development program, and its laboratories are contributing elements of that historic landscape. The September 2025 record gives future readers a full account of a Cold War test building that demolition will erase.
doe-osti-3365644-mitigation-for-the-demo:
Desert Research Institute cultural resources report LR120424-3-MIT documents preservation mitigation for demolishing Building 25-3153. Nicole Brannan wrote it, submitted September 2025. The building is the fire station of the Nuclear Rocket Development Station in Area 25 of the Nevada National Security Site. Built in 1961, the one-story concrete block station is the most prominent building left near Gate 500, with four equipment bays and an L-shaped plan.

The station housed responders protecting nuclear rocket development throughout the district's period of significance. Mitigation produced an updated resource assessment form with interior notes, engineering drawings, and current and historical photographs, surveyed in December 2024. The letter report covers the building's significance. As with its companions, the package preserves the record of a contributing historic building that demolition will remove.
doe-osti-3365669-mitigation-for-the-demo:
Desert Research Institute cultural resources report LR120424-4-MIT documents preservation mitigation for demolishing Building 25-4314, the Radiation Services Building. Megan Stueve wrote it, submitted September 2025. The site is Area 25 of the Nevada National Security Site. The building is a plain 33 by 45 foot concrete block box with a flat roof, tan walls, and a chain link fence. It was later used by the Yucca Mountain Project as construction management space.

Its original work was radiation study and control for the nuclear rocket station. The mitigation package updates the resource assessment form with an eligibility check, interior notes, drawings, and photographs. Integrity checks weigh location, design, materials, and association. The letter report completes the standard recording required before a contributing element of the historic district is demolished.
doe-osti-3365704-mitigation-for-the-demo:
Desert Research Institute cultural resources report LR120424-5-MIT documents preservation mitigation for demolishing Building 25-4838, the Vehicle Maintenance Shop. Cheryl Collins wrote it, submitted September 2025. The site is Area 25 of the Nevada National Security Site. Built in 1967 in the Central Support Area, the shop is a prefabricated steel building 27 by 90 feet with a front gable. A fuel island once stood in front of the main entrance.

Alterations tell the shop's working history: the center rear bay was raised for taller vehicles, and two rollup doors were replaced with siding and personnel doors. The mitigation package updates the Architectural Resource Assessment form, documents accessory resources down to propane tank foundations and a flagpole, and adds photographs and an eligibility narrative. Recording precedes demolition under the site agreement.
doe-osti-3367528-speed-to-power-solution:
Berkeley Lab report by Fredrich Kahrl and Natalie Mims Frick, published June 2026 through UC eScholarship, tackles the queue strangling new data centers and factories. Connecting large electrical loads to the grid now takes years. The authors survey why studies crawl and what grid operators are changing. Proposed rule sets from the Southwest Power Pool, including its CHILLS framework, are compared configuration by configuration for loads paired with generation.

Solutions span faster study methods, conditional and bridge service while upgrades are built, and rules letting flexible loads connect sooner. Federal orders from 2018 through 2026 frame the regulatory shift. For utilities facing gigawatt-scale requests, the report is a menu of reforms already in motion somewhere, with citations to steal from.
doe-osti-3369038-assessment-of-vibration:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21851, printed in June 2026, by Joseph A. Ronevich, Benjamin B. Schroeder, and Brian D. Ehrhart weighs how vibration and shock loads on railroad steel interact with hydrogen embrittlement. Moving hydrogen at large scale takes pressure vessels, tubing, and rail transport, so rail steels may face hydrogen exposure along with years of shaking and impact loads. The team set out to judge whether that mix raises the risk of cracking.

The report reviews past work and test data on tensile strength, Charpy impact results, and fatigue crack growth in steels with and without hydrogen. One pattern it draws out is that crack growth rates fall at higher test frequencies, so the harmful effects of hydrogen shrink and growth starts to look like behavior in plain air.
doe-osti-3377882-sustainable-ethylene-vi:
North Carolina State University and SABIC deliver the Phase I final report for award FE0032513, dated July 16, 2026. The subject is making ethylene by chemical looping oxidative dehydrogenation. The report was prepared by Md Sumon Reza, Dennis Chacko, Kyle Vogt-Lowell, William Joe Sagues, and Fanxing Li, the principal investigator. Ethylene is a core chemical feedstock. The looping route aims to cut the carbon cost of making it from ethane.

The team presents a conceptual design, then experimental results on catalysts. The catalysts include a sodium tungstate promoted magnesium manganese oxide. Advanced sodium magnesium tungsten formulations appear as well. A life cycle section bounds the assessment at the plant gate. Carbon dioxide comes mainly from the power block. That block burns natural gas and fuel gas byproducts to meet the plant's own power needs.
doe-osti-3419444-fuel-performance-modeli:
Idaho slide set INL/RPT-26-94809, dated August 2026, is Cecilia Jean Harrison's final talk on a fuel performance modeling internship. The slides model metallic uranium-zirconium fuel rodlets in HT-9 cladding inside steel capsules. Tests ran in the Advanced Test Reactor. The BISON code did the modeling.

Models tracked gap heat transfer, contact, and plenum pressure over time. Fission gas release came out lower in the model than in tests. Low modeled fuel heat and burnup may explain part of that gap. Cladding wastage in the model matched marks seen in metal samples.
doe-osti-3422011-integrated-hydrogen-ene:
NLR/TP-5D00-100324 is a August 2026 report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies that covers testing of an integrated hydrogen energy system. Kumaraguru Prabakar, Ben Kroposki, Deepthi Vaidhynathan, Meghan Pearson, and Yaswanth Nag Velaga were the lab contacts. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-21-18272.

One task modeled grid-forming fuel cell inverters inside a microgrid. The model checks how the inverters act with other power gear. A later task built a power hardware-in-the-loop test setup. Real gear can then be tested against simulated grids safely. Hydrogen systems must prove they support, not shake, local grids.
doe-osti-3422582-non-conformal-interface:
Argonne report ANL-26/22 studies a shifted boundary method for modeling cracks and bonded interfaces that do not share a mesh. Cheng-Hau Yang, Mark C. Messner, and Tianchen Hu wrote the study. Mismatched meshes are common when parts are designed apart.

Tests checked whether points fall inside unions of immersed shapes. One case joined a built circle with an L-shaped boundary from a mesh file. Another joined a sphere shell with a tetrahedron from an STL file. Background grids as coarse as 8 by 8 by 12 still classified points well. Engineers can model joined parts without forcing one shared mesh.
doe-osti-3453384-no-band-gap-no-problem-:
Sandia report SAND2026-25162R closes LDRD project 242427 on atomic defects in narrow bandgap materials. Peter A. Schultz led the project, with Leopoldo Diaz. Radiation-hard infrared imagers and fast electronics need defect answers that standard theory struggles to give.

Standard density functional theory suffers a band gap problem in these materials. The project built a band-avoiding, occupation-constrained method to work around it. Past studies of indium arsenide defects disagreed with each other, the report notes. No shared theory had emerged before this work. Chip designers gain a cheaper path to defect insight for space hardware.
doe-osti-3827140-xct-supported-triso-oxi:
X-ray scanning sharpens TRISO fuel oxidation tests in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4760, dated August 2026. Five authors are printed: Grant Helmreich, William Cureton, Stephen Trewhitt, Martino Hooghkirk, and Tyler Gerczak. TRISO particles guard their fuel with a silicon carbide shell. In an air-ingress accident that shell slowly burns away, so its recession rate matters for safety cases. Older tests weighed particles but could not see the shell thin. The team scanned particles before and after furnace runs instead.

Sets of thirty fresh and thirty irradiated AGR-5/6/7 particles went through the scans. The furnace held them at fourteen hundred degrees in twenty percent oxygen for up to four hundred hours. Only three irradiated particles survived whole, but they proved the method can track shell loss directly. Scans showed the outer oxide skin peeling away, which fools weight-based checks.
double-trouble-or-every-hero-his-own-vil:
Herbert Quick builds a comic novel on a doubled self in Double Trouble, issued by Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis in 1906 with pictures by Orson Lowell. The hero, Eugene Brassfield, wakes with a gap in his mind: the first chapters are called A Sleep and a Forgetting and The Riddle of Raiment and Dates. Another life seems to have run in his place while he slept.

Adventures in Benares, a wrong house, and legal minds fill the middle chapters, and a fortune hangs on which Brassfield did what. A fortune teller figure, Madame Le Claire, works on him with a strong voice: sleep, she says, and wake as the old Eugene, at home with all around him. Quick plays the double for farce and for a jab at business honor. The plot asks whether a man is the self he recalls or the one his deeds have made.
early-britain-roman-britain:
Edward Conybeare tells the story of Roman Britain in a 1903 volume for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, with a map of the occupation. A long errata list at the front corrects dates and Latin words page by page. His bibliography points readers to the Antiquary, local society reports, and more than fifty ancient authors quoted in the text.

Chapters run from Caesar's landings through the revolt years to Agricola and the civil wars of the empire. One passage tells how a new governor, Petronius Turpilianus, let fighting lapse and dressed the slackness up as peace with honour. Conybeare writes dry, exact history for general readers. Roads, walls, towns, and garrisons take shape from coins, inscriptions, and the Roman writers themselves.
elsie-s-kith-and-kin:
Martha Finley draws the clan tighter in Elsie's Kith and Kin, dated 1886. Chapter one belongs to the young married pair Edward and Zoe Travilla. Zoe weeps in her husband's arms, lonely at first with them all gone at once, above all mamma, for months.

Edward laughs, hugs her, and owns he would cry himself if he were a girl. The book follows the spread family through visits, partings, and returns. In one scene a daughter pleads mutely for a kiss from her papa, the first in a whole year, and gets several, given with grave tenderness. Finley writes marriage and kinship as a warm discipline of prayer and affection. The Elsie books by this point were a family institution, and this volume serves the faithful with more of the same tender household gospel.
erastus-repetitio-disputationis-lamiis-1:
Thomas Erastus, the Swiss Reformed doctor and theologian, wrote this Repetition of the Disputation on Witches at Basel in 1578. The Latin text answers Johann Weyer, the great skeptic who held that accused witches were melancholy women fooled by the devil, not partners with him. Their clash is the great sixteenth-century debate on the reality of witchcraft.

Erastus grants the devil real power and urges the death penalty for true witches, yet even he trims the wildest charges of the witch hunters. He writes as both physician and churchman, and the two callings pull against each other on the page. The book marks the limit of skepticism in its age. Weyer lost the round, and the burnings went on.
erema-or-my-father-s-sin:
R. D. Blackmore's Erema, or My Father's Sin, opens with a curse that has followed its narrator always: a father's sins visited on his children for generations. Erema's father, a resolute man, falls and dies alone in the desert, in a silence beyond the grave.

At a dark, narrow gorge off the mountain track, her father leaves the wagon train to seek still remoter solitudes, and Erema closes his eyes herself. The novel follows her struggle with the inheritance of that fatal life, and with the question of guilt passed from parent to child. Readers who know Blackmore from Lorna Doone will find Erema darker, more personal and equally strong in landscape.
errores-gazariorum-latin:
The Errores Gazariorum is an anonymous Latin treatise from Savoy, written around 1430. Its title means the errors of the Cathars, a name now pinned on supposed witches. Scholars prize it as the founding document of the witches' sabbath, the first full description of that fateful idea.

The text describes secret night assemblies where heretics renounce Christ and feast with demons. Before this treatise, such elements lay scattered in separate charges. Here they fuse into the sabbath stereotype whole. That stereotype would condemn thousands across the next two centuries. Cold, brief, and fateful, the Savoyard text marks the moment the witch of legend took her lasting shape.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-romans-cor:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on Romans and Corinthians covers Paul's letters in sermon form. Alexander Maclaren takes Romans whole, then First Corinthians, then Second Corinthians to chapter V. Each sermon starts from a short verse or clause. The contents show a dense run of entries for Romans alone.

Romans entries include The Gospel the Power of God and No Difference. Let Us Have Peace and Access into Grace treat chapter V. Sons and Heirs and More Than Conquerors come from chapter VIII. Love's Triumph closes that chapter's run. The Corinthian sermons follow the same close pattern. Maclaren reads Paul as a pastor, pressing doctrine into daily duty and hope.
eymerich-directorium-inquisitorum-1578-l:
Nicholas Eymerich, inquisitor of Aragon, wrote the Directorium Inquisitorum in 1376, the manual that taught inquisitors their trade for two hundred years. The text here is the Rome edition of 1578, with the commentaries of Francisco Peña. Eymerich wrote from a hard life of hunting heresy in Catalonia and at the papal court.

The manual covers the whole craft: how heresy is found, how witnesses are heard, how torture is ruled, and how sentences are framed. Its sections on witchcraft and sorcery later fed the Malleus tradition of the witch trials. Peña's notes bring the old text up to the age of the Spanish Inquisition. It is the procedural root of the early modern persecution.
facts-and-arguments-for-darwin:
Fritz Müller's Facts and Arguments for Darwin argues for Darwin's theory of evolution from the study of crustaceans, the group that includes crabs, shrimps and barnacles. William Dallas translated the book from German into English, with additions by Müller himself, and the London edition carries illustrations throughout.

Müller builds his case from body structure and from the growth of young crustaceans into adults, showing how unlike forms can share a common pattern. Chapters take up the species of Melita, the shape of crustacean bodies, breathing in land crabs, the heart, and the rules for sorting species into groups. The closing chapters turn to the wider progress of evolution itself, and to what crustaceans in particular reveal about it. Readers who want an early, detailed defence of Darwin from a working naturalist will find it here.
ficino-de-vita-1529-latin:
Marsilio Ficino, the Florentine priest-philosopher, wrote his Three Books on Life in the fifteenth century. This Latin edition of 1529 spread his manual of astrological medicine and natural magic. Ficino taught how the planets shape the body, and how a scholar might live long under their influence.

Diet, music, scents, and stones all enter his regimen for the learned life. He writes for melancholy scholars like himself, in danger from their own desks. The book is the philosophical root of learned Renaissance magic. Physicians and magi read it side by side for generations. Ficino's Florence speaks here: Platonism turned into a daily art of health.
ficino-de-vita-libri-tres-1498-latin:
Marsilio Ficino, the leading thinker of Florence's Platonic Academy, wrote Three Books on Life in 1489. The Latin text here comes from the Venice edition of 1498. The work is a guide to health for scholars, built on astrology, medicine, and natural magic.

Ficino teaches readers how to guard their health, live long, and draw strength from the planets and stars. He covers diet, sleep, herbs, music, and talismans, the images meant to catch heavenly power. The book, with its added defense of his magic, became the base work of Renaissance medical astrology.
ficino-pimander-1481-latin:
In 1463 Marsilio Ficino set aside his Plato to translate a Greek manuscript that had just reached Florence: the discourses of Hermes Trismegistus. His Latin version, the Pimander, was printed in 1481. It lit the Hermetic fever of the Renaissance. No English version of Ficino's own text exists in the public domain.

The discourses tell of God as light and life, the making of the world, and the fall and return of man. Ficino and his readers took Hermes for a sage older than Moses, a gentile prophet of Christian truth. The book reshaped Renaissance thought on magic, the soul, and the stars. This early printing is the form in which Europe first read it.
from-boyhood-to-manhood-life-of-benjamin:
Thayer traces Benjamin Franklin's life from his Boston boyhood upward. Franklin was the fifteenth child of a tallow chandler. The early chapters show him at school and at work. He pays too dear for a whistle and learns the lesson. At ten he is cutting candle wicks in his father's shop.

The biography follows his search for the right trade. Readers see the runaway printer's apprentice reach New York and Philadelphia. Franklin's rise rests on industry, reading, and self-command. Thayer tells the story as a model for young readers. Anecdotes carry the moral at each stage. The full career unfolds from these poor beginnings. It is a life written to teach by example.
gerson-de-erroribus-artem-magicam-1402-l:
Jean Gerson, chancellor of the University of Paris, wrote De Erroribus circa Artem Magicam in 1402. The Latin title means, in plain words, on the errors that gather around the magic art. The text here comes from the 1706 collected works issued under Dupin.

Gerson lists the mistakes he saw in charms, spells, and claims of hidden power, and judges them by church teaching. He wrote early, before the great witch trials of later years had taken shape. His short treatise shows a leading church scholar drawing a firm line around magic. It marks an opening move in a long debate.
golden-steps-to-respectability-usefulnes:
John Mather Austin, author of Voice to Youth, gave these lectures to young people of both sexes in 1851. Golden Steps to Respectability, Usefulness and Happiness takes up character, principles, associates, amusements, religion, and marriage. Its motto verse urges the reader onward and upward, to fix the goal amid the skies. The first lecture treats the value of a good reputation.

Austin writes as a minister who believes a life is built by daily choices. He warns against bad company and cheap pleasures, and praises steady work and faith. The style is earnest and direct, with rules a young clerk or schoolgirl could carry in mind. Books like this lined the shelves of striving families. It is a clear sample of the self-help teaching of its age, before the term was coined.
goldsmith-s-friend-abroad-again:
Mark Twain writes these seven letters in the voice of Ah Song Hi, a Chinese labourer sailing from Shanghai to make his fortune in America. The title reverses Goldsmith's Citizen of the World, in which a Chinese philosopher observed England. Twain's prefatory note insists no experience in the letters had to be invented; plain fact, he says, is amply sufficient.

Ah Song Hi writes home to Ching-Foo in perfect faith. America is the land of the free, which has welcomed Germans, French, and Irish and will surely welcome him. The second letter already shows the machinery working on him: passage money advanced against his labour, his family held as security, and a consul pocketing two dollars a head for certificates. The satire needs no commentator; the letters' innocence does the work.
govdocs-archive_org-TheFinalNailInMalach:
Malachi Martin was an Irish ex-Jesuit priest whose books on the Catholic Church and exorcism made him famous and controversial. The Final Nail in Malachi Martin's Coffin, dated 2019, is a polemic written against him from within traditionalist Catholic circles.

Its charge, stated in the file's own framing, is that Martin worked as a triple agent, serving masters beyond the church he wrote about. The piece argues its case sharply and expects readers who already follow the quarrels around Martin's life. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, as a record of that infighting.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BelliMelvin_Bel: Melvin Belli was San Francisco's flamboyant trial lawyer, and he entered the Kennedy case as Jack Ruby's defense counsel, representing the man who shot Lee Harvey Oswald on live television. Belli's courtroom performance and his defense of Ruby became part of the case's legend. This file holds the government material filed under Belli's name in the assassination records. It is kept as issued, under the name of the most theatrical lawyer the case produced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrownHRapBombin:
Newsweek's Terrorism on the Left surveyed a wave of political bombings that shook the United States in the early 1970s. Radical groups of the New Left had turned to explosives, and bombs at government and corporate buildings had become regular news.

The article takes stock of the campaign: the groups behind it, the targets chosen, and the official response as the bombings mounted. It comes from the moment when domestic terrorism first became a standing fear in American public life. Preserved among the research files, it shows the climate in which the era's investigations and surveillance programs grew.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DiesMartin_Dies:
Martin Dies was a Texas congressman who chaired the House committee that hunted alleged communists, the body that grew into the House Un-American Activities Committee. His book Martin Dies' Story was published by Bookmailer in New York in 1963. It is his own account, written after his years at the center of those hearings.

Dies writes as the man who built the committee's methods and defended them for years. A memoir from the chairman lets readers hear the case for the investigations in his own words, rather than through his many critics. It is a primary source on the politics of the early Cold War at home.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DymondFIrwin_Dy: Nsia-DymondFIrwin Dymond F Irwin: the made public government document, captured as titled, subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued, an obscure item, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBINewOrleansFi:
An FBI memorandum records a request from staff of the House Select Committee on Assassinations. The committee wanted all assassination files held by the Bureau's Dallas and New Orleans field offices. The scale was large: about 154 volumes, some 170,000 pages of records.

Numbers like those explain why the committee's work took years. Two field offices had gathered a library on one crime, and Congress asked for all of it. The memo preserves the Bureau's side of that handover, a measure of how much paper the Kennedy investigation produced. The request itself came as Congress reopened the case in the late 1970s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-InternationalTr: An advertisement by I. E. Zollinger Co., appraisers and auctioneers, lists photographs among its offerings. The file is kept under the International Trade Mart in New Orleans, the city's trade exhibition center. Trade ads like this one were business ephemera, printed to draw buyers to a sale. The surviving record gives the firm and the form but no date, so the piece stands as an undated auctioneer's advertisement.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingMartinLuthe:
The House Select Committee on Assassinations held hearings on the killing of Martin Luther King Jr. on November 17, 20, and 21, 1978. The sessions belonged to the committee's second great task, ten years after King's death in Memphis. They form part of the record of the 95th Congress, second session.

Congress gave the King case three November days of sworn public examination. Witnesses and investigators revisited a murder many believed had never been fully explained. The hearing volume preserves those days whole, questions and answers in order, as the official late inquiry into King's assassination.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PostalInspector:
A postal inspector's notes, made in Dallas on November 22, 1963, concern Oswald's New Orleans post office box. Box 30061 was rented in the name L. E. Oswald. The rental listed A. J. Hidell and Marina Oswald. The notes record two copies of The Worker found on hand, and Oswald's apartment on Magazine Street.

Postal inspectors were among the first federal men on the Oswald paper trail. A box rental card could prove an alias in a suspect's own hand. The Hidell name mattered because the rifle that killed Kennedy was ordered under it. These notes, dated the day of the assassination itself, show that trail being opened within hours, in Dallas, from records kept in New Orleans.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pre-Assassinati:
A letter from Washington, D.C., dated November 16, 1942, and addressed to 'Dear Frank,' pitches story outlines to its reader. One outline concerns William Power Maloney. Maloney was a special assistant to the attorney general who was preparing sedition cases for trial. The author's name is not clearly identified in the text.

Washington in 1942 was full of writers selling stories to magazines hungry for war material. Sedition trials of pro-Nazi agitators were among the era's biggest stories. A pitch letter shows the trade from inside: subjects weighed for sale, angles offered, a prosecutor's name used as bait. The letter preserves both the outlines and the selling, a freelancer's work caught mid-pitch.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ScottWin_Scott_:
An article titled 'The Spy Who Loved Him' tells the story of Michael Scott's long effort to read his father's memoirs. His father was Winston McKinley Scott, a senior CIA officer who ran the agency's Mexico City station. Before he died, Scott wrote his memoirs. The CIA holds those memoirs and will not release them, even to his son.

A station chief's memoir is the kind of document agencies are built to suppress: names, operations, and judgments in the author's own hand. The son's campaign to read it became a case about who owns a spy's memory. The article preserves the family's side of that fight, and the agency's silence, in the form the magazine gave its readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WalshKevin_Wals: Kevin Walsh wrote to Harold Weisberg on September 21, 1995, enclosing papers about Weisberg's books. Readers and younger researchers often sent Weisberg clippings, reviews, and questions. His mailbox stayed active for decades after his first book appeared in 1966. The Walsh letter, with its enclosures, shows that readership still feeding material back to the author in the mid-1990s.
govdocs-archive_org-questioning-of-migue: Miguel Serrano, a Chilean diplomat and writer, built a body of esoteric work that mixed myth, history, and extreme politics. Questioning Miguel Serrano gathers essays that examine the man and his ideas. The library holds the set as an archive item, without backing. Such collections serve readers who study fringe movements from the outside, testing claims and tracing where a writer's system came from.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Au:
Australia's intelligence services helped the CIA in Chile, and their records stayed hidden for decades. Australian Spies Aided and Abetted CIA in Chile was published for the forty-eighth anniversary of the 1973 coup.

The briefing book posts Australian intelligence records that had never been seen in public. They widen the Chile story beyond Washington and Santiago, showing a third country quietly assisting the American effort against Allende. For historians, new national archives change old stories. The collection reminds readers that covert campaigns usually have more partners than the headlines name.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Br:
Brazil's military government helped bring down Salvador Allende in neighboring Chile. Brazil Abetted Overthrow of Allende in Chile presents the record of that role in the 1973 overthrow.

Brazil had its own generals in power and its own reasons to fear a Marxist neighbor surviving in office. The briefing book shows Brazilian support flowing into the Chilean coup story, which is usually told as an American and Chilean affair. Adding Brazil changes the map of the plot. The page capture preserves the Archive's documents and its account of the neighbor's hand.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Chiquita, the banana company, made illegal payments in Colombia, and a large paper record of them survived. Michael Evans edited this briefing book, number 593, on that record and its legal afterlife. The National Security Archive sent 48,000 pages of the Chiquita Papers to prosecutors at The Hague.

Groups asked the International Criminal Court to investigate company executives for facilitating crimes against humanity. That makes the papers more than corporate history. They became evidence in a filing that tests whether business leaders can be held criminally responsible for paying armed groups in a war zone.

Payments by Chiquita Brands in Colombia are the subject of this National Security Archive page, built on the company's own papers. The documents total more than 800,000 dollars paid to Colombian guerrillas. That figure comes from the records themselves, not from outside estimates.

Company payments to armed groups in Colombia later drew criminal cases and fines in the United States. A paper trail this detailed lets readers follow amounts and recipients directly. It is primary evidence for how a major fruit company financed fighters during Colombia's long internal conflict. The amount gave investigators a fixed starting point for wider inquiries.

Colombia's Palace of Justice siege in 1985 ended with many judges and hostages dead, and blame reached the army officer who had run military intelligence. This briefing-book page records his conviction in the killings, under his nickname, the godfather of Colombian army intelligence. The evidence here is the headline alone, with no documents described. The page marks a court outcome in one of Colombia's most painful cases, and researchers will need the linked record for the trial's details.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: BALTIC GHOST: Supporting NATO in Cyberspace - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia-rus: Memoranda of conversation and telephone call records, called memcons and telcons, are the near-verbatim notes of presidential diplomacy. This briefing-book page reports that an Archive lawsuit opened the records of Vladimir Putin's conversations with American leaders. Such records are usually withheld for decades, which is why a lawsuit was needed. The evidence here is the title alone, and the conversations themselves are not quoted. The page documents a transparency win whose contents researchers can now request and read.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_New:
A recently declassified document on the 1953 Iran coup makes a charged claim about the coup's Iranian helpers. Malcolm Byrne and Mark Gasiorowski edited this briefing book, posted in March 2018. The passage alleges that senior Iranian clerics received large sums of money from the United States.

Clerical involvement has long been debated by historians of the coup against Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. Money flowing to religious leaders would help explain street mobilization against him. A single declassified passage does not settle the debate, but it adds a concrete document where mostly inference existed before, and scholars of 1953 will have to weigh it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_The:
Thirty years after the Iran-Contra affair broke, Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, number 567, published in November 2016. Declassified records recall official deception carried out in the name of protecting a presidency. The affair joined secret arms sales to Iran with illegal support for Nicaraguan rebels.

The posting calls Iran-Contra a milestone in post-truth politics. That framing argues the scandal taught later officials that surviving a story could matter more than telling the truth. The documents let readers test that claim against memos and testimony from the cover-up itself, rather than taking the anniversary judgment on faith.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In the autumn of 1991, President George H.W. Bush announced unilateral withdrawals of American nuclear weapons. This briefing book, posted in September 2016, covers that pullback and the answer it drew from Moscow. The Soviet Union matched the move with rapid cuts of its own.

Unilateral means Washington did not wait for a treaty or a negotiation. It simply withdrew whole classes of weapons and invited a response. That gamble produced one of the fastest nuclear reductions of the Cold War, weeks before the Soviet Union itself dissolved. The documents show disarmament by announcement, a method arms control rarely attempts.

In 1957 the CIA debriefed a witness who had seen a Soviet hydrogen bomb test up close. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 623, published in April 2018. It presents newly declassified intelligence reports from 1957 on Soviet atomic development.

The witness described air crackling with pressure, as if the air was tearing up. CIA analysis also credited German scientists with greatly accelerating Soviet nuclear research. Eyewitness color of that kind is rare in intelligence files, which usually trade in estimates and photographs. The reports show analysts piecing together a rival's bomb program from human fragments in the years before satellites.

Greenland's size and position made it vital to American defense in the early Cold War, and nuclear plans followed. This briefing book is the first part of a series on episodes in that nuclear history, from 1947 to 1968. Its named landmark is Thule Air Base, the early-warning site in the far north.

Evidence gives the span and the Thule focus, and the description stays within them. Radar at Thule watched for Soviet bombers and missiles over the pole, which put a Danish territory inside America's nuclear warning system. The episodes collected here show how a quiet Arctic island became a working part of the superpower standoff.

In September 1979 a flash over the South Atlantic raised the question of a secret nuclear test, and the event became known as the Vela Incident. This briefing-book page presents the Archive's record under that name. A fuller companion volume, The Vela Flash, prints a CIA judgment putting the chance of a test at ninety percent or more. The evidence here is the title alone. This page is the shorter entry point to a mystery that governments have never officially solved.

Iceland sat astride the North Atlantic sea lanes, yet no American nuclear weapons were ever deployed there during the Cold War. This briefing book, posted in August 2016, shows how close the question came to a different answer. A recently declassified State Department record documents the internal debate.

Officials debated whether to deploy the weapons in Iceland, including through secret deployments hidden from the Icelanders. A secret deployment in a democratic ally that opposed such weapons would have carried real political danger. The record matters because the debate happened at all: geography kept pulling planners toward a country whose consent was doubtful, and restraint, in the end, won.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
What Boris Yeltsin heard from Western leaders about NATO expansion became a lasting Russian grievance. This briefing book, posted in March 2018, publishes declassified documents from the American side and others on those conversations. Its companion volume covers what Gorbachev heard a few years earlier.

Evidence here is a truncated dateline, so the description must stay general. The subject itself is precise: exact words spoken to a Russian president about whether NATO would move east. Transcripts and memos let readers compare those assurances with later claims from both sides. In a dispute where memory is the battlefield, paper is the only referee.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_vietnam_:
South Vietnamese president Ngo Dinh Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup in November 1963, with American knowledge. Briefing Book number 730, edited by John Prados and Luke Nichter and published in November 2020, brings new evidence to that old event, including material from President John Kennedy's own files.

A newly released Kennedy tape and the president's intelligence checklists fill gaps in the known record. They suggest Kennedy leaned toward regime change more strongly than earlier accounts believed. Most striking are notes by Diem himself, published for the first time, written hours before his assassination. For readers, the release sharpens the hardest question of the Vietnam story's first act: how far did Washington go in toppling its own ally?
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Explo: Russian social media operations around the 2017 violence in Charlottesville, Virginia became a case study in how foreign influence campaigns exploit American divisions. A National Security Archive briefing book page gathers its material under the heading of exploring that campaign. It covers the posts, pages, and provocations attributed to Russian operators. They appeared as a white supremacist rally turned deadly. Only the page capture survives here. Its subject remains significant, because Charlottesville showed influence work aimed not at an election directly but at a wound in American public life.
greifenstein:
Greifenstein, by F Marion Crawford, opens at Sigmundskron with the old baroness, Frau von Sigmundskron. Her hair is very white, Crawford writes, and she is thin and pale. Her bold features show the framework of departed beauty. She carries her head erect and high. Her blue eyes forbid sympathy at a glance. She is the proudest of women, and one of the most reticent. Her only child has been raised in her image.

Poverty, Crawford says, is too insignificant a word for the family's state. Greifenstein is a novel of German aristocratic pride at bay. Crawford, the American cosmopolitan of Saracinesca, sets his tragedy among castles, codes of honor, and a love the code forbids. The baroness's silence governs the first chapter as it governs the house. What she will not say, the novel spends itself discovering.
harvey-de-motu-cordis-latin:
William Harvey proves the blood's circuit in his Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis, in Latin from 1628. The heart works as a pump, driving blood in an endless round. Valves, ligatures, and vivisection build his case step by careful step in the most important medical book ever written by an Englishman.

Harvey counts the blood's volume and shows no other path is possible. Galen's old system, master for fourteen centuries, falls before his trials. The slim Latin volume remade physiology from the ground up at once. Readers meet modern medicine at its birth, in the author's own words, argued with a clarity that still instructs.
home-again:
George MacDonald wrote this novel of country life and second chances. Two elderly folk sit in a farmhouse parlor at dusk as it opens. The husband mourns his vanished youth over the scent of roses. His wife believes mainly in mahogany, linen, and hams, MacDonald writes.

Their son's world, and the heiress Lufa, widen the tale. Lufa writes, yet those who know her doubt her depth of faith. Talk of love, art, and religion fills the evenings. MacDonald blends plain farm talk with his tender moral vision. Readers get a quiet story of age, youth, and coming home to oneself.
how-to-observe-in-archaeology-suggestion:
The British Museum issued this field guide in 1920. Sir F G Kenyon wrote the preface. G F Hill opens with method's twin: how to look. W M Flinders Petrie adds his own chapter on method, and another on Egypt.

Chapters parcel the Near and Middle East among experts. Greece, Asia Minor, Cyprus, Syria, Palestine, and Mesopotamia each get a guide. Hogarth, Myres, Macalister, and Hall are among the hands. Sun-dried brick walls and ploughed-up figurines teach what to record. An appendix sums up the laws of antiquities. Travellers got a small book that could save a site, if used in time.
in-the-irish-brigade-a-tale-of-war-in-fl:
George Alfred Henty's In the Irish Brigade follows Gerald O'Carroll from Ireland to war in Flanders and Spain. The contents match a full edition, from Fresh from Ireland to a final chapter named for Gerald. The preface blames religious persecution for driving Irish soldiers abroad. Their service for France is the book's ground.

A king's threat frees imprisoned officers in exchange for Huguenots in one late scene. Ambush, kidnapping a minister, and the battle of Oudenarde raise the stakes. Gerald is captured, then finds an old friend. This copy gives the complete twenty-chapter tale.
isidore-etymologiae-latin:
Isidore, bishop of Seville, compiled the Etymologiae in the seventh century to save the learning of the ancient world. This text is the full Latin work in W. M. Lindsay's Oxford edition of 1911. Twenty books hold nearly all the knowledge a medieval reader could reach.

Isidore explains words and things together, from grammar and law to stones, ships, and food. Book Eleven treats man and the monster races of the far East. Book Twelve covers beasts, the seed of every later bestiary. Monasteries copied the work for centuries. It is the Middle Ages' own encyclopedia, and its wonders fed a thousand years of marvels.
jack-of-the-pony-express-or-the-young-ri:
Frank V. Webster wrote Jack of the Pony Express, or the young rider of the mountain trails. Jack is seventeen, tall and bronzed, waiting for his late father at Mrs. Watson's cottage. He thinks more of his pony Sunger than of his father's horse. Postmistress Jennie and important letters open the plot.

Jack faces a man who claims to be a post office inspector in one sharp scene. Never mind who I am, but who are you, Jack shoots back. Pony express rider, he answers grimly. A secret mine, masked man, and rides for life fill the tale. Webster writes a western for young readers.
judgments-of-the-court-of-appeal-of-new-:
Judgments of the Court of Appeal of New Zealand records the court's ruling on the Mount Erebus aircraft disaster inquiry. The case number is C.A. 95/81. Air New Zealand and two officials applied to review parts of the Royal Commission's report. Justice Peter Mahon, who ran the inquiry, was first respondent.

The full bench sat: Woodhouse, Cooke, Richardson, McMullin, and Somers. Hearings ran on October 5 through 9 and 12, 1981. Counsel appeared for the airline, the pilots' association, the Attorney-General, and the Civil Aviation Division. The document gives the court's judgments on how far a royal commission's findings could stand. It is a legal record of one of New Zealand's gravest public disputes.
kalitan-our-little-alaskan-cousin:
Mary F. Nixon-Roulet wrote this children's story for the Little Cousin series, published in Boston by L. C. Page and Company with a 1907 copyright. Her preface says she wrote it to interest American girls and boys in Alaska and its native peoples. She explains that the United States had taken charge of them after buying the land from Russia. The hero is Kalitan Tenas, a boy of the Thlinkit tribes of the southeast coast.

Kalitan fishes through spring storms, hears tales round the camp-fire, and travels to a glacier, Nome, and the gold country. Along the way the chapters explain totem poles, a berry dance, tea in an eglu, and how his people live and work. Young readers of the time got both a story and a plain tour of Alaskan native life as one of its own children lived it.
keziah-coffin:
Keziah Coffin is a novel by Joseph C. Lincoln, set in the Cape Cod village of Trumet. Every chapter title begins the same way: 'In which Keziah...' She talks with the parson, argues with Captain Nat, and opposes Captain Eben. The brig Sea Mist sails in chapter five, and Trumet talks in chapter six.

Keziah receives unexpected callers, visits Kyan Pepper's shop, and dresses a doll. Her next-door neighbor makes a call, and discord sounds in the parish. Captain Eben tells a story, and Keziah falls from grace in her neighbors' eyes. A last chapter tells who Keziah sees and what she does. Lincoln builds a whole village comedy around one sharp-tongued, warm-hearted Cape Cod woman.
king-olaf-s-kinsman-a-story-of-the-last-:
King Olaf's Kinsman is Charles W. Whistler's story of the last Saxon struggle against the Danes. His preface notes that no English chronicler mentions King Olaf coming to England. Yet two churches, one at each end of London Bridge, testify to his presence. Whistler fits Olaf's deeds from the Saga of King Olaf the Holy into the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's order.

That order runs from Swein's death to the accession of Cnut. A hard fight at Ringmereheath gets a Suffolk home in his retelling. Whistler imagines an English kinsman of Olaf telling the tale from inside the saga world. His novels of Saxon England always rested on this kind of chronicle checking. This one braids Norse saga and English record into a single adventure.
lectures-on-art-delivered-before-the-uni:
John Ruskin delivered these Lectures on Art at Oxford in Hilary term, 1870. The contents list an inaugural lecture first. Then come art's relation to religion, and art's relation to morals.

Ruskin had just become Oxford's first Slade Professor of Fine Art. He used the chair to preach art as a moral force. Students heard that drawing trains both eye and character. Later lectures treat landscape and Greek art in the full series. These talks helped shape British art education for a generation. Dana, his editor, was a noted author himself. Their friendship helped preserve Allston's thought for American art.
letters-and-journals-of-james-eighth-ear:
The letters and journals of James Bruce, eighth Earl of Elgin, appeared after his death. Dean Stanley of Westminster supplied a preface. Elgin's family and friends consulted Stanley about publishing a record.

Stanley says Elgin's career touched many critical points of empire. Elgin governed in Canada and served in China and India. His letters mix public duty with private reflection. The journals show a Victorian statesman at close range. Readers of imperial history will find a candid, careful self-portrait here. Elgin's role in Canada fills much of the early record. His later China mission brought fame and controversy alike.
life-of-chopin:
Franz Liszt wrote this life of his fellow composer Chopin. Martha Walker Cook translated it from the French. The original edition appeared in 1863, the notes to this text explain. A fourth, revised edition of 1880 underlies this electronic version.

Cook dedicates her translation to Jan Pychowski, a Polish pianist. She praises his earnest patriotism, like Chopin's own. Liszt knew Chopin personally, which gives the memoir special weight. Seven chapters carry the pianist-composer's story in Liszt's romantic voice. Cookery of the text cut pages apart for scanning, its notes confess. She dedicated the work without Pychowski's consent or knowledge beforehand.
little-britain:
Washington Irving sketches a small London neighborhood in this piece. Little Britain hides among narrow streets and venerable houses. Christ Church School and St. Bartholomew's Hospital bound it westward. Smithfield, Long Lane, and Aldersgate Street frame its other sides.

St. Paul's dome looks down with motherly protection over it. The quarter once housed the Dukes of Brittany, Irving says. Fashion later rolled west, and trade took the deserted homes. For a time the district became a great mart of learning. Bull-and-Mouth Street's gulf separates it from Butcher Lane. Dukes of Brittany once resided in the ancient quarter.
looking-seaward-again:
Sir Walter Runciman published these sea tales in 1907. The Walter Scott Publishing Company issued them in London. He inscribes the fragments affectionately to his wife. His preface says the tales were told by firesides first.

Runciman claims only unvarnished matters of fact for them. Early desertion of home for sailing vessels limited his schooling. Steam was already taking the wind from sailing ships then. Contents promise torpedoes, ice, smugglers, and a Russian port. A pasha before Plevna and Dutchy and his chief appear. Fair trade and foul play open the contents' sea stories.
lord-dolphin:
Harriet A. Cheever published this children's sea story in 1903. Diantha W. Horne illustrated the volume. Lord Dolphin introduces himself in the first chapter. Under the waves and a coral grove follow quickly.

A mermaid's cave, gardens, and treasure grounds await young readers. The dolphin narrator reports what he saw one strange day. A great vessel strains and tugs in the frontispiece. His adventures end with a surprising visit onto land. Madame Angora and Mother Bunny preceded Cheever's dolphin tale. Billy Trill's strange adventures headline her earlier children's books. Cheever had written Madame Angora and Mother Bunny for children before.
lord-elgin:
Sir John George Bourinot wrote this life of Lord Elgin. The Makers of Canada series issued it at Toronto in 1903. Duncan Campbell Scott and Pelham Edgar edited the series. Bourinot finished and revised the pages shortly before his death.

Editors praise his breadth of political vision and factual mastery. Elgin's Canadian career required unusual insight into constitutional law. Contents cover the Indemnification Act and two ministries' ends. Clergy reserves, seigniorial tenure, and American relations close it. Farewell to Canada closes the ten-chapter contents list. Canada and the United States receive the ninth chapter's attention.
lord-kilgobbin:
Charles Lever sets this tale of Ireland at Kilgobbin Castle. It first ran as a serial in the Cornhill Magazine. Luke Fildes illustrated that run from October 1870 onward. Smith, Elder published the three-volume book form in 1872.

Lever dedicates it in breaking health and broken spirits. The task once his joy became linked with sorrow, he writes. Prince Kostalergi and the chums enter the castle's home life. A drive through a bog shows how friends may differ. The blue coat and the cousins follow the Trinity chapters. Kilgobbin Castle's home life anchors Lever's final novel.
marie-an-episode-in-the-life-of-the-late:
Marie is an episode in the life of Allan Quatermain by H. Rider Haggard. His dedication, dated at Ditchingham in 1912, recalls southern Africa. He lists the annexation of the Transvaal and the Zulu and Boer wars. Against that history he sets young Allan's first love.

Allan learns French, then rides to the rescue at Maraisfontein. Marie Marais is the girl whose farm is attacked. A shooting match, a parting, and a camp of death follow. Dingaan's bet and Retief's treaty bring the Great Trek into the tale. Haggard mourns the innocent blood of those years. The novel is a moving prequel for Quatermain's many readers.
mark-twain:
Mark Twain, by Archibald Henderson, is an early life of the humorist. Photographs by Alvin Langdon Coburn illustrate the volume. A poem by Bliss Carman pictures Twain jesting among the great dead. Henderson's preface speaks of a world in debt to Twain's humor.

His own feeling, he says, began in childhood with warm affection. It grew from the works first, then from knowing the man. Henderson traces the Hannibal boy who became a river pilot and miner. Newspaper work in the West sharpened the young humorist. World fame, the white suit, and the sage's drawl complete the portrait. The book glows with personal gratitude and knowledge.
martin-arles-tractatus-superstitionibus-:
Martin of Arles was a canon from Navarre who wrote a Latin treatise on superstition in 1517. The work was printed at Rome in 1559 under the title Tractatus de Superstitionibus. Its full title adds that it argues against harmful magic and sorcery, the twin fears named in Latin as maleficia and sortilegia.

Martin sorts the false beliefs and secret rites of his day and argues that clergy should correct them. He writes as a churchman close to daily parish life, not as a distant judge. The treatise stands between older pastoral teaching and the sharper demon manuals of the next century. Readers can see early modern fears of magic taking fixed, written form.
memoir-of-fleeming-jenkin:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the Memoir of Fleeming Jenkin for Scribner's in 1901. Jenkin's kin meant to print his papers, with this life at their head. In America the life came out alone, without those papers.

Stevenson warns that Jenkin was more than his work shows. His force lay in friendship, in brave views of life, and in hard thought. Chapter one traces the Jenkins of Stowting and Fleeming's father at sea. Stevenson wrote the preface at Saranac in October 1887. St. Helena and King Tom stand in his father's sea tale. A life of cables and college work grows from those roots.
morgagni-sedibus-1761-latin:
Latin was still the tongue of learned medicine when Morgagni issued De sedibus in 1761. The full title promises five books on the seats and causes of diseases, studied by anatomy. This Latin first edition holds the complete original text. Its final line, Finis Tomi Secundi, closes the second Latin tome.

Morgagni spent decades gathering cases from Padua's hospitals and his own practice. He set each patient's story beside the autopsy that followed death. From that pairing grew modern pathology. An English translation by Alexander, in three volumes, is also held. Scholars use the Latin to check every term. The original carries an authority copies cannot match.
moths-of-the-limberlost-a-book-about-lim:
Gene Stratton-Porter wrote this nature book about the moths around her Limberlost Cabin in Indiana. She dedicates it to Neltje Degraff Doubleday. The first chapters cover moths generally: their eggs, caterpillars, and winter quarters. Then the book takes up species one by one, under the folk names she loved.

The Robin Moth, the Yellow Emperor, and the Lady Bird get chapters. So do the Moths of the Moon, the King of the Hollyhocks, and Hera of the Corn. Bloody-Nose of Sunshine Hill and the Modest Moth close the list. Stratton-Porter reared moths at home and photographed them, mixing science with storytelling.
muslin:
George Moore first published this Irish novel in 1886 as A Drama in Muslin. A new edition came out in September 1915. The tale opens at the Convent of the Holy Child. White-dressed schoolgirls flutter in the green garden like doves.

It is prize day, and a bishop's visit stirs the school. Plain Alice Barton has written the day's musical sketch. Moore watches the girls with a cool, close eye. Their dresses, hopes, and ranks all matter here. The novel follows convent girls into Dublin's marriage market. Moore's plain style was bold for its day, and the book made his name.
my-first-picture-book-with-thirty-six-pa:
Joseph Martin Kronheim printed this first picture book in rich colors. Routledge issued it in London and New York. It holds thirty-six pages of pictures for small children. A first alphabet leads the contents.

Old tales follow: the Old Woman in a Shoe, and Babes in the Wood. Little Bo-Peep and Five Little Pigs come next. Mother Goose and her son Jack close the set. Each letter pairs a word with a bright picture. Kronheim was a pioneer of color printing for children. The book shows Victorian picture books at their gayest, made to teach letters through charm.
my-robin:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells the true tale behind her famed robin. A reader of The Secret Garden wrote to ask one question. Had she owned the real robin from that book? Burnett says the letter thrilled her to the center of her being.

She answers that she did not own him at all. He owned her, or perhaps they owned each other. Her robin is the small English kind, not the American bird. He wears a red satin waistcoat on a plump breast. Each tilt of his head seems full of drama. Burnett's sketch is a love letter to one bold garden friend.
mysterious-mr-sabin:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this spy novel, copyrighted in 1905 by Little, Brown. Its first chapter is a supper party at the Milan. A drama of the pavement follows at once. Felix gives a warning in chapter three.

Chapter four moves to the Russian ambassador's rooms. A frontispiece shows a girl's face lit like fine statuary. The old text opens with a toast among men at supper. Densham lifts his glass under rose-shaded lights. Sabin, the mysterious man of the title, drives the intrigue. Oppenheim builds an early spy tale of plots, warnings, and high society masks.
nasa-tm-19630013134-stress-corrosion-of-:
