T. S. Humphries of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on June 24, 1963. It studies stress corrosion in strong aluminum alloys. Stress corrosion cracks metal held under load in a harsh setting. The alloys named are 2014, 2024, 2219, 7075, 7178, and 7079.

Tests dipped samples in salt water, then exposed them to air, in turns. Humphries reports that nearly all the alloys cracked badly along one grain direction. Two tempers, listed as 7075-T73 and 2219-T87, resisted that cracking. Plain protective coatings failed, but coatings plus a zinc chromate primer helped a great deal. Rocket builders needed such warnings.
nasa-tm-19630013938-studies-on-ablation-:
Ernst W. Adams, John D. Warmbrod, and Benton K. Berry of Marshall wrote this study on June 19, 1963. It reviews theory work on ablation heat shields. Ablation protects objects that cross an atmosphere at high speed. The shield chars and sheds material, carrying heat away with it.

The authors came from Marshall's Aeroballistics Division. Their review rests on numerical solutions worked out by computer. Catalog notes say both Earth and Mars entries were treated. A Mars craft meets a thin, strange atmosphere, unlike Earth's. Pulling the theory together in one review helped shield designers plan for planets beyond our own.
nasa-tm-19640018168-an-experimental-stud:
Robert W. Graham, Robert C. Hendricks, and Robert C. Ehlers of Lewis wrote this study. It was prepared for a cryogenic engineering meeting in August 1964. Their subject is heating liquid hydrogen in a pool. Liquid hydrogen is a key rocket fuel, stored near absolute zero.

The team varied pressure across low and very high ranges. They also varied acceleration, to mimic tanks in flight and on the ground. Pool heating drives boiling on the tank's warm surfaces. How bubbles form and break away sets how fast heat moves. Knowing that behavior helped engineers design hydrogen tanks that would not overheat, vent badly, or starve an engine.
nasa-tm-19650012585-the-motion-of-gaseou:
Su-Shu Huang, of Goddard and Catholic University of America, studied how gas streams move in a close binary star system. In such a system, two stars orbit each other closely. Gas can flow between them and around them. Huang asks what rules govern that flow when particles collide.

He first examines a statistical property of the constants that describe particle motion. He then shows that the rate of change of angular momentum does not depend on speed. Those results lead to formulas for the gaseous flow. The work is theory, aimed at explaining real pairs of stars that exchange gas.
nasa-tm-19650070881-studies-of-pilot-con:
C H Woodling of Langley and Carl C Clark of the Naval Air Development Center presented this study in New York in January 1959. Pilots practiced control of space vehicles during launch and reentry on a human centrifuge. A centrifuge spins its rider to copy the forces of flight. Woodling notes that pilot-controlled simulators had become a necessity as aircraft grew more complex.

Real flight was too risky for first tries at such tasks. The centrifuge let pilots feel real forces while staying on the ground. Their performance showed whether a person could still control a vehicle under launch and reentry loads. That question stood at the center of the coming crewed space program.
nasa-tm-19650076351-on-the-use-of-dynami:
Perry W Hanson and George W Jones Jr at Langley explained, in a September 1963 symposium paper, how scaled dynamic models help study two hard loads. Transonic buffet shakes a vehicle in flight. Ground winds bend a tall rocket standing on its pad. Both forces are random and complex, which makes pure calculation difficult, the authors say.

Their answer is the aeroelastic model, scaled to bend like the real vehicle. Tested in wind, such a model reveals response that formulas miss. A two-percent Saturn model appears among their examples. The paper shows model testing at its most practical, aimed at loads that could shake a launch vehicle apart.
nasa-tm-19660020099-a-simulator-study-of:
Lindsay J Lina and Martin T Moul at Langley studied a dangerous stall in a fixed-base simulator, in a paper given in Los Angeles in November 1965. Aircraft with a T-tail, the tailplane set atop the fin, can fall into a deep stall. There, the wing's wake blankets the tail and the nose will not drop. Jet fighters with high tails had long shown pitch-up faults, the authors note.

Newer T-tail transports with rear engines raised the same fear. A simulator lets pilots meet the trap safely and practice recovery. Lina and Moul examine how the aircraft behaves in that state. Their study served a design question with several fatal accidents behind it in that era.
nasa-tm-19670005827-ionospheric-polar-bl:
Yukio Hakura, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this August 1966 paper with Yugoro Takenoshita and Koichi Matsuoka. The co-authors came from the Hiraiso Branch of Japan's Radio Research Laboratories. It builds daily measures of ionospheric blackouts, events where the upper atmosphere absorbs radio signals. Coverage spans the polar cap and the auroral zone, for 1957 through 1965.

Each daily index runs from 0 to 9 and grows roughly with the logarithm of the day's total blackout hours. The auroral zone index generally rose and fell with polar geomagnetic activity. The polar cap index instead tracks activity caused by solar cosmic rays entering the cap, and its yearly average moved with sunspot numbers. The auroral index also showed a clear 27-day repeating pattern, pointing to control by the solar wind.
nasa-tm-19670022994-search-for-the-gamma:
William K. Roberts and David C. Liu, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this report in August 1967. It describes a search for a rare process predicted by quantum electrodynamics. In that process, a photon interacts with a nucleus's electric field and two photons come out. Seeing it would test the theory's picture of the vacuum itself.

The experiment fired gamma rays at lead and copper targets. Detectors sat where the two secondary photons should emerge at right angles to each other, and an energy-summing coincidence technique picked out true pairs. No signal rose above background, so the team set upper limits on the process's cross section for both metals. Those limits sat far above the theoretical predictions, so the theory escaped a rigorous test. Still, the authors argue, the experience shows the predicted range is reachable with improved technique, and they discuss the needed improvements.
nasa-tm-19680012452-modulo-acquisition-o:
Solomon Levine, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1968. It treats modulo acquisition of ambiguity resolving tracking codes, the signals ground stations use to measure a spacecraft's range. Before any ranging can happen, the station must lock onto the incoming code at exactly the right repeating point.

With sidetone ranging, Levine explains, phase locked loops make acquisition easy. A pure pseudo-random code system is slower: the local copy must be shifted bit by bit against the received code until the two correlate. A hybrid system using both can exploit the sidetone's ambiguous range reading to acquire the pseudo-random code automatically and rapidly. Compared with the code-only approach, this modulo technique cuts acquisition time to a small fraction, raises the detection threshold, and considerably reduces encoder complexity.
nasa-tm-19680013859-human-information-pr:
T. E. Wempe and D. L. Baty of NASA's Ames Research Center measured how fast people handle information while tracking in this 1968 study. Subjects flew one-axis and two-axis tracking tasks while also doing a second listening task. The work asks how much a person can take in before performance hits a clear limit.

Adding a second tracking channel or the listening task lowered the rate on each channel. Apart from that drop, the channels acted like parallel paths that add together. Total rate still stopped at a limit tied to the order of the system being controlled. The results help predict pilot workload on complex aerospace missions with many tasks at once.
nasa-tm-19680016283-on-the-dynamics-of-a:
Joseph A. Burns and Gerald Halpern of Goddard Space Flight Center study charged particle motion in a spiral magnetic field in this May 1968 preprint. The spiral field is an ideal model of the interplanetary magnetic field. Energetic particles follow a guiding center path as they drift through that field.

The authors present formulas for every part of the drift velocity. Comparing the parts shows the electric drift is by far the largest for cases of physical interest. They then derive a fuller expression using only that dominant drift. The results help scientists track how energetic particles move through interplanetary space between the Sun and Earth.
nasa-tm-19680019214-a-study-of-refrigera:
Jesse P. Blalock of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston studied a cold-based first aid treatment for pit viper snakebite in this June 1968 memorandum. The method pairs refrigeration with a constricting band on the bitten limb. Blalock asked whether it could replace the standard incision and suction procedure.

A literature search showed experts already doubted incision and suction, citing limits and possible harm. Blalock injected rabbits with eastern diamondback rattlesnake venom. Treated animals were then compared with untreated animals for survival time. The treated group showed a significant increase in survival time. Blalock closes with recommendations for first aid procedures based on the study.
nasa-tm-19680020381-pressure-induced-mic:
W. Ho and I. A. Kaufman, linked to North American Rockwell and Columbia University's Radiation Laboratory, studied how nitrogen gas absorbs microwaves under pressure. Nitrogen on its own should pass microwaves freely, yet squeezed gas absorbs some of the signal. Their report measures that pressure-induced absorption at one microwave frequency, across wide ranges of heat and pressure.

All readings were taken at a single frequency while pressure rose to well over a hundred times normal air pressure. The authors express the loss in a compact formula tied to gas density and temperature. Combining their result with earlier far-infrared work, they then calculate a lasting property of the nitrogen molecule, its quadrupole moment.
nasa-tm-19680027714-radiative-transfer-b:
James E. Hansen of the Institute for Space Studies at Goddard Space Flight Center develops a faster way to compute radiative transfer in this paper. The problem is diffuse reflection of light from a plane parallel atmosphere. Exact solutions exist only for very simple scattering patterns, so practical cases need numerical work.

Hansen builds on a doubling principle first used by van de Hulst. Start with a layer so thin that its scattering follows directly from the phase function. Then double the layer repeatedly to reach full atmospheric thickness. The method skips solving the full transfer equation numerically. Hansen applies it to spectral scattering by clouds in the near-infrared. There the phase function peaks strongly in the forward direction.
nasa-tm-19690018532-a-note-on-the-plasma:
J. M. Grebowsky wrote this March 1969 preprint, numbered X-621-69-42, on the plasma moment equations in a dipole field. A dipole field, like a bar magnet's, models the magnetism of Earth and other planets. Plasma trapped in such a field follows its curved lines, which makes the motion equations awkward in ordinary coordinates.

Grebowsky sets up a coordinate system fitted to the field itself. One direction runs along the field, one circles around it, and one follows the dipole's equipotential lines. He then rewrites the speed terms of the continuity and momentum equations in those directions. The short note gives plasma theorists a cleaner frame for studying distributions and waves in planetary fields.
nasa-tm-19690020177-effects-of-thermal-s:
John J. Smithrick of Lewis Research Center thermal-shock tested thin-film cadmium sulfide solar cells in this report. Cells on Kapton, copper, and molybdenum substrates were heated, then dipped into liquid nitrogen. The cycles ran in an inert atmosphere, with heating held at a set warm temperature.

Kapton substrate cells split in the cadmium sulfide layer and delaminated. Their voltage and fill factor held steady, while current and power fell in proportion to lost area. The single copper cell survived over thirteen hundred cycles without delamination or degradation. The single molybdenum cell also avoided delamination but did degrade. Comparable molybdenum cells degrade in shelf storage too, Smithrick notes.
nasa-tm-19700008652-method-for-determini:
David G. Evans of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in January 1970. It gives a method for matching the main parts of a turbojet engine. The compressor and turbine must work together across the engine's full range of speeds.

Evans builds charts that pair the compressor and turbine of a single-spool engine. From them he finds the pressure ratios and temperature ratios that meet the matching needs. Those needs cover air flow, power, and shaft speed. Engine designers could use the method to predict how a matched engine would run before it was built.
nasa-tm-19700016392-measurements-of-fluc:
Raymond J. Karabinus and Bobby W. Sanders of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in May 1970. They measured unsteady pressures inside the center's 8-by-6-foot supersonic wind tunnel. The tests spanned speeds from just over half the speed of sound to about twice it.

The team checked the tunnel's bellmouth, test section, and diffuser for pressure swings. The strongest disturbance in the test section came near Mach 0.75, they found. It pulsed hundreds of times each second and seemed to be a flow resonance in the porous wall region. Knowing such swings exist helps staff judge when tunnel data can be trusted.
nasa-tm-19700016396-comparison-of-flame-:
Charles R. Andracchio and John C. Aydelott of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in May 1970. It compares how flames spread over thin flat materials in normal gravity and in weightlessness. All tests ran in an oxygen atmosphere, where fire risk is a grave concern.

The team burned thin square samples of paper and plastic in both settings. They photographed the flame shape and spread pattern for each run. They also measured how fast the flame moved across each sample. Results like these fed the fire safety rules for crewed spacecraft, where a flame in weightlessness behaves in new ways.
nasa-tm-19700024929-effects-of-roughness:
Meyer Reshotko, Donald R. Boldman, and Robert C. Ehlers of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 engineering meeting in New York. It studies how surface roughness changes heat transfer in conical nozzles. Rocket and jet nozzles pass very hot gas at high speed.

Roughness peaks can poke through the calm layer of gas next to a wall. When they do, more heat passes into the wall, the authors note. The team tested two cone-shaped nozzles with different angles, using heated air. They varied the roughness over a wide range. Such results help designers predict wall heating and pick safe nozzle finishes.
nasa-tm-19700024989-the-effects-of-wind-:
Donald L. Dietrick of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this internal note on January 23, 1968. It studies wind forces on a thrusting launch vehicle during a Mode I abort. A Mode I abort happens early in flight, while the launch escape system can still pull the crew away.

Wind pushes on both the rising rocket and the escape system as they fire. Those pushes can bend the flight path at the worst moment. Dietrick works out how strong the effects are. Studies like this one set the wind limits for a safe launch. They also helped crews plan an escape that stays clear of the failing rocket.
nasa-tm-19700025191-csm-fuel-requirement:
Ronald W. Simpson of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this Apollo internal note. It works out the fuel the command and service module would need to rescue the lunar module in lunar orbit. A rescue would be needed if the lunar module could not fly itself back up to meet it.

The figures rest on a piloted simulation study run to aid planning of the lunar landing mission. That study also tested whether improving the state vector with ranging data would change the fuel needed. Both the primary and the backup rendezvous modes were covered in the runs. The cockpit setup paired digital and analog computers, with a projected view of the target craft for the pilot.
nasa-tm-19700026507-development-of-a-spa:
The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this internal note, number MSC-67-EE-12. It reports the development of an atomic timing system for spacecraft. Exact timekeeping on board supports navigation, tracking, and the timing of events in flight, where a drift of seconds can throw off a whole plan.

The document is built in parts that move from the ground up. Early parts cover the system's principle of operation and a description of its working parts. A test plan section then lays out how the timing system would be proven before flight. That plan includes an engineering evaluation and flight-related checks, the stages any new spacecraft clock had to pass.
nasa-tm-19700027853-orbital-reconnaissan:
Richard N. Green and Sue W. Souders of the Langley Research Center in Virginia wrote this report for Project Viking. It presents a computer program for planning orbital reconnaissance of Mars. Viking orbiters would photograph the planet to pick landing sites.

The program follows two things over time, the authors state. One is the spacecraft ground track, and the other is the camera footprint on the turning surface of Mars. Users can set where and how the photographs are taken. A photo run can be placed inside a band of good lighting. Planners used such a tool to design missions before launch.
nasa-tm-19710007936-dynamic-data-analysi:
Robert C. Ward of the Langley Research Center wrote this report in February 1971. It explains the dynamic data analysis techniques inside Langley's time series computer program. The program studies records that vary with time, such as vibration data from flight tests.

Ward describes how the program handles random but steady series of readings. Spectral methods in the program show which frequencies carry the energy in a signal. The report also prints corrections to some lines and table headings. Guides of this kind let engineers across the agency run the same analysis the same way. That sameness makes results from different centers easy to compare.
nasa-tm-19710023840-energy-exchanges-dur:
R E Morris of the Lewis Research Center published this short theory study in August 1971, as NASA TM X-67917. It asks where the energy goes when two moving masses strike head on and bounce only partway back. His test case was a model of a spherical reactor vessel hitting a concrete block. Reactor safety studies needed the answer.

Morris derived a formula for the motion energy turned into work, heat, and sound. It depends on the two masses, their starting speeds, and a bounce factor. For a fixed pair and bounce factor, the changed energy stays constant at a fixed closing speed. The total changed also stays below one simple bound. He tied that bound to the smaller mass.
north-american-free-trade-agreement-1992:
Tariff phasing descriptions for the North American Free Trade Agreement, dated October 7, 1992, form this record, tied to Canada. The sampled text is Annex One of the agreement, in plain legal form. It explains how each party lists reservations in its schedule. Those lists name existing measures that break certain duties.

The duties named cover national treatment and most favoured nation treatment. Local presence, performance needs, and nationality rules for managers are also listed. Each reservation states its sector, sub sector, and trade class. It also gives the type of reservation, level of government, and legal citation. Lawyers and trade officials, not general readers, were its users.
observations-of-an-orderly-some-glimpses:
Ward Muir, a lance corporal in the Royal Army Medical Corps, wrote Observations of an Orderly about an English war hospital. Simpkin, Marshall in London first published it in July 1917. Muir dedicated it to the officer in command of the Third London General Hospital. Passages had run earlier, in shorter form, in many papers.

The Spectator, the New Statesman, and the Daily Mail stand among those papers listed. The subtitle promises glimpses of life and work in the hospital, seen from an orderly's low place. Muir had also edited Happy, Though Wounded, the book of that same hospital. Wounded men, nurses, and daily routine fill his sketches from inside the wards.
our-american-cousin:
Tom Taylor's comedy Our American Cousin, in three acts, made its name at Laura Keene's Theatre in New York in October 1858. Its cast pairs English aristocrats of Trenchard Manor — Sir Edward Trenchard, his daughter Florence, the drawling Lord Dundreary — with Asa Trenchard, the rough American cousin whose visit upends the house. Joseph Jefferson's Asa and E. A. Sothern's Dundreary became theatrical legends.

The play's fame is inseparable from a darker night: Abraham Lincoln was watching it at Ford's Theatre when he was assassinated, in the middle of the second scene of act three. The text here opens on the manor drawing room, luncheon spread, French windows giving on an English park. Dundreary's mangled proverbs, the transcriber notes, are largely absent from this early printing.
our-little-korean-cousin:
H. Lee M. Pike wrote Our Little Korean Cousin for the Little Cousin series, which introduced American children to the children of other lands. His hero is Yung Pak, a Korean boy. His name, house, clothes, shoes, and tongue all seem queer to the reader. Pike turns the joke around at once. Yung Pak would open his eyes just as wide at an American child's peculiar ways.

The chapters walk through Yung Pak's home and a glimpse of the king. His school follows, where boys sit upon the floor. A monk's story and a journey to a monastery come later. The book ends with the day he earns a full-fledged top-knot. Illustrated by L. J. Bridgman, the book teaches geography by sympathy, one ordinary boy at a time.
penny-plain:
O. Douglas opens Penny Plain at tea-time in Priorsford, a little town on the river Tweed. Mist shrouds the circling hills on a chill October afternoon, and the bridge stands almost deserted. Peel Tower looms over neat houses where brown teapots warm on hobs and servants lay tea-tables in the big houses on the Hill.

The title comes from a toy-theatre joke: penny plain or twopence coloured, and the solemn small boy chooses penny plain as better value. Douglas writes of a Scottish Borders town and its households with warmth and humour, finding drama in ordinary, decent folk.
pico-oratio-de-hominis-dignitate-latin:
Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a young Italian count and scholar, wrote his Oration on the Dignity of Man in 1486. He meant it as the opening speech for a public debate on 900 claims about philosophy and faith. The Latin text is the speech as he prepared it.

Pico argues that humans have no fixed place in creation and can shape themselves by free choice. He defends learning from many sources at once, including Jewish Kabbalah and learned magic. Later readers named the speech the manifesto of the Renaissance, and it still anchors debates on human freedom.
pomponazzi-de-incantationibus-1556-latin:
Pietro Pomponazzi, a philosophy professor at Padua and Bologna, wrote his book On Incantations early in the sixteenth century. This Latin edition of 1556 spread his argument after his death. Pomponazzi asks why marvels, cures, and apparitions happen, and answers that nature alone can cause them, without demons or miracles.

Images work on the imagination, faith heals the body, and celestial influence moves the rest. His naturalistic critique was daring in an age of inquisitors. The book became a turning point for demonology and the philosophy of magic. Later skeptics built on Pomponazzi's ground. His calm professors' Latin still reads like a door opening in a stuffy room.
practical-rules-for-the-management-of-a-:
Charles Hutton Gregory, civil engineer, published his Practical Rules for the Management of a Locomotive Engine in the 1841 edition. Covering the engine in the station, on the road, and in cases of accident. His preface makes a pioneer's claim: engineering literature offered valuable treatises on the theory and construction of locomotives, but no work yet illustrated their use. The paper was read in abstract before the Institution of Civil Engineers in February 1841.

Gregory wrote from the footplate side, as resident engineer of the London and Croydon Railway. He appends the regulations he framed for the first appointment of engine-men on that line, plus a table of railway velocities he used to save calculation. Safety is the drumbeat throughout. In 1841 the locomotive was new, its drivers were newer, and this little book is among the first to treat driving as a profession with rules.
quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of-mark:
Quotes and Images from Mark Twain, prepared by David Widger, gathers quotations from Twain's works and marks a first run of them as some of the editor's favorites. The lines run alphabetically, and Twain's bite is present from the start.

The aim and object of the law and lawyers, he writes, was to defeat justice, and all life seems to be sacred except human life. A house should not be built by beginning at the top, there are liars everywhere this year, and contempt of court may be committed by a horse. Grief too deep for outcry stands beside the coyote, a living, breathing allegory of Want.
ranke-history-popes-vol-2-austin:
Sarah Austin put Ranke's History of the Popes into English in 1840. Volume 2 treats the papacy in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Reformation, Catholic revival, and the Baroque age fill its wide span.

Ranke drew on the archives of Venice and Rome for his tale. He shows popes as princes, patrons, and foes of reform at once. The work helped found the modern, source-based study of the past. Protestant readers praised its fairness toward a church not its author's. That rare balance made the book famous across Europe at once. It remains a landmark of history writing in any tongue.
ranke-history-popes-vol-3-austin:
Volume 3 of Ranke's History of the Popes appeared in Austin's version in 1841. The Catholic revival stands triumphant across the book's main span. Trent's great council and the new Jesuit order lead the renewal.

A papacy once sunk in scandal rises to fresh power and discipline. Ranke tells the turn with care for proof and a fair hand. He praises reform where he finds it, though a Protestant himself. Saints, soldiers, and statesmen crowd his rich, ordered narrative here. The book's fame rests on that rise above mere party feeling. Great history, many said, had found a new and higher road.
red-robin:
Jane Abbott wrote this story for young readers, copyrighted in 1922 by J. B. Lippincott and reissued by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Harriet Roosevelt Richards drew the pictures, and the book is dedicated to Betsy. A prologue is billed as a story before the story.

Robin enters through chapters named The Orphan Doll, A Prince, and The House of Forsyth. She asserts herself, writes a letter, and meets the Lynchs, Susy Castle, and a lady of the rushing waters. A gift to the queen and a Forsyth heir add to the plot. One picture caption promises a very Christmasy effect, in a tale of a girl finding her place.
remy-daemonolatreiae-1595-latin:
Nicolas Rémy, a judge in Lorraine, published his Daemonolatreiae Libri Tres, Three Books on the Worship of Demons, at Lyon in 1595. The text is the Latin original. Rémy drew his book from the capital trials of some nine hundred persons put to death for witchcraft in his own courts. With the Malleus Maleficarum, it is the most weighty early work on demons and witches.

Case by case he tells of pacts, sabbaths, weather magic, and the marks of the devil, all sworn in his courtroom. Rémy believed every word and hanged on the strength of it. His casebook armed a generation of judges across Europe. The library holds the English version beside this Latin root of it.
reuchlin-de-arte-cabalistica-1517-latin:
Johannes Reuchlin, a German lawyer and scholar of Hebrew, published De arte cabalistica at Hagenau in 1517. The Latin work, in three books, is the founding text of Christian Kabbalah. It mixes Hebrew and Greek passages into a staged debate among three speakers.

Simon the Kabbalist, Marranus the Muslim, and Philolaus the Pythagorean argue over the Messiah, number lore, and the hands-on use of Kabbalah. Reuchlin aimed to show that Jewish mystic teaching could support Christian truth. The book shaped how Europe's scholars read Kabbalah for the next two centuries.
rituale-romanum-latin:
The Rituale Romanum is the Catholic Church's official book of rites outside the Mass. Pope Paul V issued the first edition in 1614. The Latin text here is the standard 1925 edition from Ratisbon, which kept the older rites in their classic form.

Priests use the book for baptisms, weddings, funerals, blessings, and prayers for the sick and dying. Its most famous part is the Rite of Exorcism, word for word the same since 1614. The book shows the Church's daily ritual life as it stood before the reforms of the 1960s. Latinists value its exact, formal wording.
robin:
Frances Hodgson Burnett, author of The Secret Garden, published this novel with Stokes of New York under copyright of 1922. It continues the world of her Head of the House of Coombe: an outline called The Years Before, arranged by Hamilton Williamson from that book, stands at the front. The story opens in Mayfair in the years when Victorian standards began to falter.

Robert Gareth-Lawless and his lovely young wife live there in a slice of a house between two stately mansions. So light and airy is she that she is known as Feather. The house was a rash venture of the honeymoon. Robert, well born and irresponsible, has no resources, and the outline traces what followed for them and theirs.
saint-augustin:
Louis Bertrand wrote Saint Augustin, translated here by Vincent O'Sullivan. In a translator's note O'Sullivan explains that quotations from Saint Augustin's Confessions are taken from Canon Bigg's scholarly version, which he thinks the best in English. Where Bertrand's reading of the Latin differs from Bigg's, O'Sullivan felt bound to follow the author of the book. These differences, he says, never gravely affect the meaning of a passage. Sometimes the choice is a mere matter of wording, as with one Latin word that Bigg renders twin and Bertrand, like Pusey, renders foster-brother.

To let curious readers judge, O'Sullivan prints an instance in full. The Latin, from the Confessions, book six, chapter fifteen. It tells how a mistress was torn from Augustin's side as a bar to his marriage. His heart, where it clung to hers, was cut and wounded and drew blood.
secretum-secretorum-1501-latin:
The Secretum Secretorum, the Secret of Secrets, pretends to be Aristotle's private counsel to his pupil Alexander. This Latin edition was printed at Bologna in 1501. The medieval work is a mirror for princes, a guide to ruling, with health lore, physiognomy, and talismanic matter worked through it.

Kings across Europe and the Islamic world prized copies of the Secret. Its advice runs from choosing ministers to reading faces and timing journeys by the stars. The magical streak sets it apart from plainer mirrors of rule. Few medieval books traveled so far in so many tongues. The 1501 printing shows the text still current at the dawn of the press age.
selections-from-the-works-of-john-ruskin:
Chauncey B. Tinker, professor of English at Yale, edited this college choice from John Ruskin's works, issued by Houghton Mifflin in 1908. Tinker adds an opening essay and notes. A first essay treats Ruskin's style, that rich and urgent voice of Victorian art writing.

Chosen parts of Modern Painters cover Alpine sunrise, mountain glory, and what Ruskin named the pathetic fallacy. Parts of The Stones of Venice follow, opening with The Throne. Students meet Ruskin on landscape, building, and truth in art, in passages that show why his praise or blame could make or mar a painter's name.
sinistrari-demoniality-1879-english-lati:
Ludovico Maria Sinistrari was a Franciscan friar and demon expert in late 1600s Italy. His Latin treatise on demoniality stayed in manuscript until it was found in 1872. The first English version came out at Paris in 1879, printed side by side with the Latin.

Sinistrari argues that incubi and succubi, the night demons of old lore, are real bodily beings with minds of their own. He asks how the law and the Church should judge acts tied to them. The odd, careful book is a late high point of Catholic demon thought.
spadacrene-anglica-the-english-spa-fount:
Edmund Deane, a doctor of Oxford, wrote Spadacrene Anglica, or The English Spa Fountain, the first work on the waters of Harrogate. The 1922 reprint, from John Wright and Sons at Bristol, adds a first note by James Rutherford and life notes by Alex. Butler. Rutherford asks what Deane would think of the modern Harrogate his labors helped to bring into being.

In Deane's day, the year 1626 being named, Harrogate was a small scattered hamlet in the great Royal Forest of Knaresborough. Since then, more than eighty mineral springs have been found within a few miles, a count no other health resort in Europe can match. The healing powers of the waters were not unknown before Deane praised the Tuewhit Well, and Rutherford traces their fame back toward old times and St. Mungo's well.
spee-cautio-criminalis-1631-latin:
Friedrich Spee was a German Jesuit priest who heard the last words of many women condemned as witches. His Cautio Criminalis, printed at Rinteln in 1631, attacks the witch trials from inside the system. The Latin text is that of the first edition.

Spee lays out 51 doubts about how the trials worked. He shows how torture forced false claims, how one claim led to the next arrest, and why no accused person could ever prove innocence. The book helped turn opinion in Germany against the burnings. It remains one of the bravest books of the witch-trial age.
stories-for-the-young-or-cheap-repositor:
Volume VI of Stories for the Young, or Cheap Repository Tracts, is by Hannah More and others. It came out in a new revised edition. The American Tract Society issued it from 150 Nassau Street, New York. The tracts aim to be at once entertaining, moral, and religious fare for young readers.

The contents run from Black Giles the Poacher, about a family that would rather live by wit than work, through the tales of Widow Brown's apple tree and Tawney Rachel the fortune-teller. The Happy Waterman, Parley the Porter told as an allegory, and a Christmas tract on the right way to mark the season round out the set of short, pointed lessons.
the-american-republic-its-constitution-t: Title and dedication pages open The American Republic: Its Constitution, Tendencies, and Destiny, by O. A. Brownson, printed in New York by P. O'Shea in 1866, with copyright entered in 1865. Brownson offers the book to historian George Bancroft, praising his learning, patriotism, and public service in memory of old friendship. He calls his own work a feeble attempt to set forth the rules of government and to explain and defend the Constitution. The contents begin with an introduction and a chapter on government.
the-ancient-life-history-of-the-earth-a-:
H. Alleyne Nicholson, professor of natural history at the University of St Andrews, sets out the main facts of fossil science in this outline of the earth's ancient life history. His many degrees are listed on the title page. In his preface he divides the study of fossils into two paths that run side by side.

One path treats buried forms as living things in their own right, weighing their build and parts with little care for when they lived. The other treats them as marks in the world's old record, tied to the layers of rock where they lie. Even then, Nicholson notes, their build cannot be ignored, since form and age explain each other.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-01-nov: The first number of The Atlantic Monthly, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, dated November 1857, is present only as an alphabetical contents index. Headings run from the Abbé de l'Epée through the Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, the Battle of Lepanto, and Henry Ward Beecher. Aaron Burr and Thomas Carlyle appear in the index. So do the catacombs of Rome and child-life by the Ganges. A piece called The Diamond Lens is listed as well. A financial flurry and the Indian revolt close the set.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-02-dec:
Volume one, number two of The Atlantic Monthly, dated December 1857, leads with the closing part of Florentine Mosaics. Its subject is the Carmine church in Florence, where fire in 1771 spared one treasure: the Brancacci Chapel. There stand the wall paintings of Masolino da Panicale, among them the Preaching of Saint Peter and the Healing of the Sick.

Masaccio, Masolino's pupil, carried the series on, and Filippino Lippi finished it. The writer praises the hearty resolve of Masolino and Masaccio to deal with actual life. They grappled visible human forms to their souls, he says, and breathed them back in new shapes of dignity and keen action, to the great gain of art.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-04-feb:
The February 1858 Atlantic Monthly leads with an essay called The Great Failure. Its crucial fact, the writer argues, is not the stoppage of this firm or that, nor banks halting cash payments. It is the paralysis of trade across the civilized globe.

Within the last quarter, business has been struck down at once in the United States, England, France, and most of the Continent. It fell in deep peace, with no failed harvests, no waste, no plague or famine or rumor of revolt to numb it. Yet shocks of ruin ran from Chicago to Constantinople, toppling firms past counting.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-13-nov:
Railway engineering in the United States leads the November 1858 Atlantic. America, the writer grants, can boast no Watt, Brunel, or Stephenson, and no Thames Tunnel or giant steamer. Yet her own engineers yield to none in skill.

He names Evans and Fulton, Whistler, Latrobe, Roebling, Haupt, Ellet, Adams, and Morris. Their works include a railroad bridge of eight hundred feet in clear span. It hangs two hundred fifty feet above a wild river. Their engines climb the Alleghanies at five hundred feet per mile. The country already runs twenty-five thousand miles of railroad, with five thousand locomotives and eighty thousand cars.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-16-feb:
February 1859 leads with a bold question: ought women to learn the alphabet? Paris smiled in 1801, the essay recalls. In that year the satirist Sylvain Maréchal slipped in a plan for a law barring the alphabet to women. He placed it among Napoleon's grand schemes for remaking faith and rule.

Maréchal's mock statute ran to eighty-two clauses, backed by a hundred thirteen weighty reasons. He swept through history for the dread results of a woman's taste of the tree of knowledge. He also quoted the Encyclopédie. A woman who knows the alphabet, it claimed, has lost part of her innocence. His friend Madame Gacon Dufour took the joke in earnest and answered it, which the essay treats as proof of her own folly.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-25-nov:
November 1859 leads with a life of E. Felice Foresti. Late in the autumn of 1836, an Austrian brig-of-war dropped anchor in New York harbor. Seldom, the writer says, have travelers come ashore with such thrilling joy as some of those passengers felt.

Theirs was not the joy of homecoming, of reaching a sought land, or of seeing a new country fresh. It was the relief of men set free: devotees of liberty loosened from a chain, escaped from watching eyes, breathing at last where liberty is law. They were exiles, but the bitterness of exile was forgotten in pride at having earned it by loyalty to freedom.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-26-dec:
The Experience of Samuel Absalom, Filibuster, leads the December 1859 Atlantic. In the winter of 1856, its narrator admits, his outlook had grown troubled and scarcely respectable. As a gold-digger in California, fortune had used him unkindly, and he had sunk to one of the ragged children of the earth.

His shame could be read at a glance: stamped on once-white canvas on his back ran the label Stockton Mills Self-Rising Flour, then the best-known badge of failure in California. One morning, after sleeping in the streets of Oroville, he rose and read in the town paper that frost would soon drive the crowd of street-sleepers out to work for warmer quarters.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-37-nov:
November 1860 leads with a life of Thomas Hood. He was first meant for business and entered a counting house, but failing health at fifteen forced him out. He went to Scotland for two years, to the great gain of both body and mind.

Back in London he set himself to learn engraving, though his frame again stopped the work. What skill he did gain, joined to his genius for comic watching of life, served him well later. His start was purely literary, in a low post on The London Magazine. That post put him among the magazine's bright writers, and Charles Lamb took a strong liking to the young sub-editor, finding in him a talent much like his own.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-38-dec:
The United States and the Barbary States leads the December 1860 Atlantic. Mention those ties at the century's start, the writer says, and most countrymen think only of the war with Tripoli. Ask after that Yankee crusade and their knowledge stops at Preble's attack.

That bright spot fixes the American mind, he charges, while the dish the nation ate for twenty-five years is forgotten. Nor is it true, he adds, that America first refused tribute to the Moorish pirates and so set a new rule of the sea. That, too, is a patriotic dream. The quarrel between President and Pacha was simply one of amount: Tripoli's price was too high to swallow.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-40-feb:
February 1861 continues the series on American artists in Italy with William Page. Among artists, the essay begins, William Page is a painter. The claim may sound needless to a public long familiar with him and his works.

Few do not know his pictures, the writer grants, and men argue whether they are great and whether his Venus is pure or gross. On one point all agree: the world calls the hand that wrought them a painter's. Yet the title, as it comes from Page's studio, carries a higher charge. Not everyone who uses pigments can say, I also am a painter; the name belongs to him who makes the ideal visible.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-49-nov:
George Sand leads the November 1861 Atlantic, under a Latin motto from Horace about a proud, unhumbled woman in triumph, first sung of Cleopatra. The essay turns those words on another woman of royal soul. She has yielded to her age's world, it says, without letting it plunder the secrets of her life.

The public has long clamored at her gates in blame and in praise. Now, in her Histoire de ma Vie, she lets the eager crowd in. They find parentage, birth, schooling, faith, marriage, motherhood, writing, travel, and lawsuits set out in full. But the passionate loving woman, and whom she loved, are not there, and the essay honors the reserve that keeps them out of the world's triumph.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-50-dec:
The Home of Lafayette leads the December 1861 Atlantic. General Lafayette visited the United States in 1824. After that visit, the piece recalls, a pattern set in. Every American who went to France felt he had a right to the old man's time and welcome. He took as much of both as he chose.

Happily for Lafayette's purse and patience, travelers were then few, though a week seldom passed without two or three new faces at the Rue d'Anjou or La Grange. Ocean steamers were still a doubtful thing, and packets rarely ran over five hundred tons. The writer confesses his own part in it. A boy of sixteen, he had no more restraint than his elders. His first use of a Paris cabriolet was a drive to number 6, Rue d'Anjou.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-52-feb:
February 1862 leads with the Battle Hymn of the Republic, printed in verse at the head of the number. Its eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord, who tramples out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored. He has loosed the fateful lightning of his terrible swift sword, and his truth is marching on.

Later verses place God among the watch-fires of a hundred camps and hear a trumpet that will never sound retreat. Men are sifted, the hymn says, before a judgment seat, and the singer's feet are urged to be swift and jubilant in reply. No singer is named on the pages shown.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-62-dec:
The Procession of the Flowers leads the December 1862 Atlantic. In Cuba grows a blossoming shrub whose crimson flowers so charm humming-birds that they hover all day buried in its blossoms, till petal and wing seem one. The bells droop, fall unwithered, and are called by the Creoles Cupid's Tears.

Frederika Bremer, the essay tells, brought home handfuls of these blossoms daily, and nightly they vanished. One morning she saw them on her wall in a long crimson line, climbing one by one to the ceiling. Each was borne onward by a tiny colorless ant, much smaller than its lovely burden. So, the writer says, would the march of a zone's flowers across the year look to a watcher from the sky.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-64-feb:
Sovereigns and Sons leads the February 1863 Atlantic, opening on the sudden death of Prince Albert. That death, it says, caused deep regret, and the royal family of Britain had the sincere sympathy of the civilized world.

The Prince Consort was a man of brilliant talents, trained with true German thoroughness. His knowledge was wide, varied, and exact, and his regard for letters, art, and science held no affectation. He held no official post, yet his place in the empire ranked among the highest open to one not born to the sceptre. The sovereign's trust made his sway a fact whatever the constitution said, and he directed the schooling of the princes and princesses.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-73-nov:
The Spaniard and the Heretic leads the November 1863 Atlantic. It picks up a story told in the August number as The Fleur-de-Lis in Florida. That story told of Huguenot attempts to settle the country. Their attempts roused Spain's jealousy and brought on the crusade recorded here.

The monk, the inquisitor, the Jesuit: these, the essay charges, were the lords of Spain, sovereigns of her sovereign. They had formed and fed the dark, narrow mind of that tyrannical recluse her king. They had formed the minds of her people too, quenching every spark of rising heresy in blood and giving a noble nation over to bigotry as blind as doom. Pride, ambition, and greed worked with them in a rich, strong nature.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-74-dec:
The Man Without a Country leads the December 1863 Atlantic. Very few casual readers of the New York Herald of August 13, the narrator supposes, noticed a small death notice in an obscure corner. It read: Nolan, died on board the U.S. Corvette Levant, on the 11th of May, Philip Nolan.

He noticed it for a plain reason. He was stranded at the old Mission-House in Mackinac, waiting for a Lake Superior steamer that would not come. He was devouring all the print he could get. He read down to the deaths and marriages. His memory for names is good, he says, and he had reason enough to remember Philip Nolan. The tale that follows explains that reason.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-76-feb:
Genius leads the February 1864 Atlantic. When Paul Morphy plays seven games of chess at once, blindfold, or young Colburn solves on the spot a problem running to fifty-six figures, we are struck with hopeless wonder. Such power seems cut off from our own mental work by its very size.

These feats, the essay notes, come with little or no fatigue: they are play, not strain. We see in them a new kind, not merely a new degree, of intelligence. The men leap to their results rather than laboring step by step. Colburn sees the values, Morphy the moves, as plainly as we see the relation of two and two.
the-autobiography-of-charles-darwin:
Charles Darwin's private recollections, edited by his son Francis Darwin, were written for his wife and children with no thought of publication. Francis explains that the sketch began on May 28, 1876, and was worked on for about an hour on most afternoons. Some private passages were left out of the printed version.

Contents run from Cambridge in 1828 to 1831 and the Beagle voyage from 1831 to 1836. Later sections cover marriage in 1839, life in London, and settlement at Down in 1842. Darwin also looks back at his several publications, giving readers his own plain account of how his mind and work developed.
the-barbarism-of-berlin:
G. K. Chesterton published a wartime argument in 1914, opening with what he calls the facts of the case. Four main parts follow: a war on the word, a refusal of reciprocity, the appetite of tyranny, and the escape of folly.

Chesterton says a story lies behind even a confusing event, just as a burned house points back to whoever set the fire. He then states his facts plainly: Prussia, France, and England had promised not to invade Belgium. Prussia proposed to break that promise to reach France, while asking trust for the future. For Chesterton, that offer joins present wrongdoing with a pledge no one should accept.
the-beldonald-holbein:
Henry James opened his tale, in a Macmillan edition of 1922, with a painter telling how Mrs Munden came to his studio. She hints that he might paint her beautiful sister-in-law, Lady Beldonald, if he cares to throw the handkerchief. Lady Beldonald has seen and admired his work.

Talk turns on why the lady has not got on. Mrs Munden says, to begin with, that she is American, and that being American is one way to get on and also a way to be out of things. Beauty itself, she adds, can be taken in different ways. James builds a social puzzle from hint and pause.
the-boys-life-of-mark-twain: Albert Bigelow Paine wrote The Boys' Life of Mark Twain. Only the list of parts is shown, and it maps the whole life in order. School and Tom Sawyer and His Band come early, then the printer's trade and Orion's paper. River Days, the wreck of the Pennsylvania, and The Pilot fill the mid list. The Territorial Enterprise, the birth of the name Mark Twain, and the find of The Jumping Frog mark the turn to fame. Hawaii, lectures, and Roughing It close the arc shown.
the-bravest-of-the-brave-or-with-peterbo:
The Bravest of the Brave; or, With Peterborough in Spain, by G. A. Henty, opens with the same preface as the short-titled form of the book. Henty tells his dear lads that the Earl of Peterborough has all but vanished from fame. His years in command came to just over one, yet in them he won feats fit to stand with the brave deeds of chivalry. His gift for war, Henty says, has never been passed.

Marlborough's glory hid him, the cause was not felt as England's, and the war failed though the fault was not his. Above all, his talent lacked fixed principle and a steady aim. Still, Henty finds much good in him: a warm heart, care for his troops, and a word kept like a bond.
the-broncho-rider-boys-with-funston-at-v: Frank Fowler wrote The Broncho Rider Boys with Funston at Vera Cruz, or Upholding the Honor of the Stars and Stripes. The A. L. Burt Company of New York put it out, with rights dated 1916. A plate shows Billie well hid behind a giant cactus, with the remark that this is no place for him. The tale opens with a daring adventure. Donald reaches for the field glass through which Broncho Billie gazes down, and no more of the page is shown.
the-chase-of-saint-castin-and-other-stor:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood gathered tales of the French in the New World here, in a volume dated 1894. The title story opens at nightfall in April woods, around a bark and pole lodge. The Penobscot River foams along its bed half a mile to the east.

The lodge is the color of the woods and barely reads as man's work, yet smoke rises straight from its top in the cool air. Such a camp usually rings with Indian noise at night, above all after a good day's hunting, but this one holds a deep silence. Fresh-cut pole tops and newly fastened bark mark it as one night's camp for a traveling party. Two French hunters and their Abenaqui companions read those signs as the tale begins, and the hunt of the title takes shape from close woodland watching.
the-coming-of-cuculain:
Standish O'Grady retells the coming of Cuculain, hero of the Red Branch Knights of Ulster. His preface sorts Gaelic literature into three great cycles. The first treats of the gods, the second of the Red Branch Knights and their contemporaries, and the third is the Ossianic cycle.

Finn is the chief figure of the Ossianic cycle, O'Grady notes, while Cuculain rules the Red Branch tales. He insists that Cuculain and his friends were historical people, seen through mists of love and wonder. Men could not forget them, and for centuries they kept the heroes alive in countless songs and stories. Mere inventions of idle fancy, he argues, do not live and flourish so in a people's memory. As for their giant stature and superhuman feats, all art magnifies its subject, like the bronze Grattan in Dublin, twice the size of the real man.
the-confessions-of-ars-ne-lupin: Maurice Leblanc's Confessions of Arsene Lupin, headed with the year 1913, appears here in a Three Owls edition from W. R. Caldwell and Company of New York, copyrighted in 1912 and 1913. Only the front matter and the first line of the contents are present, naming an opening chapter called Two Hundred Thousand Francs Reward! A frontispiece line shows Lupin suddenly rushing at a woman and catching her by the arm. No story text follows.
the-continental-classics-volume-xviii-my: Volume XVIII of The Continental Classics, dated 1909, gathers mystery tales from Russia, Denmark, and Hungary. Its contents list Pushkin's Queen of Spades, an extract from Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment, and Chekhoff's Safety Match among the Russian pieces. Danish stories by Bergsöe, Ingemann, and Blicher follow. Hungarian ones by Ferencz Molnar, Maurus Jokai, and others close the list. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the tales themselves do not appear.
the-cruise-of-the-dolphin:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich tells The Cruise of the Dolphin as an episode from The Story of a Bad Boy, with Tom Bailey as narrator and hero. Every Rivermouth boy, Tom says, sees the sea as mixed up with his fate: He hears the breakers' boom in his cradle. He watches sails fade into the blue as he grows.

The town feeds the dream with rust-red roofs, salt air, fog, shipyards, wharves, and wrecks thrown on shore. Tom's earliest ambition is to own part of a rowboat. When the trim sailboat Dolphin comes up for sale in late May, three shares go fast. They go to Phil Adams, Fred Langdon, and Binny Wallace. With four dollars and fifty cents in hand and a loan from the treasurer of the Centipedes, his secret society of twelve schoolboys, against his silver pencil-case, Tom takes the fourth share.
the-destiny-of-man-viewed-in-the-light-o:
John Fiske's The Destiny of Man Viewed in the Light of His Origin reached its twentieth edition with Houghton, Mifflin and Company of Boston in 1893, under an 1884 copyright. Fiske dedicates the essay lovingly to his six children, Maud, Harold, Clarence, Ralph, Ethel, and Herbert.

In his preface Fiske explains that the Concord School of Philosophy invited him to address its summer discussion of immortality. He took the chance to gather his thoughts on the origin of man and his place in the universe. On a question of future life, he argues, one should start well within the limits of the known. Science may place the subject outside its proper range, yet that does not bar us from holding an opinion about it.
the-effects-of-cross-self-fertilisation-:
Charles Darwin's The Effects of Cross and Self-Fertilisation in the Vegetable Kingdom sets out years of plant trials. His contents lay out the plan: how crosses are favoured, what good they do, how the trials were run across many generations, and how height and fertility were weighed. The first test plant is Ipomoea purpurea, tracked through ten generations.

Crossed plants beat self-bred kin in height, vigour, and seed. Darwin counts stems and weighs seed like a bookkeeper of nature. The book backs his case that nature shuns close breeding, with tables upon tables of proof.
the-entire-project-gutenberg-works-of-ma:
The Entire Project Gutenberg Works of Mark Twain binds Samuel Clemens's whole Gutenberg shelf, over sixty files, into one vast text. An editor's note says many hands made the files over many years, and that each work can be had alone in far smaller size. New finds will be added as they come, the note adds.

Albert Bigelow Paine's Twain bibliography sets the order, by first issue date where it can. Novels, tales, speeches, and sketches all stand in line. The file is less a book than a whole author's works in one heap, made for search and study.
the-epic-of-gilgamish-a-fragment-of-the-:
Stephen Langdon's The Epic of Gilgamish, issued by the University Museum at Pennsylvania as Babylonian Section volume ten, number three, prints a fragment of the Gilgamish legend in transliteration. Line by line, the old signs are spelled out in Roman letters. Gilgamish tells his mother a dream: a star-like mass fell from heaven, too heavy for him to lift, while the land gathered round it.

His mother, who knows all things, reads the dream for him. A second dream brings an axe in Uruk's street, loved like a wife. Langdon's text serves scholars who read cuneiform; no English rendering stands beside it.
the-ethics-of-drink-and-other-social-que:
James Runciman's The Ethics of Drink and Other Social Questions, subtitled Joints in Our Social Armour, was printed at London in 1892. Runciman opens by doubting cold figures: gallons and millions move no one, he says, any more than word of a thousand dead Chinamen. A pet terrier's ailment stirs more feeling than a reformer's vast sums.

So he argues from life, not ledgers: pubs, homes, and streets he knew. Runciman, who wrote A Dream of the North Sea, brings a sailor's bluntness to social ills. Drink is his first joint in the armour; others follow.
the-fall-of-the-grand-sarrasin:
William John Ferrar wrote The Fall of the Grand Sarrasin as a tale of Guernsey in the Norman seas, set in and about the year 1057. Sir Nigel de Bessin, a knight, stands at the heart of the tale, and Harold Piffard drew the pictures.

In his preface Ferrar says the book grew from a summer holiday spent walking the island end to end. He peopled its cliffs and glens with folk of eight hundred years before. Notes at the end mark where fact stops and fancy starts. Raiders, knights, and an island church world give the tale its shape.
the-foolish-virgin: Thomas Dixon wrote The Foolish Virgin as a novel in twenty-nine chapters, given to Gertrude Atherton. Only the front matter is present here: the contents and a list of the chief folk. That list names Mary Adams, an old-fashioned girl; Jim Anthony, a modern youth; Jane Anderson, an artist; Ella, a scrubwoman; and Nance Owens, Jim's mother. Chapter heads run from a friendly warning and temptation to a wedding, a trial, and a soul born. No chapter text can be read here.
the-founder-of-new-france-a-chronicle-of:
Charles W. Colby wrote The Founder of New France as a tale of Samuel de Champlain, volume three of the Chronicles of Canada, printed at Toronto in 1915. The first chapter sums Champlain's whole life in one tight sketch.

Born in 1567 at Brouage, Champlain sailed to the West Indies, then up the St. Lawrence in 1603. He founded Quebec in 1608, found the lake that bears his name, and fought the Iroquois. Taken to London as a captive in 1629, he came back in 1633 and died at Quebec on Christmas Day 1635. Colby shows a tireless pioneer who held a frail colony alive.
the-glittering-plain:
William Morris wrote this tale of a quest in a made up land in 1891. Its full name is The Story of the Glittering Plain. Morris, poet and craftsman, had by then made his own line of prose romance in a high, old style.

A young man of the Raven kindred sails to seek his lost bride in the Glittering Plain. That land grants long life, yet its gift turns sour for those who take it and stay. The book is a landmark of the fantasy line Morris made, the line that taught Tolkien his craft.
the-golden-triangle-the-return-of-ars-ne: Maurice Le Blanc wrote The Golden Triangle: The Return of Arsene Lupin. The Macaulay Company printed it in New York. Its copyright is dated 1917. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and the start of a contents list. The first heads name Coralie and Right Hand and Left Leg. They name The Rusty Key and Before the Flames. A front note quotes a scroll from page 205. Send Coralie up by herself, it says, and her life shall be saved. No chapter text is present.
the-haunted-man-and-the-ghost-s-bargain:
The Haunted Man and the Ghost's Bargain opens with chapter one, The Gift Bestowed. No author is named in the pages present. The narrator challenges the common saying that a certain man looked like a haunted man, then grants that the saying held true in his look, his manner, and his slow, grave voice.

The man is described as a learned teacher of chemistry, with a hollow cheek, a sunken bright eye, and grizzled hair. At night he sits alone in a room that is part library and part laboratory, among drugs, instruments, and books. Firelight throws strange shapes on the wall while he ponders in silence before the grate.
the-hollow-needle-further-adventures-of-:
Maurice Leblanc wrote The Hollow Needle, further adventures of Arsene Lupin, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. Leblanc is named as the author of Arsene Lupin and The Blonde Lady. The contents list ten chapters, from The Shot and Isidore Beautrelet, Sixth-form Schoolboy through An Historic Secret, From Caesar to Lupin, and The Treasures of the Kings of France.

Chapter one, The Shot, opens at night in a big country-house. Raymonde listens to a noise repeated twice, clear enough to stand out from the vague sounds of the night yet too faint to place. The sound might lie within the walls or out among the dark recesses of the park.

Maurice Leblanc wrote The Hollow Needle, further adventures of Arsene Lupin, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, with a heading in the record dated 1909. Leblanc is named as the author of Arsene Lupin and The Blonde Lady. The contents list nine chapters in the pages present, from The Shot and Isidore Beautrelet, Sixth-form Schoolboy through An Historic Secret and Open, Sesame. A sibling record in the library lists a tenth chapter, The Treasures of the Kings of France. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-impostures-of-scapin:
Molière's Les Fourberies de Scapin appears here in English prose translated by Charles Heron Wall, with short introductions and explanatory notes. The headnote dates the first performance to May 24, 1671, at the Palais Royal, where it had great success. Wall calls it nothing more than a farce, drawn partly from classical, partly from Italian or French sources, and notes that Molière acted the part of Scapin himself.

The cast, set at Naples, supplies the plot's engine. Two fathers, Argante and Géronte, have sons, Octave and Léandre, who have fallen in love across the family lines, with Hyacintha and the supposed gypsy girl Zerbinette, really Argante's daughter. Scapin, servant to Léandre, works with Octave's man Silvestre to trick the old men. The servant's impostures give the play its title and its enduring place in French comedy.
the-insurrection-in-dublin: James Stephens published this account with Maunsel and Company in 1916. Dublin and London share the imprint. The year matches the rising it describes. A list of his other books faces the title page. It shows poems and prose side by side. The Crock of Gold and The Charwoman's Daughter appear. Only the title pages and contents start are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The contents begin with chapter I, Monday. Stephens arranged the book as a day-by-day witness record. Easter week supplied the days.
the-land-of-contrasts-a-briton-s-view-of: James Fullarton Muirhead, author of Baedeker handbooks to Great Britain and the United States, published his account of American kin in Boston in 1898. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The list names an introduction, a chapter on contrasts, and lights and shadows of American society. An appreciation of the American woman follows in the list. The later chapters and the observations themselves do not appear in this record.
the-land-of-little-rain:
Mary Austin wrote about a dry country she knew well, naming places as Native people named them when she could. Her preface explains that habit at length. She says a name should fit the place itself, not honor the person who first mapped it.

Chapters in the contents move along water trails, into Shoshone land, and through small towns such as Jimville. Readers meet a pocket hunter, a basket maker, and neighbors who live by scarce water. The book treats desert life as full and ordered, not empty. Her place names carry that same close attention throughout.
the-last-of-the-peterkins-with-others-of:
Lucretia P. Hale published the final Peterkin papers in Boston in 1906, from an 1886 copyright. Her preface calls these pieces the last records of a family that left its native land and never returned. Elizabeth Eliza commonplace book, found among family papers, appears here for the first time.

The preface reports sad guesses about the family fate after Tobolsk. Mr. and Mrs. Peterkin may have died in a fire, Agamemnon in Madagascar, and Solomon John in Rustchuk. Hale keeps a straight face while the beloved Lady from Philadelphia loses her most helpless clients.
the-legacy-of-cain:
Wilkie Collins dated his dedication December 6, 1888, thanking Mrs. Henry Powell Bartley for copying his manuscripts for the printer. His novel then opens in a prison during 1858 and 1859, told by its governor. The governor withholds town and personal names by design.

He recalls the night before a woman execution, with a chaplain, a minister, a doctor, and a young woman present. That child of the condemned prisoner grows into the legacy of the title. Secrecy governs both households from the very start. Collins builds a tale of inherited guilt, family secrets, and second chances across two households.
the-life-of-john-milton-volume-5-of-7-16: David Masson wrote his life of John Milton alongside the history of his time, and volume five appeared with Macmillan in London in 1877. Only the title page and the start of detailed contents are present here, covering September 1654 to June 1657 under Oliver Cromwell first Protectorate. Entries promise Milton secretaryship, a four days debate on Cromwell powers, toleration fights, and the case of John Biddle the Socinian. The biography itself remains outside this record.
the-life-of-john-ruskin: W. G. Collingwood wrote his life of John Ruskin, dated at Coniston in May 1911. Only the title page and contents are present here. The plan divides the life into the boy poet from 1819 to 1842 and the art critic to 1860. A hermit and heretic book covers the years after 1860. Chapter titles trace Modern Painters, The Seven Lamps, Stones of Venice, and the Working Men College. The biography itself is missing from this record beyond that plan.
the-lion-s-skin: Rafael Sabatini's novel The Lion's Skin carries a 1911 date in its heading. What is present stops at the title page and contents; the story itself does not appear. The contents name eighteen chapters, opening with The Fanatic and moving through At the "Adam and Eve," The Witness, Mr. Green, and Moonshine. Later titles include Hortensia's Return, Father and Son, Temptation, The Champion, and Amid the Graves.
the-major-operations-of-the-navies-in-th: A. T. Mahan wrote The Major Operations of the Navies in the War of American Independence. Sampson Low, Marston and Company published it in London under a 1913 copyright, with portraits, maps, and plans. Mahan is identified as a captain in the United States Navy and author of The Influence of Sea Power upon History. Only the title page and the contents' start are present, so the text does not appear. The contents list a preface at page five, a list of illustrations, and a list of maps.
the-makers-of-canada-champlain: N. E. Dionne wrote Champlain for The Makers of Canada series, published in Toronto by Morang and Company in 1912. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the biography itself does not appear. The nine chapters follow Champlain's first voyage to America, Acadia and Port Royal, and the founding of Quebec. The voyages of 1610, 1611, and 1613 follow, with the Récollet missions and war against the Iroquois in 1615. The fur trade, Champlain with the Jesuits, and the Company of New France, also called the Hundred Associates, close the list.
the-minister-and-the-boy-a-handbook-for-:
Allan Hoben, associate professor of practical theology at the University of Chicago, published The Minister and the Boy in 1912. Its subtitle calls it a handbook for churchmen engaged in boys' work. Hoben also served as field secretary of the Chicago Juvenile Protective Association. The contents move from the call of boyhood through village and city boys, organized play, vocation, and citizenship, ending with the church boys' club.

Chapter One argues that Christian apologetic today rests less on speculative theology than on social results. A pragmatic public, Hoben says, asks what an institution accomplishes for the common good. Growing social science exposes crying needs, and socialist dreams of welfare press the church to heed the present life. Individual views of salvation in the world to come no longer fully satisfy modern hearers. Readers get a Progressive Era case for youth work as the church's practical proof of worth.
the-mutineers-a-tale-of-old-days-at-sea-:
Charles Boardman Hawes's The Mutineers is a tale of old days at sea and adventures in the Far East. Benjamin Lathrop supposedly set it down. Only dedication pages and the start of a contents list are present here, so the story does not appear. Hawes thanks, under the heading To Pay My Shot, the ship Hunter's master, mate, and men, whose voyage forms the backbone of his tale.

He also thanks Captain David Woodard, an English mariner wrecked on Celebes more than 120 years earlier, and Captain R. G. F. Candage of Brookline, Massachusetts, a party to an original contract in melon seeds. Contents begin with Part I, In Which We Sail for Canton, China, in five small chapters.
the-nursery-no-107-november-1875-vol-xvi: Number 107 of The Nursery, a Boston monthly for the youngest readers, is dated November 1875, in volume XVIII, published by John L. Shorey at 15 cents a copy. Nothing past the title pages and contents is present here; the tales and verses themselves stay out of view. Listed pieces include Flora's Looking-Glass by Anna Livingston, Chinese Scenes, Minos by Elizabeth Sill, Grandma's Garden, Captain Bob, The Soldier-Dog, and The Parrot's Lament.
the-outdoor-girls-at-ocean-view-or-the-b: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls at Ocean View, or The Box That Was Found in the Sand, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The lists name five earlier Outdoor Girls books, from Deepdale to Florida, plus Hope's Moving Picture Girls and Bobbsey Twins series, each volume at 50 cents postpaid.
the-pied-piper-of-hamelin:
Robert Browning's poem The Pied Piper of Hamelin appears here with illustrations by Kate Greenaway. Frederick Warne and Co. of London and New York issued the edition. The poem is told in numbered verse sections. The narrator begins by placing Hamelin in Brunswick, near Hanover, with the river Weser washing its southern wall.

Hamelin is called a pleasant spot, yet the story starts almost five hundred years before the telling. In those days the townsfolk suffered badly from vermin. The second section opens with a single blunt word for the plague: rats. Browning's bouncing lines and Greenaway's pictures made the old legend a favourite children's poem. The bargain the town strikes with the piper grows out of this rat-filled opening. So does what follows when payment is refused.
the-princess-and-the-goblin:
George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin is laid out in a contents list of thirty-two chapters before the tale begins. Titles trace the young princess's adventures: she loses herself, lets well alone, and meets the little miner. The goblins get their hall and their counsels, and Curdie gets his clue and his grief. Irene's clue, the escape, the subterranean waters, and the king and the kiss close the plan.

Chapter 1, Why the Princess Has a Story About Her, opens in the old storybook manner. It begins with a small princess, daughter of a king who rules a mountainous land from a palace set on one of the peaks. That opening, following the full map of chapters, sets the fairy-tale terms at once. A small royal child, a mountain kingdom, and goblins waiting below ground are all in place.
the-prose-of-alfred-lichtenstein:
Alfred Lichtenstein's prose opens with The Winner, the story of Max Mechenmal. Max manages a newspaper kiosk, eats and drinks well, and tops up his salary from Ilka Leipke, a small, elegant prostitute who calls him her sweet dwarf. Max, angry all his life at being small, came from an impoverished family and was dismissed early from an institution for backward children. He wandered homeless, lived by petty larceny, and was trained as a locksmith in a home for neglected children.

His skill with keys tempted him toward grand burglary, fine clothes, and showy women. Fear of capture held him to seductions and small, safe break-ins, leaving his ambition unsatisfied. He tormented weaker comrades, set stronger ones against each other, and had no friends. One tired evening walk begins to change the direction of his life.
the-romanization-of-roman-britain: F. Haverfield's study asks how Roman ways took hold in Britain. The Clarendon Press at Oxford issued it in 1912. That printing was a second edition, greatly enlarged. It carried twenty-one illustrations. Presented here are just the title page and contents. Haverfield's argument itself is absent. The contents promise chapters on Romanization across the empire. Later chapters treat Britain through language and material civilization. Others cover art, local government, and the land system. A chronology follows. The closing chapter turns to the Celtic revival in the later empire.
the-rulers-of-the-lakes-a-story-of-georg:
Joseph A. Altsheler's The Rulers of the Lakes was copyrighted in 1917. D. Appleton and Company held the copyright. The subtitle calls it a story of George and Champlain. A prefatory summary sets the tale in the French and Indian War. The time is just after Braddock's defeat. A character list names Robert Lennox and Tayoga. He is a young Onondaga warrior. The hunter David Willet and several French officers appear.

According to that summary, Lennox and Tayoga travel through the northern wilderness. Their errand is dangerous. They must warn Fort Refuge of hostile forces. The garrison and settlers there are in peril. Afterwards the pair join the army as scouts. They precede it toward Lake George and Lake Champlain. The story concludes with the battle of Lake George. The summary calls it the colonists' first great success of the war.
the-saddle-boys-of-the-rockies-or-lost-o: Captain James Carson published The Saddle Boys of the Rockies with Cupples and Leon in 1913. Its subtitle is Lost on Thunder Mountain. A frontispiece caption describes a big black horse acting as though it had gone wild. Preserved here are the title pages and the start of the contents only. The story itself is left out. Early chapters promise a challenge accepted and the strange actions of Domino. A note of warning waits at the spring hole.
the-second-violin: Grace S. Richmond wrote The Second Violin, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company. Richmond also wrote Red Pepper Burns and Mrs. Red Pepper, the title page notes. Copyrights of 1905 and 1906 are listed. The book was published in September 1906. The portion shown gives the title matter and contents only. Two books are listed, each with ten chapters. The first book shares the volume's title. The second is called The Churchill Latch-string. No chapter titles are given, and no story text appears.
the-spirit-of-the-border-a-romance-of-th:
Zane Grey published this romance of the early settlers in the Ohio Valley in 1906, dedicating it to his brother with memories of days in forest solitude. His introduction refuses to apologize for the story's wild spirit. He insists that its brutality is true to western border life. That life lay a little more than a hundred years in the past.

Grey says he holds papers of undoubted truth. Chief among them is a long-lost journal. His ancestor Colonel Ebenezer Zane kept it. Zane was a leading hunter and pioneer of the western settlement. From those notes he means to show the fever of freedom. It lured pioneers toward unmarked graves. He hopes their heroism and sacrifice will gain a higher place in history books.
the-story-of-porcelain: Sara Ware Bassett wrote this industrial story for young readers. Her companion volumes cover lumber, wool, leather, glass, sugar, and silk. The Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia published this book in 1919. Isabel W. Caley illustrated it. Only the title pages are present here, with two short pieces. Bassett's inscription to Margaret Huxley is affectionate. The opening lines of a piece called The Bowl follow. A master-craftsman in it makes porcelain for the Emperor, the Son of Heaven. The story itself does not appear beyond its threshold.
the-tale-of-squirrel-nutkin:
Beatrix Potter's Squirrel Nutkin was published by Frederick Warne in 1903 as a story for Norah. Potter calls it a tale about a tail, the tail of a little red squirrel named Nutkin. He has a brother, Twinkleberry, and many cousins living in a wood beside a lake. On an island in the lake stands a hollow oak, home of an owl called Old Brown.

One autumn, when the nuts ripen, the squirrels paddle to the island on little rafts of twigs to gather food. Their visits to Old Brown's tree set the story in motion. Potter mixes real woodland habits with a cheeky hero who teases a dangerous neighbor, and young readers learn why Nutkin's tail matters.
the-treasure-train:
Arthur B. Reeve's Treasure-Train gathers Craig Kennedy detective stories, opening as Maude Euston visits Professor Kennedy in his laboratory.
